rows: XPO / NPO / CPO ROADMAP WITH DATES: SVP Cloud and AI Networking Tyson Lamoreaux said 'XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that is where we start to see some of that CPO ramp occur'. The sequence is copper as long as possible, then NPO/XPO (XPO is the NPO-based architecture) for the multi-rack density copper cannot reach, then CPO once it can be built at scale - early CPO adoption expected, but a completely different manufacturing technology whose yields will be very challenging early on. Arista builds CPO or NPO switches when customers ask; XPO timing is partly aligned with scale-up form factor and bandwidth density needs.
XPO early deployments second half of next year, really ramping in 2028, and probably 12 months behind that

FIRST HARD SIZING OF THE CPO TEST MARKET, PLUS WHO WINS WHICH INSERTION (CEO Greg Smith): the test-equipment TAM for silicon photonics co-packaged optics is about $100 million in 2026 and is expected to be between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, reaching about a billion dollars of test equipment by 2030 (optical alignment, interface hardware and material handling are a separate TAM). Today it is 'a very concentrated market' - one customer and a very small number of devices drive most of the 2026 capital intensity. A CPO device has four major optical test insertions: (1) the photonics wafer, (2) the silicon photonics wafer with the electronic ICs bonded to it, (3) the singulated optical engine dielets with the mounting plate for FAU alignment, (4) the assembled CPO device. On this first device at this first customer, 'Advantest is strongest in insertion one, Teradyne is strongest in insertion two, a Taiwanese supplier is strongest in insertion three, and Teradyne is strongest in insertion four.' Management flags scaling pain as the reason for 'increasing excitement about copper networking for scale-up' and for NPO, which avoids the yield risk of a full CPO device.
CPO/SiPho test equipment TAM about $100 million in 2026, between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, about a billion dollars by 2030
Teradyne Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-10-2026)

OPTICAL TIMELINE TIGHTENED - CONNECTOR REVENUE 2027, NPO REVENUE IN 2H 2027, CPO AT 400G PER LANE: Mohan said optical revenue starts in 2027 with component-level sales of the glass coupler/connector from the aiXscale Photonics acquisition closed 'in December of last year', which customers are qualifying for their own CPU scale-out applications and which 'might very well end up becoming the first revenue that we see in 2027'. Next is NPO, which Astera considers the right answer at '200 gig per lane data rates' because it does not stress the supply chain while delivering the distance and density scale-up needs; 'we will start to see initial revenues in the back half of 2027 from our NPO efforts. Then full year ahead in 2028.' At '400 gig per lane data rates and even higher densities' CPO takes over, with Astera supplying the full optical engine - its own electrical IC, its own photonics IC (PIC) and the fiber-to-silicon-photonics packaging - landing both on an optically enabled Scorpio SKU and on the XPU side, so a link that previously had no such component gains two. He also corrected a pricing assumption for multi-rack scale-up: as cluster sizes go from 72 to 144, 288 and 576 GPUs the switch radix rises and 'contrary to popular belief that price per lane goes down, it actually goes up with radix'.
initial revenues in the back half of 2027; 200 gig per lane; 400 gig per lane
Astera Labs Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Photonics timing sharpened: Corning is planning to build out a $10 billion business by the end of the decade, from no sales today, selling into NPO and CPO applications inside the server tray, and is building out the supply chain now — hopefully next year we will start to see some sales there. The single biggest variable for the Springboard high-confidence gap is CPO adoption; the CPO supply chain at the scale required does not exist today and is the largest build investors should watch, though management sees no showstopper. Schlesinger expects the adoption inflection in the next four or five years rather than in 2027, with near-term content coming from traditional product sets (polarization-maintaining fiber, FAUs) and GlassBridge-type products a 2030-plus opportunity. Scale-up of the network should begin at the end of next year and run 2028 through 2030; today's growth is scale-out, where clusters above 130,000 GPUs add another network layer.
$10 billion photonics business by the end of the decade from no sales today; first sales hoped for next year; adoption inflection in the next four or five years, not 2027; 130,000 cluster barometer

CPO REVENUE RAISED AGAIN AND THE CUSTOMER BASE IS BROADENING. CEO Mike Slessor: 'we started the year with a view of maybe $10 million-$20 million in revenue. Have now successfully upgraded that to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter' — i.e. the top of the original full-year range is now hit by the end of Q3. More important than the dollars, the concentration is changing: 'one of the exciting things that we're now seeing in the second part of the year is broader production adoption of this TRITON high-volume manufacturing platform at multiple foundries with multiple fabless customers'. Today it is 'pretty concentrated, with one major foundry fabless partnership', but FormFactor is 'building backlog and building the breadth of the backlog where this diversifies a little bit beyond that one customer set'. Installed base: 'hundreds of systems installed worldwide' at close to as many customers, with 'installed now tens of systems' specifically ramping in CPO production. The 2025 acquisition of Keystone Photonics is described as 'really an enabling technology for optical probing'. On the NPO-versus-CPO debate, Slessor said FormFactor has built one fundamental optical probing technology applicable across CPO, NPO and pluggables, and that NPO is not yet pulling in at the scale CPO is affecting 2026 revenue, though there is 'lots of activity' across the customer base. He also embraced the bottleneck label: photonics test is where the industry is constrained, and FormFactor is resolving technical and operational challenges in real time on installed systems.

CPO revenue view upgraded from $10 million-$20 million for the year to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter; hundreds of systems installed worldwide; tens of systems in CPO production

Kathy Ta sized the optical bandwidth step-up per interconnect tier for the first time: if Data Center Interconnect / telecom is a 1x multiple, scale-across and scale-out are each roughly 10x DCI; the first instance of CPO going to scale-up, starting in the second half of 2027, is 'probably 3x to 4x above the 10x that we are seeing for scale-out', and when all of scale-up goes optical it is 'a full 10x above the 10x of scale-out', with scale-in another 10x multiple beyond that. Wupen Yuen framed the same ladder as scale-across 1, scale-out 10, scale-up 100, scale-in 1,000, and positioned Lumentum as 'going all the way from scale across to scale out, to scale up, and later to scale in'.
scale-across and scale-out each about 10x DCI; scale-up CPO 3x to 4x above the 10x of scale-out from the second half of 2027; full optical scale-up a full 10x above scale-out; scale-in another 10x

Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.

CPO half and NPO half of the optical scale-up market; ILS about 25% of the overall market; NPO engine 1 inch by half an inch packing 6.4T vs a 1.6T module today; 120, 150 milliwatt and above vs traditional 70 milliwatt

Three-wave ultra-high-power (UHP) laser capacity ramp laid out for the first time: wave one is the San Jose fab, ramping today with line of sight through 2027; wave two is the U.K. fab, which 'will come in in second quarter 2027' and continues ramping through 2028; wave three is the Greensboro fab, starting to ramp in 'second quarter 2028 or mid 2028'. All three are on schedule and the biggest variable is customer qualification timing - Lumentum must submit a PCN for the customer to qualify the product, and accelerating that qualification can pull the ramp in. Capacity is additive rather than reallocated: a new clean room in the U.K. fitted with 'the latest and greatest state-of-the-art equipment', and the added capacity is '6-inch capable', so current telecom and scale-across products are not sacrificed - 'by and large, we do not sacrifice. We add.'
San Jose ramping through 2027; U.K. fab second quarter 2027 ramping through 2028; Greensboro second quarter 2028 or mid 2028; new 6-inch capable capacity

Kathy Ta quantified the first ELS win announced on the Q4 FY2026 call: it is with the existing CPO customer, it covers only 'a relatively small portion of their ELS total demand', first ELS shipments are expected in the second half of calendar 2027, and Lumentum estimates 'maybe 15%-20% of their fleet is about the right amount of their share that we think that we will win'. She expects a bigger ELS share opportunity in NPO because the majority of the NPO opportunity looks ELS rather than ILS, and many of those ELS customers want Lumentum to supply the complete ELS module rather than only laser chips. No NPO win has been announced yet, but management expects to announce a first NPO customer 'in the next handful of months'.
about 15%-20% of the lead CPO customer's ELS fleet; first ELS shipments in the second half of calendar 2027

Competitive read on high-power CPO/NPO lasers: Yuen named Coherent as the single competitor - 'we see the one competitor, right, who is Coherent' - and said Lumentum is 'really not seeing anybody else in this high-power laser area'. He described why the part is hard (power, RIN noise, linewidth and mode hop all have to be achieved simultaneously at volume with good yield, and mode hop is the biggest problem with today's silicon photonics lasers), noted Lumentum is already ramping these lasers and seeing good real data, and then said the industry needs a second source: from a customer's point of view Coherent would need to be ramping 'sometime in 2027... Probably second half' to support the scale-up build in 2028.
Coherent second source needed around the second half of 2027 to support the 2028 scale-up ramp

Scale-up optics raised for a second time in two weeks: a quarter ago the next-fiscal-year outlook was zero to $300 million, on the Q2 call Murphy said it would be much higher, and at Citi he told investors to imagine that number is even greater, with NPO and scale-up optics a big part of the guide-up. Marvell already sells TIAs and drivers into third-party NPO modules built for hyperscalers, which he called a billion-dollar business for us already just on analog components, and said Marvell content is very high in the NPO module ecosystem with TIAs and drivers. NPO and CPO will coexist rather than replace each other, with a big NPO ramp in calendar 2028 and 2029 as CPO layers in.
next-year scale-up optics: prior guide zero to $300 million, now greater still; TIAs and drivers a billion-dollar business for us already just on analog components

Content economics of the 1.6T transition, with ASPs: 'if you look at 800G, most of the market data will say ASPs are running, I don't know, $35 to $50 probably, versus a 1.6T, which is probably $80 to $100 plus the cost of the TIA, which pushes it above $100.' Rushmore is in customer qualification and is 'expected to go to market mid-next year,' with full scale production 'in the following year,' sold alongside the Washington TIA. Looking further out, architectures disaggregate: at 3.2T expect a standalone TIA, a standalone driver and the SerDes 'incorporated differently. Maybe it is not in a DSP'; in a CPO or NPO application the driver (today integrated into the DSP) becomes standalone and the SerDes 'ends up being in a chiplet', so versus the DSP and a TIA today 'the content is higher in a CPO or an NPO application.' Pricing is expected to hold: 'I don't anticipate pricing coming down much, between now and the end of next year.'
800G ASPs $35 to $50 versus 1.6T $80 to $100, above $100 with the TIA; Rushmore to market mid-next year, full scale production the year after

On the silicon photonics opportunity split, management said inspection will for sure be the largest opportunity and that this is reflected in the backlog Onto holds now - the bulk is inspection - but Onto is also selling metrology tools with multiple customers adopting a couple of different metrology tools, and sees opportunities for other tools in the space too. On what drives upside or downside to the opportunity, Plisinski said it is not a question of if it happens but how quickly the technology is adopted at the server level and then at the rack level, with Onto playing in both; he cited NVIDIA, Broadcom and AMD as committed to driving it forward and the hyperscalers as committed from a data center perspective, with everyone convinced on the economics and performance benefits. Silicon photonics is also one of the named drivers behind Onto's expectation that it can outperform the market in 2027, alongside the Dragonfly G5 opening front-end markets and Atlas G6 logic expansions.
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

CFO Lorenzo Grandi on the AI data-center mix: the connectivity flow (silicon photonics, microcontrollers and BiCMOS EICs for optical transceivers) generates the strongest revenue, and for 2027 ST expects 'mostly of our revenue will be in MDRF for around 80% of the billing' with only 20% in APMS (thermal and power flows). ST is 'marginal today' in data-center power and is building its portfolio for the 800V architecture, expecting 'meaningful revenue after 2028 for the power'. Silicon photonics is described as accretive to the gross-margin target. For NPO/CPO, ST says it has 'all the ingredients', including packaging, and the timing will be driven by customers.
around 80% of 2027 data-center billing in MDRF (connectivity), 20% in APMS; power meaningful revenue after 2028

Optics positioning sharpened and the price of this year's optics technology acquisition disclosed: TE made a '$200 million acquisition earlier this year to help buffer the portfolio' in optics (the company is not named in this session). TE plays in scale-up and 'we do not play as much in the scale out'; it expects NPO and CPO to show up 'more at the switch level is where you are going to first see it', and its own entry is the fiber attach unit — 'essentially a fiber connector that would actually help enable CPO or NPO' — which is incremental TAM on top of the copper portfolio. The milestones to watch are the customer's architecture intercept point, engineering qualification, then scaling to AI/hyperscaler unit volumes.
$200 million acquisition earlier this year to buffer the optics portfolio
TE Connectivity Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

CEO Tim Breen on the silicon photonics growth targets: 'the industry adoption needed to reach those targets has already happened. So I think we now have very limited adoption risk baked into that.' The constraint is now supply, not demand - 'All indicators right now from a demand point of view are flashing kind of bright green relative to those targets... we see much more demand than we can supply out of our current install base, so we will definitely be accelerating that.' Pluggables alone get GF 'pretty much all the way' to the first milestone, with NPO rollout already picking up steam on top. The upside case is co-packaged optics: if CPO sees really broad adoption in the latter part of the period GF 'could blow past those targets materially', because CPO is the technology for the scale-up transition and 'you are replacing 10x the links of scale-out with those solutions, so you are not going to see a linear growth story'.
co-packaged optics replaces 10x the links of scale-out

First photonics customer count disclosed: 'We have more than 40 customers in photonics today, and that number keeps growing as players really invest in their optical roadmap.' Breen added that 'everyone who was touting copper two years ago has either launched an organic or inorganic effort to get into optical'. On the form-factor transition, near-package optics and co-packaged optic designs are 'even taping out in our fabs today' and are 'going into production in 2027 and 2028', while pluggable optical transceivers ramp strongly now; the NPO rollout is being led by 'many of the same players who are in pluggables today'. The core photonics platform roadmap runs from 100 gig per lane to 200 gig per lane to 400 gig per lane and beyond with new materials and modulators, paired with advanced packaging (hybrid bonding, fiber-to-chip attach) as the optical link moves closer to the XPU and switch ASIC.
more than 40 customers in photonics; NPO and CPO designs taping out today and going into production in 2027 and 2028; 100 gig per lane to 200 to 400 gig per lane roadmap

AI portfolio catalysts: WaveLogic 6 Extreme — after 18 months still the ONLY 1.6 Tb high-performance modem on the market — with a ramp already exceeding WaveLogic 5 Extreme and output doubled. RLS holds roughly 70% market share in disaggregated optical line systems; next-generation RLS HYPER-RAIL (co-created with the hyperscalers for scale-across / distributed AI training over greater distances) is on track for initial customer standardization by the end of calendar 2026 and will ramp to SEVERAL HUNDRED MILLION DOLLARS of revenue in 2027 (could be faster with more components), with economics a step function above RLS and accretive to corporate average margins. Interconnects: Q3 800 ZR pluggable shipments MORE THAN TWICE the previous quarter's volume; strong market receptivity to Nitro, the linear redriver for active copper cable solutions; VESTA, the open co-packaged optics (CPX) solution, received SAMPLE ORDERS FROM SEVERAL ANCHOR CUSTOMERS in the ecosystem — CPX revenue expected to begin in 2027 and ramp into 2028. Coherent moving inside the data center is viewed as inevitable with the right general-market intercept at 3.2 Tb; OCS is welcomed as driving coherent adoption inside the data center faster (no comment on Ciena entering the OCS market itself). The major-hyperscaler WaveLogic 6 Extreme win announced last quarter — DSP, drivers, TIAs and coherent expertise in a complete module deployed across the customer's own global optical platform, a significant takeaway from a component competitor — is one of two bespoke performance-optics consumption-model relationships. TAM expected to effectively double from approximately $25 billion today to approximately $50 billion by 2029; scale-across is a major demand driver, almost entirely North American/US-based and just beginning, with asynchronous training and inference traffic still ahead.

Hyper-Rail standardization by end-2026, several hundred million dollars of revenue in 2027; 800 ZR plug shipments more than twice QoQ; Vesta CPX sample orders, revenue from 2027; TAM ~$25B to ~$50B by 2029

Scale-up optics push: Credo joined the Open Compute Project MSA consortium (open CPX) and sees increasing customer activity around NPO for scale-up networks, with CONFIRMED DESIGN WINS expected to begin ramping in fiscal 2028. Scale-up requires roughly 10x more density than scale-out pluggables — the industry conversation spans XPO, CPX, NPO and ultimately CPO — and Credo is approaching it agnostically: leading with the silicon photonics PIC in all NPO solutions including CPX, pursuing component sales where customers prefer them and complete optical engines / system-level solutions long term, bringing pluggable-ecosystem advantages (telemetry, interoperability, serviceability) to the consortium.
NPO scale-up design wins confirmed, ramping fiscal 2028; 10x density improvement needed vs scale-out

→ Marvell: Celestial AI CPO photonic fabric was framed last quarter at about $150 million of revenue for FY2028 within a ~$300 million scale-up optics category; that category is now accelerating further and is a significant driver of the $1.5 billion FY2028 raise; Celestial team integrated well and remains a key part of the program, with CPO a key part of FY2028 and FY2029
value: ~$150 million FY2028 CPO photonic fabric revenue (prior framing, now biased higher)

→ Lumentum: Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston said the discussions with NVIDIA 'have emerged with, one, a very substantial long-term agreement that we’ve characterized as a multibillion-dollar deal, and then, of course, the investment where they helped us considerably buy that fab and equip it and outfit it' (the Greensboro fab he had just described). He added that 'it was a year cycle for us to get qualified at Nvidia', and that before investing in more capacity for NPO customers he would 'need to see a similar type of commitment as we ultimately got from Nvidia.'

CW laser engagement across pluggable transceivers (production-ready 70 milliwatt and 100 milliwatt laser singles and arrays), near pluggable optics / extra dense pluggables (200 milliwatt singles and 100 milliwatt arrays sampling now), and co-packaged optics (needs from 200 to 400 milliwatt lasers, with and without SOA combinations); beyond Jabil, three pluggable module makers are in alpha sample evaluation and another three in technical engagement and supply assessment; $3.4 million new program with SemiNex focused on semiconductor optical amplifiers for co-packaged optics in AI data centers
$3.4 million new program with SemiNex; lasers spanning 70 milliwatt to 400 milliwatt

Strategic shift from a fab-lite to a hybrid manufacturing model for indium phosphide lasers — laser demand outstrips supply for the next 3 to 5 years; a new foundry partner has brought on tremendous committed capacity available now, Glasgow Phase 1 expansion capacity comes online end of Q4 2027, and the long-term model is one-third internal manufacturing and two-thirds foundry partners; production capacity not seen as the bottleneck versus the pipeline

→ Jabil: With Jabil, alpha builds have been completed for preliminary system validation; beta builds in Q4 2026, followed by customer qual cycles; initial production orders expected in the first half of 2027 with the production ramp planned second half of 2027

→ GlobalFoundries: Sivers continues to stay closely engaged with GlobalFoundries on their partnership; progress driven by customers working with the solutions and evaluating them in their systems rather than by U.S. Department of Commerce funding

MARKET / ROADMAP DATA POINTS: 800G transceiver INDUSTRY volume went from ~20 MILLION UNITS/YEAR two years ago to ~90 MILLION UNITS/YEAR this year — the industry entered the year forecasting 50M units and Semtech is 'now hearing the number 80, 90 million'; 800G bookings are still INCREASING (not decreasing), and 800G and 1.6T both have 'a really very healthy runway over the next two years'. 3.2T TIMING: design window starts opening in ~12 MONTHS, EARLY MOVERS ~18 MONTHS OUT, MEANINGFUL DEPLOYMENT IN ~2 YEARS (i.e. H2 CY2028) — that is the cut-in for Semtech's content step-up, and above 200G/lane is where TIA + photodiode CO-OPTIMIZATION becomes necessary. MPO/NPO called a strong trend driven by BANDWIDTH-DENSITY limits against fixed shoreline: Semtech is engaged on '10, 15 DIFFERENT PROGRAMS' with module manufacturers, some tied directly to end customers, as a leading supplier of TIA ARRAYS and (linearized) LASER ARRAYS; higher density tightens element spacing and crosstalk, changing packaging requirements. LPO has generated meaningful revenue since Q1 FY2027 and is growing moderately, but its bigger effect is PROVING THE LINEAR ARCHITECTURE, which now carries into MPO, XPO and 'some form of CPO'. Stated R&D priority: lasers, photodiodes, drivers and TIAs for 3.2T coherent light, XPO, MPO and CPO applications. Analyst day 10-15-2026 (San Jose) will publish TAM, share and the multi-year model.
800G industry units ~20M/yr (2024) → ~90M/yr (2026); 3.2T volume ~2 years out; 10-15 MPO/NPO programs

CO-PACKAGED OPTICS: ADI views the nascent CPO space as a SAM EXPANDER - the criticality of its precision control technology increases further as THERMAL AND SERVICEABILITY challenges rise in co-packaged architectures. Combined with market growth, expanding content and increasing share, management says data center optics will remain a strong growth vector for ADI over the coming years.
CPO framed as SAM expander; no specific figure

CPO PIPELINE AND CPO MARGIN STRUCTURE: Murry said AOI has 'five companies' it is talking to about CPO, some of which are also in real NPO discussions, and expects MORE THAN ONE CPO customer - but probably not all five, because it will not have enough capacity for everyone. On economics, CPO ELSFP or laser-diode margins 'should be meaningfully above 40%', with the bare laser chip 'most likely above 60%' and modules in between, so CPO/NPO mix can pull group margin above the 40% long-term target once it scales.
five companies; margins should be meaningfully above 40%; most likely above 60%

SCALE-UP LASER CONTENT - THE INDUSTRY CAPACITY GAP QUANTIFIED: Murry agreed scale-up optics is 'an order of magnitude-ish increase' in the NUMBER of lasers per rack versus scale-out, and added the die itself is 'five or six times larger size per laser', so the wafer real estate the industry must process rises enormously. He said there is not enough capacity in the industry right now to come close to meeting scale-up demand, let alone scale-out - which is why AOI and its competitors are all investing in laser fabs. He called the AI shift in optics the most impactful game changer he has seen in 30 years in the business.
an order of magnitude-ish increase; five or six times larger size per laser

First margin math on NPO/CPO: on a typical product, if COGS is 100%, roughly 70%-80% is material and 20% is value add. For NPO the material content is much lower - in many cases the wafer is consigned by the customer and Fabrinet singulates it, does the packaging and the testing at die and device level - so it is much higher value add, probably a lower ASP but a higher margin, and Grady said NPO 'would be much better gross margin than our traditional business'. He cautioned the business needs a mix of both higher-volume lower-margin work and this higher-margin lower-ASP work, and described NPO as probably a little bit more straightforward than CPO, with the opportunity in NPO extending well beyond ELSFPs to the packaging of the devices themselves.
typical COGS about 70%-80% material, 20% value add

Optical speed transitions are running CONCURRENTLY rather than sequentially - 'pretty unprecedented... 800G is still sort of the underlying technology, but 1.6T is scaling, and typically that would have been spaced out a little more'. Transceiver manufacturers are RAPIDLY SCALING 800G AND 1.6T optical transceivers on Keysight's industry-leading 224G digital communication analyzers, and customers are 'ramping production of 1.6T as we speak right now' with very strong demand - Q4 wireline mix is expected to tilt further toward PRODUCTION test as a result. Customers are ALREADY ENGAGING KEYSIGHT ON 3.2T (demo run at a conference earlier this year). Optical component ecosystem investment continues to ramp and key players are adopting the lab portfolio including the INDUSTRY'S FIRST 220 GHz LIGHTWAVE COMPONENT ANALYZER, introduced at OFC this year. Wireline R&D-vs-manufacturing mix has shifted from ~80/20 historically to ~70/30 and roughly two-thirds / one-third over the last couple of quarters.
800G+1.6T scaling concurrently on 224G DCAs; 3.2T engagements live; first 220GHz LCA

Raytek (Raytec Semiconductor) will add wafer-level packaging capacity in Thailand ON FABRINET'S CAMPUS, so that the full set of packaging capabilities required for CPO and NPO devices sits under one roof - either in Fabrinet's own production lines or in partnership with Raytek. Fabrinet also recorded an approximately $56.7 million non-cash gain remeasuring its existing ~14% investment in Raytek in fiscal Q4 2026.
$56.7M non-cash remeasurement gain on Fabrinet's ~14% stake; new Thailand capacity on Fabrinet's campus

CPO TEST - TIMING AND WHERE VIAVI SITS: Khaykin said Viavi has been working on a CPO test 'now for well over 12 to close to 2 years. We are now started shipping, I would say even this quarter is early shipments.' Test capacity is facilitized ahead of demand and the next increment is added at about '60%, 70% utilization'. CPO pulls Viavi into semiconductor test next to Advantest, Teradyne and FormFactor - the configuration is an IC tester plus a prober plus an optical rack, all interconnected - and he expects a HIGHER share for Viavi there than in pluggables because Viavi sells an automatable integrated platform with '2,500 SKUs' of measurement modules rather than a point solution. Content per port rises sharply: pluggable is power, dispersion and insertion loss, CPO is multiple insertions plus extensive functional test, with known-good-die, optical-engine and interconnect-platform insertions all before the ASIC and memory go on a module worth 'thousands of dollars' - skip them and 'you will be throwing away tens of millions of dollars'.
CPO test in development well over 12 months to close to 2 years, early shipments this quarter; capacity increments added at 60%, 70% utilization; 2,500 SKUs of measurement modules

FY2027 framed as a significant acceleration: having just delivered its first $2B revenue quarter, Coherent expects its FIRST QUARTER ABOVE $3B OF REVENUE BY THE END OF FISCAL 2027, with EPS again growing significantly faster than revenue. Confidence rests on three stated factors: (1) record bookings again in Q4 with demand still growing, (2) rising supply of critical components led by the indium phosphide doubling, and (3) multiple new revenue streams ramping — optical circuit switching, co-packaged optics, multi-rail systems, and advanced materials for data-center thermal and power management. Data center and communications was 79% of total Q4 revenue.
first >$3B revenue quarter targeted by end of FY2027; DC+comms = 79% of revenue

Integrated optics: CPO, NPO and other forms represent MORE THAN $15 BILLION of incremental addressable market. At ECOC in September (launch event September 21) Coherent unveils COHERENT PHOTONLINK, a complete integrated-optics platform spanning the full optical signal chain — light generation, beam shaping, transmission, detection and conversion back to an electrical signal for the XPU or switch chip — supporting CPO, NPO and other optical integration. Initial PhotonLink-related revenue begins in the DECEMBER QUARTER. Engagement intensity with customers on CPO and/or NPO 'has really gone up over the last three to six months', with almost every large strategic customer running a CPO or NPO project (some both). Content per socket is COMPARABLE between CPO and NPO — 'just a different attach point' — because Coherent supplies the laser, external laser module, isolators, polarization-maintaining fiber, full fiber-attach kit assembly and SiPho PICs rather than a single ingredient. CPO for SCALE-UP applications starts generating revenue in the second half of calendar 2027; the CPO ramping now goes first into scale-out. The 200G VCSEL is expected to be adopted in NPO/integrated-optics applications.
integrated optics >$15B incremental TAM; PhotonLink unveiled Sept 21, first revenue Dec quarter; CPO scale-up revenue 2H CY2027

Potential U.S. import restrictions on optical transceivers (a Reuters report management called speculative) would benefit Coherent as 'the largest U.S. supplier of transceivers'. Coherent has OVER 20 PRODUCTION FACILITIES IN THE U.S., including Sherman, Texas, which makes critical components for transceivers AND for CPO/NPO applications, plus U.S. sites producing fiber optic cable and growing the garnet used in transceiver isolators. Management said it would be open to increasing U.S. manufacturing further, and confirmed that a number of customers have since reached out to discuss manufacturing options — 'that has spurred some new customer demand and supply discussions.' Separately, Coherent does not expect to sell indium phosphide lasers externally in the near future because data-center transceiver demand absorbs every bit of capacity 'and then some'.
>20 U.S. production facilities; possible import restrictions spurring new customer supply discussions

→ NVIDIA: The Texas facility HAS BEGUN RAMPING the ultra-high-power CW laser for CPO solutions, 'including those covered by our NVIDIA partnership', with revenue expected to begin ramping in fiscal Q2 (the December quarter). Management reported NO push-out of CPO demand — the opposite: 'we have seen demand increase and request from customers' demand getting pulled in.'

H1 networking-product revenue grew strongly on higher switch volumes and rising ASPs as AI racks push network bandwidth and interconnect needs. The target of roughly doubling 800G-and-above switch revenue this year is unchanged, and CPO optical switches are on plan for volume production and shipment in Q3 - CPO switches have already begun shipping, currently used mainly for scale-out links between AI racks and later extending as platform generations and system architecture upgrade. Foxconn is also building out optical modules, optoelectronic integration, advanced packaging, cables/connectors and high-speed transmission and power-management modules to lift in-house content; it sees optical communications and networking as the next major AI-infrastructure growth leg, with a market that could exceed US$100 billion, and its research institute announced an ultra-high-capacity silicon photonics technology for supercomputing transmission.
800G+ switch revenue on track to double in 2026; CPO switch volume production and shipment from Q3

Networking is now an explicit DCBBS pillar: the total solution spans CPU and GPU compute, storage, energy and a 1.6T HIGH-SPEED SWITCH plus 'upcoming optical networking', sold with the Supermicro management software suite (SCM, SuperCloud Composer, SVM, SOM). The new 32-acre Silicon Valley DCBBS campus features an ADVANCED OPTICAL PHOTONICS NETWORKING LAB alongside datacenter-scale manufacturing, and management calls out high-speed switch and optical technology as areas of very aggressive continued investment, with the 'high bandwidth switch and the whole networking design management tool' cited as a big room to grow toward the ~20%-of-gross-profit DCBBS target. Customer networking readiness (alongside power and cooling) was one of the causes of the Q4 revenue push-out.
1.6T switch shipping in DCBBS; optical networking upcoming; SV photonics lab

1.6T optical-module PCB: current orders are mainly 1.6T high-speed optical-module boards; 2026 optical-module related revenue is guided to double, 1.6T keeps growing sharply in 2027 and becomes the main shipping spec in 2028, and 3.2T boards are already being sampled. Customers are already pre-booking 2027 capacity; target is to become the world's largest high-end optical-module PCB supplier in 2027. 800G-and-above optical-module boards require M7-class ultra-low-loss laminate (1.6T effectively mandates it); management says roughly 20 players claim to be entering optical modules but few master M7 high-layer board production, which is why Zhen Ding's substrate-derived M7 technology gave it the 1.6T breakout. 1.6T optical-module board yield is described as industry-leading at above 90%, including the newly ramped Thailand lines. On a potential US FCC ban on Chinese optical modules: Zhen Ding supplies the PCB inside the module, not the module itself, so sees no direct hit, and can shift production to Thailand where customers require it. On CPO: the company says it will participate in both pluggable and CPO/NPO architectures as they develop; most PCB equipment is transferable between product types so a CPO shift would strand little capacity.
2026 optical-module revenue to double; 1.6T main spec by 2028; 3.2T sampling; 1.6T board yield above 90%; goal: largest high-end optical-module PCB supplier in 2027

Named by AOI management on its Q2 FY2026 call as one of the very few suppliers able to serve the high-power CPO laser market: AOI, Lumentum, Coherent and Broadcom are all 'invest[ing] huge money' in laser capacity, yet 'even combined... it's still very tough to meet the customer demand in the next few years'. Sizing: CPO/ELSFP needs a 300mW laser (vs 70mW for 800G, 100mW for 1.6T) with ~6x larger die, so the industry laser market must grow 8-10x; DWDM ELSFP carries 40-50% worse yield loss than 1310nm, and laser equipment takes 21-24 months from order to high-volume output. AOI states only AOI, Lumentum and Coherent can hit acceptable DWDM CPO laser / CPO module yields.
Industry high-power laser capacity must grow 8-10x for CPO; 21-24 month equipment lead time

NPO and XPO positioning: MACOM has BETWEEN 10 AND 20 ACTIVE NPO DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS across various customers and use cases, and expects some of that revenue to kick in IN 2028, with NPO starting to grow significantly from 2028. Critically, MACOM says it will NOT build or supply optical engines - in Data Center it is a chip supplier, not a multichip assembly or module supplier. It describes the architectural evolution as pluggable transceivers with DSPs, to LPO platforms that remove the DSP, morphing into smaller package-less NPO platforms; those architectures still need drivers and TIAs, but with much higher density - smaller parts, more channels, lower power, and varied form factors using wire bonds, bumped devices or flip chip, plus through-silicon-via options. Because these solutions are specific to the architectures hyperscalers are driving, the design wins come directly to MACOM. Related applications include LPO and LRO on single mode or multimode.
10-20 active NPO development projects; NPO revenue expected to begin in 2028

THE NPO / SCALE-UP THESIS AND THE III-V ROADMAP: SiPho pluggables (800G/1.6T) have 'for the most part ALREADY REPLACED COPPER for scale-out connections outside the rack'; the NEXT FRONTIER IS SCALE-UP, where Tower has SEVERAL NEAR-PACKAGED-OPTICS (NPO) DEPLOYMENTS PLANNED OVER THE NEXT YEAR and many more in design — NPO expected to be 'in the TENS OF PERCENT' of SiPho shipments by H2 2027 (it reuses the pluggable ecosystem, easing hyperscaler reliability/serviceability/multi-source concerns). Content growth comes from HETEROGENEOUS INTEGRATION: III-V-on-silicon INTEGRATED InP LASERS (several tens of $M of revenue expected in 2027; chip-to-wafer bonding moving in-house), die-to-wafer/wafer-to-wafer bonding, and next-gen modulators (400G/lane silicon with Coherent; TFLN and InP in development); multi-year IQE EPI SUPPLY AGREEMENT resolved the InP-substrate crunch. SiGe: 100G/200G-per-lane drivers and TIAs in HVM across all three 200mm fabs (pluggables + LPO/LRO), 400G/lane next with tight EIC-PIC co-design. Adjacent read-through: image-sensor demand SURGING for machine-vision inspection driven by 'the accelerated build-out of DDR and HBM MEMORY ASSEMBLY LINES.'
NPO = tens-of-% of SiPho shipments by H2-2027; integrated InP lasers = tens of $M in 2027; pluggables already displaced copper for scale-out

Silicon photonics and indium phosphide lasers are Veeco's clearest AI-linked growth vector, with a projected $700 million SAM by 2030 for its role in InP laser manufacturing and a stated opportunity of AT LEAST $2 BILLION over the coming years across the laser manufacturing flow - epitaxy, wet processing and laser facet coating. Announced with the results: a global leader in optical and photonics technologies selected Veeco's Lumina+ MOCVD system to fabricate indium phosphide lasers for the datacom industry; Lumina+ offers the largest batch size in the MOCVD industry, best-in-class throughput, lowest cost per wafer, and can deposit high-quality epitaxial layers on InP wafers of any size. Veeco is also a market leader in WaferEtch/WaferStorm wet processing and in the SPECTOR ion beam deposition tool used for the critical laser facet coating step, where its IBD is differentiated as the industry moves to higher-power lasers with stricter film specifications. Management framed the driver as the industry 'overcoming the copper wall,' with hyperscalers advancing EML pluggables, silicon photonics pluggables and the longer-term near-package and co-packaged optics architectures - all of which rely increasingly on InP lasers.
InP laser SAM ~$700M by 2030; total laser-manufacturing opportunity at least $2B; Lumina+ MOCVD selected by a global optical/photonics leader for datacom InP lasers

Singapore-based indium phosphide IDM (20 years in optical communications, all R&D and production in Singapore, part of the non-Chinese supply chain) making CWDM laser gain chips and SOAs; current mass production is at 100 milliwatts, with 200 and 400 milliwatts the future mainstream for CPO and optical engines. Capacity is expanding with more machinery in Q3 this year and Q1 next year and significant expansion through next year. Lite-On is taking a 21% stake and one board seat.
mass production at 100 milliwatts; 200 and 400 milliwatts the future mainstream; Lite-On taking 21% stake

→ Lite-On: Lite-On's board approved a strategic investment to procure 21% of DenseLight's shares and one board seat; DenseLight's laser chip will become part of Lite-On's modules as the light source for its optical communication products, with joint development targeting 1.6T and 3.2T light engine / CPO solutions. No exclusivity, and revenue contribution to Lite-On expected only in late 2027 or early 2028.
value: 21% equity stake, amount not disclosed

The new Turing design center began trial operation in Q2 running small and mid-size projects and is expected to be in full use in H2; it adds some depreciation/R&D cost but is aimed squarely at 3nm, 2nm and even more advanced process work plus advanced packaging. The R&D roadmap already includes CPO, IVR (integrated voltage regulator), next-generation UCIe die-to-die, and N2-on-N2 advanced-process development; opex should grow only modestly versus a clearly larger revenue increase next year.

CPO remains at the incubation stage - how the cooperation models and mass-production timing shake out is not yet clear - but management views optical as inevitable as bandwidth grows: beyond the two small announced customers there are large customers actively engaging, still too early to disclose. On memory: GUC confirmed it does have HBF (high-bandwidth flash) cooperation underway. For HBM base die, memory makers currently keep the logic die to themselves (Samsung using its own logic process, SK Hynix working with TSMC); GUC sees its opening coming when a memory maker's main product splits into many SKUs, and notes its existing cooperation with SK Hynix on other product lines has been good.

Entering the optical engines, optical modules and rack-scale optical connection markets via the DenseLight strategic investment, leveraging existing strengths in advanced packaging, optical coupling, system integration and global manufacturing; focus is on back-end optical engines and CPO for next-generation optic communications (1.6T and 3.2T), with clear revenue numbers expected in 2027 or 2028.

448G SerDes development progressing well with a co-packaged copper system solution, IP expected ready in the second half of next year; beyond 448G the roadmap most likely needs to go optical, and MediaTek continues to develop CPO system solutions on TSMC's COUPE platform for next-generation system connectivity, plus an end-to-end 3.5D platform (IP, packaging, design flows) and industry-leading D2D IPs.
448G SerDes IP ready second half of next year (2027)

→ TSMC: MediaTek continues to develop CPO system solutions on TSMC's COUPE platform to enable next-generation system connectivity beyond 448G SerDes, and works through deep design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) with TSMC on advanced nodes such as 2 nanometer for high-performance ASICs across very large chip sizes using CoWoS and EMIB-T technologies.

Technology roadmap. PANEL: ASE's fully automated panel line starts PRODUCTION IN Q1 2027 in a 310mm x 310mm form factor — described as COMPLEMENTARY to foundry CoWoS, serving the SAME CUSTOMER SET with identical reticle size and pitch/line-width coverage; adoption depends on capacity, performance and speed of execution. GLASS SUBSTRATE: NOT in production and not within the next 12 months; R&D is evaluating feasibility and economics with substrate suppliers, the foundry and customers. FULL-PROCESS (CoWoS-like): on track for ~USD 300M of revenue in 2026 with aggressive capacity expansion and substantial growth in 2027; margin not yet fully reflected but expected to be margin-accretive. CPO: launching toward the END OF 2026 in initially small volume, yielding benchmark data on bandwidth, system performance and thermal dissipation; more detail promised in two quarters. Bigger reticle sizes drive panel/more-complex CoWoS first, then POWER DELIVERY becomes the next constraint over the following two to three years.
panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027; glass substrate not within 12 months; full-process ~USD 300M 2026; CPO launches late 2026

DEMAND DRIVERS AND CUSTOMERS: optical connectivity deployment in AI data centers is accelerating 'as hyperscalers scale GPU dense architectures and look for higher speed lower power photonics'. Near term the pull is the industry migration to 1.6T transceiver modules, 'for which indium phosphide based lasers and detectors are essential'; longer term, hyperscalers advancing toward NEAR-PACKAGED AND CO-PACKAGED OPTICS 'will continue to drive increasing demand for our material' — pointing to a durable multiyear demand cycle. AXT signed strategic LONG-TERM SUPPLY AGREEMENTS with COHERENT and another partner, and announced one with LUMENTUM the week of the call. US cloud/AI capex is the primary driver for EML and silicon-photonics transceivers plus high-speed photodetectors; AXT believes its material is used at MULTIPLE US HYPERSCALERS with end-customer use expected to broaden, alongside 'huge growth in China'. Corporate: subsidiary Tongmei withdrew its STAR Market IPO application (06-26-2026) and is redirecting to a HONG KONG EXCHANGE listing (~1 year); this created a redemption right on $49M of 2021 PE investment, though those investors currently wish to remain.
1.6T migration + CPO/NPO drive multiyear InP cycle; LTAs with Coherent and Lumentum; Tongmei to HKEX

Microsystems & Photonics growing; progress in co-packaged optics, data communication, AR/VR and quantum-computing-related applications through the LIGENTEC collaboration; photonics volume production expected to start in 2028; awarded EUR 127.4 million under the European Chips Act to expand Microsystems & Photonics manufacturing in Erfurt (Fab4Micro)
Microsystems & Photonics revenue $28.7 million, up 14% year-over-year; EUR 127.4 million Chips Act award

Photonics: customers ramping production of high-speed optical transceivers for 800G and beyond; SEMI's pluggable optical transceiver solutions revenue almost tripled year-on-year in H1 2026, with further growth expected for the rest of 2026. CPO is still small, with the packaging-equipment inflection point seen between 2027-2028, more likely 2028; ASMPT's portfolio (Amicra ultra-high-precision bonders, TCB, hybrid bonding, flip chip mass reflow) covers EIC/PIC integration, optical assembly and fiber attach.
pluggable optical transceiver revenue approximately $75 million in H1 2026, almost tripled year-on-year

Optical/CPO roadmap: the Broadcom cooperation has brought PTI into optical communications - it will build Optical Engines using its panel fan-out technology, with small-volume production of the first OBO and OSFP versions starting around end-2026; integrating the Optical Engine into a switch (a CPO switch) is targeted to start shipping in H2 2027, and integration of the Optical Engine into AI chips is expected around 2028 or later once designs mature (engineering simulations already completed). Separately, TSV interconnection for DRAM co-developed with a partner has completed DDR-5 trial production and moves to volume production and shipments in Q4 2026 - a foundation for future HBM manufacturing that management expects to start shifting DRAM packaging from 30-year-old wire-bond formats toward advanced packaging, with a meaningful revenue and margin contribution from next year.
Optical Engine small-volume production from end-2026 (OBO, OSFP); CPO switch shipments from H2 2027; AI-chip integration ~2028; TSV-based DDR-5 DRAM volume production from Q4 2026

→ Broadcom: PTI and Broadcom will form a joint venture in Singapore - a major milestone making PTI a strategic and preferred partner of Broadcom. Built on PTI's fan-out PLP AI packaging experience, the JV will co-develop and produce additive-process fine-line-width redistribution-layer (RDL) packaging directly on advanced substrates (fan-out based), and will serve Broadcom exclusively without affecting PTI's fan-out PLP work for existing and future customers. An NDA is signed and the deal awaits Taiwan investment-authority approval, after which details will be disclosed; the JV funding goes in staged installments and does not raise PTI's NT$500 hundred million capex. The cooperation also brought PTI into the optical-communications field (Optical Engine, CPO switch roadmap).

CALL-ONLY: ADVANCED-PACKAGING PROGRAM COUNT RESTATED - 2.5D: 11 customers; HDFO (high-density fan-out): 5 customers across 10 active engagements; still on track for FOUR 2.5D and FOUR HDFO product launches in 2026, of which the data-center CPU program now ramping 'is definitely the largest from a scale perspective'. Active leading-edge engagements also span emerging CO-PACKAGED OPTICS, across AI infrastructure, HPC and networking applications. BRIDGE-type packaging technologies are 'more of a 2028 type timeline'. Utilization has moved from the 50s into the 70s across the manufacturing network (Q2 in the high 70s) and 'several technology platforms are now operating at FULL CAPACITY' - advanced application spaces very high, with remaining open capacity mainly in mainstream (notably the Philippines); assets in transit for the Korea-to-Vietnam SiP move are effectively stalled capacity that understates true utilization.
2.5D 11 customers; HDFO 5 customers / 10 engagements; 4+4 launches in 2026; util 50s -> high-70s

Networking cadence: 1.6T mass production ramps commence in Q3 2026 with two hyperscaler customers; 10 active 1.6T programs 'really surging' in 2027 with additional awards likely in coming quarters; 400G 'remarkably resilient' from 2026 into 2027 alongside strong 800G growth. The 1.6T CPO switch win: samples 1H 2027, mass production 2H 2027. Scale-up TAM expected to grow substantially over next 3 years; also winning scale-up networking programs from one of its largest customers.
1.6T MP from Q3 2026; 10 active 1.6T programs; CPO samples 1H27, MP 2H27

SCALE-UP PROTOCOL AND THE END STATE OF THE OPTICAL TRANSITION. An AMD executive (named 'Farosh' in the transcript): 'on MI450, we support UALink transported over Ethernet. ESUN is a set of extensions to Ethernet', and AMD expects 'UALink over Ethernet brought forward and being available in MI500 as well'. MI500 is 'the one where we begin transitioning from a purely electrical interconnect for scale-up networking to start to see optical play a role as well' — 'We don’t view this as a light switch.' The terminus, 'generations out in the future is, Co-packaged optics on all the major components and optical really being the backbone of many connections within the rack as well as between.'
MI450: UALink over Ethernet; MI500 begins electrical-to-optical scale-up transition; end state Co-packaged optics on all the major components

Hybrid bonding customer adoption increased from 15 at year-end 2025 to 21 at the end of Q2 2026; use cases expanded across logic, memory, co-packaged optics and consumer; Q2 hybrid orders came from two repeat customers (one for co-packaged optics, one for logic) and one new hyperscaler customer, probably for wearables such as smart glasses
hybrid bonding customers 21, up from 15 at year-end 2025

Photonic SOI addresses pluggable transceivers, near package optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO); most current revenue and growth comes from scale-out, mostly pluggables, with NPO taking share and CPO expected to ramp on scale-out at the end of the year; scale-up is starting with pluggables and will move to CPO; roughly the same Photonic SOI content in all these architectures

Q3 FY2026: networking & communications grew more than 50% YoY, fueled by a strong networking ramp in India (revenue ~doubled YoY) and customers investing in greater high-speed-interconnect capacity for AI workloads; InfiniBand and Ethernet both cited as demand drivers. Silicon photonics remains an active participation area and a margin-accretive driver within Intelligent Infrastructure, building on the co-packaged-optics / near-package-optics business acquired from Intel.
Networking & comms +50%+ YoY; India networking ~2x YoY; silicon photonics margin-accretive

HPE is the FIRST OEM to productize a Broadcom Tomahawk-6-based, 100% liquid-cooled switch (1.6 Tbps, 'HelioStack' reference architecture, introducing in fall 2026), with a roadmap extending through co-packaged optics for lower power. Raised the cumulative FY2026 Networks-for-AI order target to at least $2B; data-center networking & routing revenue grew 69%, with Juniper PTX (800G density) winning data-center-interconnect deployments at large cloud service providers. Scale-up (Helios switch) + scale-out (QFX fabric) + scale-across (PTX DCI) covered.
First Tomahawk-6 liquid-cooled switch; Networks-for-AI >= $2B FY26

Booked $1.8B in new AI systems orders, bringing cumulative AI systems bookings to $16.4B; entered Q3 with $5.9B AI backlog (primarily enterprise + sovereign). Networking (Juniper integrated, ahead of plan) revenue $2.7B (+10% normalized); raised cumulative FY2026 Networks-for-AI order target to at least $2B. First OEM to productize a Broadcom Tomahawk 6-based 100% liquid-cooled switch; QFX AI scale-out fabric; Juniper PTX 800G scale-across; co-packaged-optics roadmap. Data-center switching orders +~20%, routing orders +~30% (data-center interconnect for large CSPs).
AI systems bookings $16.4B cumulative; Networks-for-AI target >=$2B

Capacity: Kulim (Malaysia) plant 1 successfully running high volume production of advanced substrates, with the next generation of larger advanced substrates under development; new customer-financed capacity expansion for AI-related substrates announced in Chongqing under a long-term contract (accretive from the start, high double-digit EUR million bottom-line impact); Leoben and Fehring in Austria being rebuilt for embedding of high-power electronics (partly single source) with revenue impact from the second half of the year; Shanghai focused on accelerator cards, co-packaged optics and embedded optics. T-glass shortage managed by expanding allocation from existing suppliers and qualifying new ones, though some effects remain on finished product availability; inflationary input cost increases (an ABF price increase was flagged by an analyst) are passed through to customers with a delay of a couple of months.

Optical generation shift: SiTime expects meaningful adoption of 1.6 terabit optical modules in 2026, with higher frequencies and resilience needs driving demand for its advanced oscillators at a higher price than those used in 800G, while oscillators for 400G and 800G keep shipping strongly for at least the next two years. Vashist said 1.6T is 'growing, as we said the last time, at a higher rate than we had anticipated last year', and connectivity demand includes AEC active cabling. AGENTIC WORKLOADS ARE THE CPU DEMAND DRIVER, AND IRELAND IS THE SUPPLY ANSWER: CFO David Zinsner quantified the workload shift for the first time - comparing a regular training data center with an agentic-like activity, 'it's like a 4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements'. Server CPU units, which used to decline low single digits, are now growing double digits with core counts growing at multiples of that, and ASP per core - which fell almost 20% in some years - has at least stabilized and in some like-for-like cases is going up, so core-count growth now flows straight through to revenue. The constraint is supply, not competitive performance: 'as we look at this year, next year, probably even into 2028, this is going to be less about competitive performance of CPUs and more about can you get the CPUs to the customer', and share will follow whoever can supply. Granite Rapids, the data-center flagship, is built in Ireland on Intel 3; part of next year's CapEx is to ramp Ireland where Intel wants to 'more than double the output there next year'. Even so Intel will 'under-supply for sure this year', 'probably under-supply next year', and hopes to be in a good position by 2028.

MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

CALL — THE ATE-TAM RERATING AND THE DUAL-VENDOR SHARE MACHINE: AI-driven revenue is now >60% OF TOTAL COMPANY REVENUE. New TAM frame: test equipment has rocketed from ~4% of semiconductor capex (2023) to 7% (2025) to 8% (first five months of 2026), expected to SETTLE AT 7-9%; with WFE approaching $250B by end of decade, Teradyne sees a path for TOTAL ATE TAM TO REACH OR EXCEED $20 BILLION — after a decade of semi-cap outgrowing test, THE TREND REVERSED IN 2024 and test now outpaces fab equipment (transistor production +15-20% CAGR = first-order SoC-TAM predictor; correlation runs on a ~1-YEAR LAG, strong over 3-5-year windows). Test intensity: accelerator:CPU ~4:1, but 'ALL the wafers that get fabbed need to get tested' — mix-agnostic at the wafer level. 2027: 'a RESURGENCE in growth' on TAM expansion + share; target-model update at the Q4 call. Networking test: CPO test TAM $300-700M BY 2028 (2027 nearer ~$200M), Photon 100 + Quantifi + MLTP JV cover pluggable->XPO->CPO and copper; SiPho nuance — the polymer LENS is applied after EIC-PIC bonding, so key loss/polarization tests CANNOT happen at insertion 1.

END-MARKET TRANSFORMATION COMPLETE — from EV silicon carbide to AI: two years ago OVER 95% of Aehr's business was tied to silicon carbide for electric vehicles; in fiscal 2026 almost 95% of revenue came from markets OTHER than EV SiC. WIDE TC bonder launch imminent (hybrid-bonder delay = TC extension); 2.5D packaging entry; Micron now a disclosed customer

industry-wide component shortages; $8.9B purchase commitments; GM pressure

smartphone wafer starts 4 times larger than data center a few years ago; one to one today; two to one data center versus smartphone in a couple of years

chip complexity/size up 48x over the next five years (TSMC roadmap); customers would otherwise need 2x more engineers every year; exponential projected to 2042

emulation runs ~1,000 times faster than CPUs; 10, 15-year design lead; record hardware year for the last 6 years

it will be above 20%; Gartner talking about 20% growth, TechInsights in the high 20s

WHY NOVA IS NOT OUTPERFORMING WFE AS USUAL IN 2026 (the '2x WFE' framing was the moderator's, not management's): Kizner said Nova historically outperforms WFE significantly ('2024, we grew by 30%', '2025, we grew by 31%' while WFE did not grow much) but 2026 breaks the pattern because of investment MIX. Three reasons: (1) NAND contributes to WFE but nothing to Nova because the spend is upgrades, not greenfield capacity; (2) heavy DRAM investment, where metrology intensity is lower than logic; (3) most important, the AI customers did NOT transition to Gate-All-Around - they are 'still using the N-1, 3 nm and 5 nm' and are spending on 3 nm capacity expansions in both the U.S. and Taiwan, so the metrology intensity of 2026 spending went down on mix.
2024, we grew by 30%; 2025, we grew by 31%; still using the N-1, 3 nm and 5 nm

it will happen in 2028 and going forward

it is around 30% of our revenues; 25% to 30% over all WFE spending; it will be another growth year for China for us on a nominal basis

First cost and gating condition put on the EUV plan the Q3 call described only as partnerships: 'we have a plan to go to EUV, but a full EUV program would cost us about $300 million. For a company generating $850 million to $900 million in annual revenue, you're very cautious about doing that... you could end up crippling the company if you're not careful.' The approach is to introduce certain EUV capabilities in stages over what Moreau called 'probably takes us a good maybe a five-year investment cycle', spreading the cost while waiting for the captives to release EUV work to merchant suppliers. The demand gate today is thin: 'At the moment, there's one company out there that's requesting EUV masks. That's not a big enough market for you to incur that $300 million.' EUV is critical from 14 nanometers down to 3 nanometers and essentially all of that mask business is captive today.
full EUV program would cost about $300 million against $850 million to $900 million of annual revenue; one company currently requesting EUV masks; EUV critical from 14 nanometers down to 3 nanometers

Mask-set ASP ladder and share, quantified: citing a Morgan Stanley Japan initiation report on a competitor, Moreau said a 90 nanometer design is about 25 masks per set and roughly '$50,000 of revenue for that one chip design'; at 14 nanometers the set goes to close to 80 masks and 'we're talking about $1 million in revenue contribution'; at five nanometers 'you're talking about $10 million to $20 million for that one semiconductor chip design, for the photomask set' - 'a very parabolic move'. Photronics holds about 10% of the total photomask market including captives, captives are about two-thirds of the market and gained share in 2025 purely on ASP (conceivably going to 70%), while display share is about 28% and has held steady for five years. On units, Photronics estimates it manufactures about as much volume as TSMC does in-house, but that TSMC's fully captive mask output would be worth 'at least five or six times' Photronics' roughly $620 million of semiconductor photomask revenue last year if it carried an external price.

90 nanometer set about 25 masks and about $50,000; 14 nanometer set close to 80 masks and about $1 million; five nanometer set $10 million to $20 million; Photronics 10% of the total photomask market, captives about two-thirds going possibly to 70%; display share about 28%; semiconductor photomask revenue about $620 million last year

Node-capability roadmap by site, more granular than the Q3 call. Boise is the U.S. high-end facility and 'can produce masks down to seven nanometers' today, with little revenue at 7 nanometers so far, and 'with the same equipment, we are advancing our capabilities to actually go down to four' - not ready and no revenue presented today. Allen, Texas is being taken from 180 nanometers and 130 nanometers up to 65 nanometers and 'we should be up and running in the next month or two'; production then shifts out of Boise to Texas, freeing Boise to capture more 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometer business. Korea is the other upgrade: the bulk of that facility's business today is about 40 nanometers, the expansion to 8 nanometers is expected 'in about a year from now', and Photronics expects significantly greater 8 and 10 nanometer business there 'largely because of customers that are very close to that facility'. The U.S. is 17%-19% of revenue today and is expected to be a higher share of total revenue in fiscal 2027.

Boise down to seven nanometers today, advancing toward four; Allen, Texas from 180 and 130 nanometers to 65 nanometers up and running in the next month or two, freeing Boise for 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometers; Korea about 40 nanometers today to 8 nanometers in about a year; U.S. 17%, 18%, 19% of revenue rising in fiscal 2027

→ Samsung: Moreau: 'Samsung is a 10% customer of ours today, and we supply masks to them on both the semiconductor side and the display side.' Samsung runs a captive mask operation and designs 'a lot of the photomasks in-house' for its own needs but does outsource some; Photronics is working with Samsung and the other captives, which are expected to outsource more at the near-leading edge as their internal teams move to five, four, three and two nanometer.
value: Samsung is a 10% customer of Photronics

→ TSMC: Moreau named TSMC as a customer: 'If you looked at Taiwan Semiconductor, which is a customer of ours, they're actually a top 20 customer of ours.' He added that Photronics estimates it manufactures on a unit volume basis about as much as TSMC does in house, and that if TSMC's fully captive mask output were given an external revenue value it would be 'at least five or six times greater' than Photronics' roughly $620 million of semiconductor photomask revenue last year - the ASP gap, not units, is why captive share keeps rising. Photronics is also working with TSMC, Intel and SMIC as those captives look to outsource more of the near-leading edge.
units: top 20 customer; Photronics unit volume about equal to TSMC in-house mask volume

Third-party commentary from a competitor, not Toppan management: Photronics' IR head Ted Moreau named Tekscend - the photomask business spun out of Toppan, which IPO'd in October of last year - as Photronics' largest competitor, and gave its EUV status: 'Our largest competitor is this company called Tekscend, which went public in October of last year. They were spun out of a company called Toppan... Tekscend is based in Japan. They have been subsidized by the Japanese government in order to produce masks at what's called extreme ultraviolet technology, EUV.' That capability is close to live - they are 'about to start producing capabilities for masks for that technology in the coming, I would say, probably any minute now.' Moreau added that clean-room capabilities on both sides are otherwise very comparable and both buy the same equipment, so the differentiator is geometry capability, capacity and turnaround time.

CEO split the GaN roadmap into two supply models. Lateral GaN (GaN-on-Silicon) is sourced through partners: 'We have announced a partnership with Innoscience and a partnership with GlobalFoundries... We are partnering with very strong partners externally to get access to the GaN-on-Silicon devices,' while onsemi keeps the control and driver silicon internal on Treo; the combined go-to-market was announced at PCIM. Vertical GaN is fully organic (plus a small tuck-in acquisition for IP) and is built in onsemi's own fab in Syracuse, New York: 'we have the fab. It is up and running. We are sampling, so we have physical samples at customers on their boards being tested.' He claims onsemi is the only company in the world manufacturing vertical GaN today and that competitors would have to work around its patents, and positions it as complementary to silicon carbide for size- and density-constrained sockets.

FOUNDRY BREAKEVEN TARGET END OF 2027 - BUT SUCCESS COULD PUSH IT INTO 2028: Zinsner said Intel is driving the foundry business to breakeven by the end of 2027 as its internal target, while acknowledging that winning more customers carries porting investment and startup expenses that 'could elongate the time to breakeven' - 'I could see us going into 2028 and not being there yet, and maybe it's the end of 2028 even that we get there.' Foundry operating profit has been running at 'like a $2.5 billion loss or so per quarter', and regardless of the crossover date he wants relative steady improvement every quarter. Separately he confirmed an Analyst Day is planned but not this year - sometime next year - and said investors should not expect Intel to announce foundry customers at it: 'that's not done in the foundry industry, and we're not going to be an outlier.'
$2.5 billion loss or so per quarter; breakeven by the end of 2027

THE CAPITAL RAISE IS A SUBSTRATE-AND-FAB SPENDING EVENT: Zinsner explained the August equity raise as 'the capital raise precedes capital investment' - 2026 CapEx has already been upticked 'by a couple of billion dollars from $18 billion to $20 billion', next year's will be significantly higher, and 'substrates are really constrained and we're going to need to make investments associated with substrates as well next year, given the significant demand.' Committing to 14A high-volume manufacturing in 2028 means placing long-lead supplier orders now, which was one of the biggest drivers of the raise. On footprint: Ireland's shell is being equipped now; Fab 52 in Arizona is running Intel 18A and Fab 62 is almost ready, with next year's investment accelerating its equipping; Oregon stays the pilot line but will also run volume Intel 14A as 18A is pushed into Arizona; Ohio shells are in progress with the ability to have 'eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio', mod one being built as fast as possible. Zinsner said 2027 CapEx is not locked - the businesses gave him a number and 'I've told them no', sending them back for more efficiency before he guides.
from $18 billion to $20 billion; eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio

INTEL 14A: 0.9 PDK IN OCTOBER, RISK PRODUCTION 2027, HIGH-VOLUME 2028: Zinsner said Intel is within two months of the 14A 0.9 PDK, so 'you can pretty much now expect us to land in October with that 0.9 PDK', and the remaining step from 0.9 to 1.0 is much smaller than 0.5 to 0.9. Defect density on Intel 14A is tracking better than the target curve and is coming down faster than any previous node - 'we haven't seen this performance since 22 nanometer, which is arguably one of the best nodes Intel's ever put out' - while 18A yields are beating internal milestones. Demand side: internal product teams, 'probably the most cynical bunch out of anybody', are now designing products on Intel 14A, and external foundry engagements have increased enough that Lip-Bu Tan and the team meet customers weekly and the conversation has moved from data to 'how much capacity can I get? What does that supply look like?'. That sequence forces risk production in 2027 ahead of high-volume manufacturing in 2028.
0.9 PDK in October; risk production in 2027; high volume production in 2028; 22 nanometer

EMIB-T ADVANCED PACKAGING SIZED FOR THE FIRST TIME - REVENUE FROM 2H 2027, MULTIPLE BILLIONS PER CUSTOMER: Zinsner said EMIB-T, which removes the interposer from EMIB and can increase reticle size significantly, is a differentiated solution not available elsewhere, and that packaging revenue will 'start to ramp in the back half of 2027', become a run-rate business in 2028 and be 'definitely hitting its stride in 2029'. Scale: 'this business is in the billions... by customer, it will be multiple billion dollars per customer per year of business', at margins of '40% gross, 30% operating margin' with low capital intensity relative to the front end, so 'the ROIC is phenomenal'. He framed advanced packaging as the on-ramp that tests Intel operationally and creates cross-sell into front-end foundry, something Intel has 'already seen that show up even now'. He also pointed to the hire of Seokhee, former CEO of SK hynix, to lead the business as the signal of the opportunity size.
back half of 2027; multiple billion dollars per customer per year; 40% gross, 30% operating margin

INTEL 3 OFFERED AS A BASE-DIE PROCESS FOR OTHER COMPANIES: Asked whether the Ireland Intel 3/4 nodes are internal-only, CFO David Zinsner said 'Intel 3 would not be a great logic process for external, but we use it for base die, and it can be used for base die for other companies. And the fact that we have advanced packaging and all these things kind of all under one roof, there could potentially be some opportunities there.'

HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY is named as one of the three drivers of Keysight's record semiconductor quarter, alongside advanced nodes and silicon photonics, with semiconductor wafer test seeing significant capacity expansion across all three dimensions (memory explicitly included) and wafer-fab-equipment capital forecasts continuing to expand. Test intensity is rising in parallel on the compute side: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean design margins are shrinking and customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' - a compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts, and memory fabrics are among the interfaces being characterized across the GPU/CPU/DPU mix.

AI / HBM / ADVANCED PACKAGING framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the company says the surge in AI semiconductor demand has raised the importance of HBM and advanced-packaging processes, pushing up the technical barrier for high-purity chemicals and precision polishing materials; the global semiconductor market is growing at an unprecedented pace on AI data-center memory and on-device AI, and the introduction of sub-2nm GAA processes and volume production of 300+ layer V-NAND are driving continued demand for high-performance etchants and next-generation precursors. Seasonality has flattened because AI and cloud enterprise demand now leads, producing a longer up-cycle. Product positioning: special etchants for sub-2nm GAA, next-generation CMP slurry and precursors for HBM4 stacking; ultra-high-purity chemicals supplied at near-exclusive levels to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix from the leading-edge ramp and ultra-high-layer V-NAND development stage; a completed portfolio of TSV formation and planarisation materials for HBM4 and chiplet structures to lift high-value-added revenue; display unit expanding into glass-substrate processing materials for next-generation packaging; customers' processes moving to GAA and to HBM / 400+ layer NAND, with joint development from the process-design stage. US entities Soulbrain TX LLC (2022) and Soulbrain RASA TX LLC (2024) respond in real time to customers' new fab lines in Texas and North America; the Xi'an entity supports China memory lines. Semiconductor material ASPs +5% vs FY2025 while raw-material costs rose +14%; semiconductor materials 85% of H1 revenue, +31% company-wide revenue growth.
HBM4 CMP slurry / precursors / TSV materials portfolio; sub-2nm GAA etchants; 300-400+ layer V-NAND; glass-substrate materials; Texas entities for US fab ramps

AI / HBM framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the memory market is leading semiconductor growth on AI and big-data demand, and the equipment market is expected to keep growing over the medium-to-long term on the aggressive DRAM-centric investment memory makers are making to break the HBM SHORTAGE caused by the explosive expansion of AI end-markets. 2022-2024 is described as a harsh down-cycle (memory price collapse, utilisation drop); 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase driven by generative-AI infrastructure build-out, led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than commodity products. The AI-accelerator and HBM demand surge is forcing the equipment market onto a single high-end track where marginal technology or adequate tools have no place; foreign vendors from the US, Japan and Netherlands still hold the largest shares but Korean localisation is rising and the company's tools are now in mass-production lines of major customers at home and abroad, with overseas sales rising (China semiconductor revenue KRW 63,346M in H1 2026 vs KRW 42,017M in H1 2025). Company cannot estimate market share because device makers' total orders are not observable.
HBM shortage-driven DRAM capex cited as multi-year equipment driver; 2025-2030 structural growth phase (HBM, sub-2nm foundry)

panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027; glass substrate not within 12 months; full-process ~USD 300M 2026; CPO launches late 2026

Credo's 10-K describes a fabless model: in fiscal year 2026 Credo exclusively used TSMC for semiconductor wafer production and outsources all of its IC manufacturing to TSMC; after wafer fabrication it uses third-party contractors Amkor Technology and Advanced Semiconductor Engineering (ASE) for packaging its IC products, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC) and Sigurd Microelectronics for testing its IC products, and BizLink Technology for manufacturing its AEC products. Except for its agreement with BizLink for the manufacture of certain AEC products, Credo does not maintain long-term supply contracts with TSMC or its other contract manufacturers or suppliers; none of TSMC, BizLink or its other manufacturers or suppliers has provided contractual capacity assurances, and Credo has not entered capacity commitment arrangements with TSMC. It expects a transition to new foundry or assembly providers would take approximately 9 to 12 months.
