At the most advanced logic node, Entegris has secured strong POR (position of record) positions in CMP consumables, advanced deposition and implant materials, liquid purification and filtration, and wafer handling. The team is now focused on winning incremental share and PORs at subsequent advanced nodes. Separately, the CEO said it takes time to grow two-nanometer and to transition to new nodes such as 1.4 nanometer. Management expects 'middish single-digit' industry MSI (wafer starts) growth in 2026 and strong WFE growth. Fab construction CapEx should grow modestly after last year's high single-digit decline, weighted to the second half, with a bigger acceleration in 2027 as work starts on new fabs. Management flagged ongoing memory shortages as a possible second-half 2026 risk for mainstream end markets; guidance assumes no impact.
middish single-digit industry MSI growth expected in 2026; advanced logic utilization near 100%

CEO Sanjiv Lamba: the project backlog stands at a record $10 billion, not including over half a billion dollars of investment for rocket propellants for contracted space launch customers; two-thirds of the backlog supports contracted clean energy projects. record project backlog $10 billion; $2.5 to $3 billion of projects to start up in 2026

Advanced-node gas intensity (CEO Sanjiv Lamba, answering on TSMC's Phoenix fabs): after the yield from the first couple of fabs positively surprised, 'the commitment to major investments in advanced nodes at Phoenix is strong, and with that comes higher gas intensity'. Moving to advanced nodes raises gas usage per node and, 'more importantly', new gases are being introduced and used in much bigger quantities, which together raise overall gas intensity for the new fabs. 'The next round of fabs is now under discussion and being worked through.'

→ TSMC: Asked about TSMC's Arizona Fab 2, CEO Sanjiv Lamba said Linde's plants for Fab 1 and 2 are in operation ('those assets are on the ground. They have been commissioned'): Fab 1 is fully utilized, and Fab 2 is ramping up at TSMC's end 'and, obviously, we're there fully supporting them on that'. The next round of Phoenix fabs is under discussion, and advanced nodes bring higher gas intensity.

Supply-side position (management): 'For handsets, we don't buy memory'. Apart from some memory that gets stacked, customers buy most memory directly. Qualcomm says it is 'probably among the first to be qualified with every memory provider', including CXMT and other smaller companies. Its platforms have a multi-generation memory controller that works with both newer and older memory, so 'we're going to work with whatever is available'. On foundry supply: 'leading nodes are constrained on the wafer side as well. But we have great relationships with our suppliers, and so we're confident that we'll have enough wafers to address the demand.'

CALL-ONLY: A LEADING-EDGE NODE SHORTAGE GATES THE MARCH QUARTER. Cook: 'we exited December with very lean channel inventory due to that staggering level of demand. And based on that, we're in a supply chase mode to meet the very high levels of customer demand. We are currently constrained and at this point, it's difficult to predict when supply and demand will balance. The constraints that we have are driven by the availability of the advanced nodes that our SoCs are produced on. And at this time, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal.' Asked why Apple is constrained (the analyst framed it as advanced packaging), Cook named the node: 'it's the advanced nodes that we, like three nanometer to be specific, where our SOCs are the latest SOCs are produced on is what is gating the Q2 supply', 'a direct result of the 23% growth' far outstripping internal estimates, with 'more limited flexibility in the supply chain for some period of time'. The March-quarter revenue outlook of 13% to 16% 'comprehends our best estimates of constrained iPhone supply during the quarter'. Cook declined to comment on supply beyond Q2.
'three nanometer' advanced nodes gating Q2 supply; March-quarter revenue outlook of 13% to 16% includes constrained iPhone supply

more than half of wafer requirements from third-party foundries such as TSMC

HBM GROWTH DECOMPOSED, AND THE THIRD DRAM CUSTOMER OPENS UP. On the roughly '70% growth on a year-over-year basis' in HBM in the first half, Slessor attributed it to three things: share gains from 'adding a second HBM customer'; industry bit growth as HBM3 moved to HBM4; and ASP uplift that came not from price increases but from delivering a higher-value configuration 'able to test at the 11 gigabit per second spec of HBM4 and test hundreds of die at once'. FormFactor's largest customer is the HBM leader, where it is the strong incumbent. At the third DRAM maker the major competitor is the entrenched incumbent and FormFactor sees less adoption of its high-speed stack-die configuration — but 'there is a very active conversation with that customer about what to plan for in 2027 and into 2028, as we have more capacity available to serve them'. On the HBM de-spec debate, Slessor called it 'much ado about nothing': fewer/simpler stacks would be offset by more HBM units and by more networking infrastructure to transact data across those units, leaving it 'net net... neutral'. He framed the whole test tailwind as a chiplet problem — in an HBM stack 'one of the 16 die actually causes the entire stack to be essentially scrapped and lost' without known-good-die certainty.
HBM revenue up about 70% year-over-year in the first half; test at the 11 gigabit per second spec of HBM4 and hundreds of die at once

DE-SPECCING DOES NOT DENT HBM PROCESS-CONTROL INTENSITY: asked about customer de-speccing (the analyst's framing - AI servers putting in less memory and stepping from 12 high to 8 high), Higgins argues 'the roadmap dynamics I talked about earlier, those are generally unchanged in the HBM environment' - redundancy, IO count, die size and performance specs still hold, and 'You cannot bin an HBM device'. He reads the behaviour as a reaction to today's memory pricing and supply-demand imbalance rather than a roadmap change, and says KLA does not like paying today's memory prices either. Supporting context he gave on intensity: HBM carries less redundancy, larger die and more logic-like attributes with more logic in the base die, 'the actual device only performs as good as the weakest DRAM in the device', and 'In some products, we have seen intensity in High-Bandwidth Memory that has been consistent with what we see in advanced logic.' Conventional memory is also improving for KLA, with more EUV layers in conventional DRAM devices than in the past.
HBM roadmap dynamics generally unchanged despite de-speccing; you cannot bin an HBM device

Growth split disclosed: this year the biggest growth was in packaging at 80% growth while advanced nodes was about 35% growth, and for next year management expects not those numbers but similar dynamics, with advanced packaging still probably growing stronger than advanced nodes and both growing fairly well. Within advanced packaging the memory (HBM) versus 2.5D logic mix is fairly well split, generally around the 50/50 mark or 60/40 depending on the quarter, because logic requires the memory around it so the whole packaging requirement grows across both. On share, Onto has always had very high share in memory and maintained it, with incremental gains tied to 3D bump metrology as bumps get smaller and denser (3DI); in logic packaging there is room to gain share because of the very high resolution the Dragonfly G5 provides.
packaging 80% growth vs advanced nodes about 35% growth; advanced packaging memory/logic mix around 50/50 to 60/40

Some of the components are very tight.' For Helios it is not just GPU, CPU and HBM — 'there are also a lot of other small component that we need to ensure we have'. We need to build ourselves to buy the equipment, do the consignment to support the ramp' — i.e. AMD is buying the equipment itself and placing it on consignment to support the ramp. He credited a widening foundry ecosystem: 'Now it is not just TSMC, it is Intel, it is Samsung, it is Rapidus. We are working with them all', while holding company incremental margin at 50%.
IP at a $1 billion clip by the end of the year; IP growing north of 40%; 50% incremental margin

HIGH BANDWIDTH COMPUTE (HBC) IS AN EXPLICIT ALTERNATIVE TO HBM, WITH SPECS AND A SHIP DATE. Durga Malladi (EVP Tech Planning, Edge & Data Center): HBC puts compute right next to memory and was 'a direct take on an alternative way of doing things as opposed to HBM'. Claimed '6x improvement compared to HBM in terms of tokens per second per watt'; where 'HBM today is about give or take 21, 22 terabytes per second. We are, like, in hundreds of terabytes per second'. Against SRAM the argument is TCO/area (more racks for the same work). Proof points: the silicon is taped out and 'back in the lab ... coming along very well', with silicon validation and engineering plus commercial samples on track. Generation 1 is 'slated to be commercial and shipping in 2027'; generation 2 lands in 2028 and is benchmarked against HBM4E, where Malladi says the relative gain looks even better because more arithmetic is moving into the logic die under the DRAM stack.

6x improvement compared to HBM in terms of tokens per second per watt; HBM today about 21, 22 terabytes per second vs hundreds of terabytes per second; gen 1 commercial and shipping in 2027, gen 2 in 2028 vs HBM4E

HBC SUPPLY CHAIN AND DIVISION OF LABOUR: Qualcomm is not a memory vendor - 'We're not doing the DRAM stacking ourselves. What we prescribe is this is how things should be done. These are the TSVs that need to occur.' The compute die comes from Qualcomm, and 'We still have to work with the likes of TSMC to tape it all together'; Qualcomm positions itself as the overall system integrator and the single front end to the hyperscaler customer. On supply: right after Investor Day Malladi was 'in Korea with two memory vendors' and, instead of pushing back on the HBM comparison, they asked how to work more closely - 'we have been working with them because we need to make sure that we have the right supply as we do the commercialization', with additional inbound interest from the wider memory community. Hyperscaler engagement is modular across three independent tracks (standalone HBC, HBC plus Qualcomm CPU, or the full stack), and a hyperscaler taking HBC brings 'certain volume commitment, some sort of a demand signal'.

Asked whether High Bandwidth Flash (the moderator named SK hynix and SanDisk) could undercut High Bandwidth Compute on TCO, Durga Malladi gave his own view after in-depth talks with memory vendors: 'HBF is trying to solve a slightly different problem. It is not quite exactly the same problem.' HBF uses flash in addition to DRAM for something else, which 'is not the same thing as increasing the memory bandwidth to the point that the decode performance becomes really good', though 'it has its own use case' and more work remains. He sees HBF as a stack 'kind of independent of this', while the HBM vendors are opening 'a parallel track' because they cannot offer anything like HBC through HBM for the foreseeable future ('Maybe 5 years down the stream, it is going to be a different story').

→ Samsung: Samsung Foundry named among the customers that validated Multiphysics Fusion (up to 10x faster design closure, 3x faster runtime). Separately, on Korea revenue trending up close to 20% this year, management cited the Samsung relationship 'across the portfolio... from IP with our custom HBM and HBM engagements with the lead customers to EDA and to Ansys.'

CRESCENT ISLAND DELIBERATELY SKIPS HBM AND GDDR FOR LOW-POWER DDR: Anil Nanduri, VP of AI Products and Go-To-Market for Intel's Data Center, described Intel's inference GPU roadmap scaling up from the Arc series to Crescent Island and said that 'with Crescent Island, we intentionally chose low-power DDR instead of GDDR or HBM memory' to land on an energy- and cost-efficient point rather than ultra-premium low-latency tokens - a PCIe card an enterprise can plug in and scale. He positioned the portfolio as Xeon plus Crescent Island plus the SambaNova partnership (SambaNova serving the high-interactivity, high-volume token pipe), sold on TCO and ROI rather than peak performance, deployable from on-prem to a neocloud.
low-power DDR instead of GDDR or HBM memory

HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY is named as one of the three drivers of Keysight's record semiconductor quarter, alongside advanced nodes and silicon photonics, with semiconductor wafer test seeing significant capacity expansion across all three dimensions (memory explicitly included) and wafer-fab-equipment capital forecasts continuing to expand. Test intensity is rising in parallel on the compute side: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean design margins are shrinking and customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' - a compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts, and memory fabrics are among the interfaces being characterized across the GPU/CPU/DPU mix.
HBM one of 3 named drivers of the RECORD semi quarter; memory wafer-test capacity expanding

Electronic Industrial Solutions Group delivered a record quarter, and SEMICONDUCTOR was itself a record, driven by ongoing CAPACITY EXPANSION FOR ADVANCED NODES, HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY AND SILICON PHOTONICS. Semiconductor wafer test is seeing significant capacity expansion across all three of those dimensions, and forecasts for wafer fab equipment and capital going into those markets 'continues to expand'. Given increasing adoption of optical interconnects, COMMERCIAL PRODUCTION OF SILICON PHOTONICS IS ACCELERATING ACROSS LEADING FOUNDRIES AND IDMs. Semiconductor R&D solution demand was also healthy, and engagement with industry leaders gives good visibility into next year's requirements. In general electronics, test intensity keeps rising for high-performance components - MULTILAYER PCBs AND CAPACITORS for next-generation compute - as higher frequencies, tighter tolerances and greater GPU/CPU density raise production complexity and quality requirements, pushing test from the board level down to the COMPONENT level. Automotive and energy orders grew solid double digits on software-defined vehicle architectures, in-vehicle network and cybersecurity test, and grid/high-power-charging validation.
EISG record $501M (+21%); semi record on advanced nodes + HBM + SiPh wafer test

US entities Soulbrain TX LLC (2022) and Soulbrain RASA TX LLC (2024) respond in real time to customers' new fab lines in Texas and North America; the Xi'an entity supports China memory lines. Semiconductor material ASPs +5% vs FY2025 while raw-material costs rose +14%; semiconductor materials 85% of H1 revenue, +31% company-wide revenue growth.

Filing frames test and inspection equipment as the fastest-growing equipment segment because HBM-style advanced packaging requires 100% inspection at each process step, raising both ASP and unit counts. AI / HBM framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the memory market is leading semiconductor growth on AI and big-data demand, and the equipment market is expected to keep growing over the medium-to-long term on the aggressive DRAM-centric investment memory makers are making to break the HBM SHORTAGE caused by the explosive expansion of AI end-markets. 2022-2024 is described as a harsh down-cycle (memory price collapse, utilisation drop); 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase driven by generative-AI infrastructure build-out, led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than commodity products. Supply and manufacturing: 'TSMC has once again come through, and we have the wafers needed to fuel our growth' - wafer supply positioned 'not just for the remainder of this year, but for the next year as well' (CFO); 5 nm node where 'wafers are less expensive and supply is less constrained'; 'we don't use HBM memory, CoWoS packaging, or require 3 nm fab capacity'. manufacturing capacity 4 times above 1H 2025; more than 10x increase in 2026

Order intake has accelerated sharply: MORE THAN $600 MILLION of orders received year to date, with deliveries scheduled through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027, materially improving visibility well into 2027. Approximately 80% of those orders are advanced packaging applications. OSATs accounted for MORE THAN 50% of total order intake, HBM players for OVER 20% of the $600 million (against the $260 million of POs and forecasts discussed on the prior call), and photonics for about 5%. Order flow started in Q1 and has grown steadily since. Most orders now being received are for 2027 rather than 2026, and management says a nice 2027 backlog is already building, with additional 2027 OSAT orders already in discussion.
>$600M orders year to date; ~80% advanced packaging; OSATs >50% of intake; HBM >20%; photonics ~5%

The HBM4 transition is a direct order driver: CEO Rafi Amit said 'the industry transition to HBM4 together with continued capacity expansion has resulted in significant orders from MULTIPLE LEADING HBM MANUFACTURERS.' In parallel, ongoing expansion of 2.5D and 3D IC packaging capacity is producing large multi-system orders from leading foundries, IDMs and OSATs. Within the HPC/AI portion of the business the two main segments are HBM and CoWoS (and CoWoS-like) applications, both expanding quickly and growing at roughly similar pace, with the faster one depending on which customers add capacity. Growth is attributed to a combination of share gains and genuine market capacity additions across HBM, CoWoS, fan-in and fan-out.

Advanced packaging mix is stepping up through the year: it was approximately 75% of Q2 revenue and is expected to reach around 80% by Q4. The advanced packaging business is expected to grow approximately 45% in the second half versus the first half, and Q4 advanced packaging revenue is expected to be approximately 70% HIGHER THAN Q1. HPC and AI-related products are already around 55% of revenue and may reach closer to 60% by the end of the year, with conventional advanced packaging roughly another 20%. Non-advanced-packaging business is stable with modest growth, helped by significant CMOS image sensor orders and early signs of recovery in consumer-related areas.
Advanced packaging ~75% of Q2 revenue rising to ~80% by Q4; AP +45% H2 vs H1; Q4 AP ~70% above Q1; HPC/AI ~55% of revenue rising toward ~60%

Custom HBM begins at HBM4E and HBM is becoming a one-to-two-supplier market. Asked when custom HBM can be material: 'HBM4E is when there is going to be a custom SKU of HBM as we work with customers on, and there is plenty of opportunity for differentiation in HBM.' Beyond the custom opportunity, the core design and qualification of HBM is so time-consuming, R&D-intensive and expensive that it is not practical for customers to do business with all three HBM suppliers for all projects: many projects, platforms and several customers will end up using ONE OR TWO HBM suppliers and only a very small number will use all three, so HBM becomes a two-supplier market and 'oftentimes, just a single-sourced opportunity.' On supply mix, the HBM-to-DDR trade ratio of 3-to-1 at HBM3E (to produce 100 bits of HBM, 300 bits of DDR supply must be given up) worsens to CLOSER TO 4 TO 1 by the time Micron reaches HBM4E.
custom HBM SKU starts with HBM4E; HBM3E-to-DDR trade ratio 3-to-1 worsening to closer to 4 to 1 at HBM4E; HBM a one-to-two-supplier market per platform

Sadana cited an HBM3E power lead as an example of co-engineering with customers: 'If you look at the HBM3E product, we came out with capability that was 30% lower power consumption than anyone else, the next best product.' He said engineering engagements now give Micron visibility into customer 'roadmaps at our customers that are beyond 2030 timeframe', whereas years ago it was rare even to know a customer's next-year products.
HBM3E 30% lower power consumption than anyone else; customer roadmap visibility beyond 2030

Electroplating momentum on both front-end and back-end: in logic, larger die sizes and steadily higher interconnect layer counts; in memory, HBM packaging demands higher levels of DRAM stacking and thus more copper process steps. ACM shipped its 2,000th electroplating chamber in the quarter (500th in 2022, 1,500th in 2025); the copper plating market is now almost $1.5 billion, with backside power and HBM DRAM stacking driving more plating tool demand.
2,000th electroplating chamber shipped; copper plating market almost $1.5 billion

Memory is expected to show strong year-over-year growth in 2026 with momentum into 2027 as customers accelerate clean room investments to support growing DRAM and high-bandwidth memory demand driven by AI; 2026 is a significant improvement over the low 2025 base with significant DRAM memory revenue, and second-half memory revenue probably looks similar to the first half because customers are solving bottlenecks in existing fabs until new clean room space comes online.

Memory customer portfolio is expanding: a recent order for multiple high current systems in the current quarter, and additional orders from the leading North American memory manufacturer (referenced last quarter) after the successful completion of its system evaluation, to support new fab investments. High current is the important implant category for memory; medium current also competitive; high energy has less memory content.

2027 memory: too early to size, indications are another year of growth but at a much lower percentage growth rate than 2026 given the low 2025 base; customers have ambitious capacity plans and Axcelis is expanding beyond its traditional position into other areas of the memory market and other customers. no specific figure (analyst estimate ~$120 million annual memory run rate)

NAND: a little activity but no trend yet; anyone with clean room space is using it for higher-value DRAM. Vertical scaling of NAND does not change implant density, so NAND only helps Axcelis when customers add wafer capacity; historically NAND has followed DRAM. Memory systems carry lower-than-corporate-average gross margin but drive higher-margin CS&I aftermarket over the tool life.

Memory: despite the anticipated sequential decline from a strong Q1, customer engagement remains robust; strong year-over-year growth expected in 2026 with momentum into 2027 as customers accelerate clean room investments to support DRAM and high-bandwidth memory demand driven by AI. Recent order for multiple high current systems in the current quarter, and additional orders from the leading North American memory manufacturer after its system evaluation, to support new fab investments.

Growth catalysts: GAA sales were about JPY 5 billion in Q1 and are expected at over JPY 20 billion for FY March 2027. Advanced packaging revenue, JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026, is now expected at JPY 15 billion in FY March 2027 (Q1 was JPY 4.5 billion) - a significant upward revision from the JPY 6 billion prior plan, driven by both rising customer CapEx and additional POR wins for its film deposition technology. In NAND, demand-supply is not fully adjusted - memory players are allocating clean room to DRAM while NAND wafer output needs to increase - so greenfield NAND investments are expected to resume, which converts all of Kokusai's PORs to sales and is broadly favorable. In DRAM, the D1C transition is complete and D1D is progressing. NAND sales could approach record highs, and DRAM plus NAND plus advanced packaging support growth above WFE (targeting more than a 20% sales increase).
GAA JPY 5 billion in Q1, over JPY 20 billion FY March 2027; advanced packaging raised to JPY 15 billion FY March 2027 from JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026

ADVANCED PACKAGING set a record and contributed nearly one-quarter - 'nearing 25%' - of overall product revenue in Q2, driven by the dimensional metrology portfolio and fuelled by customers' continued investment in advanced packaging and HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY capacity to support AI-related device demand. Nova had guided advanced packaging to between 20 and 25% of product revenue for the year and now sees it 'inching towards the 25% for the year.' Management frames advanced packaging as a MULTI-YEAR STRUCTURAL growth opportunity that has gone from essentially no revenue several years ago to a meaningful contributor, now spanning optical, chemical AND materials metrology, and becoming increasingly similar to front-end manufacturing in complexity across both logic and memory. Chiplets, HYBRID BONDING, PANEL-LEVEL PACKAGING and 2.5D integration all increase both the number of measurements required and their criticality; hybrid bonding is described as 'an additional layer that will accelerate this growth for Nova.'
Advanced packaging a record at nearly 25% of Q2 product revenue, inching toward 25% for the full year (initially guided 20-25%)

The Nova WMC dimensional-metrology platform won a recent TOOL OF RECORD SELECTION BY A LEADING FOUNDRY CUSTOMER (not named on the call) for MULTIPLE LAYERS MEASUREMENT in advanced-packaging production flows. Nova is also seeing accelerating WMC adoption across BOTH memory and foundry customers, 'positioning us to benefit from further investment in advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory manufacturing.' A new configuration of the Nova WMC extends its dimensional metrology capabilities to PANEL-LEVEL PACKAGING.

Memory and others was 27% of Q2 product revenue and Nova projects MEMORY AT ABOUT 30% for full-year 2026, a slight increase on the 70/30 logic-to-memory ratio of 2025, against a long-term model of about 60/40 in favour of logic because process-control intensity in logic is higher. The MAJORITY OF NOVA'S MEMORY EXPOSURE IS DRAM, where demand is strong, while 3D NAND remains 'somehow muted' this year because its growth is driven by UPGRADES rather than capacity expansion - even though metrology intensity between DRAM and NAND is 'more or less similar.' Nova sells to ALL THE TOP PLAYERS IN THE NAND MARKET (positions vary by product line) and expects to benefit once NAND capacity investment returns, which management hopes will be sometime next year. Coming DRAM technology transitions - 4F-squared, 6F-squared, advanced DRAM architectures and eventually 3D DRAM - all increase process complexity and metrology requirements. A new generation of the Nova PRISM platform is targeted at advanced memory structures.
Memory 27% of Q2 product revenue and ~30% expected for 2026 (2025 was 70/30); long-term model 60/40 logic/memory; DRAM strong, 3D NAND muted and upgrade-driven

THE NPO / SCALE-UP THESIS AND THE III-V ROADMAP: SiPho pluggables (800G/1.6T) have 'for the most part ALREADY REPLACED COPPER for scale-out connections outside the rack'; the NEXT FRONTIER IS SCALE-UP, where Tower has SEVERAL NEAR-PACKAGED-OPTICS (NPO) DEPLOYMENTS PLANNED OVER THE NEXT YEAR and many more in design — NPO expected to be 'in the TENS OF PERCENT' of SiPho shipments by H2 2027 (it reuses the pluggable ecosystem, easing hyperscaler reliability/serviceability/multi-source concerns). Content growth comes from HETEROGENEOUS INTEGRATION: III-V-on-silicon INTEGRATED InP LASERS (several tens of $M of revenue expected in 2027; chip-to-wafer bonding moving in-house), die-to-wafer/wafer-to-wafer bonding, and next-gen modulators (400G/lane silicon with Coherent; TFLN and InP in development); multi-year IQE EPI SUPPLY AGREEMENT resolved the InP-substrate crunch. SiGe: 100G/200G-per-lane drivers and TIAs in HVM across all three 200mm fabs (pluggables + LPO/LRO), 400G/lane next with tight EIC-PIC co-design. Adjacent read-through: image-sensor demand SURGING for machine-vision inspection driven by 'the accelerated build-out of DDR and HBM MEMORY ASSEMBLY LINES.'
NPO = tens-of-% of SiPho shipments by H2-2027; integrated InP lasers = tens of $M in 2027; pluggables already displaced copper for scale-out

Memory is described as a significant long-term growth opportunity as AI compute architectures accelerate DRAM and NAND demand and create new thermal processing and material requirements. Veeco is the production tool of record at A TIER 1 HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY MANUFACTURER that is accelerating its investments in 2026. CALL — CXL REVIVAL, TAURUS EXPANSION, CUSTOM SILICON: CXL momentum is back, driven by (1) MEMORY PRICING/SUPPLY dynamics — CXL-attached memory as a cost alternative to expensive local memory/HBM for memory-intensive inference and agentic workloads, (2) GPU-attach with KV-CACHE ACCELERATION improving inference latency, (3) memory-intensive general compute (SAP-class). Closed a NEW standard Leo design win at a U.S. hyperscaler in Q2; in 2027 expects VOLUME shipments of BOTH standard and custom Leo CXL controllers to TWO U.S. HYPERSCALERS. Taurus: 100G/lane smart cable modules in pre-production for 800G AECs; new 3.2T smart retimers/redrivers at 200G/lane (first with 'smart swap') support next-gen Ethernet AND UALink and DOUBLE the Taurus TAM to OVER $4 BILLION by 2030. Custom: NVLINK FUSION-BASED designs for hybrid rack architectures plus custom Leo controllers — initial shipments 2027, 'multi-billion dollar incremental opportunity.' China stays single-digit % of revenue (open protocols: PCIe, Ethernet, increasingly NVLink).
CXL: 2 US hyperscalers in volume 2027 (memory-cost + KV-cache drivers); Taurus TAM doubles to >$4B/2030; NVLink-fusion custom ships 2027

Semiconductor Technologies net sales $744 million, up approximately 3% sequentially and 17% organically year-over-year, driven by demand strength especially for advanced logic and HBM chips; semi gross margin ~49% and adjusted operating EBITDA margin ~34% (right around 35% for the first half, expected to continue).
Semiconductor Technologies $744 million (+17% organic YoY); EBITDA margin ~34%

Advanced nodes portfolio grew more than 20% in Q2 (Investor Day plan was ~7%): continued growth at three nanometer, emerging activity at two nanometer, really strong pull for 2 nm and 18A, and successful scale-up of HBM3/HBM4 on the memory side; advanced nodes were about 40% of the portfolio exiting the first half versus the 45%-50% Investor Day target, which Qnity expects to reach early.
advanced nodes +20% YoY; ~40% of portfolio vs 45%-50% target

utilization: advanced logic mid-80%, mainstream logic low 80%, DRAM high 80%, NAND low 80%

Musk names memory as the binding constraint on AI compute: 'Limiting factor currently is memory. The memory output is increasing by around 20% per year... the demand is increasing by 200% a year, maybe higher. If you have got demand increasing much faster than supply, Economics 101 would suggest that the price increases. It does not decrease.'
memory output +20% per year vs demand +200% per year

For 2026 Ichor expects revenue growth in alignment with the high end of WFE expectations, an increase of at least 30% from full year 2025; the steepening customer demand ramp indicates sequential revenue growth exceeding 10% in each of the next two quarters and second half revenue volumes at least 25% higher than the first half. Demand drivers unchanged: advanced etch and deposition applications supporting AI infrastructure, gate-all-around architectures, advanced memory and leading-edge process technologies.
2026 revenue growth at least 30% vs 2025; H2 at least 25% above H1; >10% sequential growth in each of Q3 and Q4

Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. HBM price cited from ~240 early in the year to 700-900 (as spoken), passed through to customers

CPO remains at the incubation stage - how the cooperation models and mass-production timing shake out is not yet clear - but management views optical as inevitable as bandwidth grows: beyond the two small announced customers there are large customers actively engaging, still too early to disclose. On memory: GUC confirmed it does have HBF (high-bandwidth flash) cooperation underway. For HBM base die, memory makers currently keep the logic die to themselves (Samsung using its own logic process, SK Hynix working with TSMC); GUC sees its opening coming when a memory maker's main product splits into many SKUs, and notes its existing cooperation with SK Hynix on other product lines has been good.

On approaches trying to replace HBM (such as LPDDR-based designs) due to the supply issue: for hyperscalers requiring the absolutely high performance, HBM is still the best, and for the segment MediaTek's AI accelerators aim at, HBM will remain the mainstream memory at least for the near term.

AI data center applications drive the WFE market: sales to AI data center are expected to grow by five times or more in the five years from calendar 2023 through calendar 2027, spanning not only GPU and HBM but also DDR, CPU and 3D NAND. Technology transitions expected within two years: logic scaling from the 3 nanometer mainstream toward 2 nanometer with backside PDN adoption, DRAM evolving to the 1D node (1C to 1D transition), HBM stacked DRAM count rising from 12 to 16, and NAND evolving to 300 layers and further to 400 layers. Agentic AI is the driver of the overall WFE market; CY2026 WFE application mix is about 60% logic and 40% memory, versus 65%/35% last year.
AI data center WFE sales to grow five times or more CY2023-CY2027; HBM stacks from 12 to 16; NAND to 300 then 400 layers; logic mainstream 3 nanometer moving to 2 nanometer

HBM INSPECTION RAMPING ACROSS GENERATIONS: during Q2 Cohu shipped additional FINAL INSPECTION SYSTEMS FOR HBM3, HBM4 AND HBM4E devices to a US-BASED IDM (not named), with a strong forecast into the second half of 2026, and says it continues to invest to stay ahead of customer road maps INTO HBM5 AND BEYOND — calling HBM 'the memory backbone of AI training and inference infrastructure'. Cohu also QUALIFIED ITS NEON PLATFORM AT A TAIWAN-BASED OSAT (not named), establishing a foothold in high-volume outsourced assembly from which it intends to pursue further advanced-package and AI-adjacent inspection opportunities. New capability released in the quarter: a vision inspection sensor with SHORTWAVE INFRARED that detects INNER CRACKS in complex silicon devices — described as a step-change in outgoing quality for advanced packages.
HBM3/HBM4/HBM4E final-inspection shipments to a US IDM; roadmap to HBM5; Neon qualified at a Taiwan OSAT

HBM: continued repeat orders from HBM manufacturers; installed tools at one customer now deployed to HBM4 in high volume manufacturing, plus low volume manufacturing with multiple memory makers for HBM4; entered an exclusive joint evaluation program with a key memory player for HBM5 advanced memory packaging. HBM stack height could relax from the current 775 micron to beyond 900, which would extend TCB use beyond HBM4 into HBM5; hybrid bonding (second-generation tools in sampling) inflection seen around 2029, 2030 or even 2031.
HBM stack height possibly from 775 micron to beyond 900

Record June quarter: revenue $6.72B (+15% QoQ, +30% YoY), non-GAAP EPS $1.82; September-quarter guide $8.1B (+>20% QoQ). DRAM = 23% of systems revenue. DRAM technology drivers: leveraging foundry-logic capabilities into DRAM PITCH SCALING — VECTOR hard-mask and diffusion-barrier tools 'critical for next-generation requirements'; Argos surface-treatment expanding into a growing set of DRAM applications; Equipment Intelligence / Dextro self-maintaining-tool solutions now expanding from NAND INTO DRAM. HBM-relevant: advanced packaging revenue on track for >70% YoY growth (raised from >50%) on TSV etch & electroplating leadership; AI driving 'more advanced DRAM and foundry architectures' and 'larger and more complex advanced packages'.
DRAM 23% of systems; VECTOR critical next-gen DRAM; adv packaging +>70% YoY

CALL — DRAM TO LEAD 2027 WFE: Lam expects DRAM to be the FASTEST-GROWING WFE segment in 2027 (then foundry/logic, then NAND — same order as 2026). June-quarter DRAM dollars were flattish AT THE RECORD March-quarter level (23% of systems revenue; 1-alpha/1-beta/1-gamma wafer additions + upgrades enabling DDR5/LPDDR5/HBM). Technology detail: DRAM customers adopting VECTOR hard mask for low-K film patterning (co-optimized with conductor etch; >20% COST SAVINGS vs traditional approaches) and VECTOR diffusion barriers (~5% CAPACITANCE REDUCTION vs competing tech); AKARA has won strategic tool-of-record positions including 'the most challenging GATE ETCH applications' in advanced DRAM. Thesis: 'as you push DRAM performance ahead, it starts to look A LOT LIKE LEADING-EDGE FOUNDRY LOGIC' — more EUV layers pull Lam's patterning etch, verticalization makes everything '3D-NAND-like.' HBM4/HBM4E raise capital intensity (taller stacks = longer process times + more equipment; unquantified). Down-payment rebound: deferred revenue +$213M QoQ largely on customer down payments.
DRAM = fastest WFE grower in 2027; Vector >20% cost save / ~5% capacitance cut; Akara advanced-DRAM gate-etch TOR wins

Memory market: AI servers keep driving HBM demand and high-end memory packaging demand stays very strong; DRAM and NAND market demand and prices are rising together, with customers maximising output of committed capacity - customer revenue gains are mostly price-driven as supply is limited, but PTI's packaging volumes are still growing and utilisation keeps improving. Packaging material costs keep rising and PTI is passing them through to customers gradually (its customers are large long-term partners, so price adjustments are made carefully each quarter). AI-server eSSD demand keeps rising with shipments expanding QoQ and YoY.

Optical/CPO roadmap: the Broadcom cooperation has brought PTI into optical communications - it will build Optical Engines using its panel fan-out technology, with small-volume production of the first OBO and OSFP versions starting around end-2026; integrating the Optical Engine into a switch (a CPO switch) is targeted to start shipping in H2 2027, and integration of the Optical Engine into AI chips is expected around 2028 or later once designs mature (engineering simulations already completed). Separately, TSV interconnection for DRAM co-developed with a partner has completed DDR-5 trial production and moves to volume production and shipments in Q4 2026 - a foundation for future HBM manufacturing that management expects to start shifting DRAM packaging from 30-year-old wire-bond formats toward advanced packaging, with a meaningful revenue and margin contribution from next year.
Optical Engine small-volume production from end-2026 (OBO, OSFP); CPO switch shipments from H2 2027; AI-chip integration ~2028; TSV-based DDR-5 DRAM volume production from Q4 2026

WFE is expected to grow about 20% in calendar 2026 and a similar level in calendar 2027. Updated CY2026 growth by application: advanced logic foundry over 20%, DRAM over 25% (raised), NAND about 20% (raised from a bit less than 15%), power devices a bit less than 10%. Foundry AI-driven leading edge investment is the primary WFE driver; advanced DRAM and HBM are in shortage and even existing DDR is in shortage, so CapEx is going into both HBM and general DDR, with strong NAND investment also expected as data center demand recovers. Memory device makers are asking for accelerated delivery - demand is now stronger than SCREEN's current capacity. Average equipment lead time is about 4.2 months. Chinese demand for advanced AI-related tools is at record-high inquiry levels.
WFE about 20% growth in calendar 2026 and 2027; DRAM over 25%, NAND about 20%, advanced logic foundry over 20%; lead time 4.2 months; demand stronger than capacity

CALL — TIER-1 HYPERSCALER HBM IP WIN CONFIRMED: 'an exciting DESIGN WIN WITH A TIER-1 U.S. HYPERSCALER FOR NEXT-GENERATION HBM IN FUTURE AI CHIPS' — clarified in Q&A as an IP (LICENSE) win, not a product: the hyperscaler defines the SoC/memory-subsystem architecture with Rambus engaged BEFORE standards are finalized, and the chosen implementation then PROLIFERATES — whoever builds the silicon (in-house or ASIC partners) licenses the IP (multi-license, not volume-based). Management: hyperscalers are playing a growing role defining their own architectures on complex subsystems like memory — a key reason confidence in the 10-15%/yr silicon IP growth 'continues to build.' PCIe 7 SWITCH IP (128 GT/s): license revenue lands 'in the coming quarters,' WELL AHEAD of end products (which ramp 12-24 months later) — early engagement doubles as market intelligence. CXL stance reconfirmed: an interconnect protocol, not a product — product market looks FRAGMENTED/ASIC-like, so Rambus serves it with IP and keeps chip investment in STANDARD products. Patent licensing: 'every company that builds memory has to have a license agreement with us' — including CXMT, whose rise is a long-run licensing positive.
Tier-1 US hyperscaler NEXT-GEN HBM IP design win (license; proliferates with the architecture); PCIe7 license revenue near-term; CXMT licensed

HBM hybrid bonding at a decision point: evaluations ongoing at one of the three memory companies with another starting its evaluation; all three are preparing to adopt hybrid bonding at some point because the device performs significantly better and produces far less heat; H2 2026 will clarify which HBM applications (HBM4E or even HBM3) adopt the technology and at what scale; the JEDEC height relaxation does not change that characteristic

TC Next customer base expanding for sub-20 micron bump pad pitch, fluxless applications; single systems ordered (one customer has several), not yet major volume; also finding its way into development of HBM with smaller geometries; first hybrid bonded device adoption (the M5) into high-end laptops noted last quarter, expected to reach high-end smartphones at some point

HPC rose 20% sequentially to 66% of Q2 revenue, and advanced nodes (7nm and below) were 77% of wafer revenue. Critically for HBM stack assembly, TSMC's advanced PACKAGING capacity is now the binding constraint — CEO C.C. Wei: 'our packaging capacity is so tight that now it's LIMITING MY CUSTOMERS' GROWTH' — with the newly announced additional $100B Arizona investment including advanced packaging fabs and 10-20% of 2026 capex going to advanced packaging, testing and mask making.
Capex raised to $60-64B; HPC 66% of revenue; packaging capacity limiting customer growth

MEMORY-RELATED NET SYSTEM SALES NOW GUIDED TO GROW OVER 75% IN 2026 — memory was 49% of Q2 net system sales (EUR 6.6B total). Driver per CEO Christophe Fouquet: 'the supply challenges driving up both DDR AND HBM PRICES have prompted significant investments in fab expansion', with customers adding meaningful capacity this year AND planning MULTIPLE MEGA FABS that come online in phases over the coming years. Growth is a combination of (1) much higher VOLUME for both HBM and DDR — 'HBM will require more wafer, there's a volume effect' — with some product mix shifting toward DDR on very strong DDR pricing, and (2) rising LITHO INTENSITY as customers migrate to advanced nodes: the 1c node ('going to be enormous') and 1b use more EUV layers, with Low-NA EUV growth driven by replacing multi-patterning with more cost-effective SINGLE-EXPOSE EUV, plus more immersion DUV. Fouquet: 'this combination which create a bit the perfect storm for ASML on DRAM this year and most probably the next few years to come.' Company-wide: Q2 net sales EUR 9.3B above guidance, FY2026 raised to EUR 43-45B; ~65 Low-NA EUV systems shipping in 2026 with 2027 Low-NA EUV nearly sold out and capacity being raised ~30%.
FY26 memory system sales +>75%; memory 49% of Q2 systems; 1c/1b add EUV layers

Segment growth for FY2026 quantified: ADVANCED LOGIC foundry-related net system sales to grow OVER 25%, and MEMORY-related net system sales to grow OVER 75%. DRAM: supply challenges driving up BOTH DDR AND HBM PRICES have prompted significant fab expansion including plans to build MULTIPLE MEGA FABS phasing in over coming years; litho intensity rising as customers migrate to advanced nodes (1b/1c use more EUV layers), with Low-NA EUV growth driven by replacing multi-patterning with more cost-effective SINGLE-EXPOSE EUV. FY26 logic system sales +>25%, memory +>75%; ~65 Low-NA EUV shipped; EUV sales +>45%

Jabil contract-manufactures AI server/GPU PCBs populated with MLCCs and high-density interconnect.
HBM lead times extending; high-density-interconnect PCBs in high demand; DDR4 shortages, DDR5 decent

N3 AI accelerator for the #1 North American customer is READY FOR PRODUCTION - shipments begin JUNE 2026; Alchip secured the required capacity across ALL suppliers (wafer, CoWoS, substrate, COOLING, tester) for on-time delivery. N3 MP ships June 2026; monthly peak from mid-Q3; 2026 upside capped by 6-7mo turnaround

Backlog KRW 573.7B; top customer 42.2% of sales; new orders KRW 489.7B > shipments

NAND +55-60% QoQ; MonTitan cloud-AI ramp; SSD controllers +45% YoY

HAMR MP ~FY2028; nanocomposite bonding material industry-first MP (100 W/mK)

WFE outlook (CEO): customers are quoting $140 billion-$145 billion WFE in 2026, 18%-20% year-over-year growth, and talking about 15% and above for 2027. 2026 WFE $140 billion-$145 billion; 18%-20% growth; 15% and above for 2027

Demand drivers (CEO): hyperscalers and cloud providers are expected to spend around $600 billion in 2026 on data center capacity. AI capacity has been gated by memory capacity for the past three, four quarters; all the major memory customers are now investing in greenfield factories and upgrading existing fabs, which unlocks constrained capacity, and new leading-edge factory launches are seen at all three leading customers, TSMC, Intel and Samsung. Memory: Aehr achieved the correlation a key memory supplier asked for and is discussing system specs for its next-generation flash and high bandwidth flash; it hopes to close in the next few months on a development agreement, followed by a 12- to 18-month development of memory-optimized blades for FOX-XP/NP. 12- to 18-month development; orders possible in fiscal '27, ramps in fiscal '28

Entegris is gaining traction in DRAM and HBM, particularly with CMP consumables and advanced packaging solutions. The CEO said advanced packaging revenue grew nicely in 2025, to 'roughly a $100 million plus minus', and should keep growing in 2026. advanced packaging revenue roughly $100 million (2025), expected to keep growing in 2026

AI / HBM / ADVANCED PACKAGING framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the company says the surge in AI semiconductor demand has raised the importance of HBM and advanced-packaging processes, pushing up the technical barrier for high-purity chemicals and precision polishing materials; the global semiconductor market is growing at an unprecedented pace on AI data-center memory and on-device AI, and the introduction of sub-2nm GAA processes and volume production of 300+ layer V-NAND are driving continued demand for high-performance etchants and next-generation precursors. Seasonality has flattened because AI and cloud enterprise demand now leads, producing a longer up-cycle. Product positioning: special etchants for sub-2nm GAA, next-generation CMP slurry and precursors for HBM4 stacking; ultra-high-purity chemicals supplied at near-exclusive levels to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix from the leading-edge ramp and ultra-high-layer V-NAND development stage; a completed portfolio of TSV formation and planarisation materials for HBM4 and chiplet structures to lift high-value-added revenue; display unit expanding into glass-substrate processing materials for next-generation packaging; customers' processes moving to GAA and to HBM / 400+ layer NAND, with joint development from the process-design stage. US entities Soulbrain TX LLC (2022) and Soulbrain RASA TX LLC (2024) respond in real time to customers' new fab lines in Texas and North America; the Xi'an entity supports China memory lines. Semiconductor material ASPs +5% vs FY2025 while raw-material costs rose +14%; semiconductor materials 85% of H1 revenue, +31% company-wide revenue growth.
