Q1 OP KRW 51.3B EXCEEDED all of FY2025 (49.1B); export ASP +29% on high-end mix; substrate capex extended to 2027 + new building expansion disclosed 05-11-2026

Advanced-packaging growth outlook RAISED to ~80% CY2026 (from ~50% a quarter earlier); inspection (Dragonfly) +30% QoQ on 2.5D + HBM; >$200M of Dragonfly orders from a SINGLE OSAT partner, majority delivering 2027; record backlog >$1.1B (~30-40% covers 2027); panel-level packaging revenue to MORE THAN DOUBLE YoY (JetStep for 500x500+ panels, Firefly now carrying Dragonfly G5 optics, plus TSMC CoWoS 310x310); not capacity constrained (~$2B in-house + an equal amount from Asian extended factories)

tables.title: Latest graph signals (auto-derived)
rows: SHARE INSIDE BUMP-PACKAGING INSPECTION, AND HYBRID BONDING AS THE NEXT STEP: Ahmad Khan (President of Semiconductor Products and Customers) says KLA entered advanced packaging about five, six years ago with 10% share and is 'Now we are above 50%, 56%, 57% share in advanced packaging', driven by capability requirements; he notes this is still bump packaging. Hybrid bonding / die-to-wafer bonding in logic (SOIC) brings 'a 10x change in specifications of defects that kill the die', pulling KLA's most advanced front-end systems into packaging, and the introduction of hybrid bonding in memory will tighten specs significantly as well. Economics: a logic wafer out of the front-end fab is worth '$30,000, $40,000, $50,000' and a memory wafer '$50,000, $60,000, $70,000', so a loss in packaging also loses that wafer's value and customers 'want to inspect every step'.
10% share about five, six years ago to 56%, 57% share; hybrid bonding a 10x change in specifications of defects that kill the die

Component-level breakdown of the upstream bottleneck: 'Packaging is a challenge. DRAM is a challenge. LPDDR DRAM is a challenge. Connectors are challenging. Everything is challenging. Voltage regulators are challenging. Everything is challenging. Wafers are obviously challenging.' Huang framed downstream (land, power, shell) as NVIDIA's advantage because 'we are tracking every single gigawatt of land, power, shell around the world', with neoclouds, OEMs, clouds and AI natives all reporting capacity back to NVIDIA.

CEO Gary Dickerson walked through how the 2026 revenue forecast has been raised through the year: in February Applied said greater than 20% revenue growth, in May greater than 30% revenue growth, and now it is approaching 40% revenue growth. 80% of wafer fab equipment growth this year is leading foundry logic, DRAM including High-Bandwidth Memory and advanced packaging, and management sees that same mix in 2027 and going forward.
approaching 40% revenue growth (from greater than 20% revenue growth in February and greater than 30% revenue growth in May); 80% of wafer fab equipment growth

Capital allocation: Applied will return 80%-100% of cash to shareholders. Management said large M&A is not possible in the current geopolitical environment, so the company is doing smaller deals - the panel plating acquisition and an X-ray technology company - plus strategic investments, including hybrid bonding, where Applied is combining a partner technology with five technologies from Applied Materials on an Applied Materials platform.
80%-100% of cash returned to shareholders; hybrid bonding combines a partner technology with five technologies from Applied Materials

First size disclosure for the advanced packaging business alongside the raised growth rate: packaging is forecast to grow over 70% this year with a midpoint between $2 billion and $3 billion in terms of the size of the business for Applied Materials. High-Bandwidth Memory and 3DIC are the fastest-growing segments this year. Applied's inspection and measurement business, both eBeam and optical, is growing over 50% this calendar year, and management is highly confident that in the next three to five years there will be incredible inflections in how computing components are connected.
advanced packaging over 70% this year, midpoint between $2 billion and $3 billion; inspection/measurement over 50% this calendar year

CUSTOM ASICs CROSS INTO ADVANCED MEMS IN 2027-2028 — THE NEXT TECHNOLOGY PIVOT. Slessor named the category directly: 'custom ASICs, things like Google's TPU, AWS's Trainium'. Their power envelope, both consumed and produced, is driving them out of legacy wire-based needle probe technology: 'We see custom ASICs really crossing this brink in 2027 and into 2028 of needing an advanced MEMS probe technology... much the same way GPUs did a few generations ago.' It will be mixed rather than wholesale — chiplet architectures mean some chiplets stay on legacy wire probes while the advanced compute chiplets require MEMS. FormFactor builds every probe with proprietary MEMS metallurgy and patterning, vertically integrated in Livermore, California and the ramping Farmers Branch, Texas site, enabling higher current, higher speed and higher/lower temperature test. Engagement is with 'all the names you'd expect us to be engaged with and their foundry and OSAT partners'; initial revenue has been booked on some projects, with designs and qualifications won in late 2026 and ramp in 2027. These may not appear as 10% customers because FormFactor is 'essentially operating at a billion-dollar annual run rate now', raising the 10%-customer bar.
custom ASICs crossing to advanced MEMS probe in 2027 and into 2028; FormFactor at a billion-dollar annual run rate

HOW LAM GETS PAID ON THE PANEL TRANSITION: the growth rate itself was already on the Q4 FY2026 call - Bettinger repeated that 'Our advanced packaging business is growing north of 70% this year', with foundry and logic the big contributor. NEW is the panel readiness argument: he said the industry has not moved to the panel form factor yet but will, that it will show up in foundry and logic, and that Lam needs nothing inorganic for it because the wafer-level TSV skill set (silicon etching plus copper electroplating) carries straight over - 'we're going to be extraordinarily strong there' - helped by a company Lam acquired in Austria a few years ago that already had panel form-factor capability and 'accelerated our R&D progress there'.
no specific figure (advanced packaging growth north of 70% this year was already disclosed on the Q4 FY2026 call)
Lam Research Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Supply: over the past year the supply chain has been able to flex up 50%, taking the two-year revenue plan from $20 billion to $30 billion. Marvell reaches production more than 90%-plus of the time on first-pass silicon on advanced nodes. TSMC remains the sole-source fab vendor, with long-term deals also struck on substrate and back-end capacity plus capex and prepays. Murphy spent a week in Asia with existing and new suppliers ahead of the October 6 Investor Day; conditions are very acute right now in some areas, and he warned that some substrate capacity cannot be obtained until the end of the decade by anyone who did not start five years ago.
supply chain flexed up 50%; two-year plan from $20 billion to $30 billion; 90%-plus first-pass silicon success on advanced node

Management explained what sits behind the >$200 million single-OSAT Dragonfly order: with the industry constrained on heterogeneous integration, end customers are looking at alternative packaging technologies (EMIB among them), and separately 'TSMC is well-publicized. TSMC is looking at how to release more capacity' given fab constraints - taking its lower-end process steps and outsourcing those to the OSATs to free precious fab capacity for the higher end. Plisinski said that dynamic was in play in the order, and that OSAT capital intensity is really volume-driven, with the volume expected to come both from that outsourced capacity and from the OSATs' own technology that they will be selling. On share at the OSATs versus the foundries, Onto has very high share on the 2D side at the higher-end applications and has gained nice traction on 3D bump metrology at at least a couple of the OSATs; share is lower in low-end or China work.
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Growth split disclosed: this year the biggest growth was in packaging at 80% growth while advanced nodes was about 35% growth, and for next year management expects not those numbers but similar dynamics, with advanced packaging still probably growing stronger than advanced nodes and both growing fairly well. Within advanced packaging the memory (HBM) versus 2.5D logic mix is fairly well split, generally around the 50/50 mark or 60/40 depending on the quarter, because logic requires the memory around it so the whole packaging requirement grows across both. On share, Onto has always had very high share in memory and maintained it, with incremental gains tied to 3D bump metrology as bumps get smaller and denser (3DI); in logic packaging there is room to gain share because of the very high resolution the Dragonfly G5 provides.
packaging 80% growth vs advanced nodes about 35% growth; advanced packaging memory/logic mix around 50/50 to 60/40
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

First sizing of the panel-level packaging opportunity: Plisinski said Onto has publicly put the market at around a $1 billion SAM (competitors have said even more), covering process control - inspection as well as lithography - and that while Onto will not get 100% of it against competitors, '$200 million, $300 million' would be a reasonable expectation over the next few years. The accelerant is that constraints in AI packaging and heterogeneous integration are pushing customers to panel as an alternative: as die and therefore packages get bigger the economies of scale at the wafer level stop working - at 310 by 310 they get better, but that is still much smaller than 600 by 600 or 510 by 515 - so customers are moving capacity to companies with a proven process that can ramp right now. Adoption is still early and management expects it to continue over the next several years. The enterprise-server driver (advanced IC substrates, where Intel and AMD were constrained during COVID) is also working its way back, addressed by the JetStep X500 and Firefly.
around a $1 billion SAM; Onto share expectation $200 million, $300 million over the next few years
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Timing moving from discrete components into the package, quantified and dated for the first time. Vashist on chiplets, substrates and modules: 'that can be rather large. We think it could be anything from a billion to 1.5 billion more of SAM. The reason for all of this, of course, is because timing needs to get closer, timing needs to get more clean, the signal needs to be less attenuated, and just like in power, you have VPD, vertical delivery, we think there's a concept called VTD, which is getting closer and closer to the chip, either below, embedded in the substrate or above. I think that this could start as early as 2028, maybe 2029.' He called it 'mostly incremental' rather than cannibalistic because it lands at the very high end.
a billion to 1.5 billion more of SAM; could start as early as 2028, maybe 2029
SiTime Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

THE SHAPE OF THE DATA-CENTER CUSTOMER BASE (CEO Edwin Roks): TTM will not name customers - 'we cannot disclose our customers. We have very strict NDAs with them. But these are the big guys. These are the big guys you read in the newspaper every day, correct? 10, 15 of these big customers, and then a tail of another 50. Which is helping us to understand the landscape, to understand what are the trends.' On hyperscaler roadmap alignment: 'the first thing what we do is align with our customers, and these are the multiple hyperscalers. We also like to show, let's say, demonstrators. I hate to go with only PowerPoints to our customers... So alignment with these hyperscalers, by the way, with all our customers, is going very well.' Management also framed N+M as the start of a technology curve rather than a one-off: 'where you do N+M, which is a new technology, only the first generation of that new technology trend, is working out very well. We're ramping up.'
10, 15 of these big customers, and then a tail of another 50
TTM Technologies Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

DATA CENTER AND NETWORKING IS SET TO OUTGROW DEFENSE INTO THE MIX (CEO): asked about the long-term split of the ~80% of the business tied to AI and aerospace/defense, which is roughly even today, 'If you look at how fast data centers and networking is growing right now, it will likely get aerospace and defense to a 30% portion. Now it's 40%. But who cares, because the business is growing nicely in double digits, and it is very sustainable.' The strategic direction is away from a pure PCB identity: 'we are indeed coming from a traditional PCB company, but we have to find another word for PCB... We're moving into, let's say, a more, I would say, communication and sensing company' - built on heterogeneous, very compact packaging and then modules, subsystems and systems, plus geographic expansion into Europe where management expects to do more acquisitions. The CEO's framing of the AI role: with Moore's law slowing, 'What we provide is, let's say, combining these chips. That's why we like to call ourselves the nervous system... combining these chips in a very efficient way with low latency and high bandwidth.'
data center and networking growth likely takes aerospace and defense to a 30% portion from 40% today
TTM Technologies Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

COPPER AND GLASS ARE THE TWO WATCHED INPUTS - NO ISSUES YET (CEO): asked about supply-chain constraints that could temper delivery, 'We are focused every day, every hour on the supply chain... this is almost a full-time job of our COO. We follow, let's say, what's happening with copper. We follow what's happening with glass and making sure that we don't get tied here. So far so good. We are very transparent to our customers also.' The mitigations named were multiple qualified suppliers and TTM's position at the top of the technology stack: 'The good thing is that these suppliers also focus more on the high-end, and that's exactly where we play. We don't see issues right now, but absolutely it's our focus every day.'
TTM Technologies Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

CAPACITY IS ADDED IN SMALL BROWNFIELD STEPS AND IS NOT EXPECTED TO CONSTRAIN GROWTH (CEO and Cathy Gridley, President of Aerospace and Defense): 'we do it in a more, I would say, in a disciplined way. When we see growth... we do a $50 million investment here and $100 million there. You don't see us a lot in, although we did it... with Syracuse, and we have examples with Penang in Malaysia, where we did greenfield, but we love brownfield. We love, let's say, a building which is next door, which we can use... and now we put all these drill stations... We can follow the demand cycle very carefully.' On the defense side: 'in North America, in the U.S., we have 16 facilities that are dedicated or largely dedicated to defense... We have to add pieces of equipment to expand the capacity within that footprint, but it's a measured approach. Capacity is not going to be a constraint for us.' The Syracuse Ultra-HDI plant was a true greenfield next to the 2018 Anaren facility and went 'from greenfield and within 23 months, I handed the keys over to operations so that they could go into production'; UHDI itself 'is not a new technology. It's been built in Asia for quite a long time... What is new is the application of that capability in defense and defense systems, and that has to be done here in the U.S.'
a $50 million investment here and $100 million there; 16 facilities dedicated or largely dedicated to defense; Syracuse greenfield to production within 23 months
TTM Technologies Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

SUPPLY BREADTH AND THE COST PASS-THROUGH RULE. Jean Hu listed the tight points by name: 'not only wafers, advanced process node, HBM tight packaging, substrate. Some of the components are very tight.' For Helios it is not just GPU, CPU and HBM — 'there are also a lot of other small component that we need to ensure we have'. On capex: 'The primary increase for CapEx is to build the capacity to support the recipe ramp, especially Venice... capacity is not enough. We need to build ourselves to buy the equipment, do the consignment to support the ramp' — i.e. AMD is buying the equipment itself and placing it on consignment to support the ramp. On pricing, a rule not given on the Q2 call: 'if there's a component cost increase, we do need to make sure we share that cost increase with the customers... If wafer price increase, you should expect us to increase the CPU price, too', while stressing AMD will not raise price purely to expand gross margin. CPU growth is coming from both units and ASP, with 'unit increase probably is more than ASP increase'.

→ TSMC: Asked whether AMD would consider Intel as a foundry partner, CFO Jean Hu said AMD co-develops much of its technology with TSMC, is diversifying geographically with TSMC (a fab in Arizona), and 'you should expect us to continue to view TSMC as our primary supplier on the wafer side.' Matt Ramsay added that for 'anything that’s advanced packaging or anything that’s advanced wafers, we’re going to evaluate and due diligence on technology from every vendor in the market', while the TSMC partnership stays significant for the foreseeable future.

CEO Hock Tan disclosed the multi-die XPU roadmap in explicit terms - the clearest statement yet of how Broadcom is 'substituting Moore's law with something else'. He said Moore's law has ended ('Moving down process node, you cannot achieve double transistor performance anymore. You barely eke out 5% improvement, but you get power'), that physics caps a single die at '800 square millimeters' ('That's the largest size die you can make'), and that Broadcom now puts '2 die together in one chip. So effectively, you now have 1,600 square millimeters, double.' Critically: 'The current generation we are working on has 4 dies. You can just imagine. The one after that probably will go to maybe no limit, 8 die. 8 die in one chip. So your chip size is equivalent of, say, 800 times 8, over 6,000 square millimeter running as one single chip.' He stressed this enabling technology 'is not just created at a wafer fab or with the memory guys. It is us designing it', and listed the moats as high-speed SerDes/IO IP, multiplier density per square millimeter, die-to-die communication at low power, and advanced packaging.

largest size die you can make 800 square millimeters; 2 die = 1,600 square millimeters; current generation has 4 dies; next probably 8 die in one chip = over 6,000 square millimeter; process node shrink now yields barely 5% improvement

Tan unpacked what 'supply constrained' means behind the 2027 and 2028 AI revenue forecast, and it is not silicon. On chips: 'We understand the need for wafers, leading-edge wafers, and memory, as well as even substrates. That is pretty well locked in. We can pretty well lock that in for sure in 2027, and the process of locking in 2028 gives us within some limits. That is more within our control.' The less deterministic constraint is a site that is power READY, not merely power available: 'If you want to make it power ready, say, in 2028, got to start construction on the sites now. That is not us, our customers, has to start construction on the site now to make it available and ready by 2028' - a year and a half to two years out, gated by transformers, gas turbines, local permitting and the rate of construction. 'It's a judged number based on not just supply of memory wafers, but availability and readiness of power sites.'
wafers, memory and substrates locked in for 2027, being locked for 2028

President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel disclosed the next Silicon One scale-out chip: the G300, which has close to a quarter trillion transistors on 100-millimeter package substrate. Cisco operates in both scale-out systems (the G300) and scale-across systems (the P-Series chips), and sells hyperscalers full systems rather than chips alone. He framed scale-across as the answer to power limits - data centers are starting to get to be hundreds of kilometers apart but need to operate like one logical unit, which requires different chip design including debuffering so packet loss does not force a training run to restart.
Silicon One G300: close to a quarter trillion transistors on 100-millimeter package substrate
Cisco Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-08-2026)

HYBRID BONDING IS THE PACKAGING SHARE PRIZE - TIMING GIVEN: Kizner said the main advanced-packaging share-gain opportunity ahead is hybrid bonding, which brings front-end capability into the back end: copper-to-copper bonding requires wafer-to-wafer and die warpage control, CMP uniformity and flatness control, all of which raise metrology intensity and pull in both Nova's dimensional and materials metrology portfolios. The work right now is QUALIFICATIONS - high-volume manufacturing 'capacity is not big story in 2027', it comes later. He added that Nova's materials metrology is not yet exposed to advanced packaging at all and that early customer discussions to apply it there are another growth engine on top of the ancosys and Sentronics acquisitions and the PRISM front-end tools already deployed into packaging.
the capacity is not big story in 2027

Dell's constraint list runs the length of the semiconductor chain: 'just about every product going through a leading node is constrained', mature nodes building MOSFETs, power ICs, microcontrollers and drivers are constrained, and there are shortages of ABF substrate, T-glass and optical components. Jeff Clarke adds that the AI supply chain is 'working red line all out' to build CDUs and power racks.

Mix: Q2 product mix was server 78%, networking 15%, notebook 5%, other 2% - server share has climbed from about half in 2020 to 64% in 2023 (when AI demand started) to 78% now, while notebook shrank from about 20% to 5%. AI server boards were roughly four to five tenths of Q2 revenue (management: approaching but not yet half). Over nine tenths of revenue comes from US end customers, served from five production sites: Taiwan, Suzhou, two Changshu plants, and Thailand. Products span high-layer-count boards, thick-copper boards, backplanes and HDI (including HDI server boards and AI PC).
Q2 mix: server 78%, networking 15%, notebook 5%; AI server roughly four to five tenths of Q2 revenue; server share 64% in 2023 vs 78% now

Outlook: Q3 is the seasonal peak - server demand should keep improving with AI server growth more pronounced, networking should also beat Q2, notebook seen flat. 2026 capex announced so far is about NT$190 hundred million, with further additions expected to be announced in H2 and capex to keep increasing next year.
Q3 AI server and networking to grow QoQ; 2026 capex announced so far ~NT$190 hundred million, more to come

ACM Shanghai's August 14, 2026 investor-relations record (Exhibit 99.1) gives delivery timing for its 2026 horizontal panel-level electroplating orders: the first 510 × 515 mm volume-production system (existing advanced packaging customer in mainland China) is planned for delivery in the first quarter of 2027, and the 310 × 310 mm evaluation system (leading panel packaging customer in Asia) by the end of 2026. The technology supports 310 × 310 mm, 510 × 515 mm and 600 × 600 mm panels.
510 × 515 mm volume-production system: delivery Q1 2027; 310 × 310 mm evaluation system: delivery by end of 2026; 600 × 600 mm panels also supported

THE CAPITAL RAISE IS A SUBSTRATE-AND-FAB SPENDING EVENT: Zinsner explained the August equity raise as 'the capital raise precedes capital investment' - 2026 CapEx has already been upticked 'by a couple of billion dollars from $18 billion to $20 billion', next year's will be significantly higher, and 'substrates are really constrained and we're going to need to make investments associated with substrates as well next year, given the significant demand.' Committing to 14A high-volume manufacturing in 2028 means placing long-lead supplier orders now, which was one of the biggest drivers of the raise. On footprint: Ireland's shell is being equipped now; Fab 52 in Arizona is running Intel 18A and Fab 62 is almost ready, with next year's investment accelerating its equipping; Oregon stays the pilot line but will also run volume Intel 14A as 18A is pushed into Arizona; Ohio shells are in progress with the ability to have 'eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio', mod one being built as fast as possible. Zinsner said 2027 CapEx is not locked - the businesses gave him a number and 'I've told them no', sending them back for more efficiency before he guides.
from $18 billion to $20 billion; eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio

EMIB-T ADVANCED PACKAGING SIZED FOR THE FIRST TIME - REVENUE FROM 2H 2027, MULTIPLE BILLIONS PER CUSTOMER: Zinsner said EMIB-T, which removes the interposer from EMIB and can increase reticle size significantly, is a differentiated solution not available elsewhere, and that packaging revenue will 'start to ramp in the back half of 2027', become a run-rate business in 2028 and be 'definitely hitting its stride in 2029'. Scale: 'this business is in the billions... by customer, it will be multiple billion dollars per customer per year of business', at margins of '40% gross, 30% operating margin' with low capital intensity relative to the front end, so 'the ROIC is phenomenal'. He framed advanced packaging as the on-ramp that tests Intel operationally and creates cross-sell into front-end foundry, something Intel has 'already seen that show up even now'. He also pointed to the hire of Seokhee, former CEO of SK hynix, to lead the business as the signal of the opportunity size.
back half of 2027; multiple billion dollars per customer per year; 40% gross, 30% operating margin

INTEL 3 OFFERED AS A BASE-DIE PROCESS FOR OTHER COMPANIES: Asked whether the Ireland Intel 3/4 nodes are internal-only, CFO David Zinsner said 'Intel 3 would not be a great logic process for external, but we use it for base die, and it can be used for base die for other companies. And the fact that we have advanced packaging and all these things kind of all under one roof, there could potentially be some opportunities there.'

EDA / MULTI-DIE: AMD's newly launched Instinct MI455X GPU was delivered using Synopsys 3DIC COMPILER, described as the industry's only exploration-to-sign-off platform for multi-die and advanced-package co-design. Management said the 2024 forecast that ~30% of EDA software demand would come from MULTI-DIE has ACCELERATED, driven by advanced packaging and 3DIC architectures. MULTIPHYSICS FUSION LAUNCHED in Q3 — the first joint Synopsys+Ansys product and the industry's only solution with thermal analysis fully integrated into the chip design flow; NVIDIA, Cisco, MediaTek and Samsung Foundry have validated up to 10x FASTER DESIGN CLOSURE and 3x faster runtime (3x faster SPICE-accurate multiphysics timing). Revenue contribution expected to begin in FY2027, not FY2026; $400M synergy commitment in year four reaffirmed. Hardware-assisted verification: 12 NEW + 66 REPEAT customer wins in the quarter and a record hardware revenue year.
MI455X on 3DIC Compiler; Multiphysics Fusion 10x design closure / 3x runtime; HAV 12 new + 66 repeat wins

CAPACITY, BACKLOG & PRICING: RECORD BACKLOG — the remainder of FY2027 is 'all booked' and OVER 70% OF FY2028 is already booked. CEO warns the capacity secured MAY NOT BE ENOUGH to support FY2028, ESPECIALLY H2 FY2028, and says there is room in the industry to secure ANOTHER 50-100% of capacity. Actions: acquired an ALREADY FULLY-FACILITIZED FAB in close proximity to the existing photonics site, raising fab capacity 3-4x BY END OF FY2027 (on track); adding BACK-END TESTERS and qualifying ADDITIONAL OSAT partners (test, packaging, die-separation) partly to MITIGATE GEOPOLITICAL RISK; front-end capacity being expanded with a leading partner via PREPAYMENT / CapEx / other means. CapEx was 2% of net sales in Q2 (fab capacity for gain chips and CW lasers) and is expected to grow but stay GENERALLY BELOW 5% of sales. PRICING: 'availability is more important to the customers than the pricing' — NO price erosion expected in the near term and none on orders already in backlog; CFO confirms NO price erosion at 800G. Input costs rising slightly and being PASSED THROUGH to customers.
>70% of FY2028 booked; fab capacity 3-4x by end FY2027; room for +50-100% capacity; no price erosion

Electronic Industrial Solutions Group delivered a record quarter, and SEMICONDUCTOR was itself a record, driven by ongoing CAPACITY EXPANSION FOR ADVANCED NODES, HIGH-BANDWIDTH MEMORY AND SILICON PHOTONICS. Semiconductor wafer test is seeing significant capacity expansion across all three of those dimensions, and forecasts for wafer fab equipment and capital going into those markets 'continues to expand'. Given increasing adoption of optical interconnects, COMMERCIAL PRODUCTION OF SILICON PHOTONICS IS ACCELERATING ACROSS LEADING FOUNDRIES AND IDMs. Semiconductor R&D solution demand was also healthy, and engagement with industry leaders gives good visibility into next year's requirements. In general electronics, test intensity keeps rising for high-performance components - MULTILAYER PCBs AND CAPACITORS for next-generation compute - as higher frequencies, tighter tolerances and greater GPU/CPU density raise production complexity and quality requirements, pushing test from the board level down to the COMPONENT level. Automotive and energy orders grew solid double digits on software-defined vehicle architectures, in-vehicle network and cybersecurity test, and grid/high-power-charging validation.
EISG record $501M (+21%); semi record on advanced nodes + HBM + SiPh wafer test

Catalysts / pipeline (half-year report): (1) Financing - 4th-series KRW 130,000M zero-coupon private convertible bond issued 2026-04-29 (board resolution 2026-04-21; arranged by Korea Investment & Securities and NH Investment & Securities), conversion price KRW 54,603 = 2,380,821 shares (17.7% of the 13,462,007 shares outstanding), conversion window 2027-04-29 to 2031-03-29, maturity 2031-04-29, investor put from 2028-10-29, issuer call 2027-04-29 to 2028-10-29; KRW 20,768M used for working capital by 2026-06-30, KRW 109,232M parked in deposits/MMT/wrap. Cash KRW 70,529M plus short-term instruments KRW 60,808M; debt ratio 133.3%. (2) R&D - H1 R&D spend KRW 20,875M (32.09% of separate revenue) versus KRW 10,807M for all of FY2025, with KRW 14,559M capitalised as development costs; consolidated R&D outlay KRW 22,438M. Named programmes: Samsung 2nm Arm Neoverse V3 ADP620 HPC platform with DDR5 RDIMM, 16-lane PCIe Gen6, CXL 3.0, UCIe chiplet-to-chiplet interface and BMC/UEFI secure boot, running 2024-11 to 2028-07 with silicon bring-up targeted at first-pass success; Arm Neoverse N2 ADP-600 HPC platform (CMN mesh, USB/PCIe/Ethernet/DDR, 2025-01 to 2026-12); 2nm and 4nm Foundation-IP (standard-cell library + SRAM compiler) and HPC design kits as a Samsung Foundry Foundation-IP service partner (to 2026-12); 2.5D chiplet design methodology combining HBM3e PHY/controller and a 2nm big die in one package with 14.4Tbps-class 112G PAM4 SerDes, silicon-interposer stitch-line avoidance and integrated silicon capacitors for PDN (2023-03 to 2026-12). (3) Corporate - Arm Total Design partner since 2023-10, Synopsys IP OEM partnership since 2023-07; charter amended 2026-03-30 to raise CB/BW issuance flexibility and adopt electronic AGMs; RSUs (224,700 shares) granted 2026-02-24; credit rating BB+ reaffirmed by NICE D&B on 2026-05-14; seven patents filed since 2025-09 (radiation-hardened flip-flop, dynamic-latch standard cells, multi-bit flip-flop, library verification). R&D KRW 84,267M (22.09% of sales); 3D NAND selective-removal and panel-level RDL PVD in development; EGM 2026-09-04 (treasury-share plan, new director); credit A+ 2026-05-04

→ Daeduck Electronics: Daeduck's H1 2026 half-year report (filed 08-13-2026) lists Ajinomoto Fine-Techno Co., Inc. as the main supplier of ABF - purchases KRW 12,496M, 7.85% of raw-material purchases (total KRW 159,224M). ABF unit price KRW 34,591 per m2 in H1 2026 vs KRW 36,611 in FY2025.
units: H1 2026, ABF build-up film, per m2 pricing; value: KRW 12,496M (7.85% of raw materials)

Supply and manufacturing: 'TSMC has once again come through, and we have the wafers needed to fuel our growth' - wafer supply positioned 'not just for the remainder of this year, but for the next year as well' (CFO); 5 nm node where 'wafers are less expensive and supply is less constrained'; 'we don't use HBM memory, CoWoS packaging, or require 3 nm fab capacity'. Manufacturing capacity is 'already 4 times above where we were in the first half of 2025' and will increase 'more than 10x in 2026', with new factories being built with Flex and Sanmina; 'We already have contracted facilities three or four times more for growth in 2027'.
manufacturing capacity 4 times above 1H 2025; more than 10x increase in 2026

New-generation AI rack (Vera Rubin) on plan: volume production from Q3 (production preparation in Q3) with shipments starting in Q4, ramping over subsequent quarters to become the main product next year. Foxconn is still working toward roughly half of the new-platform market and argues product standardization raises rather than lowers entry barriers, favoring suppliers with scale delivery and vertical integration - its new-generation Compute Tray line reached 100% automation. Next year's overall rack volume hinges on how much CoWoS capacity the chip customers secure; the market expects CoWoS capacity to grow more than 50% next year, with final rack output depending on chip supply. GB-platform demand remains stable and GB-series demand should last at least into next year.
Rubin racks: volume production from Q3, shipments from Q4, main product next year; new-platform share target about half; market expects CoWoS capacity +50% next year; Compute Tray automation 100%

Raw-material purchases and named suppliers H1 2026 (DART half-year report): package substrate (PCB) purchases of KRW 85,750M were 90.3% of raw-material spend, bought from Simmtech, Daeduck Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Fast Print and Daisho Denshi; gold wire KRW 7,333M (7.7%) from LT Metal and MK Electron; solder ball KRW 1,030M (1.1%) from MK Electron and Duksan Hi-Metal; EMC moulding compound KRW 895M (0.9%) from Samsung SDI, Hitachi, Nepes and KCC. The average PCB input price rose to KRW 822 from KRW 447 in FY2025 on a richer high-end substrate mix and a weaker won, and gold wire rose to KRW 272 from KRW 206 on the LME gold price - substrate and gold are the cost items inflating this OSAT's bill of materials.
PCB substrate purchases KRW 85,750M = 90.3% of raw-material spend, unit price KRW 822 vs KRW 447; gold wire KRW 7,333M (7.7%), unit price KRW 272 vs KRW 206; solder ball KRW 1,030M; EMC KRW 895M

R&D and product pipeline (DART half-year report): H1 R&D spend KRW 1,519M, 0.65% of revenue. Completed developments include fine-pitch Cu pillar bump packages, ELK (extreme low-k) flip-chip mass-production infrastructure with several new product wins, flip-chip flux jetting and SDTT wafer dicing. The forward programme targets large-body FCBGA (85 x 85), high-density large-area FCBGA no-pressure low-warpage bonding (national consortium project), laser-assist bonding, land-side capacitor attach, large-die thermal-compression flip-chip attach, fine-pitch Cu pillar and thick-RDL WLCSP, GaN and SiC wafer bumping, high-voltage power fine-pitch flip-chip bumping (national consortium project) and a glass-composite large-area multilayer wiring package (national consortium project). Bumping, added as a new business in 2014, is described as the company's growth engine alongside a push from memory into system LSI.
R&D KRW 1,519M (0.65% of sales); pipeline: large-body FCBGA 85 x 85, glass-composite multilayer package, laser-assist bonding, GaN/SiC wafer bumping, thick-RDL WLCSP

1.6T optical-module PCB: current orders are mainly 1.6T high-speed optical-module boards; 2026 optical-module related revenue is guided to double, 1.6T keeps growing sharply in 2027 and becomes the main shipping spec in 2028, and 3.2T boards are already being sampled. Customers are already pre-booking 2027 capacity; target is to become the world's largest high-end optical-module PCB supplier in 2027. 800G-and-above optical-module boards require M7-class ultra-low-loss laminate (1.6T effectively mandates it); management says roughly 20 players claim to be entering optical modules but few master M7 high-layer board production, which is why Zhen Ding's substrate-derived M7 technology gave it the 1.6T breakout. 1.6T optical-module board yield is described as industry-leading at above 90%, including the newly ramped Thailand lines. On a potential US FCC ban on Chinese optical modules: Zhen Ding supplies the PCB inside the module, not the module itself, so sees no direct hit, and can shift production to Thailand where customers require it. On CPO: the company says it will participate in both pluggable and CPO/NPO architectures as they develop; most PCB equipment is transferable between product types so a CPO shift would strand little capacity.
2026 optical-module revenue to double; 1.6T main spec by 2028; 3.2T sampling; 1.6T board yield above 90%; goal: largest high-end optical-module PCB supplier in 2027

Materials supply: T-glass is currently in shortage; Zhen Ding says it keeps long-term strategic partnerships with upstream material makers, has signed strategic-cooperation / supply-guarantee agreements with suppliers, and is qualifying second sources to diversify. Whether next-generation glass-core substrates relieve the glass supply-demand balance is 'not yet knowable' given long certification. CCL price increases are being passed through to customers smoothly with small impact on gross margin; across AI and non-AI products management says most raw-material increases can be passed on.

Capacity and outlook: 2026 capex is around NT$800 hundred million, with similarly high investment maintained for 2027-2028; 13 plants are under construction and 16 more planned. Capex split roughly: 25% to 30% optical-module boards, 35% to 40% IC substrate (substrate is the most capital-intensive - a dollar of high-end substrate investment yields only about half a dollar of output, versus six to seven tenths for server/optical boards). Thailand: PA01 reached breakeven and turned profitable in July 2026 (mass production began Q3 2025); additional Thai buildings and a data/computing center complete around end-2026; Thai plants 1-2 make server and optical-module boards, plant 3 flex, plant 4 high-layer-count server boards. Huai'an HD campus broke ground 04-22-2026, three buildings already topped out, production starts March 2027 with fast ramp since qualification is shared with the existing campus. Shenzhen third campus broke ground 07-24-2026 for AI 1.6T optical-module high-layer boards and high-end AI flex; its supplier conference drew 217 supply-chain companies and 410 representatives. Capacity for the next three years is largely bound to customers through LTAs and project-based binding agreements (visibility to 2029); 2027 AI PCB order visibility described as optimistic with capacity still insufficient. By 2030 the target is server + optical-module + IC-substrate at 45% to 50% of group revenue. GPU customer motherboards are produced both in mainland China and Thailand depending on customer requirements. Subsidiary Peng Ding filed its Hong Kong main-board listing application on July 2, 2026 (under review, so details withheld).

2026 capex ~NT$800 hundred million; 13 plants building + 16 planned; capex split 25-30% optical module / 35-40% IC substrate; Thailand PA01 profitable July 2026; 2030 target 45-50% of revenue from server/optical/substrate

Order intake has accelerated sharply: MORE THAN $600 MILLION of orders received year to date, with deliveries scheduled through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027, materially improving visibility well into 2027. Approximately 80% of those orders are advanced packaging applications. OSATs accounted for MORE THAN 50% of total order intake, HBM players for OVER 20% of the $600 million (against the $260 million of POs and forecasts discussed on the prior call), and photonics for about 5%. Order flow started in Q1 and has grown steadily since. Most orders now being received are for 2027 rather than 2026, and management says a nice 2027 backlog is already building, with additional 2027 OSAT orders already in discussion.
>$600M orders year to date; ~80% advanced packaging; OSATs >50% of intake; HBM >20%; photonics ~5%

The HBM4 transition is a direct order driver: CEO Rafi Amit said 'the industry transition to HBM4 together with continued capacity expansion has resulted in significant orders from MULTIPLE LEADING HBM MANUFACTURERS.' In parallel, ongoing expansion of 2.5D and 3D IC packaging capacity is producing large multi-system orders from leading foundries, IDMs and OSATs. Within the HPC/AI portion of the business the two main segments are HBM and CoWoS (and CoWoS-like) applications, both expanding quickly and growing at roughly similar pace, with the faster one depending on which customers add capacity. Growth is attributed to a combination of share gains and genuine market capacity additions across HBM, CoWoS, fan-in and fan-out.

Advanced packaging mix is stepping up through the year: it was approximately 75% of Q2 revenue and is expected to reach around 80% by Q4. The advanced packaging business is expected to grow approximately 45% in the second half versus the first half, and Q4 advanced packaging revenue is expected to be approximately 70% HIGHER THAN Q1. HPC and AI-related products are already around 55% of revenue and may reach closer to 60% by the end of the year, with conventional advanced packaging roughly another 20%. Non-advanced-packaging business is stable with modest growth, helped by significant CMOS image sensor orders and early signs of recovery in consumer-related areas.
Advanced packaging ~75% of Q2 revenue rising to ~80% by Q4; AP +45% H2 vs H1; Q4 AP ~70% above Q1; HPC/AI ~55% of revenue rising toward ~60%

New platforms are carrying the mix: the Eagle G5 and Hawk generated approximately 50% of systems revenue in Q2, with contribution expected to keep rising as adoption accelerates, and they lift ASPs. Hawk targets high-volume, high-end applications - HBM is cited as the example where Camtek is selling more Hawks - and combined with new AI technology is enabling penetration into additional process steps INCLUDING HYBRID BONDING. Eagle G5 offers better resolution, optics, throughput and cost of ownership, and existing Eagle customers are switching to it. Camtek is also launching NanoProf, a new metrology platform built on the FRT business acquired three years ago plus Camtek-developed technology, installed at selected customers from Q1 and covering wafer topography, shape and bow. Additional new modules include a high-resolution backside inspection module and fluorescence illumination for detecting organic residue. Further detail is promised at an investor breakfast at SEMICON West on October 14, 2026.
Eagle G5 + Hawk ~50% of Q2 systems revenue; NanoProf metrology platform launching; hybrid bonding process steps being addressed

Camtek says it is successfully managing the operational challenge of unprecedented demand: it expanded production capacity and strengthened its supply chain well in advance, has all subcontractors and supply chain in place, and COO Ramy Langer said there are no issues or obstacles regarding capacity and the company is confident of shipping machines on time. It is now further expanding manufacturing capacity, system integration capability, the sales organisation and customer support infrastructure to support substantially higher annual revenue levels. Inventory was flat in Q2 but is expected to grow in coming quarters to support forecast revenue growth.

Growth catalysts: GAA sales were about JPY 5 billion in Q1 and are expected at over JPY 20 billion for FY March 2027. Advanced packaging revenue, JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026, is now expected at JPY 15 billion in FY March 2027 (Q1 was JPY 4.5 billion) - a significant upward revision from the JPY 6 billion prior plan, driven by both rising customer CapEx and additional POR wins for its film deposition technology. In NAND, demand-supply is not fully adjusted - memory players are allocating clean room to DRAM while NAND wafer output needs to increase - so greenfield NAND investments are expected to resume, which converts all of Kokusai's PORs to sales and is broadly favorable. In DRAM, the D1C transition is complete and D1D is progressing. NAND sales could approach record highs, and DRAM plus NAND plus advanced packaging support growth above WFE (targeting more than a 20% sales increase).
GAA JPY 5 billion in Q1, over JPY 20 billion FY March 2027; advanced packaging raised to JPY 15 billion FY March 2027 from JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026

JAPAN DUAL-TRACK 300MM EXPANSION (METI-supported): TRACK 1 repurposes the Arai facility (ex-Fab 6) for 300mm SILICON PHOTONICS + advanced packaging and maximizes Fab 7 output — FULL PRODUCTION READINESS Q4 2027 (this drives the raised 2028 model; capacity 'already requested by and committed to several lead customers'). TRACK 2 builds a NEW 300mm fab adjacent to Fab 7 for a 4x INCREASE IN JAPANESE 300MM OUTPUT (SiPho, SiGe, advanced optical packaging) — installed and functioning by Q4 2028, the growth path into 2029+; intent to add AT LEAST 20,000-25,000 wpm of SiPho capacity; self-funded, no dilution. Japan chosen for GEOPOLITICAL NEUTRALITY, the Panasonic-heritage R&D workforce, and manufacturing-quality culture.
Track 1: Arai 300mm SiPho ready Q4-2027; Track 2: 4x Japan 300mm output by Q4-2028 (>=20-25k wpm SiPho)

Q1 (Apr-Jun 2026): revenue JPY 123.2 billion with electronics JPY 75.5 billion; operating profit JPY 26.9 billion with electronics JPY 21.4 billion - driven by strong demand for GPU and high-end CPU, stabilized Cell 8 production and improved utilization at existing plants pushing sales volume above the initial plan, plus strong selling prices for high value-added products. First-half forecast raised: revenue to JPY 253 billion (+10%), operating profit from JPY 38 billion to JPY 54.5 billion (+43%), electronics OP from JPY 33 billion to JPY 47 billion (+44%), net profit from JPY 23 billion to JPY 34 billion (+48%).
Q1 revenue JPY 123.2 billion (electronics JPY 75.5 billion), OP JPY 26.9 billion (electronics JPY 21.4 billion); H1 OP forecast raised 43% to JPY 54.5 billion

Full-year FY2026 forecast raised: revenue from JPY 500 billion to JPY 550 billion (+10%), electronics from JPY 350 billion to JPY 375 billion (+14%); operating profit from JPY 90 billion to JPY 127 billion (+41%, operating margin expectation raised from 18% to 23%), electronics OP from JPY 75 billion to JPY 110 billion; net profit raised to JPY 84 billion. Biggest driver: ASP and product mix with a positive impact of JPY 26.5 billion (majority is ASP - the planned quarterly price-reduction curve became less steep or prices were not reduced at all, plus general substrate price increases in an industry-wide supply shortage; not concentrated in a particular customer - GPU, CPU, switching IC and PC ASPs rising across the board). Revenue growth expected in all sub-segments: AI server, switching IC, and general-purpose server/PC.
FY revenue guide JPY 550 billion (from JPY 500 billion); OP JPY 127 billion (from JPY 90 billion, +41%); ASP/mix impact +JPY 26.5 billion

Supply-demand: 'The situation where demand exceeds the industry supply capacity is expected to continue' - substrates are getting larger and more difficult toward next fiscal year and the one after, AI server demand keeps rising, and current selling prices are expected to at least hold at present levels. Customers accepted fewer price cuts, and in some cases none, because of industry-wide shortages. Glass cloth and CCL cost increases are passed through to ASP in a timely manner. Utilization: apart from Intel Cell 5, almost everything was at full capacity utilization; sourcing for the revised FY2026 plan is already secured, though industry-wide competition for materials and equipment could constrain material supply in coming years.
Demand exceeds industry supply capacity; near-full utilization except Intel Cell 5; prices expected to at least hold

Capacity: Cell 6 and Cell 8 are about 50% through equipment ordering, will commence operations within FY2027 with positive business contribution in FY2028 (timing difficult to accelerate). Next investment decision accelerated - to be made at the latest before the end of the current fiscal year; capacity enhancement is needed across the business ('almost all the customers have asked us to enhance our capacity'), with vacant land at Gama and Ono (would-be Cell 7 and Cell 9) both under consideration at the same time, plus possibly buying another plant building. Advance payments from customers continue to be discussed to fund capacity and offset fixed-cost increases; customer stance on advance payments unchanged from the Cell 6 situation despite an aggressive Taiwanese competitor.
Cell 6/Cell 8 ~50% of equipment ordered, operations within FY2027, contribution FY2028; new capacity decision before end of FY2026 (Gama and Ono, Cell 7/Cell 9)

EMIB-T (silicon-bridge embedded substrate): development done by three players including Ibiden, with Ibiden believing it is at the leading edge; a test vehicle has been shipped. Challenges: embedding the silicon bridge in the buildup and getting the interconnection right, plus stronger power supply complicating the core structure (component embedding is a general new trend adding complication) - yield expected lower, but yield has improved a lot since the beginning of development, numbers indicate shippable quality, and there is no showstopper. Small-lot production expected in the latter half of FY2027, mass production at the Gama plant from FY2028.
EMIB-T small-lot production latter half of FY2027; Gama mass production FY2028; yield improving, no showstopper

Glass cloth: procurement risks flagged at the beginning of the year have been mitigated. The number of glass cloth suppliers has increased - previously two companies in Japan and Taiwan, now a third and fourth supplier are visible, giving four glass cloth suppliers with visibility for use in mass production; the Japanese glass cloth supplier is increasing capacity, and the tight glass cloth supply situation is expected to simmer down. Ibiden believes it is in an advantageous position in the industry for glass cloth supply. Glass core substrate: joint development continuing (glass core and component-embedding structures pursued as two separate options with their own roadmaps, possibly narrowing to one later).
Four glass cloth suppliers now visible for mass production (was two); Japanese supplier adding capacity

ARM-based CPU substrates (AI inference CPU demand): specs will be similar to substrates Ibiden currently supplies and difficulty level similar to the AI GPU work, so Ibiden has the capability to supply. New business is capped at around 20% of the overall in FY2027 - there is no room to allocate more capacity, so large-scale initiatives cannot be undertaken despite expected demand; allocation between new business and value-added products of existing customers to be revisited internally by the mid-year earnings call, when the midterm plan will also be revisited.
New business capped at ~20% of overall in FY2027 on capacity limits

→ TSMC: Glass core substrate joint development with TSMC confirmed ongoing ('we are doing the joint development effort. We are working with them'): glass core and component-embedding structures are being pursued simultaneously as two separate options, each with its own roadmap; at some point Ibiden may focus on just one of the two, but for now both developmental efforts continue without preassumption.

→ Intel: Intel Cell 5 is Ibiden's one line not yet at full utilization ('apart from Intel Cell 5, almost everything was at full capacity utilization') and its utilization is improving, driving the sales volume increase from existing capacity. For EMIB-T, Core 5 for Intel will be used for small-lot production (targeted latter half of FY2027) before Gama plant mass manufacturing starts in FY2028.

Advanced Solutions, which includes the Fluxless Thermo-Compression (FTC) bonding platform, recognised revenue 20% ABOVE last quarter's record. K&S is maintaining its target of OVER $100 MILLION in Advanced Solutions revenue for fiscal 2026, and for fiscal 2027 Lester Wong guided TCB revenue to a range of $150 MILLION TO $200 MILLION - significant sequential growth. The company remains closely engaged with a broad base of IDM, OSAT and foundry customers as heterogeneous packaging goes mainstream, with particular confidence in heterogeneous integration around logic for Fluxless TCB.
Advanced Solutions revenue 20% above prior record; >$100M Advanced Solutions target for FY2026; TCB guided to $150M-$200M in FY2027

Beyond thermocompression, K&S accelerated its HYBRID BONDING program over the last year and says its hybrid bonder has unique features not currently in the market; it PLANS TO DELIVER A HYBRID BONDING TOOL TO A CUSTOMER IN THE FIRST HALF OF FISCAL 2027. It is also investing significantly in a PANEL-level project, seeing a lot of interest from IDMs, foundries and OSATs because panel geometry allows many more dies on a rectangle than a circle; specific panel applications are still being scoped with customers. Management frames FTC, vertical wire, direct copper-to-copper, hybrid and panel-based architectures as the emerging packaging set that will be critically necessary across a much wider array of semiconductor production, and stresses the industry is still in the relatively early stages of this More-than-Moore advanced packaging transition.
Hybrid bonding tool to be delivered to a customer in H1 FY2027

Capacity: the Singapore capital expansion is progressing well and remains on track for completion by the FIRST FISCAL HALF OF 2027, supporting Advanced Solutions growth over coming years. For the traditional wire bonding business, K&S has increased capacity FOURFOLD compared with about two quarters ago through its flexible manufacturing model. Management said it is explicitly focused on not losing market share because of capacity constraints, noted K&S has supported $400 million quarters before, and did not see a $450 million quarterly run rate at this point while committing to ramp further if needed.
Wire bonding capacity increased fourfold versus ~two quarters ago; Singapore expansion completing in H1 fiscal 2027

K&S made a notable structural claim about wire bonding in AI infrastructure: it estimates the DATA CENTER MARKET RELIES ON WIRE BONDING TECHNOLOGY AT LEAST AS MUCH AS, IF NOT MORE THAN, traditional semiconductor markets such as smartphones and PCs, because the majority of data center chips are still traditionally wire bonded - general infrastructure, networking, communication, power management and storage. Ball bonding is the more prevalent technology for data center power management, while wedge bonding remains more focused on automotive and high-current applications. Data center expansion therefore drives demand for BOTH the thermocompression and the wire bonding lines.
Kulicke & Soffa states in its fiscal Q3 2026 release that it anticipates its expanded Advanced Solutions production facility will be completed, as scheduled, within the second half of fiscal 2027.

Veeco plans to MORE THAN DOUBLE CAPACITY in advanced packaging and silicon photonics during 2027, expanding internal manufacturing on the East Coast plus strategic outsourcing partnerships with contract manufacturers in Southeast Asia, and adding and training personnel. The company is deliberately spending ahead of revenue in the second half of 2026: approximately $10 million of incremental operating expenses and roughly 75 basis points of full-year gross-margin impact from one-time capacity set-up and contract-manufacturer onboarding costs. This is why the full-year revenue guide rose while the EPS guide came down. The revenue ramp from the optical networking, data storage and advanced packaging orders begins slightly at the end of Q4 2026, starts in Q1 2027 and gets more up to speed in Q2 2027, with the majority falling in 2027.
Capacity in advanced packaging and silicon photonics to more than double during 2027; ~$10M incremental opex and ~75bps gross-margin impact in 2026

Advanced packaging is becoming a materially larger part of the business through the wet processing and lithography portfolio, with demand driven by heterogeneous integration and increasingly complex 2.5D and 3D architectures. Veeco projects the advanced packaging SAM will approach $1 BILLION BY 2030 and expects to gain share within it. The company is actively engaged with a Tier 1 foundry on a PANEL PROCESSING opportunity and is encouraged by the progress. Manufacturing footprint is expanding both in-house and with outsourced partners in Southeast Asia to support the growth.
Advanced packaging SAM approaching $1B by 2030; active panel processing engagement with a Tier 1 foundry

CALL — GUIDE RAISED A THIRD TIME; SUPPLY CHAIN REBUILT: FY2026 revenue raised to ~$12.6B = 40% GROWTH (+$2.1B vs the $10.5B Analyst Day plan, +$1.1B vs May's $11.5B) — the raise deliberately UNALLOCATED across AI fabrics (goal >=$3.5B), campus (>=$1.25B), core front-end data center ('isn't going to be flat' — enterprise, new logos, international) and routing; operating margin RAISED to 48-49% (Q2 hit 49.9%). Supply chain: Jayshree — 'the INDUSTRY is going to have a TWO-YEAR problem... I don't think we get out of it as an industry TILL 2028,' but Arista's specific H1 actions pay off in H2: MULTI-YEAR PURCHASE COMMITMENTS NEARLY TRIPLED YoY to $9.7 BILLION (from $3.6B; $8.9B in Q1); MEMORY SUPPLY SECURED FOR 2026 with visibility WELL INTO 2027 (DDR4/DDR5/NAND); PCB + optics capacity buildable in a 12-month window; a NEW LIQUID-COOLING SUPPLY CHAIN stood up (cold plates, quick disconnects, tubing with capacity agreements); 3 CMs + 3 distribution hubs (US/Asia/Mexico). Guidance is explicitly supply-gated: 'guiding based on what we're CONFIDENT we can get the supply for — if supply released more, there is opportunity to do better.' Price increases only help 'end of the year or more like next year' (backlog); FY GM held 62-64% including memory/silicon cost inflation. Etherlink AI-fabric customers now EXCEED 100 CUMULATIVE (from 4-5 in 2024).
FY26 raised to ~$12.6B (+40%, 3rd raise); purchase commitments ~3x YoY to $9.7B; memory secured into 2027; liquid-cooling chain built; >100 AI customers

Interconnect Solutions (ICS) net sales $685 million, up more than 30% year-over-year and 16% sequentially, organic +28%, led by the three growth platforms of advanced packaging and interconnect, AI PCBs and thermal management, which collectively grew more than 50% year-over-year again; ICS gross margin ~44%, adjusted EBITDA margin ~29%, up 290 basis points YoY, now viewed as structurally in the high 20% range.
ICS $685 million (+30% YoY, +16% QoQ); AI growth platforms +50% YoY; ICS EBITDA margin ~29%

New advanced packaging architectures (panel-level packaging, larger package formats, tighter lines and spaces on high-layer-count boards and IC substrates) all mean more material complexity and more material intensity, with fewer suppliers able to qualify; Qnity has incumbency with the same customers that commercialized the existing advanced packaging formats and expects more content per package as formats grow. Customer capacity expansions in advanced packaging underpin the durability of ICS growth.

Winning new business in pulse plating, a key metallization technology for the most advanced high-layer-count printed circuit boards used in AI applications (density, signal integrity, power delivery); thermal portfolio broadened to liquid thermal interface materials, phase change materials, thermal pads and gap fillers for AI systems and data center infrastructure.

Industry volume indicators: MSI expected in the high single digits for 2026 and PCB growth in the mid to high single digits; Qnity content outperformance sits considerably above the MSI benchmark because all logic and memory leaders are successfully commercializing their most advanced nodes at once.
2026 MSI high single digits; PCB growth mid to high single digits

Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. GUC sells the customer the finished CoWoS package with HBM inside; if HBM prices rise the chip price rises with it, so the cost risk sits with the customer, not GUC. Management cited HBM pricing going from about 240 at the start of the year to 700 and up to 900 (as spoken; unit not stated), fully passed through. Whether HBM procurement flows through GUC's own P&L or is booked as a service fee is still being worked out case by case at this early stage.
HBM price cited from ~240 early in the year to 700-900 (as spoken), passed through to customers

The new Turing design center began trial operation in Q2 running small and mid-size projects and is expected to be in full use in H2; it adds some depreciation/R&D cost but is aimed squarely at 3nm, 2nm and even more advanced process work plus advanced packaging. The R&D roadmap already includes CPO, IVR (integrated voltage regulator), next-generation UCIe die-to-die, and N2-on-N2 advanced-process development; opex should grow only modestly versus a clearly larger revenue increase next year.

LAST QUARTER'S FORECAST DELIVERED EARLY: the sale-of-gas project backlog reached a RECORD $8.1 BILLION (from $7.1B in Q1) — management had guided to exiting 2026 'with an eight handle' — and the 'couple of large electronics contracts' flagged in Q1 landed as $1 BILLION OF NEW ELECTRONICS WINS added to backlog TO SUPPORT THE EXPANSION OF ADVANCED-NODE FABS IN THE WESTERN US. Linde has ALREADY BEGUN CONSTRUCTING those plants under reimbursable letters of intent while the supply contracts are finalized, adding to its existing network of plants in ARIZONA, and says it is pursuing 'a few more large opportunities'. Separately and NOT in the backlog, Linde's TAIWAN JV will invest approximately $800 MILLION to build, own and operate air separation units and HYDROGEN production units supplying NEW SEMICONDUCTOR FABS AND ADVANCED PACKAGING FACILITIES in Taiwan (the Taiwan business is a 50% non-consolidated JV, so excluded from reported numbers). ELECTRONICS IS AGAIN THE FASTEST-GROWING END MARKET, on a combination of project start-ups and 'higher demand tied to hardware associated with AI', and is expected to remain the largest backlog contributor 'for the foreseeable future'.
Record backlog $8.1B; +$1B electronics wins for western-US advanced-node fabs; $800M Taiwan JV (fabs + adv packaging)

Product momentum in FY2027: coater developer (share of more than 90% across EUV to immersion lithography) won PORs in multiple processes in advanced logic and DRAM with the new Resive Pro Dice; full-year etch system sales of JPY 1 trillion are coming within reach; cryogenic etch systems for 400-layer NAND start deploying in customers' mass production lines from calendar 2027; a POR was won for a new low resistance metal deposition system in a new application area. For DRAM interconnect etch, five-year cumulative sales to fiscal 2030 are getting closer to JPY 1 trillion, significantly exceeding the original guidance of JPY 500 billion. In advanced packaging, prober sales show outstanding growth with full-year sales likely to go significantly beyond JPY 100 billion, and the Prexa SDP device prober for advanced logic launched in April; bonder/debonder and 3D-IC are growth areas combining leading-edge front-end and bonding technology.

Coater developer share more than 90%; etch sales JPY 1 trillion full-year within reach; DRAM interconnect etch five-year cumulative sales near JPY 1 trillion vs JPY 500 billion original guidance; prober sales significantly beyond JPY 100 billion; cryogenic etch for 400 layers in mass production from calendar 2027

Record ATM (OSAT) revenue NTD 126.1B (+12% QoQ, +36% YoY) with ATM gross margin 27.3% and operating margin 15.7%; full-year 2026 ATM revenue expected to grow ~35%. Capacity is the binding constraint — blended utilization 80-85% but 'generally very close to being full', with near-term growth gated by equipment installation and building construction. Q4 2026 ATM gross margin is likely to EXCEED the 30% structural ceiling, after which management will review raising the 26-29% structural margin range upward; pricing environment described as friendly, with material and component cost inflation passed through to customers.

Fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) for AI: chairman confirms PTI is an AMD AI-chip supply-chain partner providing fan-out PLP solutions and is actively pursuing more AMD AI-chip applications; despite equipment-delivery delays, installation issues and doing new-product qualification in parallel, the program is on schedule and PTI is confident of volume production before the middle of next year, which would make it the world's first company to mass-produce fan-out PLP for AI applications. AMD fan-out PLP volume production before mid-2027 (target: world's first FOPLP for AI); 5x reticle-size panel packages, ~45 per G7 panel vs 8-9 per wafer; FOPLP equipment lead time ~1 year

→ AMD: Chairman: PTI has become a supply-chain partner for AMD AI chips and will provide AMD fan-out PLP (panel-level packaging) solutions, and is actively pursuing additional AMD AI-chip applications. → Broadcom: PTI and Broadcom will form a joint venture in Singapore - a major milestone making PTI a strategic and preferred partner of Broadcom. rows: Deal size and density are stepping up. Shaw: 'Whereas a 250 kVA deal was a large deal for us, a megawatt is kind of the going thing now.' He gave the announced DA12 build as an example: 'we are going to be delivering, I think about 67 megawatts, and it is going to have a density of about 18 kVA per cabinet. That is denser than we have ever gone'. He added that Equinix does 'not build gigawatt data centers to perform training'. Instead, xScale is meant to bring the clouds closer to the dense metro ecosystems. The moderator named the Hertfordshire campus and the Osaka site, and Shaw said 'those are the two right now that we are looking at. They are on track.'
250 kVA deal was a large deal; a megawatt is kind of the going thing now; DA12 about 67 megawatts at about 18 kVA per cabinet

Liquid-cooling strategy is to build it into new sites, not to retrofit old ones. Shaw: 'When we think about new builds, we think about liquid cooling. We're less prone to retrofitting a building for liquid cooling' and 'We're not going back and retrofitting a bunch of buildings for liquid cooling.' He said enterprise demand has changed: liquid-cooled space used to sit empty because customers found it 'really expensive', but 'Now it's a requirement'. The optional design means Equinix is 'not stuck with liquid cooling that we're not utilizing'. CFO Ryan Burke compared the in-cage deployment to 'a NASCAR pit crew': customers who want liquid cooling pay for it, and Equinix can pull it out and deploy it elsewhere when they no longer need it.

Community opposition has not delayed Equinix builds so far. Shaw called backlash 'a real thing' but said Equinix engages community leaders before it buys land. He said 'We just did an extensive one in Minooka that was really well-received' (a town hall about the project) and 'we have not seen some of the delays or issues that have come up.' He also said Equinix has 'always paid for our usage' and invests with power companies to build out the grid it needs.

CAPACITY RAISED: THAILAND TAKES AE FROM OVER $3 BILLION TO OVER $5 BILLION OF CAPACITY BY 2028. CFO Paul Oldham: 'Today we have over $3 billion of capacity in our existing facilities... With Thailand coming on, that would give us over $5 billion of capacity as soon as 2028', which he tied to having 'sharpened our pencil a bit' and to accelerating investments (the earlier lower figure was the moderator's framing). CEO Steve Kelley said AE 'accelerate[d] the opening of our new factory in Thailand' in response to raised customer forecasts and is 'just opening a 500,000 sq ft facility, and we will be launching that facility with our largest customers, semiconductor, as well as our largest customers in data center.' Oldham said AE is 'spending roughly 2X the CapEx we would normally spend', which can return to 'a more normalized level of 3%-4%', and that the build was pulled forward out of the 2030 model because demand is running ahead.
over $3 billion of capacity today, over $5 billion as soon as 2028; 500,000 sq ft Thailand facility; capex running at roughly 2X normal versus a normalized 3%-4%

800V TIMELINE PINNED: 2027 IS THE DESIGN-WIN YEAR, REVENUE IN 2028-2029. Kelley: 'we do not expect 800V to be significant from a revenue standpoint until 2028 at the earliest. So we think 2027 is a design win year for us, and 2028 and 2029 start to see revenue on 800V product.' AE is attacking it with a modular architecture - 'we have what we call a PDU, a power distribution unit. Think of it as a motherboard, essentially, where we could plug in these different 800V modules... 800V to six volts or to some other intermediate voltage' - explicitly because 'I do not think anybody knows exactly how the architecture is going to look a year or two from now.' He confirmed AE has solutions and active customer engagements for the AC/DC move out of the rack into a sidecar or power rack, and expects content per rack to rise as it has every generation. On cadence: 'every year a new solution is required. That is loosely tied to new introductions from Nvidia and other suppliers. The power requirements go up every year. 800V: 2027 design-win year, revenue 2028 and 2029, not significant until 2028 at the earliest
Advanced Energy Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-10-2026)

2026 DATA CENTER GROWTH IS STILL ONE HYPERSCALER; THE 'SECOND WAVE' ONLY LANDS IN 2027-2029. Kelley: 'In 2026, what we have seen is a ramp based on our hyperscaler customer only. On the size of the second wave: 'in aggregate, we think the second wave customers could be as big as one of our hyperscale customers. second wave customers meaningful only in 2027 and 2028, reaching the size of one hyperscale customer in the 2028, 2029 timeframe

The consequence is that data center capacity federates around the country instead of concentrating, each site is capped by locally available power, and those clusters must be interconnected - which he said can shift the scale-across TAM quite a lot.

→ Oracle: Clay Magouyrk on the New Mexico (Doña Ana County) site: data-center construction is on track and Oracle is going through the process of acquiring its AIR PERMIT; the on-site generation technology will be Bloom fuel cells — 'by far the most environmentally friendly way' to do on-site power, with extremely low water consumption and emissions. Denton 297 MW conditionally approved plus 74 MW in the 2025 RTP study cases; Pecos 300 MW base load plus 300 MW studied load conditionally approved; Hunt 431 MW conditionally approved

units: PTX, MX and QFX routers and switches running the back end of the AI data center

5-10 GIGAWATTS DEPLOYED NEXT YEAR, WITH POWER - NOT GPUs - AS THE GATING ITEM: Johnsen said 'We talked about a range next year of 5-10 gigawatts deployed... first orbital compute satellites targeted to fly next year; large-scale orbital compute going into 2028

Structural explanation of the neocloud channel: 'If you think about what's happening at the neocloud level, and you see some of these major contracts where these neoclouds were, many of them and growing, that we're serving, they're getting hyperscaler contracts. In essence, our systems at the neoclouds are serving the hyperscalers. So they need to get those systems up and running immediately.' Deployment scale cited for these operators is '100 to 1,500 rack deployments', where slow stand-up destroys economics (Staiger cited a partner's figure that 8 racks taking 30 days to become operational costs about $3 million). That is the argument for L11/L12 integrated DCBBS racks - power, cooling, CDUs, rear door heat exchangers, storage, switching and software - over shipping bare racks, and for the higher margin content that comes with it.
100 to 1,500 rack deployments; 8 racks taking 30 days to stand up costs about $3 million (partner figure cited by management)

DDN (the AI/cloud business) sized and its power/data mix trajectory given: DDN is 'about $3 billion of our $20 billion this year' and power connections have gone from roughly a quarter of DDN three years ago to about a third today, a share management expects to keep rising as rack power architectures change. DDN is delivering around $1 billion of growth this year.
