Utility-scale solar is the renewables exposure and is running slower on regulation; Europe is now stepping up investment (including LNG facilities).
energy mid-teens growth this year in a market growing 6%-7% today versus a 1%-2% market five years ago; 70% of our business is U.S.-focused

Copper / optical / power split and the CommScope mix: 'Obviously, with CommScope, our optics position is more significant today, and we've talked about the fact that we now expect the CommScope acquisition, which when we bought it for $10.5 billion, we thought it would be a roughly $3.5 billion business. Now we expect it this year to be more than $4.5 billion in sales with higher margins and thereby better accretion. We've talked about the fact that MORE THAN THREE-QUARTERS OF THEIR BUSINESS IS OPTICS.' That puts Amphenol 'as one of the world leaders in optical interconnect,' while in power 'we are the leader in power interconnect' - a legacy of defense-market ultra-high voltage/power connectors, cable assemblies and busbars, where the risk is that 'you don't want to catch a $3 million GPU rack on fire.' High-speed copper remains a big piece, with good balance across all three.
CommScope bought for $10.5 billion, originally seen as roughly $3.5 billion of sales, now more than $4.5 billion this year; more than three-quarters of CommScope's business is optics

China / ICAPS: China is mostly ICAPS (IoT, communication, auto, power, sensors) for Applied. Applied is seeing growth this year in China and overall ICAPS and gaining a little bit of share in the areas where it can compete inside China, and expects that business to grow a little faster next year than this year. Near-term ICAPS growth is being driven by power in data center and photonics; longer term ICAPS grows mid to high single digits, slower than the AI data center segments.
ICAPS mid to high single digits longer term; China and ICAPS growing this year and a little faster next year

DATA-CENTER ORDER BOOK SIZED: CEO Lorenzo Simonelli said 'since 2025, IET has secured $4.2 billion of data center-related orders, including approximately $3.2 billion in the first half of 2026 alone', and separately that 'Chart Industries has booked approximately $600 million of data center orders over the past two years'. The combined offer is pitched as a facility-level solution rather than individual products as power density rises: Baker Hughes supplies on-site power generation, power conversion and microgrid control for reliability and uptime, while Chart adds cooling infrastructure, carbon capture, water treatment and recycling, and LNG and hydrogen storage and backup fuel systems. He said commercial engagement between the two teams is already underway, 'particularly around data center infrastructure and broader gas infrastructure opportunities'.
IET data center-related orders $4.2 billion since 2025, including approximately $3.2 billion in the first half of 2026; Chart approximately $600 million of data center orders over the past two years

THE IET BACKLOG BEHIND IT: first-half 2026 IET orders of '$12 billion', a record IET RPO of 'more than $37 billion at the end of the second quarter' - this is the IET segment figure, not the company-wide total - and a reaffirmed 'more than $45 billion of IET orders through the Horizon Two period'. IET delivered record EBITDA margins of 18.5% in 2025 and Simonelli said he expects margins 'to exceed 20% in 2026', with a clear path to 20% adjusted EBITDA margins for Baker Hughes by 2028 excluding Chart. Approximately 60% of company revenue now comes from infrastructure and industrial markets, and OFSE margins are up more than 600 basis points since 2017.

IET EBITDA margin record 18.5% in 2025, expected to exceed 20% in 2026; clear path to 20% company adjusted EBITDA margin by 2028 excluding Chart; ~60% of revenue from infrastructure and industrial (reaffirmed from the Q2 call: H1 IET orders $12 billion, IET RPO more than $37 billion, more than $45 billion of IET orders through Horizon Two)

CHART INTEGRATION MECHANICS AND THE BACKLOG RESTATEMENT: after a preliminary contract-level review and the application of Baker Hughes' own backlog definitions, Chart's reported backlog drops to 'approximately $3.6 billion at the end of the third quarter'. Simonelli insisted this is 'a methodology change to align with the integration that we are conducting... not an end market view', with Chart book-to-bill still above one in the second half. On synergies, 'we have already executed $35 million of actions to date' toward 'approximately $325 million of annualized cost synergies by year 3', roughly three-quarters of it captured inside the Chart segment - part of '500 to 600 basis points of margin expansion over the next two years' that takes Chart EBITDA margin from about 17% in the second half of 2026 to '22%-23% by the second half of 2028'. Near-term Chart margin is held back by the timing of LNG equipment volumes, soft hydrogen demand and several first-of-a-kind projects with lower margin profiles; he sees improving visibility toward an LNG order recovery moving into 2027. Second-half Chart EBITDA is weighted about 40% third quarter and 60% fourth quarter.

$35 million of synergy actions already executed (approximately three-quarters of the $325 million to be captured inside the Chart segment); Chart EBITDA margin from approximately 17% in the second half of 2026 to 22%-23% by the second half of 2028, 500 to 600 basis points of expansion; second-half Chart EBITDA split about 40% Q3 / 60% Q4 (Chart backlog restatement to ~$3.6 billion and the $325 million target were already disclosed)

MARKET SIZE RE-FRAMED WITH CHART: 'Combined with Chart, we now compete across an addressable market of more than $400 billion.' Within that, exposure to the high-growth end markets - gas infrastructure, geothermal, data centers, carbon capture, space, mining and industrial gases - rises 'nearly 60%, from approximately $36 billion today to roughly $57 billion by 2030'. Simonelli also cited 'a growing enterprise solutions pipeline of $10 billion'. This is a wider cut than the power systems TAM Baker Hughes has framed before, because it spans the full combined portfolio.

combined addressable market more than $400 billion; high-growth end-market exposure up nearly 60%, from approximately $36 billion today to roughly $57 billion by 2030; enterprise solutions pipeline of $10 billion

Development pipeline and the yield on it: 'We target 10%+ development yields,' and 'We have $20 billion under construction today, and 11.5% expected initial cash yield.' The pipeline doubled in six months - 'we have $20 billion of data center construction underway today versus $10 billion 6 months ago, or at the end of 2025' - even as permitting got harder. He stressed the yield is initial stabilized CASH on a fully loaded cost (land, generators, redundancy, contingency, losses to stabilization) and would be about 20% higher on a GAAP basis, 'so maybe your 11.5 would be 14.' Cost reference given for scale: 'a gigawatt of capacity could cost $15 billion.'
$20 billion under construction vs $10 billion 6 months ago; 11.5% expected initial cash yield vs a 10%+ target; a gigawatt could cost $15 billion
Digital Realty Bank of America conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

WHAT STAYS WITH REMAINCO FLEX AFTER THE SPIN - THE ENERGY-INFRASTRUCTURE CONTRACT MANUFACTURING (Michael, CEO of RemainCo Flex): 'This is a business that we spun the power product portfolio into SpinCo, but we're maintaining all the contract manufacturing business inside of Flex. Whether it's power generation, transmission, distribution, storage, all of that contract manufacturing work stays inside of Flex. Those areas will be positively influenced by the trends in the data center.' The spin is expected 'just after the first of the year', and RMS/ITS margins have gone 'from 5% to 5.7%' over the last two quarters with a long-term target to be set at the November Investor Day. CFO Kevin, separately, said RemainCo will retain a stake in SpinCo that 'will not exceed 19.9%' and expects to use that retained stake to de-lever, leaving Flex 'with less leverage, stronger balance sheet'.
retained SpinCo stake will not exceed 19.9%; RMS/ITS margins from 5% to 5.7%
Flex Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

WHAT EPC POWER ACTUALLY BRINGS (Chris, CTO/Chief Strategy Officer of SpinCo): EPC 'really is covering a gap that we had that was kind of upstream in the data center.' Its base product is not a normal energy-storage box but 'a grid-forming inverter' that (1) insulates the utility grid from 'some of the anomalies that happen in a GPU-based data center, some of those power fluctuations' and (2) delivers 'a very clean source of power to the IT loads in the data center' - a capability 'being required by a lot of utilities here across the U.S.' The forward technology content is the bigger prize: 'They have a centralized rectifier today, an active digital rectifier that we can use for centralized 800-volt DC deployments. This is already in the NVIDIA DGX architecture. They have a very far along SST development program that will allow us to even bolster efficiency better and improve the footprint.' The stated ambition: 'we are going to be taking the data center architecture to a blank sheet of paper soon and being able to work with customers on really helping them connect that 34.5 kV at the utility space directly to the IT load.'
centralized 800-volt DC deployments; connect 34.5 kV at the utility space directly to the IT load
Flex Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

EPC'S 2027 IS ALREADY BOOKED, AND A JULY GRID EVENT IS PULLING DEMAND FORWARD (Chris): asked what drives EPC's growth, 'It is all pinned to the data centers. It is all pinned to some of those regulatory requirements that are coming. There is also some tailwinds from bans on foreign-produced product in the critical infrastructure here in the U.S. EPC is all U.S.-based production, so that plays in very well.' Asked about visibility: 'Most of that business is booked today' and 'Really good backlog for 2027.' A specific catalyst was named: 'There was a pretty significant power disturbance in Northern Virginia back in the month of July, and that is driving more utilities to demand this type of technology in the data center.' Margin uplift is attributed to capacity that 'just came online in the month of June', supply-chain reshoring initiatives, and the fact that 'data center margins are a little bit higher than what their traditional business has been.'
Flex Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

FLEX'S OWN HIGH-VOLTAGE PRODUCT IS SHIPPING INTO EXISTING DATA CENTERS; EPC IS THE GREENFIELD PLAY (Chris): 'If you look at where Flex's primary power conversion business has been, it has all been really at the rack or near the rack... we have a pretty broad portfolio of product that allow us to take, whether it be AC power or even 800-volt DC power, all the way down to one volt, which is the voltage level that these chips operate. We are deploying both plus/minus 400 and 800-volt DC sidecars as well. And those are being implemented in data centers that are already built today or in the process of being built. So we see a next two to three years really strong outlook for that type of product.' EPC sits one step upstream and one cycle later: 'Where we see the EPC product playing more of a role is in that greenfield data center that is probably in the planning stages today, and two to three years from now, we will start seeing a lot of demand for their 800-volt DC solutions.'
plus/minus 400 and 800-volt DC sidecars deploying now; 800-volt DC greenfield demand two to three years from now
Flex Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

THE POWER-DENSITY MATH BEHIND THE DEMAND CALL (Chris): NIMBY/siting pushback is not seen changing the trajectory - 'I do not think we are going to see demand curtail in the data center space, even with some of these back pressures. It may just shift around a little bit' - because the driver is silicon power: 'you are taking chips that used to operate at 150 watts are now going to 3,000 watts. It is a 20-fold increase in power. There is not a growth estimate out there that is not below two to three times the amount of power consumption in the data center fleet here in the U.S.' Flex is spending against it: 'We are making those investments in capacity to make sure that we can meet those demands.' On procurement, the CFO said the component environment 'is challenged, but it has been challenged for a while... for the better part of 7 years', and that the 65% to 75% CPI growth guide 'contemplated supply challenges in there.'
chips from 150 watts to 3,000 watts, a 20-fold increase in power; two to three times the amount of power consumption in the data center fleet here in the U.S.
Flex Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

→ NVIDIA: SpinCo's CTO said the centralized active digital rectifier of EPC Power - the acquisition the moderator referred to as announced 'last week' - for centralized 800-volt DC deployments 'is already in the NVIDIA DGX architecture', alongside the plus/minus 400 and 800-volt DC sidecars Flex is already deploying into data centers built or under construction.

A new growth leg is forming in power semiconductors from data center power. Onto's earlier power-semi run was driven not by capacity expansion but by customers using Onto's inspection and metrology to drive yield improvement, with yields in the 60%-70% range rather than the 90s. The EV recovery has not really happened yet, but those same customers are now telling Onto they see demand from data centers driving adoption of power semiconductors and that Onto needs to prepare. Management is not seeing the actual orders yet and has no good clarity on timing, but said 2027 into 2028 is what the customers are thinking about; because the process control is already inserted in their process, Onto should benefit as they expand. Data center power is relatively small for Onto today and would be captured under specialty devices.
yields in the 60%-70% range; customers thinking 2027 into 2028
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

CFO Lorenzo Grandi on the AI data-center mix: the connectivity flow (silicon photonics, microcontrollers and BiCMOS EICs for optical transceivers) generates the strongest revenue, and for 2027 ST expects 'mostly of our revenue will be in MDRF for around 80% of the billing' with only 20% in APMS (thermal and power flows). around 80% of 2027 data-center billing in MDRF (connectivity), 20% in APMS; power meaningful revenue after 2028

Silicon carbide: capacity (still at 150mm) is the limiting factor while demand recovers, especially at European car makers. SiC revenue will grow double digit this year, and with the programs in hand ST sees SiC revenue next year 'back at EUR 1.01 billion'; the move to 200mm (Catania, and Chongqing in China) should significantly improve profitability, and ST is introducing Generation 4 and Generation 5. Satellite: the business is 'reaching closely EUR 1 billion'; with Starlink/SpaceX ST holds 'around 90% of market share', which management calls not sustainable as second sources arrive, but new entrants are already being shipped to; cumulative revenue over the next three years 'well above EUR 3 billion'.
SiC revenue next year back at EUR 1.01 billion; satellite business closely EUR 1 billion; around 90% share at Starlink/SpaceX

Tan unpacked what 'supply constrained' means behind the 2027 and 2028 AI revenue forecast, and it is not silicon. On chips: 'We understand the need for wafers, leading-edge wafers, and memory, as well as even substrates. That is pretty well locked in. We can pretty well lock that in for sure in 2027, and the process of locking in 2028 gives us within some limits. That is more within our control.' The less deterministic constraint is a site that is power READY, not merely power available: 'If you want to make it power ready, say, in 2028, got to start construction on the sites now. That is not us, our customers, has to start construction on the site now to make it available and ready by 2028' - a year and a half to two years out, gated by transformers, gas turbines, local permitting and the rate of construction. 'It's a judged number based on not just supply of memory wafers, but availability and readiness of power sites.'
wafers, memory and substrates locked in for 2027, being locked for 2028

Data-center power detail beyond the Q2 call: 'next year's data centers will be having 800 volt at the data center wall that needs to get delivered to 0.8 volts, let's say, at the chip, with as few conversion stages as possible in a very dense form factor'. GF is 'shipping GaN products to the data center today' - Breen pointed at partner Navitas having discussed that ramp the prior week - and named the BCD node for the first time: 'Our latest BCD technology, 55 nanometer... is already being used in those new conversion stages that are going into production as of now.' The revenue pull-through has yet to show up and is expected going into 2027 and more into 2028, which is also when GF is adding capacity for that technology. The newest shift is from lateral to vertical power delivery, behind which GF has put process technology, integrated passives and the recent acqui-hire of a small voltage-regulator design team so it can co-design with power semiconductor players and hyperscalers alike.
800 volt at the data center wall delivered to 0.8 volts at the chip; 55 nanometer BCD in production now; pull-through in 2027 and more into 2028

→ Navitas: Breen confirmed the GaN data-center ramp is live, not pending: 'We are shipping GaN products to the data center today. One of our partners, Navitas, talked about that last week. That ramp is already underway today.' GaN is the enabling technology for the dense power conversion required by the 800 volt data-center wall.

CEO put hard CONTENT-PER-MEGAWATT numbers behind the 800V story for the first time: inside the data center GaN is worth about $15,000 per megawatt (silicon replacement), SiC for AC-DC conversion plus the JFET for power protection is about $10,000 per megawatt, and grid modernisation (2,000-volt / 3,000-volt class solid-state transformer work) adds another 10, maybe up to 15 in the long run — roughly 25-ish in total against total power content per megawatt of probably 100, 250. The model assumes data-center deployment between now and 2030 of 220 gigawatts to 300 gigawatts and management says 'It's getting closer to 300' by the day.

GaN $15,000 per megawatt; SiC about $10,000 per megawatt in the data center; another 10, maybe up to 15 for grid modernization; 25-ish total versus total power content probably 100, 250; 220 gigawatts to 300 gigawatts deployed by 2030

SAM math updated and broken into three pieces: on a 220 gigawatts deployment assumption, GaN plus SiC for data center and the grid — excluding EV and excluding China — is about $3.5 billion in 2030; adding a billion for the JFET (SiC circuit protection / ORing circuit breakers, where it competes with onsemi and Infineon) takes it to 3.5 to 4.5; and the IVR/VPD step (the 'last centimeters' to the XPU) adds as much again, doubling the SAM. Management's argument: a vendor that participates in only one conversion stage 'is not going to sit at the big table' because architects buy the whole 35,000 volt to 1 volt path.
GaN+SiC data center and grid SAM about $3.5 billion in 2030 (ex-EV, ex-China); plus a billion for the JFET takes it to 3.5 to 4.5; $4.5 billion doubled by IVR/VPD

New detail on the pending Claros acquisition: the close is now targeted 'around the beginning of Q4. October timeframe' (tighter than the previously stated before-year-end). Claros' part is an IVR with a 3.3 volt entry, sub 1 volt output, 40 amp per chip, no caps and no inductors, arranged as an IVR array with current sensing — 'if you need 2,000 amps, you put 50 of them. If you need 4,000 amps, you put 100 of them'. Big VPD modules are shipping now, but the tiny IVR chips (Claros, Empower) are 'happening in 2028'; Claros' lead customer is an XPU customer ramping in 2028, so the deal does not change the organic 2026/2027 plan. Management cites ADI's Empower acquisition as the same move.
Claros close targeted around the beginning of Q4 (October); IVR 3.3 volt entry, sub 1 volt output, 40 amp; 2,000 amps, you put 50 of them, 4,000 amps, you put 100 of them; IVR chips happening in 2028

Go-to-market named end to end: Navitas sells both to the hyperscalers and XPU vendors that spec the design (management groups NVIDIA with Google as the vertically integrated rack designers, and separates Microsoft, Meta and Amazon) and to the merchant power companies that are 'basically the buying customers' — 'the Deltas, the Flex. The Light On, the Vertiv. The Eaton.' — and says both sides have to be convinced. The reason the customer set cares: the 'power wall' is now the bottleneck after compute and memory, with many XPU companies 'underclocking their processor because they can't get enough power delivered to the processor'. Data-center SiC is a different competitive set from EV SiC because data center runs at 1.2 kV and above.

Thermal roadmap detail the call did not give, walked along the heat flow from the chip outward. The Strategic Thermal Labs acquisition is valued because it gives Vertiv an opportunity to be very early and very inside the silicon development; liquid cooling keeps evolving and Vertiv continues to add capacity to that part of the business, which Albertazzi says is growing in a very convincing way, with CDU design and orchestration at a primary/secondary fluid network level continuing. On heat rejection - chillers, dry coolers, high water temperature for efficiency - Vertiv is excited about the ThermoKey dry-cooler acquisition and is seeing a lot of attention around the Vertiv CoolLoop Trim Cooler, physically a hybrid between a dry cooler (free cooling, no mechanical refrigeration) and a chiller, which extends the range of when a data centre can run on free cooling while keeping a cooling boost in reserve for days too hot for free cooling. Chamberlin frames this as architecting a different thermal chain by site (Minnesota versus West Texas ambient) with a controls layer such as Next Predict orchestrating the whole system.

Direct answer on hyperscalers developing their own power and cooling products, which the Q2 call did not address: Albertazzi says this is not new to the industry and the behaviours have been there for at least almost two decades or at least a good decade, only now receiving scrutiny. The majority of the hyperscalers still need to rely, at least partially, on players that can support them with technology know-how and depth, because no one is pure in that type of approach - it is not all their own IP, and even where it is their own IP there is a lot of opportunity to do things together given the ability to operate at scale. On the pipeline he says Vertiv sees no sign of weakening despite data-centre siting and financing debates, with frontier labs gradually becoming hyperscalers themselves and the build-out spreading geographically well beyond the US.

First explicit 800V DC RAMP timing, more granular than the May Investor Day or the July call: CEO Gio Albertazzi says Vertiv will start to see an acceleration in everything sidecar happening in 2027, probably second half of 2027, while a fully native end-to-end 800 volt DC powertrain would probably be commercially back end of 2027, volumes 2028. He stresses the future is multi-architecture rather than one winning standard - 800V DC either at the individual pod with a sidecar or as a native end-to-end architecture across the whole data hall - and says Vertiv is delivering nicely on the timelines shared in May with customer validations ongoing and some products already in the offering cycle. CFO Craig Chamberlin adds that 800V is a content-per-megawatt opportunity in every architecture variant (sidecar, pod level, or built into the data centre), and Albertazzi notes the powertrain is getting more complex simply because required performance is rising, which favours Vertiv on content and know-how.
sidecar acceleration in 2027, probably second half of 2027; native end-to-end 800 volt DC powertrain commercially back end of 2027, volumes 2028

Proposed acquisition of Utility Innovation Group (UIG), announced just before the conference and not covered on the July call. CFO Craig Chamberlin says UIG gives Vertiv the opportunity to influence the way the powertrain will be constructed as it goes into the actual data centre - specifically the architecture of BEHIND-THE-METER power - putting Vertiv in that design conversation earlier and, as Albertazzi puts it, physically very early, just behind the meter. The deal carries an earn-out: if the earn-out happens, we would be really happy to pay the earn-out. Chamberlin calls it a home run of an acquisition and compares the logic to the earlier PurgeRite deal - buying what is not in the portfolio to pull through more content and steer how the data centre architecture is built.

Albertazzi narrows the supply-chain congestion flagged on the Q2 call: it was not a generic situation but specifically referred to the converged infrastructure products OneCore and SmartRun, where Vertiv is industrializing something that is a field project and taking construction-site complexity onto itself. The consequences are coordination across multiple factories rather than component shortage, and timing variability - is revenue recognized this day or maybe four days later because some of the components are converging in the integration factory. Integration at this scale is a different capability than the power-module integration Vertiv has done for 25, 30 years, and that integration capacity is being deployed constantly to follow demand. He adds the current outlook already incorporates wiggle room against possible hiccups. Chamberlin separately points back to the ramp in infrastructure-solutions orders (Vertiv SmartRun / Vertiv OneCore) seen in last fourth quarter as evidence of the share gain.

H1 2026: GaN power arrived later than IQE expected but is now inflecting, and MicroLED is overtaking it - "from a technology perspective, GaN power has shifted to the right, but we are now seeing really significant pickup on that opportunity. MicroLED as part of also the overall GaN technology application footprint is really gaining more and more momentum on that and really is almost surpassing the GaN power application." The data center pull is specific on both: "gallium nitride on silicon power epitaxy, meeting the need for high efficiency power supply units within data center infrastructure", and "gallium nitride on silicon MicroLED epitaxy for partners serving hyperscalers for high bandwidth, energy efficient data transfer in AI data centers".
no specific figure (GaN and MicroLED are not separately disclosed; H1 group revenue GBP 64.6 million)

Data center design and power efficiency: Sweetwater 1 is becoming the reference design for Sweetwater 2, Kiowa, Bundey and later projects, with common layouts and equipment plus more modularisation and prefab, explicitly built for successive GPU generations and evolving cooling INCLUDING 800-VOLT DC, all developed in collaboration with NVIDIA - a direct answer to the bear case that AI data centers get rebuilt in ten years. IREN also expects to extract more from sites it already owns: existing sites have SPARE POWER BEYOND CURRENT DEPLOYMENT PLANS that can support more GPUs and revenue WITHOUT NEW GRID CAPACITY, the scarcest input in the industry, starting with new liquid-cooled installs at Mackenzie, Canal Flats and Prince George in 2027. Tools such as NVIDIA MaxLPS, which smooths GPU power draw, and the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture, which runs chips at higher temperatures without giving up performance, let IREN direct more of each megawatt to IT load. Headline PUE has been deliberately conservative at 200 megawatts of IT load for 300 megawatts of gross capacity, and IREN uses a highly efficient CLOSED-LOOP liquid cooling system with minimal ongoing water usage.
200MW IT load per 300MW gross capacity headline ratio; spare power at existing sites supports more GPUs with no new grid capacity

On Texas regulation, management addressed Governor Abbott's directive - which targets transparency, grid reliability, water usage and impact on local communities - by noting IREN funded all required grid upgrades at Childress, sited it a number of miles outside the main town with no residential neighbours, and uses a highly efficient closed-loop water-cooling system with very minimal ongoing water usage. IREN said it welcomes the additional transparency and is positioned well with two very large already-energised Texas sites, and expects a tighter interconnection process to favour real and well-capitalised projects. Co-CEO Daniel Roberts framed the macro backdrop with the observation that across eight models tracked by OpenRouter, weekly token usage across large language models increased NEARLY 17x IN 8 MONTHS, which is very difficult to serve with infrastructure on three-year lead times.

IREN's next-generation data center design, built for successive GPU generations and evolving cooling including 800-VOLT DC, was developed in collaboration with NVIDIA, and IREN expects to use NVIDIA MaxLPS power smoothing and the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture to run more compute inside the same electrical envelope. Scale-across demand driver: because data centers are power constrained, large AI workloads 'are being forced to be spread across multiple data centers because there’s just not enough power in one data center to process these large workloads', which drives demand for very high bandwidth connections between data centers. Parthasarathi split that opportunity into two functional blocks Coherent serves - data center interconnect (DCI) transceivers at the edge of the data center, and optical transport equipment (amplification, signal conditioning, fiber and signal health monitoring) sitting between the data centers - with bandwidth first and energy efficiency second as the metrics customers buy on.

Metcalf describes neoscalers as real-estate-origin operators who build out infrastructure and lease it back to a Google or a Microsoft, and says they are easier to contract with; the hyperscaler terms Powell refuses include consequential damages of 'millions and millions of dollars' for five minutes of downtime caused by its equipment, terms 'you'd never see ... in a utility contract'. POWER franchise detail: customers are pushing for greater than 98% conversion efficiency, multi-kilowatt delivery with peak power up to 2x rated load, plus protection, telemetry and fault recording. Significant design uptick for ADI protection and 800V-to-intermediate conversion technology delivering 20 kW at industry-leading power density exceeding 2.5 kW per cubic inch, as the industry transitions to 800V DC power distribution. At the intermediate-to-core conversion layer - called ONE OF THE FASTEST AND LARGEST GROWING ANALOG OPPORTUNITIES IN THE AI ERA - ADI combines advanced power conversion, intelligent system control and real-time telemetry for next-generation processors operating at 6,000 A and sub-1V. Framing on efficiency: a 97% converter loses roughly 50% more energy as heat than a 98% one, compounding into cooling infrastructure and opex.

Korea's 11th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand projects power demand growing about 1.8% a year to 129.3GW by 2038 with renewables at 29.2%, driven by advanced industry, data centres and electrification. THREE-TIER DEAL MODEL made explicit. (1) MID-TERM core AI cloud contracts of one to three years — four landmark deals closed in Q2 with REFLECTION, COHERE, an unnamed scale U.S. Neolab and a large U.S.-based quant trading firm, averaging MORE THAN $1B EACH at a yield of $20-25M PER MEGAWATT, upfront payments covering 50-60% of associated capex and payback under two years. (2) SHORT-DURATION capacity of up to six months for time-boxed needs (large training runs before a model release, RL post-training sprints) on dedicated GB300 clusters, being negotiated at $40-50M PER MEGAWATT 'and sometimes above' — roughly double the mid-term yield; one such deal signed recently. (3) LONG-TERM contracts with investment-grade customers, used primarily to finance the build-out. Management states it COULD SELL ITS ENTIRE 2027 CAPACITY TODAY on mid-term terms but is deliberately choosing NOT TO, retaining capacity for higher-value short-term demand; it has also tactically shortened how far in advance it sells, selling closer to deployment to improve realized pricing.
mid-term $20-25M/MW vs short-term $40-50M/MW; could sell out 2027 today but choosing not to

FIRST CAPACITY AUCTION as a price-discovery mechanism: it cleared at the highest price Nebius has ever seen for the BLACKWELL generation — 15% ABOVE THE HIGHEST PRICE IT HAD EVER CHARGED and 20% ABOVE its Blackwell pipeline pricing. Management framed it as letting the market set price directly in an environment where 'competitor pricing, analyst opinions, and even prediction markets are all over the place' and 'we have several buyers for every GPU'; the winning bidder plans to participate in future rounds. Both the auction and the short-term scale-training deals remain take-or-pay, use only a small portion of total capacity, and have faster close-to-deployment cycles. On competitive entry (xAI selling compute at premium prices), CEO Arkady Volozh said new entrants 'validate the market' — the AI cloud market is growing tens of gigawatts per year while Nebius plans roughly 1 GW per year, so hyperscalers 'cannot build all of it'.
first auction cleared 15% above highest price ever charged, 20% above Blackwell pipeline

Connected-power guidance for 2026 MAINTAINED at 800 MW - 1 GW, though management cautions that connected power converts to revenue only after commissioning, network build, cluster build, platform deployment and customer onboarding — a gap of a few months, so this cohort is 'active throughout the first half of 2027'. Nebius plans to build MORE THAN 1 GW OF NEW CAPACITY PER YEAR starting 2027, which it says puts it among just a few companies worldwide able to do so. New ASSET-LIGHT PARTNERSHIP MODEL introduced this quarter: partners finance, build and operate facilities while Nebius supplies the full-stack platform and the demand, generating high-margin revenue with minimal balance-sheet capital; dozens of inbound partner inquiries since announcement, still early stage.
contracted power target raised to 5 GW; >1 GW/yr new build from 2027; connected power 800MW-1GW held

Materials: memory and CPU have been severely short for over half a year; more recently PCB and power-related components turned very tight - PCB traced upstream to CCL and glass fibre (Pegatron is chasing material all the way to upstream suppliers in Japan), and in power not just MOSFET/PMIC but power-module supplier capacity is strained, while high-capacitance/high-voltage MLCC shows serious shortage in H2. Purchasing staff are stationed at supplier factories to secure allocations, and some material is brought in early at good prices since failing to pull material forward would delay later deliveries. In PC, customers have already secured H2 key components (CPU, memory, SSD).

Pegatron described a three-layer cooperation with a Taiwanese power-electronics partner: overlapping North American and European customers on power modules with non-overlapping products (a 'fight as a group' effect), the partner's wins in backup power units where Pegatron hopes to build an integrated business model serving end customers directly, and the partner's North American production investment complementing Pegatron's Texas/Mexico sites for resource sharing.

Raised 2026 cash-use guidance to bring forward project activity: operating cash use now $120 million-$150 million (prior $80 million-$100 million) on expensed first-of-a-kind Aurora-INL costs and grid-interconnection build-out; PP&E spend now $400 million-$500 million (prior $350 million-$450 million) on accelerated procurement and construction at Aurora-INL plus an opportunistic fuel purchase for isotope projects; spending weighted to the second half.

Aurora-INL (first power plant): DOE approved the preliminary documented safety analysis (PDSA); site mobilization underway with reactor-area excavation near completion; 2028 remains the targeted go-live; management is 'quite confident in having all the fuel we need for that plant to run at full power' at the 75-megawatt operating level via EBR-II recovered material, Centrus HALEU and DOE plutonium; total project cost with Kiewit still being narrowed, to be disclosed later this year.

Aurora Ohio: advancing a planned 1.2 gigawatt clean energy campus in southern Ohio designed around phased deployment of multiple Aurora powerhouses; entered an MOU with Kiewit for engineering, procurement, construction and execution planning of the initial phase; advancing PJM interconnection applications and transmission studies (more than one interconnection opportunity on the PJM docket). Future power projects 'more likely than not' take place in the Ohio campus.

Customer demand described as 'unconstrained': on the power side 'we've already had the Meta payment, we've had the Equinix payment' and those discussions are the most advanced; every execution milestone 'creates more credibility and it does help those conversations'. Data-center heat-and-power collaboration with Vertiv (heat-driven cooling) announced last year.

Fuel supply — the key deployment constraint — is being diversified: Centrus letter of intent for HALEU covering initial core and reload needs for up to five Aurora powerhouses for multiple years with deliveries expected to begin in 2029 (possible Oklo/customer prepayments to fund the Ohio build-out); DOE selected Oklo for advanced negotiations on surplus plutonium (about 20 tons in the tranche) that as blended bridge fuel 'supports up to potentially 2 gigawatts'; Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility (A3F) equipment now in production for 2027 installation; Advanced Fuel Center recycling facility in Tennessee advancing NRC license readiness.
Centrus HALEU for up to five Aurora powerhouses from 2029; plutonium bridge fuel up to ~2 GW

Execution proof point: the Groves isotope reactor in Texas reached first criticality in early August — substantial construction completed in 229 days and criticality a little over 11 months from groundbreaking, which Oklo calls the fastest greenfield-to-criticality for a privately funded full-scale reactor; the same DOE authorization pathway and in-house build/own/operate organization will be applied to Aurora powerhouses. Acquired ARMEC and Creative Engineers to internalize manufacturing and sodium-systems engineering.
Groves: 229 days construction; criticality in under a year

AI partnership: collaboration with NVIDIA and Los Alamos National Laboratory (part of DOE's Genesis Mission, in which the INL-led Prometheus project received a $60 million phase two award) to build physics-based AI models and digital twins for fuel validation and reactor design — design workflows that took weeks to months now 'done in less than a day'.

→ Meta: Execution experience from Aurora-INL with Kiewit 'can now inform the work required to supply Meta power from the Oklo 1.2-gigawatt power campus in Ohio'; Meta has already made a payment to Oklo and those customer discussions are 'a little bit more advanced'.
units: 1.2 GW campus (phased, multiple Aurora powerhouses)

Power / silicon carbide: bookings improved sequentially and through the first half exceeded the average of the past two years; orders from two new customers in China and from multiple customers for high energy channeling on advanced superjunction architectures. Data centers moving to 800 volt architectures make silicon carbide the material of choice between the grid and the rack, still small but growing quickly; Purion XEmax completed a successful evaluation at a leading foundry for power management IC production with implant energies up to 15 MeV.
SiC bookings 1H above two-year average; Purion XEmax up to 15 MeV

The earnings release states the additional 920 MW of long-term nuclear PPAs signed with investment-grade customers are 15-20 years in duration and set to begin in 2029 through 2032 (the presentation says contracts begin 2029-2031 and are fully ramped by 2032). Among them, a 176 MW agreement with Walmart will enable a 30 MW capacity expansion at the Dresden Clean Energy Center in Illinois. The presentation also says the fleet is positioned to add ~1,100 MWs of uprates, including previously announced uprates and 900 MWs of uprates possible with customer support.

920 MW of PPAs, 15-20 years; begin 2029 through 2032 (release) / begin 2029-2031, fully ramped by 2032 (presentation); 176 MW Walmart agreement enabling a 30 MW Dresden expansion; ~1,100 MWs of uprates

Constellation's 10-Q reports capital expenditures of $2,521 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 versus $1,573 million a year earlier, and attributes the increase in capital expenditures to the planned restart of Crane, the inclusion of Calpine and co-location infrastructure.
six-month capex $2,521 million vs $1,573 million (six months ended June 30, 2026 vs 2025)

The earnings presentation says its growth outlook excludes potential upside from capturing premium value for 147 million MWhs of annual and available nuclear generation in 2029 and from securing additional natural gas contracts. Its detailed base-earnings modeling inputs list contracted clean volumes of 36, 45, 53, 54 and 53 million MWhs for 2026 through 2030; the footnote says contracted clean volumes are updated annually and do not include PPAs signed in 2026.
147 million MWhs of available nuclear generation in 2029 (excluded from growth outlook); contracted clean 36, 45, 53, 54, 53 million MWhs (2026 through 2030)

Q2 GAAP EPS $1.42 and ADJUSTED OPERATING EPS $2.55, up $0.64 YoY, driven by Calpine accretion, HIGHER PJM CAPACITY PRICES and commercial-book performance (realized customer margins + portfolio optimization through volatility), partly offset by more planned nuclear refueling outage days and Illinois ZEC revenue timing ($85M of banked credits recognized vs $200M a year ago - a timing item already inside guidance; the Illinois ZEC program ENDS IN MAY 2027 and this was the final planning-year true-up). FULL-YEAR 2026 ADJUSTED OPERATING EPS GUIDANCE RAISED $0.50 TO $11.50-$12.50 (from $11-$12) at the halfway mark - 'our midpoint is now what used to be the top end of the guide' - with the outlook to be revisited on the Q3 call after summer
Q2 adj EPS $2.55 (+$0.64 YoY); FY26 guide raised to $11.50-12.50

LONG-TERM NUCLEAR CONTRACTING RESTARTED: ~920 MW of long-term nuclear deals signed since the last call, at an AVERAGE DURATION OF 18.5 YEARS, all with INVESTMENT-GRADE customers, priced 'consistent with our view of long-term value' (the $20-$50/MWh disclosure range from March is retained, and management confirmed the executed PPAs fit inside it). Roughly 30% OF CLEAN BASELOAD OUTPUT IS NOW UNDER LONG-TERM AGREEMENT, with the pipeline called 'robust and active'. Counterparties are not disclosed at customer request; the one named deal is WALMART - Walmart's FIRST nuclear PPA and the first such transaction by a major retailer. Critically, management confirmed these are signed contracts that are NOT dependent on the outcome of the pending FERC/PJM decisions. Because the new agreements have later start dates they are not expected to materially affect 2029 earnings, but they extend visibility on base-earnings growth
~920 MW signed, avg 18.5-yr term; ~30% of clean baseload now contracted

CRANE (Three Mile Island) RESTART ON TRACK FOR 2H 2027: the NRC approved the new-fuel licensing amendment request, clearing the path to receive new fuel, and FERC granted the waiver to TRANSFER CAPACITY INJECTION RIGHTS FROM THE EDDYSTONE facility (slated to close) TO CRANE - expected to clear many of the transmission contingencies identified in PJM's initial deliverability review so Crane can deliver full value to the grid. Fleet life extension continued with subsequent license renewal applications filed for GINNA and NINE MILE POINT 1, enabled by New York's extension of the ZEC program, leaving 'the vast majority of our power generation secured through 2050 and beyond'. Operations: 93% nuclear capacity factor and 40 TWh generated while completing SIX refueling outages (capacity factor down 1.8pts YoY purely on planned outage days); 23-day average outage duration - 40% better than the industry average - including a turbine upgrade at Byron Unit 1; nuclear capacity factor ran ABOVE 99% during the Mid-Atlantic heat wave before July 4
Crane restart 2H 2027 (NRC fuel amendment + Eddystone capacity rights); 93% CF, 40 TWh

REGULATORY UNLOCK FOR LARGE LOADS moving far faster than expected. FERC in June ordered EVERY RTO to justify (or revise) how its tariff provides just and reasonable interconnection of LARGE LOADS, and directed PJM to explain why co-located transmission services cannot be made available more quickly; FERC is also willing to study GENERATION AND LOAD TOGETHER AT A COMMON POINT OF INTERCONNECTION, which Constellation has advocated. PJM released proposals for the RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT (RBP) and INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE (IRAS), set a target of 6.8 GW for the RBP, and is running a BILATERAL MATCHMAKING process to pair customers with new supply and shrink the centrally procured amount; the RBP auction is proposed for this fall with RESULTS BY YEAR-END. Co-location rule clarity is now expected in Q1-Q2 2027 (PJM response due ~November 2026, FERC order Q1-Q2 2027) versus PJM's earlier 2029 target. Separately Constellation is urging the EPA to exclude FERC-tariff-directed curtailments from the 50-HOUR ANNUAL LIMIT on data-center BACKUP GENERATORS, which management says may be the most effective way to cover the few peak hours
PJM RBP target 6.8 GW, auction this fall; co-location clarity Q1-Q2 2027 (was 2029)

THE STRANDED-CAPACITY THESIS, restated as the core commercial argument: the grid has unused generation and wires capacity in OVER 99% OF THE HOURS of the year - 'we have a peak capacity concern, not an energy concern' - so the fastest and cheapest path to powering AI is harvesting that latent capacity and managing the handful of peak hours with batteries, demand response, peaking resources and customer backup generation. Management argues existing and new supply are not bifurcated: even a customer that self-manages peaks via Connect and Manage 'will still need to buy energy for all of the other hours', which is where the existing fixed-price, carbon-free nuclear fleet becomes the multi-decade product customers want. Customer sophistication about the grid is now 'as good as the energy companies themselves' - not true two years ago. Management expects the data economy to invest 'upwards of $1 trillion in infrastructure ANNUALLY' and expects PJM deal flow to 'kick off with a bit of a bang' once rules are final
grid unused >99% of hours; data economy capex 'upwards of $1T annually'

CAPITAL ALLOCATION AND PORTFOLIO: ~$2.2B of accretive share repurchases in the four months since the March outlook (just under $2B since the Q1 call plus the $335M previously disclosed), with $2.8B of authorization remaining. Agreed to sell the BRAZOS VALLEY ENERGY CENTER to LS Power for $860M (~$1,420/kW), satisfying the FINAL DOJ requirement from the Calpine acquisition; total DOJ-mandated divestitures should yield ~$5.9B gross at nearly $1,200/kW, a healthy premium to the ~$960/kW implied purchase price of the Calpine assets - a mark management reads as validation of the acquired gas fleet 'in a soft ERCOT market'. The 2029 capital-allocation sensitivity was updated to a FLOOR of $0.20/share with upside of MORE THAN $0.75/share (previously $0.50+ with no floor). The nuclear PTC 2030 strike price rises from $49.88 to $50.88/MWh on the IRS 2025 inflation adjustment (2.8%), adding ~$0.30/share to the 2030 base-earnings view and supporting the goal of double-digit base earnings growth into the 2030s
$2.2B buybacks YTD ($2.8B left); Brazos Valley $860M (~$1,420/kW); PTC 2030 strike $50.88/MWh

Q3 FY2026 (Apr-Jun) revenue $650M, +8% YoY, but ~$90M BELOW the plan given on the Q2 call — the shortfall was production delays at two new contract-manufacturing facilities that are ramping. Adjusted gross profit also carried ~$15M of costs for new-product rollout and the production delays, plus a $15M loss recorded on a planned long-term battery supply agreement (mostly one project). CEO: ex the one-time costs FY margin would have been ~12%, and Fluence remains 'very comfortably' inside its 10-15% gross-margin range on both backlog and new orders — explicitly saying it does NOT see the margin pressure a larger storage peer flagged. Implied Q4 gross margin ~11%.
Q3 revenue $650M (+8% YoY, ~$90M below plan); ~$15M ramp/new-product cost + $15M battery-agreement loss; GM range 10-15% intact (~12% ex one-timers)

FY2026 guidance CUT: revenue to $2.9-3.1B (midpoint $3.0B, ~-$400M vs the prior midpoint) and adjusted EBITDA to -$30M to +$10M (midpoint -$10M vs prior +$50M). The $60M EBITDA reduction bridges to ~$44M of lost margin on the ~$400M of revenue pushed into FY2027 plus the $15M battery supply agreement; the revenue itself is deferred, not lost. ARR of ~$180M by FY2026-end MAINTAINED. Implied Q4 revenue ~$1.4B at ~11% gross margin, of which roughly half was already produced and integrated at the time of the call. Liquidity $863M (incl. $365M cash), expected back to ~$900M by fiscal year-end; management flagged that supporting record order intake may require an ADDITIONAL $300-500M of working capital over the coming year.
FY26 revenue $2.9-3.1B (mid $3.0B, -$400M); adj EBITDA -$30M to +$10M (mid -$10M, from +$50M); ARR ~$180M held; liquidity $863M; +$300-500M working capital may be needed

RECORD backlog of $6.4B, +14% QoQ and >30% YoY, built on record Q3 order intake of $1.44B — nearly TRIPLE the $509M signed in Q3 last year. Fiscal-YTD orders $2.7B, +80% YoY, with utilities and IPPs ~90% of the total. Pipeline exited the quarter at $33.1B (+$1.6B QoQ, implying ~$3B of new opportunities after conversions), with a growing U.S. share driven by data centers. Backlog coverage for FY2027 is ~$2.2B as of 06-30-2026 vs the $1.5B of FY2026 coverage a year earlier (analyst cited ~$2.8B for the year after); CEO reiterated 80-90% (~85%) coverage is the right way to frame next year's guidance. Non-data-center orders of ~$1.1B split roughly 60% U.S. / 40% international.
Backlog $6.4B record (+14% QoQ, >30% YoY); Q3 orders $1.44B (~3x YoY); YTD orders $2.7B (+80%); pipeline $33.1B; FY27 coverage $2.2B

FIRST data-center revenue: orders and awards totaling $850M. (1) A $300M order for a BEHIND-THE-METER project with a data-center developer — Fluence's first data-center deal — where the developer was referred by one of the two hyperscalers Fluence holds MSAs with and is building that data center for the same hyperscaler; lead-to-order took under three months vs the ~12-18 month cycle in its traditional utility/IPP segment. (2) ~$550M of awards in July across MULTIPLE data-center sites under one of the two hyperscaler MSAs — awards, not yet purchase orders, with final technical points being closed and conversion to backlog expected in the coming months. Data-center pipeline grew to 16 GWh, +35% QoQ, now a mix of hyperscalers (majority) and developers (fastest-growing). Hyperscalers buy on QUALITY of power (load smoothing, low-voltage ride-through via Fluence's operating system); developers buy on SPEED-TO-POWER. All data-center projects are 2-hour duration; margins in line with the rest of the book. Manufacturing delays do NOT touch the MSAs — they affect legacy contracts signed 12-18 months ago.
$850M data-center total = $300M BTM developer order + ~$550M July hyperscaler awards; DC pipeline 16 GWh (+35% QoQ); 2 MSAs / 2 hyperscalers; 2-hour duration

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manufacturing sites missed: (1) Houston, USA — a fully automated enclosure plant with 15 GWh/year capacity that Fluence off-takes, run by the SAME contract manufacturer that operates its main Vietnam enclosure facility. Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a utility-interconnection delay (the plant has been running on generators, preventing parallel commissioning work); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected within weeks, FULL production in fiscal Q1 2027. (2) One of two new facilities in China — initial production of Smartstack components (the 'pods' that sit on the skids) failed Fluence's testing and required rework; corrections are implemented, shipping has resumed and the site reached full production in Q4. Management put a hedge and a contingency in the plan and blew through both. Organizational response: Roman Loosen (Chief Enterprise Operations Officer, 20+ years at Siemens) takes over supply chain and manufacturing and Peter Williams moves to product, both reporting to the CEO; framed as an EXECUTION/process-scaling fix, not a change of suppliers. Once Houston is fully ramped, Fluence expects domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog.
Houston 15 GWh/yr, full production fiscal Q1 2027; China site reworked, full production in Q4; ~$400M of FY26 revenue pushed to FY27

SOURCING: Fluence signed a long-term battery-cell agreement with an INTERNATIONAL supplier that covers not just supply but technology-roadmap alignment on how cells behave inside Fluence's modules — securing long-term volume and attractive pricing for FY2027-28 and letting it price future orders with more confidence, at the cost of a $15M charge on one in-flight project supplied by the same counterparty. Explicitly NOT related to AESC (the AESC review, run earlier in the year, drove some strategic expense but produced no announcement); Fluence says it is spending a lot of time talking to battery capacity across the market and sees an opportunity to work more closely with U.S. battery manufacturers. On inverters: Fluence uses ONLY non-Chinese inverters in the U.S. — mostly U.S.-made, some imported from Europe — so it expects zero impact from the FCC's inverter restrictions; in Europe it still uses a mix of Chinese and non-Chinese and is working toward a fully European solution ahead of expected European restrictions.
Long-term cell supply + tech-roadmap agreement (int'l supplier, not AESC), $15M charge; 100% non-Chinese inverters in the U.S.

PRODUCT: Smartstack was 75% of fiscal-YTD orders. Fluence announced Smartstack 10, the platform's first upgrade, raising density from 7.5 MWh to 10 MWh per unit (+33%) — Smartstack was designed as an upgradeable product platform rather than a fixed SKU, so density steps can ship without a redesign. Combined with the proprietary software stack / operating system (remote monitoring, life extension, load smoothing, low-voltage ride-through), density + safety + reliability is what management credits for the data-center wins.
Smartstack 10: 7.5 MWh -> 10 MWh per unit (+33%); Smartstack = 75% of FYTD orders

NEXT CATALYSTS: management expects fiscal Q4 order intake to set ANOTHER company record; the ~$550M of July hyperscaler awards should convert into signed orders/backlog 'in the coming months'; Houston reaches full production in fiscal Q1 2027 and connects to the grid within weeks of the call; FY2027 guidance comes on the next call, framed off 80-90% coverage of the $2.2B already in backlog for FY2027. Fluence is also bidding data-center work with both MSA hyperscalers INTERNATIONALLY, not just in the U.S.
Record Q4 orders expected; ~$550M awards -> backlog in coming months; Houston full production fiscal Q1 2027

Launched June 2026 as a founding-investor platform of KKR (lead), NVIDIA, the Kuwait Investment Authority and Vistra, combining power solutions for data centers with land and other digital infrastructure into a 'rack-to-grid one-stop shop'. KKR is staffing Helix for development; more investors are expected over time to substantially increase its capital access, and it is in direct conversations with all of the major hyperscalers. Vistra is the PREFERRED POWER PARTNER (up to $1B committed, above $500M milestone-gated) and Helix carries the powered-land / powered-shell capital that Vistra does not want on its own balance sheet.
launched June 2026; Vistra commitment up to $1B

→ Siemens: Siemens highlighted its collaboration with Infineon: integrating Infineon silicon carbide power modules into Siemens' latest solid-state circuit breakers — described as a critical enabler for safe and reliable distribution of DC power on the road to 800-volt DC data-center architecture.

Industrial and Defense revenue was a record $133.4 million, up 11% sequentially. The Defense business grew 19% last year and is expected to grow approximately 25% this year across radar, missile and missile defense, drone and drone-defense, communications and wideband electronic warfare systems. At the International Microwave Symposium in June MACOM showcased an X-band front-end module built from its GaN ICs in a highly integrated multichip module, delivering 16 WATTS of transmit power and OVER 40% power added efficiency in a footprint suited to compact high-volume radar. MACOM also received INCREMENTAL FUNDING FROM THE AIR FORCE RESEARCH LABS to support MILLIMETER WAVE GaN-ON-SILICON CARBIDE production maturation. Industrial submarkets - test and measurement, medical, automotive and general multi-market - are also improving, with test and measurement demand driven partly by AI-related engineering and production facilitation, and the small automotive business expected to double its revenue this year.
I&D revenue $133.4M (+11% QoQ, record); defense +19% last year, ~25% expected this year; X-band GaN module at 16W and >40% PAE

Compound semiconductor manufacturing build-out. In Q3 MACOM began installing a new G10 EPITAXIAL REACTOR at the MACOM European Semiconductor Center (MESC) in France to support future growth and technology development for European commercial and defense markets. MESC completed conversion of one production line FROM 3-INCH TO 6-INCH this year with two more process sets to convert in the next four to six months - a conversion that improves quality, reduces cost and DOUBLES CAPACITY, and which many defense contractors have been waiting for. MACOM expects to receive one of the largest orders in MESC's history from a U.K. defense company working on airborne defense systems within a month or two, and expects European defense revenue to start growing materially around 2028. The France site was acquired as a 'fixer-upper' for about EUR 38 million against roughly EUR 25 million of land value and approximately $100 million of capital equipment.
MESC 3-inch to 6-inch conversion doubles capacity; European defense revenue to grow materially around 2028; site acquired for ~EUR 38M

Two U.S. manufacturing notes. First, when WOLFSPEED SHUT DOWN ITS DURHAM FAB, MACOM acquired equipment at attractive prices and put it into service, and has been expanding capacity in Lowell. Second, on the CHIPS Office: a January 2025 plan contemplated $345 MILLION of total investment over five years across the North Carolina and Massachusetts fabs, roughly half expected to be funded by the U.S. government and half by MACOM. Because that plan was written in 2024, MACOM has updated and RESUBMITTED the project plan to reflect changed capabilities and actions already taken, and negotiations on the terms of any definitive agreement continue.
CHIPS plan: $345M total investment over five years across North Carolina and Massachusetts fabs, roughly half government funded

Microchip's data-center catalog revenue outside its dedicated Data Center Solutions unit is expected to grow from approximately $288 million in 2025 to about $500 million in 2026. Management identified grid-to-rack and in-rack power as one of five core applications, supplied by power-management ICs, converters, mixed-signal devices and controllers.

Management said hundreds of catalog design wins are ramping across the data-center rack, including power-management and bus-conversion sockets. Unlike the 14 identified Gen6 programs, these wins are distributed across power-supply makers, card stuffers and module manufacturers rather than contracted directly with hyperscalers.
hundreds of catalog design wins across rack power and control

→ Delta Electronics: CEO Steve Sanghi said Microchip's broad catalog wins are made at power-supply companies, card stuffers and module makers, explicitly naming Delta and Lite-On as customers that sell their products into data centers. The portfolio includes power management, mixed-signal devices, microcontrollers, timing, security and memory.
units: hundreds of catalog design wins across the data-center portfolio; Delta-specific units not disclosed

→ Lite-On: CEO Steve Sanghi said Microchip's broad catalog wins are made at power-supply companies, card stuffers and module makers, explicitly naming Lite-On and Delta as customers that sell their products into data centers. The portfolio includes power management, mixed-signal devices, microcontrollers, timing, security and memory.
units: hundreds of catalog design wins across the data-center portfolio; Lite-On-specific units not disclosed

→ SoftBank: In France, SoftBank has been building a supply chain for AI data center equipment: 'establishing a local supply chain for power modules in Dunkirk to accelerate data center development together with Schneider. SoftBank Group and Schneider are going to set the supply chain for the power module' - supporting the 5 GW France program (phase 1: EUR 45 billion for 3.1 gigawatt by 2031).

Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA $1.767B, +>30% YoY vs ~$1.35B in Q2 2025 — generation ~$994M (vs ~$593M) on favorable hedging (average realized price ~5% higher per MWh), higher PJM capacity revenues, flexible gas run-profile optimization, the Martin Lake Unit 1 restart and the Lotus assets acquired in Q3 2025; retail ~$773M (vs ~$756M). 2026 guidance REAFFIRMED: adjusted EBITDA $6.8-7.6B and adjusted FCF before growth $3.925-4.725B, with confidence in delivering AT OR ABOVE the midpoint.
Q2 EBITDA $1.767B (+>30% YoY); gen $994M / retail $773M; FY26 $6.8-7.6B reaffirmed

2027 adjusted EBITDA midpoint opportunity range MAINTAINED at $7.4-7.8B even though ERCOT forward curves are meaningfully lower than the 10-31-2025 curves the range was built on — offset by higher PJM prices, the comprehensive hedging program and nuclear PTC downside protection. CFO: those offsets 'don't fully offset the ERCOT headwinds, so we would be trending towards the LOWER END of that range.' The range still EXCLUDES the pending Cogentrix acquisition and the above-market premium on the Meta PJM nuclear PPAs, which together could reasonably add ~$700M to the 2027 midpoint. Guidance update expected on the Q3 call (or the first call after Cogentrix closes).
2027 midpoint opportunity $7.4-7.8B (trending to LOW end); Cogentrix + Meta PPA ~+$700M, excluded

FOUNDING INVESTOR IN HELIX DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE alongside KKR (lead), NVIDIA and the Kuwait Investment Authority — a platform combining power solutions for data centers with land and other digital infrastructure to create a 'RACK-TO-GRID one-stop shop' that customers increasingly prefer. Vistra's role is twofold: (1) commit UP TO $1B over time, with any amount above $500M subject to achieving certain milestones; (2) serve as the PREFERRED POWER PARTNER, participating in Helix development projects via contracted new-build or new contracts on existing assets. KKR approached Vistra for the preferred-power-partner role. Vistra retains optionality to develop projects on its own; where it does not supply the power it is 'effectively carried' in its financial investment. Helix launched in June 2026, is being staffed for development by KKR, expects to add more investors over time, and is in direct conversations with all of the major hyperscalers.
up to $1B commitment (>$500M milestone-gated); preferred power partner

Helix is designed to absorb the capital Vistra does not want on its own balance sheet: 'if it's required to do things like POWERED SHELLS, POWERED LAND, that's something we don't believe our shareholders are expecting us to put a lot of capital in.' It also simplifies what are today multi-party negotiations on Vistra's existing sites (hyperscaler + co-location developer + equipment providers). Vistra applies its usual MID-TEENS levered return threshold to any project it powers; Helix carries a different (higher) risk appetite for capital.
mid-teens levered return threshold; Helix absorbs powered-land/shell capital

LOAD-GROWTH VIEW UPDATED: annual load growth of at least 4-6% in ERCOT and 2-3% in PJM through 2030 remain reasonable estimates (Q1 2026 framing was 'at least 5-6%' for ERCOT). NEW ALL-TIME SUMMER PEAKS set in July 2026 — PJM over 168 GW and ERCOT over 91 GW — and the grids met them, which Vistra argues disproves the claim that these markets cannot handle the load growth. Data centers matter 'particularly in 2028 and beyond', but a significant part of the growth is industrial reshoring, electrification, Texas population growth and broader economic expansion: of the ~5-6% ERCOT CAGR, ~3% is non-data-center (oil & gas, residential, small business) and ~2% is data centers.
ERCOT 4-6%/yr, PJM 2-3% to 2030; July peaks PJM >168 GW, ERCOT >91 GW; DC = ~2 of the ~5-6pp

ERCOT QUEUE REALITY CHECK: Vistra's May-2024 forecast of 115-120 GW of ERCOT load in 2030 is UNCHANGED despite the queue growing to what has at times been expressed as OVER 400 GW — Vistra thinks the real data-center number is 12-15 GW by 2030, i.e. the queue overstates demand by MORE THAN 20x. Governor Abbott's directive triggers a data-center audit that will likely pause ERCOT/PUC reviews for 'a couple of months'; Batch Zero baseload results were expected imminently and will slip. Vistra supports thinning the queue. Its Comanche Peak project targets energization at END OF 2027 and is not seen as affected; Vistra has projects in Batch Zero baseload, Batch Zero to-be-studied load and the coming Batch One. Only near-term energizations are at delay risk.
ERCOT 2030 load 115-120 GW (unchanged); queue >400 GW vs real DC 12-15 GW = >20x overstated

NEW-BUILD ECONOMICS GAP: ERCOT year-to-date wholesale power has averaged $30/MWh (same as last year) versus the ~$90/MWh area cited for new-build contracting — '30 is not going to get new stuff built.' The price of generation EQUIPMENT 'has doubled, if not tripled' in some cases, so what was an acceptable build price a year or two ago no longer is. In PJM the $555/MW-day RPB cap 'might get some things built' but a spread around it will be needed for certain projects. Large-load customers are willing to contract with EXISTING assets at a PREMIUM because it is still a discount to new build; co-location can beat even an islanded new build on speed.
ERCOT YTD $30/MWh vs ~$90 new build; equipment costs 2-3x; PJM RPB cap $555/MW-day

ERCOT SCARCITY-PRICING MECHANICS (Head of Commercial): on July 22, 2026 a ~3.5-hour window as solar dropped off required ~25 GWh of battery discharge against only ~31 GWh available on the system, yet the day cleared just $57/MWh because batteries, knowing they would not run out, chased the bottom to deplete energy — 'very easy that that day could have cleared closer to a $400 or $500 day.' Battery returns since the large post-August-2023 ECRS payments have been about ONE FIFTH of investor expectations and battery queues are slowing. Vistra reads current ERCOT softness as recency bias plus lumpy load timing; the load it expects to hook up was always a 2027-2028 event.
Jul 22: ~25 GWh needed of ~31 GWh available, cleared $57 vs potential $400-500; battery returns ~1/5 of expectations

FLEET OPERATIONS: annual spring maintenance completed — planned refueling outages at three nuclear units and 92 planned gas/coal outages — delivering over 97% commercial availability across the entire fleet through the Texas and PJM heat waves. ~7,000 employees.
>97% commercial availability; 3 nuclear refuels + 92 planned outages

REGULATORY: FERC's JUNE 2026 CO-LOCATION ORDER directs PJM and its transmission owners to accommodate co-location and adopt the corresponding transmission services — 'the order itself adopted a lot of Vistra's arguments.' PJM and the TOs, ordered to make a compliance filing by mid-August, have asked for more time; a filing specifying the arrangements and applicable rates is expected within roughly 30-60 days. Vistra opposes the 'bring your own new capacity' mandate contemplated in the IRAS proposal (a 'stick' approach that could require large loads to curtail ahead of those PAID to curtail) and favors incentives for data-center flexibility; it argues IRAS may actually push customers FURTHER toward co-location with existing resources, since co-location avoids transmission build and customers bring backup generation anyway. Customer appetite in PJM remains for BOTH energy and capacity, not energy-only.
FERC co-location order (June 2026); PJM compliance filing ~30-60 days out

The PJM nuclear uprate supported by the Meta PPAs is one of the named uses inside the ~$4.5-5B growth-capital allocation for 2026-2027.

Data-center engagement runs on two tracks. (2) Auxiliary power in and around the rack — switch trays, power sidecars and other high-voltage sockets — where there is 'a healthy roster of design-ins and a strong pipeline of ongoing design activity' with 1,700 volt products for 800 volt data centers, addressable with products in hand today and pointing to revenue in 2028. Battery energy storage: already shipping SCALE-2 gate-driver boards into battery storage systems used alongside renewable installations, and won an important new customer in Q2 — a utility-scale design at a top supplier of batteries for energy storage systems and EVs (customer not named). Rising power demands are pushing storage toward higher-voltage architectures and greater silicon-carbide adoption, which requires more advanced gate drivers. A number of customer engagements are underway for battery storage specifically targeting AI data centers, described as another element of the projected billion-dollar data-center SAM in 2030. Deployments of battery storage are expected to grow at a double-digit CAGR through 2035.
One new utility-scale gate-driver design win; billion-dollar data-center SAM in 2030

These auxiliary supplies sit on the compute tray in a native 800 volt system, powering components such as MCUs, gate drivers and op-amps, and deliver space savings of about 30% compared to discrete silicon carbide designs. Alongside the aux track, the main power path to the GPU is being developed with 1,250 volt GaN as a high-density alternative to stacked 650 volt designs. Aux-power design-ins point to revenue in 2028; the main power path depends on when the 800 volt systems deploy.
units: two reference designs; 1,700 volt InnoMux aux supplies on the compute tray; about 30% space saving vs discrete silicon carbide

AEP TEXAS SUBMITTED 45 GIGAWATTS OF PROJECTS INTO ERCOT'S BATCH ZERO process, forecast between now and 2032, with ERCOT expected to determine eligibility on August 7. The credit support is already in hand: 'just over the past month, we have collected nearly $2 billion in cash or collateral for load commitments in ERCOT, which represents all the required credit support for the full 45 gigawatts included in AEP Texas's Batch Zero filing.' Of the 205 gigawatts ERCOT published as eligible for Batch Zero, AEP is 'roughly, call it, a quarter of that', and the CFO treats its 45 GW as firm — a worst case only slips projects from Batch Zero to Batch One. Critical for the equipment chain: the $78 billion capital plan assumed only about 13 gigawatts of interconnection in Texas and 'does not anticipate this magnitude of load growth', and there is 'almost 100 gigawatts in Texas behind that 45 gigawatts', with 195 gigawatts of parties actively trying to interconnect to the queue.

45 GW submitted to ERCOT Batch Zero (out of 205 GW eligible); nearly $2 billion of cash/collateral posted; $78B plan assumed only about 13 GW of Texas interconnection; almost 100 GW more queued behind it; 195 GW in the interconnection queue

TURBINE SUPPLY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND AEP IS PRE-BUYING IT: an additional three gigawatts of gas-fired turbines secured during the quarter takes total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 gigawatts for deployment through 2031, and AEP is 'leveraging our sizable market position and strategic manufacturer relationships to secure up to 10 gigawatts of incremental turbine capacity through 2035' — an option it is not committed to. Three gigawatts of turbines added in the quarter, taking total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 GW through 2031; option on up to 10 GW more through 2035; about half of the 13 GW already inside the $78B plan

HVDC ramp: plus/minus 400V and 800V systems start mass production in Q3 2026, but Q4 shipments and full-year volume stay limited - larger volume comes next year. On the 110kW power shelf and other new product cycles Delta believes its market share remains high because it engages customers earliest, and the fast generational churn of AI power architecture favors its engineering resources; it declined to quantify share for the Rubin-linked 110kW PSU but asserts market leadership. A solid-state transformer (an energy gateway, not a one-for-one transformer replacement) has its first trial customers in smaller data centers, and a first small fuel-cell line starts by year-end with the first volume line planned next year, with units at Taipower and another test site performing well.
HVDC plus/minus 400V and 800V mass production from Q3, limited volume this year, ramp next year; 110kW power shelf share seen high

H1 capex NT$275 hundred million, H2 above NT$400 hundred million, about NT$700 hundred million full year vs NT$466 hundred million last year

Component supply is tight across the board: lead times are stretching and MOSFETs in particular are short, though Delta's purchasing scale and supplier relationships keep demand largely fulfilled. Memory was the hardest hit - one business unit could not secure memory volumes at workable prices, so it switched designs to second sources and expects H2 shipments to normalize and catch up the backlog without a loss. Management does not expect power semiconductors to repeat memory's shortage dynamics - the two situations differ a lot - but notes power-semi supply is cyclical because capacity investment takes long. On wide-bandgap devices (silicon carbide, gallium nitride) Delta works early and closely with the most important suppliers, keeps talking with them continuously and gets early access to new products, but will not disclose any agreements; it is also broadening its supply chain, including Taiwanese supplier options. Supplier price increases will be negotiated and passed to customers where the business model allows, with a timing lag.

A RARE DOWNWARD REVISION TO A DATA-CENTER PIPELINE — AND WHY IT MATTERS: Exelon's data-center growth pipeline now shows a combined 36 GIGAWATTS, DOWN ROUGHLY 11 GW FROM THE 43 GW previously cited. CFO Jeanne Jones attributes the cut not to demand weakness but to Exelon's own screening discipline: it developed TRANSMISSION SECURITY AGREEMENTS (TSAs) that 'never existed in our regions', and its cluster process now requires a customer to sign a TSA and, importantly, 'PUT UP COLLATERAL BEHIND THAT'. The result: 'what this update reflects is we have now WEEDED OUT SPECULATIVE PROJECTS, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real.' Exelon says it has deliberately kept capex increases consistent with historical levels and only committed capital that was 'certain and durable', alongside its stance on CO-LOCATION and fair cost allocation to shield existing customers from infrastructure costs. This is a useful reality-check datapoint on how much of the headline AI interconnection queue is firm versus speculative.
Data-centre pipeline cut 43 GW -> 36 GW after TSA + COLLATERAL requirements weeded out speculative projects
