Component shortages were the quarter's defining constraint. Critical suppliers 'essentially shut a lot of us down with a hard stop' and the shortages hit faster and lasted longer than anticipated; Modine had previously flagged four suppliers as potential vulnerabilities in its risk-management process. Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.
450-550 bps Data Center margin impact from excess labour/overhead absorption; 150 bps warranty variance; four suppliers flagged as vulnerable; June margin back to normal

Structural response to the shortage: Modine is actively negotiating long-term agreements with its critical component suppliers covering FY 2028 and FY 2029 and expects them in place soon, its existing suppliers are expanding capacity to meet market demand, and in one instance Modine is considering vertical integration. Management noted it has doubled supply-chain spend year after year as the business has grown, and has brought in senior operations talent at plant level to negotiate these long-term contracts and dynamically rebalance launch schedules against available component capacity.
supplier LTAs targeted for FY2028 and FY2029; vertical integration under consideration in one case

Third consecutive quarter of record order intake, driving another significant increase in backlog (analysts on the call referred to backlog more than doubling; management did not quantify it). The drivers were the three largest data-center customers — a couple of hyperscalers plus one large neocloud provider — all raising their forecasts as their data-center build-outs grow; none were named on the call. Order growth is concentrated in air handling units and chillers. On coverage, Modine typically starts a fiscal year with roughly 70%-80% of revenue in firm orders, with firm POs about six months out (two quarters), softer visibility in Q3 and no firm POs yet in Q4 — those Q4 POs, including against the hyperscaler capacity LTA, arrive as the year rolls forward.
third straight record order quarter; roughly 70%-80% of fiscal-year revenue in firm orders at year start; firm POs about six months out

The hyperscaler chiller capacity LTA has begun converting into orders: Modine has already taken a couple of orders against it and expected more 'as early as next week,' in line with its Q4 order-intake expectation, on a typical four-to-six-month lead time from order to build. Management gave the roll-out cadence for the first time: 20%-25% of the agreement in 2027 and 35%-40% in each of 2028 and 2029. The LTA absorbs about half of Modine's chiller capacity, a share expected to fall over time as product manufacturing gets more efficient and the three-megawatt chiller launches. Other customers are in discussions for their own agreements, but sized at 12-18 months rather than the three-year scale of the first hyperscaler deal.
LTA cadence 20%-25% in 2027 and 35%-40% in each of 2028 and 2029; ~half of chiller capacity; follow-on agreements sized at 12-18 months

Capacity ceiling stated: with the capex already deployed and the facilities and rooftops it has in place today, Modine believes the range is 'right around $4 billion' of revenue it can support over time. Going beyond that would require a different level of capex outlay, or a combination of an incremental facility, more efficiency on existing lines, and leveraging the supply chain to produce overflow capacity; design work is moving toward a more modular systems approach in the factory to add flexibility. The remaining chiller lines in Grenada, Jefferson City and the Dallas area are expected to be up and established at some level of efficiency by the end of the fiscal year. Coils production has been consolidated into Grenada and Juarez to allow the Grenada chiller lines to expand while preserving coil capacity for data-center customers; Heat Transfer Solutions sales improved 7%, or $11 million, on strong North America coil volume supporting data-center customers.
~$4 billion of revenue capacity on current capex and footprint; Grenada, Jefferson City and Dallas chiller lines running by end of fiscal 2027; coil sales +7% / $11M on data-center demand

Technology read-through on evolving cooling architectures: asked whether higher inlet fluid temperature specs for future GPU designs reduce chiller demand, management said demand is improving and increasing for Modine because of its free-cooling technology — a higher inlet temperature lets the unit run in free-cooling mode more of the time, driving further efficiency and reducing data-center power consumption, while the chiller and refrigerant cycle stay in place as the 'insurance policy' for temperatures above that band. Chillers support both facility cooling and incorporation into direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems — similar models and SKUs sit on the same data-center rooftop doing both — so Modine cannot split its order book between the two. The enhanced three-megawatt chiller is being introduced to customers and will raise output per line versus the 2 MW unit.
3 MW chiller launching (vs 2 MW today); higher GPU inlet temperatures increase free-cooling/chiller demand

A customer program delay pushed volume out of the quarter: the modular data-center product being co-designed with a specific hyperscaler is in roughly its third iteration of the design cycle, and updates to the prints and overall product specifications moved the build out of Q1. Modine's other new product launches were described as a commercial success, with the strategic customer focus on 'high-quality hyperscalers, neoclouds, and co-location customers.'

Supply capability being expanded rapidly: cell production lines in Japan being converted from automotive applications, cell mass production at the Kansas factory planned for fiscal 2029; module production - second Mexico plant starts mass production in Q2 of fiscal 2027, third plant in fiscal 2028, with localization of the broader supply chain including power supply manufacturers advancing. BBU: full-year aim of 1.7 times or JPY 550 billion maintained, based on demand information collected from hyperscalers. Product evolution: CBU solutions (combining in-house batteries and capacitors with Industry) start mass production in fiscal 2027; preparations for mass production of next-generation BBU built for HVDC to be completed within fiscal 2027.
BBU full-year aim 1.7x / JPY 550 billion; Mexico module plant 2 mass production Q2 FY2027, plant 3 FY2028; Kansas cells FY2029; next-gen HVDC BBU within FY2027

BBU content growth with next-generation accelerators: asked about NVIDIA Rubin production starting and per-rack battery cell capacity possibly rising from 80 W to 120 W, management said the Rubin percentage will not be so high yet but Panasonic's portion will increase including capacity, and as the BBU solution evolves the unit price would go up - required output changes and the total solution expands ('it's not replacing PBU, but it's PBU plus CPU'); non-GPU demand (TPU, ASIC, including CPU racks for inference) is also expanding and is part of the JPY 550 billion full-year picture.
Per-rack battery cell capacity discussion 80 W to 120 W with Rubin; unit price to rise as BBU solution evolves

RECORD BACKLOG OF $53 BILLION - and the big work is not in it yet. Duke Austin: 'The record backlog we reported reflects the demand in front of us, but we're still in the early stages. The larger programs across the utility generation and technology load center markets are ahead of us, and we expect them to stack in the years to come.' The 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV transmission are still in engineering ('We're not in backlog on any of the bigger work yet'), and about 95% of the generation work is not in backlog either. He expects record backlog again in the third quarter and probably the fourth. Book-to-burn will be lumpy: 1:1 to 1:2 in ordinary quarters, 1:5 to 1:6 in quarters when big chunks of projects land (the 765 kV work brought in last quarter was that kind of boost) - 'lower lows and higher highs all the way through'. A large share of the technology work never touches backlog at all: MEP crews can 'book and bill $300 million on a site in a quarter' against an MSA and 'you never see it show up in backlog'. CFO Jayshree Desai on data-center backlog discipline: only items with limited notices to proceed go in, 'we don't put the rest in until the project is a confirmed go.'
Record total backlog $53B; ~95% of generation work not yet in backlog; up to $300M booked-and-burned on a single technology site per quarter, outside backlog

Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

The stacking has not started. Duke Austin: the 765 kV corridors, 345 kV and 500 kV projects and the generation work are 'just starting - a lot of it's in engineering'; they start hitting backlog in the later half of this year, crews go to the field around the second half of 2027, and the compounding effect then stacks out 'throughout what I would consider the decade' and 'well past 2030'. He compares it to 2012-2015, when a batch of big projects compounded, and says the base business is doing upper-single-digit to double-digit growth before any of that lands. The nearest concrete catalyst named on the call is the NiSource generation award: 'I do believe a significant amount of that will go into backlog in the third quarter.'

765 kV / 345 kV / 500 kV plus generation work moves into backlog in the later half of 2026, into the field in the second half of 2027, stacking well past 2030; NiSource generation award expected to enter backlog in the third quarter

VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

Technology is now 15% to 20% of Quanta's business - 'a spectrum from chips to everything, not just data centers' - grown to that share over the last two years off the Cupertino Electric platform, and Duke Austin frames it as a second TAM 'every bit as big as our utility TAM'. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.
Technology = 15% to 20% of the business; Quanta can self-perform 80% to 90% of a data-center build

WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)
Q2 2026 earnings release: Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) of $33.6 billion for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, flagged as a record quarterly or record second-quarter result.

10-Q backlog detail: as of June 30, 2026 remaining performance obligations and backlog represent increases of 41.2% and 21.5% relative to December 31, 2025, with approximately 70% of remaining performance obligations expected to be recognized as revenue within the following 12 months. MSAs accounted for 33% of estimated 12-month backlog and 41% of total backlog as of June 30, 2026. Quanta attributes the increases partly to 2026 acquisitions and partly to additional awards and increased volume with existing customers.

RPO +41.2% and backlog +21.5% vs December 31, 2025; approximately 70% of RPO expected within 12 months; Electric backlog $43,790,038 thousand ($26,680,344 thousand within 12 months) as of June 30, 2026; MSAs 33% of 12-month and 41% of total backlog

Electric RPO $29,114,647 thousand ($20,409,603 thousand within 12 months) as of June 30, 2026 vs $17,963,215 thousand (June 30, 2025); Electric backlog $30,283,298 thousand (June 30, 2025)

→ American Electric Power: Duke Austin, on collaborative delivery with integrated fabrication and VDC engineering: 'if we work together, the fabrication is exponential. It will cost less... much like we've done with AEP on 765.' Separately, the 765 kV work brought in last quarter gave backlog 'a big boost up', and he expects the 765 kV corridors plus 345 kV and 500 kV projects - today still in engineering - to move into backlog in the later half of 2026 and into the field in the second half of 2027, stacking through the decade.

Data center revenue trajectory: approximately $150 million two years ago, $200 million last year, a plan for $300 million this year that was raised to $350 million last quarter and now to $430 million for the full year - growth of about 115%. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance raised by $0.45 to a midpoint of $8.40 on additional data center volume, D&M strength and the Neptronic acquisition; the midpoint implies 27% adjusted EBITDA growth.
2026 data center revenue $430 million (was $300 million plan, $350 million last quarter; $200 million in 2025); adj. EPS midpoint $8.40; 27% adj. EBITDA growth

Total data center capacity once at full production is now expected to be approximately $1.1 billion, up from the prior expectation of approximately $750 million, because OlympusMAX throughput in Olathe and Springfield exceeded initial expectations after lean, productivity and flow-optimization work, and the core Everest cooling-tower business gained space and staffing. Full production capacity is expected in the second half of 2028, with a bias that it could be earlier.
data center capacity ~$1.1 billion at full production (prior ~$750 million); full production 2H 2028

HVAC segment backlog at quarter end was $919 million, up 59% organically year-over-year, primarily driven by strong data center demand; HVAC book-to-bill was about 1.4x. Only formal purchase orders go into backlog - long-term agreements with several customers (mainly hyperscalers) sit outside it.
HVAC backlog $919 million (+59% organic YoY); HVAC book-to-bill ~1.4x

In July SPX launched assembly of the OlympusMAX at its new Madison, Alabama facility and will add production capabilities there during the first half of 2027; Tamco's new Tennessee facility for engineered aluminum dampers is on track for full production in 2027. OlympusMAX is built in both Olathe (core cooling plant) and Madison.
Madison, Alabama OlympusMAX assembly started July 2026; production capabilities 1H 2027

Market shift toward SPX solutions: as more liquid cooling goes under the roof, dry cooling appears to be the most favored heat-rejection solution, with adiabatic and cooling towers also in demand; SPX sees significantly increasing demand from existing hyperscalers and had nice wins with colos and neoclouds. Hyperscalers give visibility several years forward because they need SPX's product to turn the data center on and send teams of 10 people into SPX facilities for two weeks at a time.

Supply chain: SPX engineers its own fans, gear reducers and heat exchangers, giving it flexibility to build in-house or use third parties; before taking any large data-center order its supply chain team scrubs every bill-of-material item to validate it can deliver, having watched competitors fall down on supply chain. Management notes some customer concentration among a small number of hyperscalers.

2026 CapEx guidance of $135 million-$165 million, back-half weighted, covers the plant expansions (some could slip into 2027); regular-way CapEx is 1.5%-2% of revenue. Data center incrementals are expected to match the rest of HVAC at high 20% to low 30% segment-margin incrementals. Neptronic acquisition (controls, electric duct heaters, humidification) adds ~$75 million of annual revenue at low-40% segment income margins, paid at about 12.5x, with data center exposure similar to or a tad higher than the HVAC segment's.
2026 CapEx $135 million-$165 million; incrementals high 20% to low 30%; Neptronic ~$75 million revenue at 12.5x

200-millimeter was still sluggish in H1 with prices declining, but a clear volume improvement is expected in H2, driven by power chip manufacturers whose business increasingly benefits from data center, power supply and power management demand; utilisation is rising but is still below 2022 levels, product mix remains negative because the higher-margin float-zone and highly-doped products (MOSFET/IGBT related) are still in low demand, and power-related inventories at customers are improving but remain elevated. Prices are expected to stabilise in H2 from a very low base before the segment contributes meaningfully to revenue or the bottom line.
200mm utilisation still below 2022 levels; 200mm prices to stabilise in H2 2026 from a low base

DATA-CENTER ORDERS NAMED AS A REFRIGERANT GROWTH DRIVER: in the Refrigerants & Applied Solutions segment, 'strong demand for refrigerants driven by the ongoing HFO transition and ACCELERATING DATA CENTER ORDERS, together with continued strength in nuclear and a recovery in health care packaging drove double-digit top line growth'. Segment Q2 net sales $850M (+12% YoY) with adjusted EBITDA $280M (-6%) at a 32.9% margin (down 648bps on plant-turnaround timing and prior-year production incentive credits); management expects the segment to deliver MID-30% adjusted EBITDA margins in H2 2026 as the 454B aftermarket develops. THERMAL MANAGEMENT is one of four secular trends management names as powering results (with AI, data centers and semiconductor manufacturing), and refrigerant solutions 'including DATA CENTER COOLING' are called core to the company post-Element Solutions. Company Q2: net sales $1.148B (+11%) above the top end of guidance, adjusted EBITDA $290M at 25.3% margin, and FULL-YEAR 2026 GUIDANCE RAISED.
Refrigerants $850M (+12%) on HFO transition + ACCELERATING data-centre orders; H2 margin mid-30s%

CONTRACTED AI/DATA-CENTER LOAD CROSSES 17 GW. Four large-load projects were signed in the quarter alone: three projects in Alabama where Alabama Power added approximately 3 GW, plus a Georgia Power 3.2 GW, 25-year electric service contract with OpenAI at its newly announced site near Savannah, Georgia. Combined, those four projects represent 6 GW of newly contracted customer load, and together with agreements previously signed they bring total contracted large load agreements across Southern's electric subsidiaries to over 17 GW by the mid-2030s. CEO Christopher Womack framed the vertically integrated, state-regulated model (one-stop shop across generation, transmission and distribution) as the differentiator winning hyperscaler and data-center developer business in the Southeast.
6 GW newly contracted in Q2 (Alabama ~3 GW + Georgia Power/OpenAI 3.2 GW); total contracted large load over 17 GW by mid-2030s

PROSPECTIVE LARGE-LOAD PIPELINE STILL ABOVE 75 GW, WITH 8 GW IN LATE-STAGE NEGOTIATION. Womack: new projects continue to be added to the prospective pipeline of large industrial and data-center projects, 'which remains well above 75 GW.' Beyond the 17 GW already contracted there are an additional 8 GW of projects in late stages, including 3 GW projected to be finalized in the near term; CFO David Poroch said those contracts are likely to go into 2028 and beyond, with a couple of them initiating their ramp-up in 2028 and running into the next decade. Womack also noted momentum migrating west, with 100 MW projects already succeeding in Mississippi and increasing activity there and in Alabama.
Prospective pipeline well above 75 GW; 8 GW late-stage of which 3 GW near-term; 100 MW projects in Mississippi

DATA-CENTER LOAD ACTUALLY ON THE SYSTEM IS COMPOUNDING FAST. System-wide data-center load now exceeds 1.2 GW, an increase of more than 500 megawatts over the prior year, and Poroch noted the company 'crossed over the 1,000 MW line this particular quarter.' Data-center usage was 55% higher than Q2 2025 and is up 49% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from large-load customers. That pulled weather-normal commercial sales up 7.4% in Q2 (+6% year to date) and total weather-normal retail electricity sales up 2.3% in the first half - the highest retail sales growth through June in nearly two decades. Q2 adjusted EPS was $1.13, up $0.21 versus Q2 2025 and $0.13 above the company's own estimate; first-half adjusted EPS was $2.46.
Data-center load >1.2 GW (+500 MW YoY); data-center usage +55% YoY in Q2, +49% YTD; commercial sales +7.4% Q2; Q2 adjusted EPS $1.13

GUIDANCE RAISED TO THE TOP OF THE RANGE ON LOAD GROWTH. Management now projects full-year 2026 adjusted earnings to be near or at the top of the $4.50-$4.60 adjusted EPS guidance range, with a Q3 adjusted EPS estimate of $1.50 per share, and reiterated the goal of being toward the top half of the long-term earnings trajectory. Drivers named were increased usage and customer growth, higher AFUDC from ongoing construction projects, higher earnings from equity-method investments, and contributions from Southern Company Gas and PowerSecure, where distributed, backup and bridge power solutions markets for data centers continue to expand.
FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance $4.50-$4.60, now expected near or at the top; Q3 estimate $1.50

GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.
10 GW of new company-owned generation approved (thermal/battery/solar) + hundreds of miles of transmission; Georgia capacity ~1 GW oversubscribed after the OpenAI contract

OPEN RFPs AT ALABAMA POWER AND GEORGIA POWER ARE INCREMENTAL CAPITAL NOT YET IN THE PLAN. Ongoing RFPs at both utilities are procuring additional generation for the early 2030s. Poroch was explicit that 'there is not placeholders in our capital plan... the RFPs that are open in Alabama, the RFPs that are open in Georgia, none of that is contemplated in our capital forecast at the moment,' and gave a sizing rule of thumb of 'about $2 billion or so, a little bit above maybe related to 1 GW of new generating capacity.' Timeline: selections known by year end 2026, a certification process running through much of 2027 with clarity in the latter part of 2027, spend feathering in around 2028, and the generation coming online in the 2030-2031 timeline. Alabama runs a near-parallel schedule.
Capital rule of thumb ~$2B per 1 GW of new generating capacity; RFP selections by year-end 2026, certification through 2027, generation online 2030-2031

HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.
About $21 billion of collateral in aggregate at full ramp across the 17 GW contracted portfolio; minimum bills cover 100% of incremental cost to serve

FIRST FLEXIBLE-DEMAND DATA CENTER: 1 GW OF DEMAND RESPONSE AT THE OPENAI SITE. The Savannah site features 1 GW of flexible demand response, and Womack confirmed this is the first time Southern has done that for a data center. Poroch said demand-response flexibility 'does enter into all those conversations' and is possible because the three electric jurisdictions are not limited to a tariff and can negotiate bilateral contracts that price hyperscaler flexibility. Womack said technical requirements - how a hyperscaler's operations affect the system and the grid, and whether it can be more than 'just a taker' - are raised very early in every hyperscaler conversation, and that peak shaving from this resource benefits the whole system.
1 GW of flexible demand response at the OpenAI Savannah site - Southern's first for a data center

NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'

SOUTHERN POWER TOLLING AGREEMENTS ROLLING OFF ARE BEING RE-AIMED AT HYPERSCALERS. As existing tolling agreements expire, Womack said the team is in the midst of recontracting conversations with a host of counterparties, screened for creditworthiness, and sees upside in pricing versus where the contracts were originally struck - contributing to the durability and length of the long-term plan. Poroch added that conversations with both current and new Southern Power counterparties are 'proving to be very fruitful', covering repricing of expiring contracts into the next decade plus the previously announced uprate/brownfield opportunities, with an update expected later in the year; the business will not 'build something and see who shows up.'

ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT ANNOUNCEMENTS IN THE TERRITORY RAN AT THE SECOND-HIGHEST LEVEL EVER. In the last quarter alone, announcements were made for nearly $14 billion of investment and more than 3,000 new jobs across Southern's electric territories, led by several new data-center facilities in Alabama and a new Amazon warehouse in Georgia - the second-highest investment level ever recorded in the electric territories. Womack said there are no state-level moratoriums on data centers in the territory (though some counties have them) and that hyperscalers need to do a better job explaining the benefits, pointing to the OpenAI announcement as the template for community and rate-stability messaging.
Nearly $14 billion of announced investment and more than 3,000 new jobs in the quarter, led by new data-center facilities in Alabama

→ OpenAI: Georgia Power signed a 3.2 GW, 25-year contract for electric service with OpenAI at OpenAI's recently announced site near Savannah, Georgia. The site is expected to take electric service in phases beginning in 2028 and features 1 GW of flexible demand response to support reliability when system demand is highest - Southern's first flexible-demand arrangement with a data center. The contract carries the standard large-load framework: minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, termination/default payments backed by collateral (lines of credit and surety bonds in this case) targeting an A- or better equivalent position. Womack noted the contract pushes Georgia beyond its recently approved generation capacity by right around 1 GW.
units: 3.2 GW of contracted load, including 1 GW of flexible demand response; service phased in beginning 2028

Mix and pricing: a broad laminate price-increase wave hit in Q2 - the lower the grade, the larger the hike (specific increases not disclosed, they vary by customer). Despite low-end prices rising more, mix still shifted up: M7/M8 ultra-low-loss laminates rose from 38% to 39% of revenue while mid/low-loss M4/M6 grades slipped from 32% to 31%, so the product mix keeps optimising toward the high end and management sees plenty of margin headroom left. The special-products line (thick-copper and special-resin boards supporting power applications) nearly doubled its share over four quarters - 8% in Q3 2025, 10% in Q4 2025, 12% in Q1 2026, 14% in Q2 - with management calling TUC a leader in that niche.
M7/M8 share 38% to 39% of revenue; M4/M6 32% to 31%; thick-copper/power special products 14% of revenue in Q2 (from 12% in Q1, 10% in Q4 2025)

LiquidStack remaining interest acquired (first half of 2026)

Q2 2026: enterprise organic bookings +37%, driving RECORD BACKLOG OF $12.1 BILLION (+70% YoY, up from $10.7B last quarter), of which approximately $6 BILLION IS SLATED FOR 2027 AND BEYOND — high visibility into 2027. Organic revenue +9%, adjusted EPS +11%. Americas Commercial HVAC bookings hit an ALL-TIME HIGH, +50% YoY, with APPLIED BOOKINGS UP 130% — a fourth consecutive quarter of >100% growth, leaving applied bookings up MORE THAN 4x on a two-year stack. Asia Pacific bookings +31% with organic revenue +10%; EMEA commercial HVAC bookings +mid-20s excluding Middle East conflict impacts. CEO Dave Regnery: 'We are certainly seeing strength in data centers, but also broad-based growth across the majority of our key verticals.'
Record backlog $12.1B (+70% YoY, ~$6B for 2027+); applied bookings +130%; FY EPS raised to $15.20-15.30

HYPERSCALER CONTRACTING AND COOLING-ARCHITECTURE MIX: 'many of our hyperscalers now have -- whether it be a MASTER PURCHASE AGREEMENT or a LONG-TERM CAPACITY COMMITMENT with us. So we're gaining a lot of visibility to what they need' (CEO Dave Regnery). On technology mix, Trane sees data-center demand weighted TOWARD AIR-COOLED chillers and, importantly, toward CLOSED-LOOP systems with less evaporative cooling — management pushing back on the 'data centers waste water' narrative. Historical rule of thumb has inverted: water-cooled used to signal a 40-year data center and air-cooled a 20-year one, but that shifted given capacity requirements, and modern air-cooled technology now reaches efficiencies similar to or better than water-cooled. Trane is also 'helping many of our hyperscalers and our big colos design' systems for the DIRECT CURRENT versus alternating current transition.
Hyperscaler master purchase agreements / LT capacity commitments; mix to air-cooled CLOSED-LOOP; DC-vs-AC design support

sales $6.7B, +13% reported and organic; ~3% price; ex-data-center mid-single-digit growth

Data center sales reached $1.5 billion, up approximately 45% year-over-year; management describes a differentiated 'power to compute' model spanning the full data center lifecycle from the grid to the building to the rack and equipment

Data centers are a little over 20% of total Wesco sales on a trailing 12-month basis, with the remaining 75% to 80% of the portfolio diversified across infrastructure, power chain and reshoring demand
data center mix a little over 20% of total sales (trailing 12 months)

Record backlog for the third quarter in a row, up approximately 60% in the second quarter with record backlogs at all three business units: CSS backlog up approximately 95%, EES up approximately 30%, UBS up approximately 80%; growth fueled by multiyear customer commitments and providing high visibility into the second half
total backlog +~60% YoY; CSS +~95%, EES +~30%, UBS +~80%

grid services $300+ million business in 2025; three consecutive quarters of double-digit growth; multiyear hyperscaler award shipping over multiple years

CSS sales +18%; data center solutions sales +~45%; CSS EBITDA margin 10.2% (+140bps)

EES sales +11%; EES data center sales +>70% YoY, ~8% of EES sales; OEM +>20%; EES EBITDA margin 9.2%

UBS (Utility & Broadband Solutions) sales increased 7% with utility up mid-single-digit and broadband up mid-teens; the business returned to a 10% EBITDA margin, with public power competitive dynamics still a near-term margin headwind while grid services accelerates and is accretive at the operating margin line

Record adjusted EBITDA of $487 million, up 24%, with margin expanding 60 basis points to 7.3% of sales on 70 basis points of gross margin expansion; record adjusted earnings per share of $4.57, up 35%

Full-year 2026 outlook raised: organic sales growth of 9% to 11% (up from 5% to 8% previously), reported sales growth 10% to 12% with total reported sales of $26 billion at the midpoint, adjusted EBITDA margin 6.9% to 7.1% (an EBITDA raise of over $100 million at the midpoint), and adjusted diluted EPS of $16 to $17.50. The CSS data center sales outlook was raised to more than 30% year-over-year on continued strength in hyperscale and data center related demand
FY2026 organic sales +9% to +11%; reported sales ~$26B; adjusted EPS $16-$17.50; CSS data center sales outlook raised to >30% YoY

Management says demand is outstripping supply across the electrical value chain: 'the constraint is power and labor' - power is the ultimate largest governor of data center construction, followed by construction labor, with a variety of in-front-of-the-meter and behind-the-meter power solutions being worked; Wesco says it is not yet seeing data center demand crowd out its own non-residential construction business, which grew high-single-digit

Acquisition of Singapore-based Newark Engineering Group closed July 1, 2026, adding mission-critical cooling and thermal management capability Wesco did not previously have - design engineering for mission-critical HVAC systems, in-house fabrication and assembly, installation and after-sales service - and strengthening presence in Southeast Asia and engagement earlier in the data center lifecycle

Third quarter outlook: preliminary July month-to-date sales per workday up approximately mid-teens percent, with third quarter sales expected to grow low double-digits year-over-year and adjusted EBITDA margin slightly lower sequentially on business mix; third quarter results are expected to be announced Thursday, October 29, 2026
Q3 sales growth low double-digits YoY; July MTD sales per workday +~mid-teens %

Wesco's Q2 2026 webcast slides state that data center sales are over $5B on a trailing-twelve-month basis, representing greater than 20% of sales, and that the acquired Newark Engineering Group (acquisition closed July 1, 2026), which adds mission-critical cooling and thermal management capability, had ~$60M in 2025 sales.
Data center sales over $5B TTM (greater than 20% of sales); Newark Engineering Group ~$60M 2025 sales

AI-driven data center infrastructure named the most exciting opportunity — power conversion, sensing, infrastructure control, cooling, photonic connectivity, silicon carbide and gallium nitride across all three business units; current data center revenue mostly from silicon carbide, photonics and CMOS
long-term revenue potential of approximately $300 million annually for data center applications; current data center revenue in the range of $20 million-$30 million

Wide bandgap revenue growing with three new silicon carbide design wins secured and the gallium nitride roadmap on track; quarterly demand still volatile due to temporary order volatility from a major silicon carbide customer
wide bandgap revenue $10.6 million, up 34% year-over-year

Data center load pipeline under contract: 1 gigawatt of data centers in operation or under construction, an additional gigawatt under signed energy service agreements (ESAs), and an expected additional 4 gigawatts of data center load secured by year-end 2027, including at least 1 gigawatt by the end of 2026. Management reaffirmed this as 1 gigawatt this year and 3 gigawatts next year.
1 GW operating/under construction + 1 GW under signed ESAs + 4 GW targeted by year-end 2027 (at least 1 GW by end of 2026)

CEO Bob Frenzel on the data center funnel: 'our high probability portfolio exceeds 20 gigawatts', focused in the Upper Midwest and the Southwest near term, ranging from urban data centers in the 10- to 20-megawatt range to 1,000-megawatt campuses; hyperscalers and large data center developers are largely aligned to larger campuses for scale benefits.
high-probability data center pipeline exceeds 20 gigawatts; projects from 10-20 megawatts to 1,000-megawatt campuses

Generation capital intensity of AI/data center load: Frenzel said that in Xcel's resource-rich regions a gigawatt of data centers would be powered largely by wind, solar, storage and backup gas, so 'for every gigawatt of a data center, you're looking at something like $5 billion to $6 billion of investments on the generation side and maybe more', with the generation ramp extending late this decade and well into the next, plus the transmission needed to support it.
$5 billion to $6 billion of generation investment per gigawatt of data center load

Capital deployment: invested $3 billion in the second quarter and over $6 billion year-to-date in generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure across all 8 states. Management now has line of sight to the $70-plus billion of total investments described in the 5-year plan from last November.
$3 billion invested in Q2, over $6 billion year-to-date; $70-plus billion 5-year capital plan

Incremental (upside) investment plan beyond the base 5-year plan grew to $10-plus billion of line of sight — $7 billion identified in Q1 plus roughly $6 billion added from the SPS RFP award. Data-center-driven capital is generally ascribed to the upside plan, and management flagged further upside from generation RFPs in Colorado and the Upper Midwest, the SPP ITP transmission tranche due later this year, and generation to support the 3 gigawatts of data center demand added to the target plan on the Q4 call.
$10-plus billion incremental investment line of sight ($7 billion in Q1 plus $6 billion added)

SPS competitive RFP result: the independent monitor filed its report on an RFP seeking 1,500 to 3,000 megawatts of incremental nameplate capacity. SPS was selected to provide 2,600 megawatts of new company-owned generation — 2,400 megawatts of renewables and 200 megawatts of natural gas-fired generation — representing 70% of the total recommended portfolio and approximately $6 billion of investment in Texas and New Mexico. CFO Brian Van Abel said the SPS build is there to serve oil and gas growth in the Permian Basin as much as data centers.
2,600 MW selected (2,400 MW renewables + 200 MW gas), 70% of the portfolio, ~$6 billion of investment

Supply chain and EPC capacity lock-in: over the past 3 to 4 years Xcel shifted to being a 'partner of choice' with its Tier 1 suppliers and EPC partners across a 5-plus year portfolio of nearly 13 gigawatts of new renewable generation and battery storage, over 3 gigawatts of new natural gas generation and nearly 2,000 high-voltage transmission line miles. Management said these partnerships 'help ensure that we have access to the labor and equipment capacity that we need to deliver with certainty for our customers well into the 2030s', supported by standardized repeatable designs and one consolidated project execution organization. Van Abel separately framed the build as 15-plus gigawatts of new generation.
nearly 13 GW renewables + storage, over 3 GW new natural gas, nearly 2,000 high-voltage transmission line miles under multi-year supplier/EPC agreements

Transmission position: Xcel remains the largest builder of new high-voltage transmission lines in the country, and Frenzel said 'we might be building 20% of the 765 kV lines in the country that we know of.' The company expects a meaningful investment opportunity from the next SPP ITP tranche, and said more transmission will be needed in SPS to serve both data center developers and electrification of Permian and Delaware Basin oil and gas load.
~20% of the 765 kV lines being built in the US

Project execution in the quarter: achieved commercial operations of Group 2 of the Colorado Power Pathway, began construction on a 150-mile 345 kV transmission project in the Upper Midwest, and placed Phase 3 of the Sherco solar facility into service, bringing that site to 710 megawatts. Cumulatively the development team is helping build 16 gigawatts of new generation and storage and over 2,000 miles of new transmission.
150-mile 345 kV line under construction; Sherco solar at 710 megawatts; 16 GW of generation and storage and over 2,000 miles of transmission in build

Large Load Tariff progress, the commercial framework that gates new AI/data center load: approved in Minnesota (crafted with input from some of the hyperscalers), filed in Colorado and Wisconsin, with Texas expected to be filed in Q3 and New Mexico to follow. Under the Minnesota 'Clean Energy Accelerator charge' construct, new large load customers pay for the generation and the interconnection needed to serve them; Colorado's filing offers two pathways including a speed-and-flexibility option.

Near-term catalysts named on the call: the 4-gigawatt NSP RFP outcome is expected by the end of the year (generation for 2030) and may or may not land in the Q3 plan roll-forward; the Minnesota commission proceeding on the Google Pine Island data center project is expected to reach approval early in 2027; and the Q3 call will roll the plan forward to a new 2027-2031 capital and financing view.
4-gigawatt NSP RFP decision expected by year-end 2026; Google Minnesota approval expected early 2027

New nuclear stance: asked about peers pursuing new nuclear with hyperscaler offtake, Frenzel said Xcel does not see a need for new nuclear in its near-term resource plans and is 'quite confident in our ability to meet the growing needs we have with a big portfolio of wind, solar, storage and gas-fired backups', adding 'we will not be an early adopter of new nuclear power plants at Xcel Energy.' Nuclear depreciation lives were also extended in the Minnesota rate case (earnings neutral).

Xcel Energy's second-quarter 2026 earnings release: SPS's October 2025 RFP solicited 870 MW of accredited capacity through 2032; the portfolio selection report was publicly filed with the NMPRC in July 2026 and project CCNs are expected to be filed in late 2026 or early 2027. SPS' preferred portfolio totals 3,928 MW of nameplate capacity, including 1,305 MW of PPAs (wind 305 MW and solar + storage 1,000 MW) alongside company-owned wind of 500 MW, company-owned solar of 1,890 MW and company-owned natural gas. From its July 2024 RFP, SPS is continuing to pursue approximately 2,800 MW of accredited resources, including approximately 4,000 MW of nameplate capacity company owned resources and approximately 500 MW of nameplate capacity PPAs.

SPS preferred portfolio 3,928 MW nameplate (PPAs 1,305 MW: wind 305 MW, solar + storage 1,000 MW; company-owned wind 500 MW, solar 1,890 MW); October 2025 RFP 870 MW accredited; July 2024 RFP ~2,800 MW accredited (~4,000 MW company owned nameplate, ~500 MW PPAs)

Xcel Energy's second-quarter 2026 earnings release: NSP-Minnesota and NSP-Wisconsin's December 2025 RFP seeks up to 3,500 MW of wind, solar, hydro, standalone storage or hybrid capacity that will achieve commercial operation by December 31, 2030; short-listed projects were announced in June 2026 and filing for regulatory approval is expected by the end of 2026. For PSCo, the CPUC in November 2025 approved a load forecast reflecting 3% compound annual sales growth through 2031 and a generation capacity need of approximately 5,400 MW; the Phase II RFP, expected to be issued in the third quarter of 2026, will seek the balance of resource needs through 2031 after consideration of 3,800 MW of approved acquisitions from the Near-Term Procurement RFP.

NSP System RFP up to 3,500 MW (commercial operation by December 31, 2030); PSCo approved load forecast of 3% compound annual sales growth through 2031 and generation capacity need of ~5,400 MW; 3,800 MW of approved Near-Term Procurement RFP acquisitions; Phase II RFP expected Q3 2026

Xcel Energy's second-quarter 2026 earnings release, in its note on NSP-Minnesota's electric service agreement to power a new Google data center in Minnesota (whose approval request includes a proposed Clean Energy Accelerator Charge for 1,900 MW of clean energy resources), states that approvals for 1,000 MW of resources for the Clean Energy Accelerator program are pending as part of existing resource acquisition processes, and that the remaining resources are expected to be requested in those processes by the end of 2026.
1,000 MW of Clean Energy Accelerator program resources pending approval; remaining resources to be requested by end of 2026

→ Google: Frenzel: 'If you took our Google data center deal, it's largely a carbon-free portfolio of generation assets serving that customer.' The project sits in Pine Island, Minnesota; Xcel has filed the proceeding with the commission, cites over $1 billion of customer benefits and strong community support, and expects approval early in 2027. Google is also making investments in STEM education and in an industry-leading distributed capacity program in Minnesota. Management called the deal a template it can replicate in its Colorado and SPS companies, with other hyperscalers and data center developers asking for a similar structure.
value: over $1 billion of customer benefits

→ Google: Large Load Agreement update: the NSP-Minnesota electric service agreement to power a new Google data center in Minnesota is expected, if approved, to result in approximately $1.1 billion of benefits to NSP-Minnesota's customers, with Google paying all costs for its new service. The approval request, including a proposed Clean Energy Accelerator Charge for 1,900 MW of clean energy resources, was filed with the MPUC in April 2026; a decision is expected in early 2027.
value: approximately $1.1 billion of benefits to NSP-Minnesota's customers

Applied Digital says its standardized AI factory design lets it consolidate purchasing around a common set of qualified partners - including ABB for electrical equipment, BASX for mechanical and cooling systems, and Caterpillar for backup generation - and place bulk orders against a multi-gigawatt development pipeline; with prefabricated skids, modular construction and early procurement of long-lead equipment this supports build cycles of approximately 12 to 18 months per 100 to 150 MW facility.
build cycles of approximately 12 to 18 months per 100 to 150 MW facility

Net sales increased 11% to $1.17 billion; Commercial & Industrial segment sales up 29% to $556 million, driven by ramping data center shipments; consolidated adjusted EBITDA $291 million or 24.8% of sales including a $71 million tariff refund; free cash flow $63 million.

Data center: recognized more than $100 million of data-center revenue in Q2 and secured two multi-year supply agreements with hyperscale customers; the first (announced early June) now includes commitments totaling nearly $700 million for product delivered in 2027; data center backlog stands at $1.6 billion after approximately $1 billion of new orders in the last 90 days, plus a new large colocator win; the second hyperscale master agreement (signed late June) is not yet in backlog and is expected to be 'at least as big as the first hyperscaler agreement... or bigger', covering 2027 and 2028 deliveries on a global basis.
DC backlog $1.6 billion; ~$1 billion orders in 90 days; hyperscaler #1 ~$700 million for 2027

Now expects nearly $450 million of data center revenue in full-year 2026 (up from prior expectation), with $250 million shipping in the second half; about $1.35 billion of backlog is scheduled for 2027 deliveries (nothing yet for 2028); C&I segment net sales guidance raised to low 30s% growth (from mid to high 20s%); consolidated net sales still mid to high teens; C&I business set to more than double in three years 'and we may crush it by next year'.
2026 data center revenue ~$450 million; $1.35 billion backlog for 2027; C&I +low 30s%

Capacity: path over the next 12 months to triple large-megawatt production capacity from the original year-end 2026 target of $1.25 billion (approaching $4 billion); Sussex, Wisconsin large-megawatt plant starts production by end of Q3 (a quarter ahead) with a second line committed; Enercon (enclosures/packaging) acquired April 1st; second packaging facility in Belvidere, Illinois operational Q1 2027 (in-house packaging to cover ~70% of tripled assembly, rest third-party); new capacity in Brazil and Mexico; CapEx raised to ~4.5% of sales; investment payback 'inside 12 months' on current backlog.
capacity tripling from $1.25 billion toward ~$4 billion within ~12-18 months

Lead-time advantage: Generac large-megawatt lead times remain 40 to 45-week versus industry 70, 80 weeks and up to two years at some competitors/nodes (partly packaging constraints); hyperscaler testing shows product 'on market or better' on spec with a next-generation engine; exclusive engine-supplier arrangement in the U.S.; the engine supplier is adding capacity including a facility in France for customers wanting European-sourced engines (passed through as higher pricing).
lead times 40-45 weeks vs industry 70-80+ weeks

Backup attach: seeing 'a healthy coverage of at least 100%, and in some cases up to 125%-130% of the power consumption of the facility' depending on customer uptime requirements (five nines or more drives higher coverage); behind-the-meter turbine/gas-recip sites are viewed as bridge power and still take backup gensets in some projects; fuel-cell sites excluded from the addressable market.
backup coverage 100% up to 125%-130% of facility load

Pricing: market price per kilowatt for large gensets is higher than in Generac's business case of three to four years ago because of a supply-demand imbalance; Generac is not getting an above-market premium for shorter lead times but is capturing share, and expects prices to hold ('price rarely goes in reverse'); hyperscale margins modestly below non-hyperscale. Final product-specific terms for hyperscaler #2 expected over the next several weeks.

Data center revenue will land in the HIGH TEENS AS A PERCENTAGE OF REVENUE for fiscal 2026 and is growing much faster than the rest of the portfolio - very healthy double digits, higher in some subsegments. Over the next THREE TO FIVE YEARS management expects data centers to become ONE THIRD OF THE COMPANY by revenue, and describes the mix as extremely accretive to the enterprise. As the installed base expands on double-digit systems growth, service attachment rates should improve and generate strong service growth, fuelling the data center mix profitably. CEO Joakim Weidemanis framed the era directly: 'this is the age of thermal management.'
Data center ~high teens % of FY2026 revenue, expected to reach one third of company revenue in three to five years

Johnson Controls introduced an AI FACTORY ABSORPTION CHILLER REFERENCE DESIGN GUIDE, which it says demonstrates how advanced thermal management can REDUCE COOLING ELECTRICAL DEMAND BY APPROXIMATELY 44% by converting waste heat into productive cooling. Because those savings free power for compute without increasing on-site generation, management claims the potential for BILLIONS OF DOLLARS OF ADDITIONAL REVENUE OVER THE LIFE OF A 1 GIGAWATT FACILITY for the customer. The approach builds on more than 65 years of YORK absorption innovation. Management noted thermal management can represent ABOUT A THIRD OF POWER in a data center, so multiple percentage points of thermal efficiency are very meaningful - and that what JCI is working on 'goes well beyond a couple of percentage points.' Efficiency now matters more because power availability constrains where data centers can be sited.
Absorption chiller reference design cuts cooling electrical demand by ~44%; thermal management is ~1/3 of data center power

The CDU (coolant distribution unit) business reaches revenue: Johnson Controls WILL START SHIPPING CDUs THIS QUARTER, with most testing and validation complete and some hyperscaler validation still in progress, and it has RECENTLY RECEIVED NVIDIA CERTIFICATION. The CDU pipeline is 'well beyond the hundreds of millions and has now reached $1 BILLION,' built on JCI's Alloy investment plus pilots and early orders. Management frames CDUs as expanding total addressable market per megawatt within a broader thermal management solution set.
CDU shipments start this quarter; CDU pipeline reached $1B; NVIDIA certification received

On the chiller-versus-liquid-cooling debate, management pushed back directly: as rack densities increase and new chips are used, the heat generated in data centers keeps rising and thermal management becomes more critical, so speculation about reduced demand for chillers is 'a very nominal impact if any.' Air handling demand continues with the Silent-Aire franchise increasing, CDUs become more important as liquid cooling is implemented, and controls matter as well. The strategy is explicitly to keep increasing DOLLARS PER MEGAWATT across the whole thermal management chain - including the Armada modular container, which is 'loaded with everything we make.'

Capacity and supply chain: Johnson Controls says it is more vertically integrated than others in its industry, controlling the manufacturing and cost of goods of all FIVE SUBSYSTEMS that make up an HVAC chiller, which gives it more control of its own supply chain; bottlenecks occur occasionally in a high-growth environment. Meaningful physical plant investments made about two years ago are ramping slightly AHEAD of expectations. At the Airside Center of Excellence, applying the business system MORE THAN QUADRUPLED CAPACITY on the computer room air handler line WITHOUT SIGNIFICANT CAPITAL INVESTMENT, while achieving 100% on-time delivery, halving customer lead times, shrinking manufacturing floor space by more than 30% and cutting inventory by 50%. Management expects to need some new physical capacity at this growth rate but believes the business system buys time to ramp it. JCI operates approximately 40 manufacturing facilities worldwide.
Computer room air handler line capacity more than quadrupled without significant capital investment; lead times halved; inventory cut 50%

Edge and modular: Johnson Controls collaborates with and holds an investment in ARMADA, building modular solutions described as 'data centers in a shipping container' in JCI factories and including everything Johnson Controls makes. They are a couple of megawatts today and are forward deployed in remote locations, oil and gas, and defense. Management believes not all future data centers will be mega sites like 1 gigawatt facilities and expects decentralized, close-to-the-edge deployments to keep growing; the TAM is described as significant but still in formation, with more detail promised over the next couple of quarters. Balance sheet: approximately $600 million of cash on hand, net debt down to 1.9x - below the long-term target range - and year-to-date adjusted free cash flow of $2.1 billion. Fire and Security revenue was flat against a flat underlying global market, with management targeting mid-to-high single-digit growth there over time.
~$600M cash; net debt 1.9x (below target range); year-to-date adjusted FCF $2.1B

CALL — COMPUTE PHILOSOPHY, BLACKROCK JV, AND COMPUTE-RESALE OFFERS: announced a NEW STRATEGIC VENTURE WITH BLACKROCK to develop a 1 GW DATA CENTER IN EL PASO, TEXAS (part of 'Meta Compute'; also the template for partnership-based funding). Zuckerberg: 'We're getting A LOT OF OFFERS FOR COMPUTE AT A SIGNIFICANT PREMIUM over what we paid for it' — Meta may sell compute directly, but believes 'there will continue to be a significantly higher margin on selling INTELLIGENCE rather than selling compute'; long-term goal is 'an efficient AUCTION over our compute' like the ads auction. Capacity philosophy: plans geared to MAXIMIZING 2026 AND 2027 CAPACITY ('near-term capacity is more valuable than long-term'); Meta is 'DEMAND-CONSTRAINED — including our core business, where we still have numerous ROI-positive places we would put compute if we had it'; the industry has historically UNDER-BUILT and capacity stays TIGHT for the foreseeable future; 2028+ strategy = flexibility (lay land/power/network foundations now, defer server decisions); NO 2027 capex outlook given; custom MTIA silicon = strategic flexibility + SUPPLY-CHAIN LEVERAGE. Cost reality: Q2 total expenses +55% partly on THIRD-PARTY AI TOKEN COSTS and third-party cloud spend (rented neocloud capacity); FREE CASH FLOW just $784 MILLION on $31.1B quarterly capex; cash $90.3B vs debt $83.7B.
BlackRock 1GW El Paso JV; compute offers at 'significant premium'; demand-constrained incl core; maximize 26/27 capacity; FCF $784M

CALL — BUILD RATE, THE $175B CY2026 NUMBER, AND RPO QUALITY: Microsoft added 31 NEW DATA CENTERS this quarter (88 in the fiscal year) across five continents, added ANOTHER GIGAWATT of capacity, cut GPU dock-to-live times ~50% over the year, and remains on track to ROUGHLY DOUBLE overall capacity in two years. 'Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity' — CPU/GPU fleet efficiency gains and faster capacity delivery are 'QUICKLY MONETIZED' (visible in Azure's +43% beat; spot-market pricing cited as evidence of tightness). ACCOUNTING CHANGE: data-center/office useful life extended 15 -> 25 YEARS from FY27, shifting future DC leases from finance to operating leases — on that basis CALENDAR-2026 CAPEX EXPECTATION IS ~$175 BILLION (investment plans unchanged; FY2026 fiscal actual was $115.9B +80%); FQ1 capex alone will be OVER $50B and FY27 capex GROWS YoY, with operating margins down <1pt and FCF staying positive. FQ4 capex $41B — ROUGHLY TWO-THIRDS SHORT-LIVED ASSETS (CPUs/GPUs, deliberately: short lead times allow fast demand response; land/builds stagger-able). RPO quality: $678B (+84%) with ALL sequential growth from customers OUTSIDE frontier-model companies (+25% ex-OpenAI); weighted average duration 2.3 years, ~30% recognized within 12 months (+37% YoY), beyond-12-month portion +112%; ~90% of the $214B FY26 cloud revenue is non-frontier customers. Azure FQ1 guide ~+45% cc with H1 growth ACCELERATING. Also disclosed: a $3.2 BILLION GAIN ON MICROSOFT'S ANTHROPIC INVESTMENT.
31 DCs in qtr / 88 in FY; +1 GW; CY2026 capex ~$175B (lease-adjusted, DC life 15->25yr); FQ1 capex >$50B; RPO +25% ex-OpenAI; Azure FQ1 ~+45%

AI represented about 16% of total revenue in Q2, up roughly another point QoQ (management cautions AI revenue measurement requires assumptions and keeps refining the model). Computing and enterprise's revenue share rose from 24.9% to 27.3% on a larger revenue base. Premium vs commodity product mix held at roughly 80% premium / 20% commodity. Beyond AI, industrial has grown six consecutive quarters (strong European comeback) and automotive shows a similar pattern; laptop/consumer/smartphone are relatively weaker but still growing in dollars YoY.
AI ~16% of Q2 revenue; computing/enterprise share 24.9% -> 27.3%; mix ~80% premium / 20% commodity

Capacity is tight: Q3 utilization rates will be raised above 90% for BOTH commodity and specialty (from about 85% blended / 80% commodity in Q2) to meet demand and rebuild healthy inventory. Capacity is being expanded across the board - Kaohsiung (the large purpose-built MLCC fab, running tight), Vietnam, Suzhou and Mexico - led by tantalum and MLCC; only less than NT$3 billion of capex was spent in H1 with larger increments planned for H2, and equipment lead times are long so expansion is planned ahead, adding capacity quarter by quarter. Channel inventory is lean and healthier than a year ago: Greater China distribution about 2 months on hand (about five to six turns, versus 3 months a year ago), global distribution about 4 months, high-service channel 5-6 months (from 7-8 a year ago).
Q3 utilization >90% (commodity and specialty), up from ~85%/80%; H1 capex <NT$3B; Greater China channel ~2 months on hand

Management endorsed as 'a fair characterization' the view that high-capacitance MLCC demand ramping alongside next-generation AI servers will force conversion of mid/low-end capacity and put shortage pressure on the rest of the portfolio - part of its customer conversations already cover securing that non-AI piece too, with peers also raising MLCC utilization. Adjacent driver: the whole AI power chain 'from the grid down to the rack of the server' has many voltage step-down/conversion stages needing filtering and ripple-current management, driving strong growth in film capacitors and aluminum electrolytic capacitors plus the magnetics (inductors) and connector lines - embedded across computing, industrial and telecom segments. In notebooks, new tantalum packaging offering higher capacitance in a smaller package positions a laptop recovery as more of a 2027 story.

2Q orders were up about 40%, with Commercial HVAC orders up about 65%, driven by continued strength in data centers where orders were up 4x over last year. Total company backlog - which excludes orders expected from long-term agreements with hyperscalers and colos - is now over $8 billion, up about 40% versus last year and up 20% sequentially; Commercial is about two-thirds to 70% of that backlog and 40% of that is data centers.
data center orders up 4x YoY; total orders +40%; backlog over $8 billion (+40% YoY, +20% QoQ), 40% of Commercial backlog is data centers

Full-year data center sales outlook raised to about $2 billion from the $1.5 billion prior guide - the second year in a row of doubling data center sales. About $500 million was delivered in the first half and $1.5 billion is the balance of the year, with the ramp starting now; the 2026 data center forecast is all in backlog. Total 2026 sales are now expected at roughly $23 billion with adjusted operating profit of about $3.5 billion and adjusted EPS of about $2.90.
2026 data center sales ~$2 billion (prior $1.5 billion); 1H $500 million / 2H $1.5 billion; 2026 sales ~$23 billion, adj. EPS ~$2.90

Data center exit rate leaving 2026 would be around $2.5 billion, which is what existing capacity can support; Q4 data center sales will be higher than Q3 and annualizing Q4 gets well north of $2.5 billion, which is why Carrier needs a new facility. Carrier has repurposed an entire North American facility to air-cooled and water-cooled chillers and expanded Charlotte by 50%, and that is not enough for the demand seen for 2027, 2028, 2029 and beyond.
data center exit run-rate ~$2.5 billion; Charlotte capacity +50%

New U.S. data-center manufacturing site: Carrier is finalizing plans, primarily looking at Texas and Alabama, with a decision expected in the next month or two and the facility to be up and running by the end of the first quarter; long-lead equipment and tooling already ordered. It will build both air-cooled and water-cooled chillers plus vertical integration such as compressors. Full-year CapEx is now about $600 million, including an about $100 million increase for the new site, with a $0.05 EPS headwind from NORESCO exit and site startup costs.
new U.S. site online by end of Q1 2027; 2026 CapEx ~$600 million (+$100 million for the site)

Liquid cooling: Carrier has a 1.3 MW CDU that saw good demand in the United States in 2Q, is launching its 2.5 MW / 2.6 MW CDU this quarter and is on track for a 5 MW CDU around the end of this year; the company looked at acquisitions in liquid cooling but decided to grow organically for now. Carrier's data center portfolio is heavily weighted toward chillers.
1.3 MW CDU shipping; 2.5 MW / 2.6 MW CDU launching in Q3; 5 MW CDU around end of 2026

Carrier is fully booked for the second half; customers are pushing to accelerate deliveries rather than push them into 2027, and management sees no double-ordering risk because it is delivering into a rotable pool under strategic relationships in which hyperscalers and colos have established the share they expect to give Carrier. Additional resources have been moved into supply chain, supplier quality and factory quality to execute the ramp.

Share and margin framing: Carrier started with about 10% share in U.S. Commercial HVAC / data centers and needs to reach roughly 15%-20% to maintain its data center volume if capex slows, versus peers that started at 30%; long-term agreements with hyperscalers and major colos give contractual confidence in coming-year volumes. Data center margins are accretive to overall Commercial HVAC margins (CSA Commercial in the mid to high teens).
share ~10% moving to 15%-20%; CSA Commercial margins mid to high teens

Driven by data centers, the Middle East delivered sales growth of about 35% in the quarter despite a very challenging operating environment; in China, Commercial HVAC saw nice data center orders in July alongside electronics fab demand.
Middle East sales +35% driven by data centers

Semiconductor Solutions organic net sales grew 31%: improved order patterns for power electronics products, growing momentum in thermal interface materials for high-power applications such as AI GPUs and CPUs, and strong and growing demand for advanced packaging solutions from OSATs in Asia. Power electronics and wafer plating both saw volume growth in the high teens; of the 30+% organic growth, 60% to two-thirds was volume and the rest price/mix from silver and gold input prices.
Semiconductor Solutions organic +31%; wafer plating and power electronics volume +high teens

HOW THE SUPER AGENTS ARE PRICED - THREE MONETIZATION VECTORS: Gu said Cadence is 'creating separate price books for these four super agents, and in terms of the pricing, it is all going to be commensurate to what a human designer's skills could be. It will be worth tens of thousands of dollars.' Second, 'Once the customer exceeds or surpass the prescribed workload within that super agent... we want to charge them additional consumption in terms of tokens and extra usage.' Third is pull-through of the underlying tools, because agents 'do not need like 80 hours sleep' and explore far more broadly than a human designer, making the model 'a lot more pay-as-to-usage.' He cited Jensen Huang at Computex saying ChipStack is delivering a 40X productivity benefit.
super-agent price books worth tens of thousands of dollars each; ChipStack cited at 40X productivity

Multi-Rail optical transport platform: scale-across customers are asking for a multifold increase in capacity, but the amplifier/fiber huts between data centers cannot grow - with today's technology a 4x capacity increase needs 4 times more space and 4 times more power, and in many of those roadside enclosures the power simply is not available. Multi-Rail lets Coherent 'increase capacity by a factor of four' within the same volumetric envelope, with power scaling sublinearly. Parthasarathi reported 'a lot of excitement from our hyperscale customers and our OEM customers.'

CRESCENT ISLAND DELIBERATELY SKIPS HBM AND GDDR FOR LOW-POWER DDR: Anil Nanduri, VP of AI Products and Go-To-Market for Intel's Data Center, described Intel's inference GPU roadmap scaling up from the Arc series to Crescent Island and said that 'with Crescent Island, we intentionally chose low-power DDR instead of GDDR or HBM memory' to land on an energy- and cost-efficient point rather than ultra-premium low-latency tokens - a PCIe card an enterprise can plug in and scale. He positioned the portfolio as Xeon plus Crescent Island plus the SambaNova partnership (SambaNova serving the high-interactivity, high-volume token pipe), sold on TCO and ROI rather than peak performance, deployable from on-prem to a neocloud.

CALL — THE FIBER-CONTENT-PER-GPU FRAMEWORK (the definitive supply-side math for optical in AI factories). Base case: enterprise grows at the rate GPUs grow; THREE drivers add on top. (1) CLUSTER SIZE: clusters ABOVE ~130,000 GPUs exceed a 512-radix switch's two-layer span and need a THIRD OPTICAL LAYER -> ~50% MORE CONTENT PER GPU for very large clusters. (2) BANDWIDTH (doubles ~every 2 years): Hopper -> Blackwell kept 100G SerDes so fibers went 8 -> 16 per GPU (content DOUBLED); the RUBIN era jumps SerDes to 200G with lane count flat -> NEUTRAL; Feynman (~2029-30): fibers double again IF SerDes stays 200G, neutral if 400G arrives (BiDi/WDM could offset) — Springboard conservatively assumes NEUTRAL. (3) SCALE-UP, today 100% COPPER: Vera Rubin Ultra NVL576 is a HYBRID step — copper inside each 72-GPU rack, DIRECT OPTICAL rack-to-rack. Bracketing a full-optical scale-up: 14.4 Tbps scale-up / 200G = 72 lanes x 2 fibers = 144, plus scale-out 1.6 Tbps / 200G = 16 fibers -> 160 FIBERS PER GPU = 10x today's 16-fiber scale-out-only content (reality lands between; % of optical ports is confidential). COMBINED: optical content per GPU +1.3-1.5x BY 2028 and 'much, much higher' toward 2030. Status: Q2 enterprise strength is 'ALL JUST SCALE-OUT — we are not yet seeing scale-up or photonics in our results'; orders accelerating; 'if we could make more, we could sell more.'
Content/GPU drivers: 3rd optical layer >130k GPUs (+50%); Blackwell 16 fibers; full-optical scale-up = 160 fibers/GPU (10x); +1.3-1.5x by 2028

Optimus 4 aspiration ~10 million units a year vs ~1 million units a year for Optimus 3

switch revenue exceeding $300 million FY2026; surpass $600 million FY2027 (prior $500 million); UALink 115T sampling second half, volume fiscal 2028

800G Q2 FY2026 revenue more than $25,000,000; demand $35,000,000 to $40,000,000; firmware fix around March; Texas full qualification by mid-year
