800V DC transition: KR says AI racks will need 800 volts DC ('This switch to 800 volts DC is a necessity and not a choice') because upcoming AI racks will consume almost 100 times more power than traditional CPU racks. Grid, turbine or engine-powered sites will need transformers, rectifiers and power-conditioning gear to convert high-voltage AC, while 'Bloom, and only Bloom, natively produces 800 volts DC today.' 'Starting now, every Bloom server we ship will be 800 volts DC ready', with a removable adapter for legacy AC environments, and Bloom offers to convert previously shipped servers with simple modifications. KR says it also cuts copper use (copper is short in transformers) and efficiency losses.
every Bloom server shipped from now is 800 volts DC ready; AI racks almost 100 times the power of traditional CPU racks

New platform 'apps' for AI data centers: (1) rapid load following of the AI load 'without requiring batteries', running islanded without backup generators; KR says this removes the battery supply-chain constraint. (2) Combined cooling: high-quality heat from on-site fuel cells drives absorption chillers that deliver chilled water at around five degrees Celsius. 'We think we can reduce electricity usage in the data center by at least 20%.' Bloom already runs this mode to cool its own factory as a customer demo. KR says the approach avoids hydrofluorocarbons and the vapor-compression chiller supply chain.
absorption chilling could cut data-center electricity use by at least 20%

LPO, LRO and copper: MACOM now has three hyperscalers embracing LPO and is 'in various phases of production' with them - in all cases 100 gig per lane for generally 800 gig modules; management expects LPO to remain a small part of the market for the next one to two years and to evolve into NPO/CPO/XPO. Customers are also investigating LRO at 1.6T using 200 gig per lane chips, and management sees LRO as more likely to happen first than 1.6T LPO. LPO interest is also appearing in PCIe, NPO and telecom front haul. On copper, there is renewed interest in MACOM's linear equalizers to extend active copper cable (ACC) reach at 800G and 1.6T and for backplanes (eliminating retimers, and important at 400 gig per lane), but Q1 contained no ACC revenue; management sees the ACC opportunity as bigger than backplane equalizers, and some customers are evaluating converting AECs to ACCs. MACOM launched a PCIe 6 optical chipset supporting sideband data streams over fiber and a new PCIe 7 equalizer, giving it new exposure to the compute side of the data center network.
three hyperscalers in LPO production phases (100 gig per lane, 800 gig modules); no ACC revenue in Q1

Data center chiller launches introduced 'earlier this week', at 'the big show that's ongoing as we speak'. The YDAM 'delivers up to 3.5 megawatts of cooling in a compact footprint, providing approximately 20% higher capacity density than competing options and enabling warm water cooling for advanced GPUs'. The YKHT offers 'the industry's widest operating range and supports waterless heat reduction, which can eliminate up to 9 million gallons of cooling tower water annually in typical deployments'. The Smart Ready Chiller provides '10 times the insights over a standard remote connected chiller', which management expects to move more customers into recurring service. JCI also released a new reference guide that 'maps the full thermal chain and outlines scalable high-performance cooling architectures for an emerging class of AI factories'. CEO Joakim Weidemanis said 'We continue to work closely with NVIDIA' and that some of the guides 'is in collaboration with NVIDIA'. An analyst asked about the technology path, noting investor worry over NVIDIA and warm water cooling. The CEO would not comment on future launches but said there is 'a significant roadmap behind that'. He said the new products' effect on orders so far is 'very minor' ('it's more about what's to come') and that he expects them to start lifting orders in the current quarter.
YDAM up to 3.5 megawatts of cooling with approximately 20% higher capacity density; YKHT can eliminate up to 9 million gallons of cooling tower water annually

Next-generation MonTitan: during 2026 Silicon Motion plans to tape out its first 4-nanometer chip, a PCIe 6 version of MonTitan targeting hyperscalers, NAND flash makers, storage system providers, CSPs and other Tier 1 customers, developed with multiple partner customers. Design wins are already secured with multiple Tier 1 customers; the controller should drive MonTitan success 'beginning in the 2027, '28 time frame' and is 'expected to ramp significantly in 2028'. CFO (point-in-time plan): the 'upcoming 4-nanometer tapeout in the second quarter' will drive higher operating expenses in the second and third quarters of 2026.
4-nanometer PCIe 6 tapeout in the second quarter; ramp significantly in 2028

NEW PRODUCTS / COMPANION CHIPS (CFO): new products grew from low single-digit contribution in 2025 to upper single digits of product revenue in Q4, in line with expectations, and are expected to grow to about double-digit contribution of total product revenue in Q1; PMIC remains the largest contributor, with customers valuing the interplay between RCD and PMIC, and volume shipments are underway. CEO: growing adoption of DDR5 PMICs contributed to 2025 revenue growth; Rambus introduced a complete client chipset and now offers a chipset portfolio supporting all JEDEC standard DDR5 and LPDDR5 modules across server and client systems. The client market remains minimal for Rambus because clock (CKD) chip adoption is limited to the very high end of the client space, and it will still be minimal in 2026; the long-run goal is 20% share there; the vast majority of the business is in the data center.
new products upper single digits of product revenue in Q4, about double-digit in Q1 2026; long-run client share goal 20%

Edge / physical AI (CEO): at the November STM32 Summit ST announced the first microcontroller built on the 18-nanometer process, next-generation wireless microcontrollers and an updated suite of edge AI software tools. ST says it is uniquely positioned in robotics (printed as 'human wind robotics') through MCUs, MEMS, optical sensors, GNSS and power management, is 'already generating revenues through engagements with major OEMs', and estimates its current addressable bill of material at about $600 per system.
addressable bill of material about $600 per system

EUV roadmap: revenue was recognized on the first 5200B, the High-NA high-volume manufacturing tool, which was shipped, installed and accepted by a customer (unnamed) looking at putting it into high-volume manufacturing for its leading nodes. High-NA customers are still qualifying the tools with good results; 2026 is a year to prepare for insertion, with the first products manufactured using High NA in 2027, '28, and High NA enabling the shift to more advanced technology around '28-'29 for DRAM and logic. The vast share of 2026 EUV growth will be Low NA going into high-volume manufacturing. The number of EUV layers is increasing at key customers, raising litho intensity. R&D: the lion's share goes to EUV across 3 work streams (High NA, Low NA and the 'high productivity platform'); the high productivity platform is an EUV platform for early next decade that can take Low NA optics (more than 400 wafer per hour), High NA optics and potentially Hyper NA optics, letting ASML decide later when to introduce Hyper NA.
first 5200B revenue recognized; first High NA products 2027, '28; high productivity platform more than 400 wafer per hour early next decade

Non-EUV products (CEO): DUV immersion 2150 launched with sub-nanometer accuracy and more than 300 wafer per hour; the NXT:870B KrF system achieves more than 400 wafer per hour and is 'creating a lot of interest' because 'productivity, again, is capacity'. 3D integration: the first TWINSCAN XT:260 was shipped last quarter with a 'lot of interest from our customer', ASML's first product for this market, with more products to be defined with customers. Metrology and inspection grew by almost 30% in 2025 (the CFO cited a 20% increase in applications) on the need for more process control at leading nodes; multi-beam e-beam inspection is progressing toward high-volume manufacturing in the next couple of years.
2150 immersion more than 300 wafer per hour; NXT:870B more than 400 wafer per hour; metrology and inspection growth almost 30% in 2025

Solid-state transformer: GE Vernova completed production of its first unit; it will be tested and validated over the summer at a new testing facility in Upstate New York 'before delivering the completed solution to our hyperscaler customer in the autumn of this year' (customer not named). CEO Scott Strazik: it 'could be a substantial order for us with a new product line in 2027 for deliveries later in the decade.'
first solid-state transformer unit completed; hyperscaler delivery in autumn 2026; potential order in 2027

served market >$500M by 2030 (light guides / generation / detection)

CEO Bill Brennan: 'by the end of this fiscal year, we will be producing HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF UNITS PER MONTH, and then we will increase that production rate to DOUBLE and then even TRIPLE BY THE END OF FISCAL YEAR 2028. The ramp is going to be quite fast. It is going to be quite significant. And we expect to even go beyond that in fiscal 2029.' Margin structure of that ramp: Credo is the only vertically integrated player - it builds its own DSP and its own silicon photonics PIC - and is targeting differentiated features rather than the IEEE-standard 1.6T commodity transceiver, so it expects to hold its margin profile as optics becomes a bigger part of the mix.
hundreds of thousands of optical units per month by the end of fiscal 2027, doubling then tripling by the end of fiscal year 2028, more in fiscal 2029

CEO Bill Brennan sized the addressable market: 'as we look at the markets that we address now, you can measure that market opportunity in tens of billions of dollars', calling Credo still early in its growth story. On M&A he said Credo has made three acquisitions: a group in Canada focused on MicroLED technology (brought in-house instead of working with startups), CoMira (protocol and security) and Dust (leading-edge PIC technology). He will keep buying engineering teams and technology, and any move outside core connectivity would have to be 'a very differentiated system-level solution'.
market opportunity in tens of billions of dollars; three acquisitions (MicroLED team, CoMira, Dust)

Photonic memory roadmap timing: Penguin's photonics work is based on its early investment in Celestial AI, which was acquired about six months ago by Marvell for $5.5 billion. Penguin continues active R&D with the Celestial AI team on an appliance giving very high-speed photonic connectivity between GPUs and HBM, expanding high-bandwidth memory beyond the directly attached HBM inside the GPU. Management said the availability of that product will be second half calendar year 2027.
availability second half calendar year 2027; Celestial AI acquired by Marvell for $5.5 billion

LASER VERTICAL INTEGRATION IS SHIFTING THE HAMR HEAD BILL OF MATERIALS IN-HOUSE: the first generation of HAMR used only external lasers; with the second generation Seagate runs a mix, some products built with its internal laser and some still with external laser, and 'more and more we will go out in future, more the mix will go into the internal laser'. Producing the laser together with the head is 'much lower' cost than buying the laser outside and attaching it to the head later, with additional process and supply-chain risk benefits - a margin tailwind that grows with the HAMR mix.

FIRST HARD SIZING OF THE CPO TEST MARKET, PLUS WHO WINS WHICH INSERTION (CEO Greg Smith): the test-equipment TAM for silicon photonics co-packaged optics is about $100 million in 2026 and is expected to be between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, reaching about a billion dollars of test equipment by 2030 (optical alignment, interface hardware and material handling are a separate TAM). Today it is 'a very concentrated market' - one customer and a very small number of devices drive most of the 2026 capital intensity. A CPO device has four major optical test insertions: (1) the photonics wafer, (2) the silicon photonics wafer with the electronic ICs bonded to it, (3) the singulated optical engine dielets with the mounting plate for FAU alignment, (4) the assembled CPO device. On this first device at this first customer, 'Advantest is strongest in insertion one, Teradyne is strongest in insertion two, a Taiwanese supplier is strongest in insertion three, and Teradyne is strongest in insertion four.' Management flags scaling pain as the reason for 'increasing excitement about copper networking for scale-up' and for NPO, which avoids the yield risk of a full CPO device.
CPO/SiPho test equipment TAM about $100 million in 2026, between $300 million and $700 million by 2028, about a billion dollars by 2030
Teradyne Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-10-2026)

China / ICAPS: China is mostly ICAPS (IoT, communication, auto, power, sensors) for Applied. Applied is seeing growth this year in China and overall ICAPS and gaining a little bit of share in the areas where it can compete inside China, and expects that business to grow a little faster next year than this year. Near-term ICAPS growth is being driven by power in data center and photonics; longer term ICAPS grows mid to high single digits, slower than the AI data center segments.
ICAPS mid to high single digits longer term; China and ICAPS growing this year and a little faster next year

OPTICAL TIMELINE TIGHTENED - CONNECTOR REVENUE 2027, NPO REVENUE IN 2H 2027, CPO AT 400G PER LANE: Mohan said optical revenue starts in 2027 with component-level sales of the glass coupler/connector from the aiXscale Photonics acquisition closed 'in December of last year', which customers are qualifying for their own CPU scale-out applications and which 'might very well end up becoming the first revenue that we see in 2027'. Next is NPO, which Astera considers the right answer at '200 gig per lane data rates' because it does not stress the supply chain while delivering the distance and density scale-up needs; 'we will start to see initial revenues in the back half of 2027 from our NPO efforts. Then full year ahead in 2028.' At '400 gig per lane data rates and even higher densities' CPO takes over, with Astera supplying the full optical engine - its own electrical IC, its own photonics IC (PIC) and the fiber-to-silicon-photonics packaging - landing both on an optically enabled Scorpio SKU and on the XPU side, so a link that previously had no such component gains two. He also corrected a pricing assumption for multi-rack scale-up: as cluster sizes go from 72 to 144, 288 and 576 GPUs the switch radix rises and 'contrary to popular belief that price per lane goes down, it actually goes up with radix'.
initial revenues in the back half of 2027; 200 gig per lane; 400 gig per lane
Astera Labs Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Photonics timing sharpened: Corning is planning to build out a $10 billion business by the end of the decade, from no sales today, selling into NPO and CPO applications inside the server tray, and is building out the supply chain now — hopefully next year we will start to see some sales there. The single biggest variable for the Springboard high-confidence gap is CPO adoption; the CPO supply chain at the scale required does not exist today and is the largest build investors should watch, though management sees no showstopper. Schlesinger expects the adoption inflection in the next four or five years rather than in 2027, with near-term content coming from traditional product sets (polarization-maintaining fiber, FAUs) and GlassBridge-type products a 2030-plus opportunity. Scale-up of the network should begin at the end of next year and run 2028 through 2030; today's growth is scale-out, where clusters above 130,000 GPUs add another network layer.
$10 billion photonics business by the end of the decade from no sales today; first sales hoped for next year; adoption inflection in the next four or five years, not 2027; 130,000 cluster barometer

CPO REVENUE RAISED AGAIN AND THE CUSTOMER BASE IS BROADENING. CEO Mike Slessor: 'we started the year with a view of maybe $10 million-$20 million in revenue. Have now successfully upgraded that to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter' — i.e. the top of the original full-year range is now hit by the end of Q3. More important than the dollars, the concentration is changing: 'one of the exciting things that we're now seeing in the second part of the year is broader production adoption of this TRITON high-volume manufacturing platform at multiple foundries with multiple fabless customers'. Today it is 'pretty concentrated, with one major foundry fabless partnership', but FormFactor is 'building backlog and building the breadth of the backlog where this diversifies a little bit beyond that one customer set'. Installed base: 'hundreds of systems installed worldwide' at close to as many customers, with 'installed now tens of systems' specifically ramping in CPO production. The 2025 acquisition of Keystone Photonics is described as 'really an enabling technology for optical probing'. On the NPO-versus-CPO debate, Slessor said FormFactor has built one fundamental optical probing technology applicable across CPO, NPO and pluggables, and that NPO is not yet pulling in at the scale CPO is affecting 2026 revenue, though there is 'lots of activity' across the customer base. He also embraced the bottleneck label: photonics test is where the industry is constrained, and FormFactor is resolving technical and operational challenges in real time on installed systems.

CPO revenue view upgraded from $10 million-$20 million for the year to reaching $20 million by the end of the current third quarter; hundreds of systems installed worldwide; tens of systems in CPO production

Yuen reframed optical scale-up as an industry-wide story rather than the single-customer CPO story assumed at OFC: to serve 2028 optical scale-up volume the industry needs both CPO and NPO approaches, and by volume 'CPO will be half of the market. NPO is the other half of the market' - roughly 50/50. On the content Lumentum sells, CPO is 'an exclusive external light source market'; half of NPO also goes external light source (ELS) and the remaining roughly 25% of the overall market is still being debated between integrated light source (ILS) and ELS, with more and more movement toward ELS because the optical engine sits so close to the accelerator heat source that an integrated laser becomes the reliability-limiting factor. Even the ILS case will not use pluggable-class lasers: an NPO engine '1 inch by half an inch' packs 6.4T versus half an iPhone for a 1.6T module today, so fewer but higher-power lasers are required and the entire NPO/CPO application moves to '120, 150 milliwatt and above', not the traditional 70 milliwatt pluggable laser. Chinese CW laser supply chatter is aimed at that pluggable market, not this one.

CPO half and NPO half of the optical scale-up market; ILS about 25% of the overall market; NPO engine 1 inch by half an inch packing 6.4T vs a 1.6T module today; 120, 150 milliwatt and above vs traditional 70 milliwatt

CW LASER YIELD NOW ABOVE EML, PRICING SIMILAR: Wupen Yuen (President of Global Business Units) said 'our CW laser yield has climbed up to be higher than EMLs' and that CW pricing 'is similar to EMLs'; with the die shrunk closer to EML size, 'the margin profile is not going to be as good as EMLs, but pretty close with CW lasers', so Lumentum's past hesitance to put more CW lasers out is 'gradually diminishing'. (The Q4 FY2026 call said the CW-EML margin gap had closed considerably; it did not compare CW yield with EML.)

Scale-up optics raised for a second time in two weeks: a quarter ago the next-fiscal-year outlook was zero to $300 million, on the Q2 call Murphy said it would be much higher, and at Citi he told investors to imagine that number is even greater, with NPO and scale-up optics a big part of the guide-up. Marvell already sells TIAs and drivers into third-party NPO modules built for hyperscalers, which he called a billion-dollar business for us already just on analog components, and said Marvell content is very high in the NPO module ecosystem with TIAs and drivers. NPO and CPO will coexist rather than replace each other, with a big NPO ramp in calendar 2028 and 2029 as CPO layers in.
next-year scale-up optics: prior guide zero to $300 million, now greater still; TIAs and drivers a billion-dollar business for us already just on analog components

DCI at 1.6T: Marvell was first to market announcing 2nm DSPs that go inside the module, bring-up has been excellent and the silicon photonics platform is tracking well, backed by 15 billion device hours of reliability data. Marvell builds the modules itself and is investing in its own module manufacturing capacity while also selling the DSPs to third-party module makers. Management cited market estimates that scale-across could 2, 3, 4, 5x the size of the DCI market on top of the ASP-per-generation growth DCI already delivers.
2nm DSP first to market; 15 billion device hours of reliability data; scale-across could 2, 3, 4, 5x the size of the DCI market

On the silicon photonics opportunity split, management said inspection will for sure be the largest opportunity and that this is reflected in the backlog Onto holds now - the bulk is inspection - but Onto is also selling metrology tools with multiple customers adopting a couple of different metrology tools, and sees opportunities for other tools in the space too. On what drives upside or downside to the opportunity, Plisinski said it is not a question of if it happens but how quickly the technology is adopted at the server level and then at the rack level, with Onto playing in both; he cited NVIDIA, Broadcom and AMD as committed to driving it forward and the hyperscalers as committed from a data center perspective, with everyone convinced on the economics and performance benefits. Silicon photonics is also one of the named drivers behind Onto's expectation that it can outperform the market in 2027, alongside the Dragonfly G5 opening front-end markets and Atlas G6 logic expansions.
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

CFO Lorenzo Grandi on the AI data-center mix: the connectivity flow (silicon photonics, microcontrollers and BiCMOS EICs for optical transceivers) generates the strongest revenue, and for 2027 ST expects 'mostly of our revenue will be in MDRF for around 80% of the billing' with only 20% in APMS (thermal and power flows). ST is 'marginal today' in data-center power and is building its portfolio for the 800V architecture, expecting 'meaningful revenue after 2028 for the power'. Silicon photonics is described as accretive to the gross-margin target. For NPO/CPO, ST says it has 'all the ingredients', including packaging, and the timing will be driven by customers.
around 80% of 2027 data-center billing in MDRF (connectivity), 20% in APMS; power meaningful revenue after 2028

Silicon-photonics customers are asking for long-term agreements that lock 'capacity, volumes, pricing, and also with cash advance for many of these agreements that we are signing'; the LTAs cover 'more than one year, two, three years'. ST says it must invest to follow demand, using its 300mm infrastructure, and that the silicon-photonics capacity is fungible with other technologies such as microcontrollers. More broadly, 'we are facing backlog and demand that is well above our ability to serve the market', with the backlog extending 'well inside 2027'; industrial lead times for some products are 'now reaching 50 weeks', and microcontroller distribution inventory is well below the normal 12-13 weeks. A Q2 hiccup at the Singapore fab was escalated immediately by automotive customers.
industrial lead times reaching 50 weeks; silicon-photonics LTAs with cash advances covering two, three years; distribution inventory below normal 12-13 weeks

Silicon roadmap commitment: 'By 2029, we will be completely independent of merchant silicon providers because we will have made our own silicon.' Cisco makes its own silicon and its own photonics, and management says it would not have a hyperscaler business without that because hyperscalers want choice and diversity from the others in the market. Being in the silicon business is a five-year planning cycle versus 24 to 30 months for hardware, and Cisco expects to keep expanding into different use cases of silicon and to keep doing the same thing on the photonic side. Scale in Silicon One comes from over 960,000 customers to amortize silicon cost across volume segments.
completely independent of merchant silicon providers by 2029; over 960,000 customers
Cisco Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-08-2026)

CEO Tim Breen on the silicon photonics growth targets: 'the industry adoption needed to reach those targets has already happened. So I think we now have very limited adoption risk baked into that.' The constraint is now supply, not demand - 'All indicators right now from a demand point of view are flashing kind of bright green relative to those targets... we see much more demand than we can supply out of our current install base, so we will definitely be accelerating that.' Pluggables alone get GF 'pretty much all the way' to the first milestone, with NPO rollout already picking up steam on top. The upside case is co-packaged optics: if CPO sees really broad adoption in the latter part of the period GF 'could blow past those targets materially', because CPO is the technology for the scale-up transition and 'you are replacing 10x the links of scale-out with those solutions, so you are not going to see a linear growth story'.
co-packaged optics replaces 10x the links of scale-out

First photonics customer count disclosed: 'We have more than 40 customers in photonics today, and that number keeps growing as players really invest in their optical roadmap.' Breen added that 'everyone who was touting copper two years ago has either launched an organic or inorganic effort to get into optical'. On the form-factor transition, near-package optics and co-packaged optic designs are 'even taping out in our fabs today' and are 'going into production in 2027 and 2028', while pluggable optical transceivers ramp strongly now; the NPO rollout is being led by 'many of the same players who are in pluggables today'. The core photonics platform roadmap runs from 100 gig per lane to 200 gig per lane to 400 gig per lane and beyond with new materials and modulators, paired with advanced packaging (hybrid bonding, fiber-to-chip attach) as the optical link moves closer to the XPU and switch ASIC.
more than 40 customers in photonics; NPO and CPO designs taping out today and going into production in 2027 and 2028; 100 gig per lane to 200 to 400 gig per lane roadmap

Quantum status update since the Q2 call: 'today we announced that we completed the deal that we announced earlier in the year with the government', a partnership that accelerates GF's investment in infrastructure, tooling and PDK enablement for the more exotic processes - compressing a plan Breen framed as 'What would it take to do those in 2 years instead of over 5, 6 years?'. He stressed the roadmap is not orthogonal to the rest of GF: the exotic materials being proven for quantum - thin-film lithium niobate and barium titanate - 'will be needed for the next generation of photonics', i.e. the next generation of photonic modulators. The platform rests on cryo-CMOS (conventional FDSOI CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin) for qubit readout, plus novel-material integration, advanced packaging and high-speed photonic interconnect.
government partnership compressing a 5, 6 year plan into 2 years; cryo-CMOS characterised at 4 degrees Kelvin

Demand for lasers — EML and CW lasers — is far surpassing industry supply; Broadcom is the leader in leading-edge optical DSPs and is more than tripling capacity year-on-year at its EML, CW and VCSEL factories and indium phosphide factories in the U.S. and Singapore, with capacity increasing significantly for the next two years; Q3 capital expenditures were $532 million with $1.4 billion expected in Q4 to invest in semiconductor capacity
laser/indium phosphide capacity more than tripling year-on-year; capex $532 million in Q3, $1.4 billion guided for Q4

→ Marvell: Celestial AI CPO photonic fabric was framed last quarter at about $150 million of revenue for FY2028 within a ~$300 million scale-up optics category; that category is now accelerating further and is a significant driver of the $1.5 billion FY2028 raise; Celestial team integrated well and remains a key part of the program, with CPO a key part of FY2028 and FY2029
value: ~$150 million FY2028 CPO photonic fabric revenue (prior framing, now biased higher)

→ GlobalFoundries: Sivers continues to stay closely engaged with GlobalFoundries on their partnership; progress driven by customers working with the solutions and evaluating them in their systems rather than by U.S. Department of Commerce funding

PHOTONICS BUILD-OUT (HieFo acquired ~5-6 months ago, plus a series of photonic acquisitions completed in under six months): portfolio now spans GAIN CHIPS (the one product shipping in volume today), HIGH-POWER CW LASERS, SEMICONDUCTOR OPTICAL AMPLIFIERS (SOA, now sampling) and newly-added HIGH-SPEED PHOTODIODES / PD ARRAYS (design team brought on under an industry leader, to be co-optimized with Semtech's own TIAs). High-power CW laser sampled to FIVE-SIX MODULE MANUFACTURERS with very positive feedback on power-conversion efficiency, beam and over-temperature performance; one CW laser splits into 4 or 8 channels for 1.6T and 3.2T transceivers. Beyond the THREE ANCHOR gain-chip customers (all increasing demand), new key customers have been added now that Semtech stands behind the asset. Timeline: CW laser + SOA available for customer sampling/qualification within ~2 months; CW-LASER-FOR-TRANSCEIVER REVENUE STARTS H1 FY2028. Content per transceiver targeted to rise from HIGH SINGLE-DIGIT DOLLARS to HIGH DOUBLE-DIGIT DOLLARS as the industry moves 800G → 3.2T — CEO explicitly clarified this means $80-90, NOT $18-19 — coinciding with the 3.2T cut-in. CFO: PD and CW laser products carry DATA-CENTER gross margins, ACCRETIVE to the ~64% post-divestiture corporate average.
Content/transceiver high-single-digit $ → $80-90 at 3.2T; CW laser revenue starts H1 FY2028

CAPACITY, BACKLOG & PRICING: RECORD BACKLOG — the remainder of FY2027 is 'all booked' and OVER 70% OF FY2028 is already booked. CEO warns the capacity secured MAY NOT BE ENOUGH to support FY2028, ESPECIALLY H2 FY2028, and says there is room in the industry to secure ANOTHER 50-100% of capacity. Actions: acquired an ALREADY FULLY-FACILITIZED FAB in close proximity to the existing photonics site, raising fab capacity 3-4x BY END OF FY2027 (on track); adding BACK-END TESTERS and qualifying ADDITIONAL OSAT partners (test, packaging, die-separation) partly to MITIGATE GEOPOLITICAL RISK; front-end capacity being expanded with a leading partner via PREPAYMENT / CapEx / other means. CapEx was 2% of net sales in Q2 (fab capacity for gain chips and CW lasers) and is expected to grow but stay GENERALLY BELOW 5% of sales. PRICING: 'availability is more important to the customers than the pricing' — NO price erosion expected in the near term and none on orders already in backlog; CFO confirms NO price erosion at 800G. Input costs rising slightly and being PASSED THROUGH to customers.
>70% of FY2028 booked; fab capacity 3-4x by end FY2027; room for +50-100% capacity; no price erosion

LASER FAB FOOTPRINT AND THE US PREMIUM: Murry said 'the lasers are only made here in the U.S.' in the Sugar Land facility, that AOI intends to add further laser production in the Houston area but does NOT intend to put laser production overseas, and that the added laser capacity lands mostly in the latter half of next year aimed at CPO/NPO devices. Asked whether customers pay up for that, he said flatly they are 'willing to pay a premium for U.S. production' - driven by the non-zero possibility of a ban on Chinese-sourced optics, which customers say would kill their ability to build new US data centers.
the lasers are only made here in the U.S.; willing to pay a premium for U.S. production
