Fleet economics: GPU utilization 97.9% (Q4: 97.5%). Of all GPUs up for renewal in Q1, the capacity was renewed or resold at a 20% PREMIUM to prior contracts — and the majority of those GPUs are four years or older ('long, useful life with increasing value'). Q1 delivery was almost three times all of Q4 and 73% of the total capacity delivered in FY2026. ABILENE: 131,000 GPUs delivered in Q1 (1.9x Q4); six of the eight campus buildings (618 MW, 75% of total capacity) now delivered to the customer; customer acceptance compressed to only 24 hours. SHACKELFORD is the next gigawatt-scale campus and is progressing well.
GPU utilization 97.9%; renewals at 20% premium; Abilene 131,000 GPUs in Q1 (1.9x Q4), 618 MW = 6 of 8 buildings (75%); Q1 delivery 73% of FY2026 total

Sites and constraints (Q&A): New Mexico and Wisconsin are ~1 gigawatt each; neither Shackelford, New Mexico, Wisconsin nor Michigan contributed to Q1's 850 MW, and large sites phase in over many quarters. NEW MEXICO: data-center construction on track; Oracle is going through the AIR PERMIT process for on-site Bloom fuel-cell generation (Doña Ana County). WISCONSIN: no on-site generation — power delivered through the grid, working with the Public Service Commission, ATC and We Energies; data-center delivery on track. Neither site affects FY2027 revenue or earnings guidance. Binding constraint has moved over time from GPUs and fabs, to power generation, to data centers. Component prices: 'in a world where demand exceeds supply, prices don't go down, they go up' — Oracle charges more to be compensated and does NOT expect an impact on gross margins; prior OCI gross-margin framework still holds.
New Mexico and Wisconsin ~1 GW each; no impact on FY2027 revenue/EPS guidance; component price increases passed through, no gross margin impact expected

On navigating memory scarcity: a set of Penguin's Integrated Memory OEM customers hold their own supply agreements directly with the memory suppliers - 'whether it is Micron or SK hynix or Samsung' - and that represents about 50% of the business depending on the quarter. For the remaining customers Penguin procures the memory itself on long-term relationships and supplier contracts, which management says gives Penguin more pricing power in a supply-constrained environment because it is both securing the memory and adding design, validation and manufacturing value on the board.

SCALE AND CAPITAL EFFICIENCY AS THE MOAT (CEO): 'Between us and our JV partner, we produce roughly a third of the world's NAND', which sets the R&D budget - 'you can roughly afford to invest R&D commensurate with your market share'. The R&D goal is explicitly capital productivity: 'How do I produce the incremental terabyte or incremental petabyte of supply with the least amount of capital?' Management also quantified how much supply growth is available without new fabs: 'just through the application of what I'll call intellectual capital, new nodal transitions, we can grow at a compounded 27% growth rate if we look at a 10-year period... that's not new CapEx.' On competition, China is characterised as 'kind of a China for China story at this point, and I expect that to continue.'
roughly a third of the world's NAND; compounded 27% growth rate over a 10-year period, not new CapEx

DEMAND IS ABOVE SUPPLY IN EVERY SEGMENT AND SEAGATE IS ALLOCATING: data center is about 80% of revenue (the big drives) and edge/IoT - consumer, client, part of video surveillance, drives of roughly 2 terabytes to 10, 12, maybe 14 - is 20%. 'Demand is above supply in every segment today', so Seagate allocates, giving priority to the big data center customers. In edge there are no purchase orders, no LTAs and no specific big customers, so Seagate changed its pricing strategy there in the last couple of quarters; high NAND pricing today is letting low-capacity HDDs take price while keeping volume 'fairly consistent'.
data center ~80% of revenue, edge/IoT 20%; demand above supply in every segment; edge drives 2 terabytes to 10, 12, maybe 14

GPU ALLOCATION IS THE ONE PIECE SPACEX DOES NOT CONTROL: Johnsen on the NVIDIA relationship - 'we came out and talked about the fact that we're NVIDIA exclusive. That strong relationship, we hope certainly will translate into good allocation from a compute perspective because that's the piece that we don't control.' He argued SpaceX earns allocation by actually standing the compute up, 'not maybe not just for themselves, but also for the industry.' On residual value he said 'you are seeing the monetization of many generations old now compute from NVIDIA still holding its own from a pricing perspective', which is creating 'a whole asset class related to GPU financing.'
SpaceX Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-10-2026)

Capacity and constraints: Corning is not fiber constrained today but expects to be, which is why it committed to significantly increase US fiber capacity at what it calls the world's largest, lowest-cost fiber factory; that capacity starts coming online in the not that distant future and is tied to customer agreements. Cable and connectivity capacity has been added quarter over quarter for close to a year, and connectivity is where Corning expects to be most constrained relative to today's capacity as scale-up drives growth. Customers are funding part of the build through deposits they earn back by purchasing, and Corning modularises capacity adds rather than bringing on a whole factory at a time.

Supply is running out in the core US market and permitting risk is now geographic. Northern Virginia: 'We are running out of available capacity in a place like Northern Virginia. We have 50 megawatts available today for lease, and probably another 96-megawatt building behind it. But after that, it could be some time.' Digital Realty is siting new capacity in markets like Kansas City instead. On moratoria: no new development exposure in places like New York or Pennsylvania; a temporary moratorium in Charlotte covers three projects that are all vested (two underway, the third buildable and approved). Customers are pulling delivery forward - asking for extra crews and paying for early handover ('May cost a little extra and they're paying for it') - because time to power is paramount.
Northern Virginia: 50 megawatts available for lease plus a 96-megawatt building behind it; three vested projects in Charlotte under a temporary moratorium
Digital Realty Bank of America conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

CAPACITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND FARMERS BRANCH IS THE RELEASE VALVE. Slessor: 'right now, the simplest way to think about our situation is we are capacity constrained. What's limiting our growth, if you will, or what's constraining our growth, is our capacity.' Farmers Branch, Texas is 'close to a 300,000 square foot site' bought a little over a year ago with a ready-to-go clean room and expansion potential; a grand opening is set for 'late October'; the site is expected to deliver 'twice the current California probe card capacity in the current phase'. Timing: 'Start to ship the initial qualification units in the fourth quarter, and again, ramping through 2027 to deliver a substantial increase, essentially 2X the existing capacity as we get through the back part of 2027.' Capacity will be turned on in tranches matched to demand to avoid utilisation and gross-margin headwinds. On the target model — '55% gross margin, $5 of earnings per share on $1.6 billion of revenue' in 2030 — he said the external high-single-digit market growth assumption was arguably too conservative and that FormFactor could 'reach the target model faster than 2030' if demand holds.

Farmers Branch: close to a 300,000 square foot site, grand opening in late October, twice the current California probe card capacity in the current phase; initial qualification units ship in the fourth quarter, 2X the existing capacity by the back part of 2027; target model 55% gross margin, $5 of earnings per share on $1.6 billion of revenue

FIRST READ ON 2028: the CY2026 WFE walk ('from $135 billion to $140 billion, now to low $150 billion'), the clean-room constraint and the '8 to 10 new, what I would call tier 1 fabs coming online ... through the end of 2027' were all reaffirmations of the Q4 FY2026 call. NEW here is the year beyond: CFO Doug Bettinger would not commit to a 2028 number, but said that because customers are telling him 2027 is still undersupplied, that 'leads you to think 2028 is probably a pretty decent year as well'. He framed the constraint as easing rather than lifting - WFE grows next year while the clean-room limit 'will get somewhat better' - with the industry still 'fundamentally under-supplying demand'.
2028 called 'probably a pretty decent year as well' (no number); reaffirmed: CY2026 WFE walked $135 billion -> $140 billion -> low $150 billion, 8 to 10 new tier 1 fabs through the end of 2027
Lam Research Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

LAM'S OWN CAPACITY RESPONSE: Bettinger said Lam is pulling hard to bring a second facility in Malaysia online sooner - 'essentially a cookie cutter of the previous facility' - and is densifying existing footprints to get more output from the same square footage of clean room it already had ('you didn't know you needed to until you needed to'), plus hiring and training so Lam is 'not going to be the bottleneck'. Lam's lead time to add capacity is shorter than a customer's clean-room lead time, and the same customer demand signals (point estimate, upside, timing, error bar) are propagated back to Lam's supply chain. With thousands of parts per tool 'there's always something that is constraining us'.
Lam Research Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

WHAT IS DRIVING THE CSPG RECORD - AND THE SERVICE MODEL BEHIND IT: the headline ('third consecutive record, nearly $2.5 billion in revenue from CSPG', more than 100K installed chambers, cobots on 8 tool types) repeats the Q4/Q3 FY2026 calls. NEW is the why: Bettinger said spare parts are the biggest individual component of CSPG and 'utilization in the industry is basically at 100%, so spare parts consumption is high. That's going to continue, for sure' - the first time the utilization level itself is quantified; upgrades carry a heavy NAND footprint; and the Reliant mature-node line is strengthening in analog and industrial. He also positioned the outcome-based service model (cobots plus Equipment Intelligence and algorithmic fleet analysis) competitively for the first time - Lam is 'quite a ways ahead of this' and he expects customers to push competitors to copy it.
industry utilization basically at 100% driving spare-parts consumption (reaffirmed: CSPG nearly $2.5 billion, third consecutive record; cobots on 8 tool types)
Lam Research Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Post-earnings supply update: the supply-demand gap is 'still extending' and Lumentum is 'still short everywhere' - DML short, CW laser short. Yuen does not see the shortage going away in 2027; the industry forecasts scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027 while laser supply does not catch up, and 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x increase of demand, so the laser supply-demand gap does not close within the next couple of years. Lumentum is still allocating capacity, in some cases on pricing and expedite fees, to serve the most profitable opportunities, and 'all the deals we are making today are equal or higher pricing than the escalated pricing that we already had before' - management's own read that the gap persists.
scale-out module volume doubling from 2026 to 2027; 2028 scale-up drives another 3 to 4x demand increase; gap does not close within the next couple of years

Three-wave ultra-high-power (UHP) laser capacity ramp laid out for the first time: wave one is the San Jose fab, ramping today with line of sight through 2027; wave two is the U.K. fab, which 'will come in in second quarter 2027' and continues ramping through 2028; wave three is the Greensboro fab, starting to ramp in 'second quarter 2028 or mid 2028'. All three are on schedule and the biggest variable is customer qualification timing - Lumentum must submit a PCN for the customer to qualify the product, and accelerating that qualification can pull the ramp in. Capacity is additive rather than reallocated: a new clean room in the U.K. fitted with 'the latest and greatest state-of-the-art equipment', and the added capacity is '6-inch capable', so current telecom and scale-across products are not sacrificed - 'by and large, we do not sacrifice. We add.'
San Jose ramping through 2027; U.K. fab second quarter 2027 ramping through 2028; Greensboro second quarter 2028 or mid 2028; new 6-inch capable capacity

Competitive read on high-power CPO/NPO lasers: Yuen named Coherent as the single competitor - 'we see the one competitor, right, who is Coherent' - and said Lumentum is 'really not seeing anybody else in this high-power laser area'. He described why the part is hard (power, RIN noise, linewidth and mode hop all have to be achieved simultaneously at volume with good yield, and mode hop is the biggest problem with today's silicon photonics lasers), noted Lumentum is already ramping these lasers and seeing good real data, and then said the industry needs a second source: from a customer's point of view Coherent would need to be ramping 'sometime in 2027... Probably second half' to support the scale-up build in 2028.
Coherent second source needed around the second half of 2027 to support the 2028 scale-up ramp

Supply: over the past year the supply chain has been able to flex up 50%, taking the two-year revenue plan from $20 billion to $30 billion. Marvell reaches production more than 90%-plus of the time on first-pass silicon on advanced nodes. TSMC remains the sole-source fab vendor, with long-term deals also struck on substrate and back-end capacity plus capex and prepays. Murphy spent a week in Asia with existing and new suppliers ahead of the October 6 Investor Day; conditions are very acute right now in some areas, and he warned that some substrate capacity cannot be obtained until the end of the decade by anyone who did not start five years ago.
supply chain flexed up 50%; two-year plan from $20 billion to $30 billion; 90%-plus first-pass silicon success on advanced node

Foundry diversification is now a selling point: 'With our 1.6T, as many of you know, we moved to Samsung. The industry is somewhat constrained by TSMC, and so this move to Samsung has caught a lot of people's attention, and they are very interested in the fact that it gives them some diversity.' The strategy is company-wide, not optical-only - 'You'll see other products and other product lines or business units that will be done on Samsung as well' - and follows years of alternating between UMC and TSMC until 'UMC kind of stopped investing on advanced nodes.' To secure capacity MaxLinear is using 'everything in the toolbox': orders, occasional LTAs (normally avoided), prepayments and letters of credit, plus technical work with the foundry on throughput, IP and chip size. On Samsung wafers for the 1.6T ramp: 'we've worked with them on the forecast and potential ramps, and we feel very comfortable that we can meet the demand of the customers.'

Order visibility extended well past the earnings call: 'We quote 26 to 28 week lead times for our optical products. That's fairly consistent, but I will say that customers have come in placing orders throughout all of next year, or at least at a minimum, given us forecasts so that we can go out and plan.' He framed it as 'a big gap between supply and demand here,' with those upfront orders needed to secure foundry capacity for next year.
26 to 28 week lead times on optical products; customer orders placed throughout all of next year

Permitting/community pushback is slowing the industry and Nebius is answering it with geographic diversification and an open-construction model. 'Specifically this year, there is a lot of delays in the industry.' Nebius builds 'not only in the U.S., we build a lot in Europe. I think we're the largest builder in Europe. We build in the Middle East. We build in India, in Japan now through partnerships.' Unlike U.S. peers whose sites were 'under NDAs', Nebius arrives openly, builds a booth showing the project, runs community education programs and employs local unions. Example cited: a France site on the brownfield of an old Bridgestone tire factory.

CFO Brian Roberts on the margin path and supply: 2026 margin gains have come from operational productivity and the move of manufacturing from the U.S. to the international extended factories - a year ago Onto was shipping its first tools from those factories and in Q2 it shipped about 70% of its tools from them. To date Onto has driven 250 basis points of gross margin and doubled that at the operating margin line. Into 2027, the accretive Dragonfly G5 and Atlas G6 add ASP lift which, alongside productivity, drives toward 'a margin that starts with a six'. The two major 2026 headwinds were memory cost and freight/fuel shortage, partly offset by being in region, and Onto is having pricing conversations with customers about the existing product portfolio for the 2027 pricing/budgeting season. On supply, the extended-factory move gave Onto partner capacity and new clean rooms without heavy CapEx; the supply chain is not perfect but Onto is using customer visibility to get ahead of bottlenecks, is carrying a higher inventory balance, is not missing customer dates and its lead times have not grown too much.
about 70% of tools shipped from international factories in Q2; 250 basis points of gross margin to date; target gross margin that starts with a six
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Management explained what sits behind the >$200 million single-OSAT Dragonfly order: with the industry constrained on heterogeneous integration, end customers are looking at alternative packaging technologies (EMIB among them), and separately 'TSMC is well-publicized. TSMC is looking at how to release more capacity' given fab constraints - taking its lower-end process steps and outsourcing those to the OSATs to free precious fab capacity for the higher end. Plisinski said that dynamic was in play in the order, and that OSAT capital intensity is really volume-driven, with the volume expected to come both from that outsourced capacity and from the OSATs' own technology that they will be selling. On share at the OSATs versus the foundries, Onto has very high share on the 2D side at the higher-end applications and has gained nice traction on 3D bump metrology at at least a couple of the OSATs; share is lower in low-end or China work.
Onto Innovation Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Silicon-photonics customers are asking for long-term agreements that lock 'capacity, volumes, pricing, and also with cash advance for many of these agreements that we are signing'; the LTAs cover 'more than one year, two, three years'. ST says it must invest to follow demand, using its 300mm infrastructure, and that the silicon-photonics capacity is fungible with other technologies such as microcontrollers. More broadly, 'we are facing backlog and demand that is well above our ability to serve the market', with the backlog extending 'well inside 2027'; industrial lead times for some products are 'now reaching 50 weeks', and microcontroller distribution inventory is well below the normal 12-13 weeks. A Q2 hiccup at the Singapore fab was escalated immediately by automotive customers.
industrial lead times reaching 50 weeks; silicon-photonics LTAs with cash advances covering two, three years; distribution inventory below normal 12-13 weeks

Pricing: with backlog and demand higher than capacity, ST is raising prices by more than its input-cost increases ('not in a way that is too much opportunistic'); average pricing in 2026 will be 'substantially flattish, slightly increasing' (engaged-customer contracts limit increases, while MCU STM32 and some analog in distribution are easier to reprice). 2027 pricing is not yet being negotiated, but this year's increases stay and 2027 is expected to be 'stable, slightly increasing'.
2026 average pricing substantially flattish, slightly increasing; 2027 stable, slightly increasing

Two supply datapoints. (1) The clock/TPD business is supply-constrained, not demand-constrained: 'if we could get more product in the supply chain, that's one place where we are constrained working through Renesas and the TSAs, we could probably be significantly higher than that number.' (2) MEMS wafer supply from Bosch is not a concern — 'it is not in my top 20 things to worry about. Bosch has been a partner of SiTime since 2007... We are the only MEMS non-Bosch company there. In other words, they are a captive fab. They are not supposed to be merchant fab.' On renewal: 'I fully expect that as our 2027 10-year deal with them sort of comes off, there will be another one that will extend the time.'
constrained working through Renesas and the TSAs; Bosch 2027 10-year deal expected to be extended
SiTime Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

Asked whether AI orders stretch out the way they do for supply-constrained component makers, the CEO said connectors are NOT tight: 'We don't have that supply tightness' — TE's order book runs typically into 2027 and 2028 orders should start arriving early in 2027, with engineering engagement on next-generation architectures (who goes 800V, liquid vs air cooling, where optics enters the rack) already running for 2028-2029. On capacity and moat: three new facilities added in Southeast Asia over the past three years for China plus one with more being added right now, and engineering headcount raised by about 2,500 people over three years; TE cites 448G speeds and signal integrity as the technical bar.
three new facilities in Southeast Asia over the past three years; engineering from 7,500 to about 10,000 (about 2,500 people added); 448G speeds
TE Connectivity Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

COPPER AND GLASS ARE THE TWO WATCHED INPUTS - NO ISSUES YET (CEO): asked about supply-chain constraints that could temper delivery, 'We are focused every day, every hour on the supply chain... this is almost a full-time job of our COO. We follow, let's say, what's happening with copper. We follow what's happening with glass and making sure that we don't get tied here. So far so good. We are very transparent to our customers also.' The mitigations named were multiple qualified suppliers and TTM's position at the top of the technology stack: 'The good thing is that these suppliers also focus more on the high-end, and that's exactly where we play. We don't see issues right now, but absolutely it's our focus every day.'
TTM Technologies Jefferies Global Industrials Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

SUPPLY, NOT DEMAND, IS THE GATE - AND CURRENT EXABYTE SUPPLY GROWTH IS ONLY LOW 20s: CFO Kris Sennesael was explicit that 'my revenue is not gated by the demand. My revenue is gated by the amount I can supply', and that Western Digital 'can't supply more than 25% right now, year-over-year growth in exabyte' while demand is running well above that. Fiscal 2026 exabyte growth was 'on or about 25% year-over-year', helped by one quarter at 34% against an easy compare, but the current run rate is 'low 20s, 22%, 23% year-over-year exabyte growth in supply' because the company is 'somewhat in between two product transitions' after four or five quarters of ramping 32TB ePMR. Three transitions are queued to re-accelerate supply: next-generation ePMR up to 40TB, first-generation HAMR up to 44TB, then a 50-plus TB generation, with a roadmap beyond to 70s and 100-plus TB per drive. He sees no digestion: every customer conversation comes back with a stronger demand signal and longer visibility.
supply more than 25% right now; low 20s, 22%, 23% year-over-year exabyte growth in supply; one quarter where we had 34%
Western Digital Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

MEMORY INFLATION IS NOW AN INPUT COST INSIDE THE HDD, SLOWING THE COST-PER-TB CURVE: Sennesael reaffirmed the long-term target of cost per terabyte down 'on or about 10% year over year' but warned it will not hold every year - being between two product transitions temporarily slows it, and 'inside the HDD, we use a little bit of DRAM, and we use a little bit of NAND, and that has become a lot more expensive', with input cost increases across the supply chain creating near-term headwinds. He still expects gross margin to keep increasing at a pretty good pace given pricing, with gross margin now 'in the mid-50s' and operating margin 'in the mid-40s' and no ceiling he can identify. On investment: long-term CapEx is framed as 'in the range of 4%-6% to revenue', below that range the last couple of years and 'slightly above that range' the next couple of years, spent mainly on heads and media (including Western Digital's own substrate and media conversion) and on factory automation, which lifts unit output without major capacity CapEx. He sized the category for context: HDDs 'might only be 4% or 5% of the total CapEx spending of the big hyperscalers' but without them there is no AI.
on or about 10% year over year; in the range of 4%-6% to revenue; 4% or 5% of the total CapEx spending
Western Digital Citi’s Global TMT Conference 2026 (09-09-2026)

SUPPLY BREADTH AND THE COST PASS-THROUGH RULE. Jean Hu listed the tight points by name: 'not only wafers, advanced process node, HBM tight packaging, substrate. Some of the components are very tight.' For Helios it is not just GPU, CPU and HBM — 'there are also a lot of other small component that we need to ensure we have'. On capex: 'The primary increase for CapEx is to build the capacity to support the recipe ramp, especially Venice... capacity is not enough. We need to build ourselves to buy the equipment, do the consignment to support the ramp' — i.e. AMD is buying the equipment itself and placing it on consignment to support the ramp. On pricing, a rule not given on the Q2 call: 'if there's a component cost increase, we do need to make sure we share that cost increase with the customers... If wafer price increase, you should expect us to increase the CPU price, too', while stressing AMD will not raise price purely to expand gross margin. CPU growth is coming from both units and ASP, with 'unit increase probably is more than ASP increase'.

On HBM de-speccing: when customers lower the number of stacked High-Bandwidth Memory in a system they are doing it to get more system output and ship more AI data center systems in total against the memory constraint, which means shipping more GPUs, more CPUs and more accelerators per memory chip. Applied views the effect on equipment demand as overall neutral and says it has not seen a reduction in demand in the business because of this phenomenon.

CFO Brice Hill detailed the leading indicators behind the demand call. Applied runs a fab tracker of well over 100 factories announced across the world, with more than 10 added in each of the last two quarters, and the rolling eight-quarter forecast from its largest customers has risen every single quarter this year. Looking one level further out, cloud service provider capex forecasts have risen all year - over $700 billion this year for the U.S. companies and almost $1 trillion for the global companies. Management says the medium-term ramp is gated by clean room, and there is more demand than there is supply.
fab tracker well over 100 factories, more than 10 added in each of the last two quarters; CSP capex over $700 billion this year for U.S. companies, almost $1 trillion globally

Capacity and supply-chain readiness: Applied has invested and is investing so that it can produce double the amount of systems each quarter that it is producing today - a capacity statement, not a revenue forecast. Clean room typically takes two, three or four years to put in place. Applied aggregates the eight-quarter customer forecasts by component type and sends them to its suppliers - typically referenced as 2,000 plus suppliers - so they get 8-quarter advance notice to add capacity, and that forecast has risen every single quarter this year.
capacity to produce double the amount of systems each quarter; 2,000 plus suppliers on 8-quarter forecast; clean room takes two, three or four years

Services model: early this year Applied talked about services growing in low double digits (11% or 12%), then raised the longer-term growth view to mid-teens because the installed base is growing faster than expected. This year's growth of over 20% is an unusual bump from utilization - leading-edge logic and DRAM at almost 100% utilization, NAND very high, ICAPS healthier - which drives spares and component buying and cannot repeat ('We cannot go to 110% next year'). The two long-term growth drivers are an installed base growing 5%, 6%, 7% every single year plus rising average revenue per tool from new, largely AI-based, service products.
installed base growing every single year, 5%, 6%, 7% every single year; Leading-edge logic and DRAM, almost 100% utilization; earlier view 11% or 12%

Tan unpacked what 'supply constrained' means behind the 2027 and 2028 AI revenue forecast, and it is not silicon. On chips: 'We understand the need for wafers, leading-edge wafers, and memory, as well as even substrates. That is pretty well locked in. We can pretty well lock that in for sure in 2027, and the process of locking in 2028 gives us within some limits. That is more within our control.' The less deterministic constraint is a site that is power READY, not merely power available: 'If you want to make it power ready, say, in 2028, got to start construction on the sites now. That is not us, our customers, has to start construction on the site now to make it available and ready by 2028' - a year and a half to two years out, gated by transformers, gas turbines, local permitting and the rate of construction. 'It's a judged number based on not just supply of memory wafers, but availability and readiness of power sites.'
wafers, memory and substrates locked in for 2027, being locked for 2028

Breen put GF squarely in a supply-constrained posture for the next couple of years: 'We are clearly in a chasing supply moment today'; 'for the next couple of years, we will be more in a supply-constrained than a demand-constrained environment'. Job number one is ramping technologies GF already produces to higher volumes, and capex is going up again - 'We already are increasing our CapEx this year from last year. We'll be increasing further again next year' - with tool install and qualification speed, not demand, the thing that 'will gate or accelerate our growth going into next year'. Two new-cycle features: customers are co-investing financially alongside GF in the ramps ('customer skin in the game... they are willing to put capital to work'), and government partnerships provide tools that let GF 'accelerate CapEx at significant recovery rates that were not there in the past'.
capex increasing this year versus last year and increasing further again next year; supply-constrained, not demand-constrained, for the next couple of years

Mobile mix and a new read-across on foundry tightness: GF was 'more than 50% mobile going back a couple of years', is 'down to the mid-30s today' and the long-term model takes it to 'the mid-20s', with absolute mobile revenue assumed relatively flat rather than growing. 2026 is a tough year in mobile but 'not as tough at the higher end', where GF has more of its exposure. The new behaviour is that handset customers are now booking forward supply: 'mobile companies were the first to the queue in COVID... Now they are worried about being late when the data center is the one pushing all the demand. You are seeing actually more visibility where they are actually still saying, I need my supply for 2027. I need my supply for 2028.'
mobile more than 50% of revenue a couple of years ago, mid-30s today, mid-20s in the long-term model; handset customers booking supply for 2027 and 2028

CEO George Kurian quantified the flash-vs-disk cost gap driving a mix shift back to hard disk: NetApp's disk-based systems have started to show growth and he sees 'strong uptake through the rest of the year as the cost of flash becomes 15 to 20 times the cost of disk.' NetApp is giving customers tools to keep high-cost flash only for data that needs it and to automate movement of colder data out of flash-based systems into cheaper disk-based configurations - a large part of the data in an all-flash array is in fact cold.
the cost of flash becomes 15 to 20 times the cost of disk

NAND and hard-disk procurement behind the raised FY2027 guide: Kurian said NetApp works with suppliers on 'a broad range of commercial vehicles, including buying in the open market as well as through Long-Term Agreements to assure access to available supply at competitive cost structures', and that suppliers prefer that range of tools. He pointed to the balance sheet: inventory was up in the quarter because NetApp wants adequate inventory on hand to meet demand.

Customer behaviour under component inflation is running counter to the historical pattern: NetApp planned for a normal pattern of X new use cases and a decrease in refresh/infrastructure upgrades when prices rise, but is 'seeing infrastructure upgrades way above normal pattern' and 'new use cases also way above normal pattern', which Kurian reads as a secular spending shift toward the storage category. Separately, NetApp is working with several clients on hybrid compute landscapes where they provision compute in the cloud as a risk mitigation strategy for not having access to supply chain components for their own data centers.

Component supply behind the doubled growth outlook: Jabre said NetApp has 'different types of arrangements with different types of suppliers. In some cases, we have LTAs. In others, we basically have agreed upon commitments' and that NetApp feels comfortable it has the supply to deliver the guided outlook. He added that for most of the commodities NetApp purchases it has more than one supplier, which helps secure supply and in some cases helps on cost. He also noted NetApp sells direct to end-customer demand, so there is no channel stocking inflating the order book.

Component cost inflation: 'we are operating in a tight supply chain environment, so it’s too early to make a call on the component pricing.' NetApp has been passing through component cost inflation 'for now a couple of quarters' and has built agility (e.g. shortening the duration of its quotes) to re-price faster when component costs rise. Product gross margin guided for Q2 through Q4 is slightly better than expected 90 days ago; the full-year gross margin guide is slightly lower only because of the richer product revenue mix.

Media mix nuance in the current component-inflation environment: hybrid flash (hard-disk based) revenue rose slightly year-on-year in Q1, the second quarter in a row after many quarters of decline, and NetApp called out strength in that business going forward. Management explicitly broke the old margin assumption: 'from a hybrid flash versus all-flash, we do not have much of a differential on the margin side', and IR added investors should not assume the historical relative margin performance of different product classes holds in this environment.

CAPACITY BUILD BEYOND THE US CLEAN ROOM: Kizner said Nova is 'doubling our production floor'; besides the US expansion it has opened 'a new clean room in Germany' and will open 'a new clean room by the end of this year for the first time in Asia', with CapEx staying focused on infrastructure into 2027 and beyond. He stressed the constraint is not only Nova's own clean-room space but the whole stretched supply chain: Nova gives its vendors forward visibility so they can ramp, and qualifies a second vendor where it identifies a bottleneck, because one crucial vendor can stop Nova meeting demand regardless of floor space.
doubling our production floor; a new clean room in Germany; a new clean room by the end of this year for the first time in Asia

MEMORY PRICING IS DESTROYING THE LOW-END HANDSET BOM: smartphone volume has gone down 'by low double digits ... low teens, over the last year', with the impact concentrated on the lowest tier and second lowest tier - 'everything below $300' - because 'memory has now become more than half of the BOM of the phone', making those device prices unsustainable. At the premium end, where Qualcomm's presence is largest, Palkhiwala says Qualcomm has 'not seen much of an impact' despite higher prices. He expects continued pressure at the low end and describes handsets as at the low point of the cycle.
smartphone volume down low double digits / low teens over the last year; impact on everything below $300; memory more than half of the BOM of the phone

Albertazzi narrows the supply-chain congestion flagged on the Q2 call: it was not a generic situation but specifically referred to the converged infrastructure products OneCore and SmartRun, where Vertiv is industrializing something that is a field project and taking construction-site complexity onto itself. The consequences are coordination across multiple factories rather than component shortage, and timing variability - is revenue recognized this day or maybe four days later because some of the components are converging in the integration factory. Integration at this scale is a different capability than the power-module integration Vertiv has done for 25, 30 years, and that integration capacity is being deployed constantly to follow demand. He adds the current outlook already incorporates wiggle room against possible hiccups. Chamberlin separately points back to the ramp in infrastructure-solutions orders (Vertiv SmartRun / Vertiv OneCore) seen in last fourth quarter as evidence of the share gain.

H1 2026: Indium Phosphide substrate supply and rare earth bottlenecks are the gating risks, and the second-half outlook already reflects them - "there is substrate supply concerns, as well as rare earth bottlenecks that are highlighted in each of the calls that you are seeing in the industry... the second half outlook already reflects these risks... not over-committing to a number that we will not be able to hit". On InP specifically: "Indium Phosphide substrates are becoming some of the bottlenecks around significant volume increases. Therefore, we are working closely with everybody in the industry and with all partners to ensure that we are locking in volume allocations to secure our demand that we are currently seeing with our customers."

H1 2026: the InP substrate diameter mix, from the epiwafer maker's own view - "3-inch is still very dominant. Then it's 4-inch with almost half of the volume driven by 4-inch, and only then comes 6-inch as the fastest-growing sort of diameter, and it's scaling right now." 6-inch maturity and line yields still need to improve and "we are not seeing truly the really demand on 6-inch yet". Management clarified that IQE's tool conversions are material conversions (Gallium Arsenide to Indium Phosphide), which "doesn't necessarily come with a dimension conversion"; IQE can support 3-inch, 4-inch and 6-inch. Tightness across the three diameters is hard to rank because "there is different types of substrates too".
InP substrate volume mix: 3-inch dominant, 4-inch almost half of volume, 6-inch fastest growing but least mature

H1 2026: capacity is being added by converting existing tooling in the second half "to increase capacity to meet the strong demand for Indium Phosphide", and every conversion is gated on a signed customer commitment - "we will also not expand capacity without a clear customer commitment and a clear visibility on what value is going to be driven with that expansion" and "we are still not converting tools without customer commitments and secured demand on these tools". Conversion cost is "definitely insignificant compared to the cost of a new reactor"; the real cost is the downtime of the tool. Customer prepayments are "definitely a mechanism for us to fund our growth", following what "some of our players in the same ecosystem" already do. Newport still has "ample clean room space to add capacity" so IQE "can scale up rather quickly compared to others because we already have the infrastructure to house these reactors".

During the second quarter of fiscal 2027, conditions of one of Everpure's long-term supply arrangements were met, triggering a commitment to acquire approximately $1.1 billion of component supply through calendar year 2027; purchases can be made by Everpure or its approved contract manufacturers, Everpure would be obligated to purchase amounts its contract manufacturers do not purchase, and it expects them to purchase substantially all of the committed volume. To support component procurement for hyperscale customers that buy from contract manufacturers, Everpure has in some cases entered into agreements under which component suppliers (not named) commit to sell specified volumes directly to the contract manufacturers, with Everpure obligated to purchase any unfulfilled portion at a price that is fixed or set within a pre-agreed range.
approximately $1.1 billion component supply commitment through calendar year 2027

Backlog surge in an extraordinary demand environment: Q3 book-to-bill significantly greater than one; backlog up $800 million quarter-on-quarter to $8.5 billion, and expected to grow at an even greater rate in Q4 — just one month into Q4, orders booked are approaching a level equal to the ENTIRETY of Q3, and Ciena projects exiting fiscal 2026 with over $10 billion in backlog extending well into fiscal 2028. Orders (demand) doubled from 2024 to 2025 and are expected up another 50% from 2025 to 2026, with backlog doubling in each of those years. The vast majority of the ~$10 billion backlog carries a customer request date in 2027, meaning the backlog covers most of the FY2027 revenue guide. Ciena also recently secured a significant increase in customer commitments that extend through 2029. Customer mix: about 50% of the business is now hyperscalers directly, and 'neo scaler' (neocloud) demand — MOFN deals, own fiber builds — is expected to become an increasingly important part of the business through 2027 and 2028; MOFN growth called explosive in markets like India, plus Japan and parts of the Middle East.
Backlog +$800M QoQ to $8.5B; >$10B backlog projected exiting FY2026; orders +50% 2025-to-2026 after doubling 2024-to-2025; commitments through 2029

Supply, not demand, is the binding constraint: the industry needs to add significant capacity and management does not see supply and demand getting back into balance BEFORE 2028 — a similarly constrained dynamic is expected going into 2027 and likely into 2028. In recent weeks Ciena FINALIZED LONG-TERM AGREEMENTS that secure supply of certain key components THROUGH 2029, including incremental capacity for those key components; the June five-year zero-coupon convertible (economic conversion premium of 114%, proceeds retiring the 5.5% interest term loan) partly provided the capital to help secure supply over the next three years, and cash from operations will step down in Q4 as those investments are dispersed. Ciena is also qualifying additional suppliers — expanding both the number of suppliers and alternative technologies for the same functionality. Capital investments this year increased capacity sufficient to support RLS, plug and Waveserver revenue growth all over 60% year to date; capex expected at the high end of the $250 million-$275 million range; $2.8 billion in cash and equivalents. Value exchange with customers: price increases from high single digits up to high teens/low 20s depending on customer and product line, some of it selectively hitting backlog, alongside payment-terms and fill-rate discussions; possible new Canadian tariff impact of ~$10 million a quarter being mitigated.
Key-component supply secured through 2029; supply/demand balance not before 2028; price increases high single digits to high teens/low 20s; capex high end of $250M-$275M

Ciena's 10-Q: remaining performance obligations were $2.5 billion as of August 1, 2026 (fulfillment timing can be impacted by supply conditions), and outstanding purchase order commitments to contract manufacturers and component suppliers for inventory were $3.3 billion, including advanced orders for certain long lead time components (only a portion of this amount is firm, non-cancelable and unconditional). Citing orders significantly exceeding revenue and an industry-wide constrained supply environment that has resulted in historically high backlog, Ciena says it has entered, and is seeking to continue to enter, multi-year supply agreements with certain suppliers, some involving firm purchase commitments and prepayment arrangements, and long-term purchase arrangements with customers.
RPO $2.5 billion; purchase order commitments $3.3 billion (as of August 1, 2026)

Pipeline: expects to add 'a handful of new projects over the next 7-15 months' (mostly complex combined cycle, some simple cycle) and is staffed to execute on 10-12 jobs simultaneously with Gemma headcount at record levels; project starts depend on developers securing PPAs with an end user such as a hyperscaler, air and water permits, gas, turbines and financing; despite Texas Governor Abbott's talk of halting 1,800 data center projects, 'there has really been no change in terms of developer behavior'.
handful of new projects in 7-15 months; capacity for 10-12 simultaneous jobs

The 10-Q states that new power generation development is constrained by a limited number of experienced EPC contractors, equipment supply limitations, interconnection delays and specialized labor availability; lead times for large gas turbines, transformers and other grid equipment have extended meaningfully beyond historical norms as manufacturer order books expanded, and equipment costs have risen accordingly. Argan says its backlog growth over the past year reflects this supply-constrained environment for large-scale power generation construction.

Cisco's 10-K: inventory purchase commitments with contract manufacturers and suppliers were $17,165 million at July 25, 2026 versus $7,599 million at July 26, 2025 (up 126%), inventories were $5,694 million versus $3,164 million (up 80%), and inventory deposits and prepayments were $1,104 million versus $825 million, principally under arrangements to secure supply and pricing for memory and certain components. Cisco attributes the increase primarily to commitments related to manufacturing Cisco Silicon One and other products to meet demand from hyperscalers and other customers, with higher memory prices and commitments to secure memory supply also contributing significantly; some commitments are long-term supply agreements for fixed quantities of memory components at variable prices, and Cisco cites the memory shortages experienced in fiscal 2026. Of the purchase commitments, $14,341 million are due in less than one year.
inventory purchase commitments $17,165 million (+126%); inventories $5,694 million (+80%); inventory deposits and prepayments $1,104 million vs $825 million

Credo's 10-Q: as of August 1, 2026 Credo had multiple manufacturing supply capacity reservation agreements with assembly subcontractors, making upfront deposits for reserved manufacturing capacity over terms of 2 to 6 years; refundable deposits were $88.4 million. After August 1, 2026 it entered an additional capacity reservation agreement with an assembly subcontractor and will pay $102.4 million of refundable deposits within fiscal 2027. Remaining performance obligations were approximately $4.2 million as of August 1, 2026.
refundable capacity deposits $88.4 million (August 1, 2026); additional agreement with $102.4 million of deposits within fiscal 2027

→ Marvell: Marvell's 10-Q states that TSMC is currently its sole source foundry for all of its advanced process-node wafers and the sole wafer supplier for its advanced node products, including its 3nm products. To secure sufficient capacity when demand is high, Marvell has entered into a capacity reservation agreement with TSMC under which it agreed to make substantial advance payments in exchange for wafer capacity over a multi-year period; it is required to purchase specified target quantities of wafers during the term and may forfeit a proportional portion of its advance payments if it does not meet them.

Compute pricing has re-rated sharply. THREE-YEAR CONTRACT PRICING IS UP ABOUT 125% SINCE NOVEMBER and five-year pricing up about 70%. Recent three-year contracts are pricing IN EXCESS OF $20 MILLION PER MEGAWATT of IT load - paying back the compute investment in around two years - while active discussions are now at AROUND $25 MILLION PER MEGAWATT, described as consistent across live customer conversations with continued upward pressure and very strong competitive tension for near-term megawatts. Recent customer prepayments are funding 45% TO 55% of GPU capex. Management stressed these are three-to-five-year deals, not two-year or spot capacity, and that it is deliberately NOT sitting on capacity to time a spot price; shorter-duration and on-demand sit above this as further upside in due course. Pricing is described as consistent globally, with possible additional scarcity in Spain and Australia from sovereign AI demand. CEO Daniel Roberts noted the announced pricing relates to GPUs ordered some time ago, so it reflects genuine price increases rather than pass-through of GPU cost inflation.
3-year contract pricing +~125% since November, 5-year +~70%; recent 3-year deals >$20M per MW of IT load, active discussions ~$25M per MW; prepayments funding 45-55% of GPU capex

IREN's 10-K names NVIDIA among the limited number of suppliers from which it sources GPUs, networking and storage equipment for its AI Cloud Services; GPUs installed and on order as of June 30, 2026 included NVIDIA H100, H200, B200, B300, GB300 and VR200 systems. The 10-K states that demand for NVIDIA GPUs and certain networking equipment far exceeds supply, and that delivery delays due to industry-wide component shortages, principally relating to NVIDIA equipment, previously delayed certain equipment required for delivery of Horizon 1 under the Microsoft Agreement.

Fab-by-fab buildout schedule: Micron has 20 investment projects going on around the world of all different shapes and sizes, bringing on both front-end and back-end capacity. Idaho ID1 has first wafer outs in mid next year; ID2 follows right after with first wafer outs close to the end of calendar 2028. The Tongluo fab purchased in Taiwan has wafer starts in 2027 with further expansions there, plus expansions in Japan and Singapore. In New York Micron has a four-fab cluster with first fab output expected in 2030 - it broke ground in January and has hit the concrete pour milestone ahead of schedule - alongside the Manassas fab in Virginia. Management flags construction talent as a genuine bottleneck: there are not enough skilled construction workers or fab technicians given simultaneous data center, power plant and semiconductor buildouts.
20 investment projects worldwide; Idaho ID1 first wafer outs mid next year, ID2 close to the end of calendar 2028; Tongluo wafer starts in 2027; New York four-fab cluster first output 2030

When industry supply actually arrives: 'We think that meaningful supply will start to ramp only in 2028. And that too, it'll be only an initial ramp. It'll gather momentum only in the years after. It will take a while for the industry to find a new equilibrium point. But when exactly that happens, we don't have line of sight to yet.' Because tech transitions no longer produce enough bit growth, the whole industry needs greenfield clean room space at the same time, which is gated by construction, permitting and infrastructure. Cycle-time context on why memory supply cannot respond quickly: roughly 2,000 process steps in the fab, three and a half plus months (approaching four months) through the fab plus a month - or a month and a half for more complex products - in assembly, packaging and test, so about a five-month cycle time from wafer start to customer shipment.
meaningful industry supply ramps only in 2028 (initial ramp); ~2,000 process steps and a five-month cycle time from wafer start to shipment

Mechanism behind the better-than-expected July quarter, which the Q3 call did not spell out. April-quarter push-outs came from customers being unable to capture memory and from Asian fabs at unusually high utilization telling chip designs 'You have to delay your design because we don't have the capacity for it'. Through the July quarter those designs started to be released because the same fabs 'added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range', and in some cases told a customer with a 40 nanometer design 'if you move that chip design to 28 nanometers or 22 nanometers, I will then manufacture it for you' - i.e. the capacity shortage is actively forcing node migration, which is the ASP-positive trend Photronics benefits from. On the display side Korea is strong on high-end consumer electronics launching this fall while China has pulled back because low-end consumer electronics cannot capture memory; Moreau relayed that the memory companies are talking about 'another 2, 3, 4 years before supply and demand comes into equilibrium'.
fabs added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range and pushed 40 nanometer designs to 28 or 22 nanometers; memory supply and demand equilibrium another 2, 3, 4 years away

Named the biggest headwind of the last couple of years as geopolitics rather than demand: Photronics lost China-market customers it had good business with after 'We were told by the U.S. government, You have to stop shipping to that customer', and in another case Taiwan put a customer on its restricted list, forcing Photronics to move that production out of its Taiwan facility into its China facility, which has less capacity - so revenue with that customer fell as well. Offsetting structural positive: regionalization and reshoring, with TSMC expanding very aggressively in Arizona and GlobalFoundries and Samsung also expanding in the U.S.; the more locations that manufacture chips, the more mask business spreads out, which is why Photronics is expanding in the U.S. and Korea.

Strategic shift from a fab-lite to a hybrid manufacturing model for indium phosphide lasers — laser demand outstrips supply for the next 3 to 5 years; a new foundry partner has brought on tremendous committed capacity available now, Glasgow Phase 1 expansion capacity comes online end of Q4 2027, and the long-term model is one-third internal manufacturing and two-thirds foundry partners; production capacity not seen as the bottleneck versus the pipeline

CFO put boundaries on capacity and inventory. Distributor channel inventory is at the target 10 to 11 weeks and onsemi holds stock back ('They would take more inventory if we'd ship it to them'); balance-sheet inventory came down 8 days to 67 days, with the bridge inventory from the earlier fab divestitures taking 'a couple more years to bleed through it all.' CapEx stays in mid-single-digit percentage intensity 'for several years': 'Our revenue has to get to about 30% higher than where it is today for us even to think about adding capacity,' and about 35% of production is managed outside, which onsemi loads last. 'We're not breaking ground on a new fab anytime soon.'
channel inventory 10 to 11 weeks; inventory down 8 days to 67 days; revenue must be ~30% higher before adding capacity; ~35% of production managed outside

NVIDIA 'helped CoreWeave, Nebius and Nscale build entire infrastructure businesses'; neoclouds collectively expected to exit 2026 at 8 GW installed (from ~3 GW end-2025), with NVIDIA now offering take-or-pay floors + revenue share to help lenders underwrite neocloud projects.
Cited by NVIDIA as a neocloud it helped build into an entire infrastructure business; NVIDIA now offers take-or-pay floors + revenue share to help lenders underwrite neocloud projects.

Building Systems (Power Solutions data-center electrical in the D.M.V. region plus National Technology Integrators structured cabling, acquired this quarter): revenue $397.5 million, about 20% of total, adjusted EBITDA $97.2 million or 24.5% of segment revenue; NTI contributed ~$22.9 million; FY2027 segment outlook raised to $1.58 billion-$1.65 billion including ~$90 million from NTI in 2H, with margins in the high teens to low 20s. 'Electricians are still in short demand ... there are still projects that we are turning away.'
Building Systems revenue $397.5M (~20% of total), adj. EBITDA margin 24.5%; FY2027 segment outlook $1.58B-$1.65B

Long-haul execution capacity: 'There is a lot of training that has to happen if you're going to do long-haul fiber splicing'; around 17,000 people on the communications side and a workforce of nearly 21,000, with a new flagship training facility in Georgia opening in 1H calendar 2027. Communications margin pressure (13.6%, -134 bps YoY) reflects investment to ramp customer fiber programs, the wireless deferral and ~35 bps of fuel cost.
~17,000 communications workforce, ~21,000 total; training facility opens 1H calendar 2027; Communications adj. EBITDA margin 13.6%

AGENTIC WORKLOADS ARE THE CPU DEMAND DRIVER, AND IRELAND IS THE SUPPLY ANSWER: CFO David Zinsner quantified the workload shift for the first time - comparing a regular training data center with an agentic-like activity, 'it's like a 4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements'. Server CPU units, which used to decline low single digits, are now growing double digits with core counts growing at multiples of that, and ASP per core - which fell almost 20% in some years - has at least stabilized and in some like-for-like cases is going up, so core-count growth now flows straight through to revenue. The constraint is supply, not competitive performance: 'as we look at this year, next year, probably even into 2028, this is going to be less about competitive performance of CPUs and more about can you get the CPUs to the customer', and share will follow whoever can supply. Granite Rapids, the data-center flagship, is built in Ireland on Intel 3; part of next year's CapEx is to ramp Ireland where Intel wants to 'more than double the output there next year'. Even so Intel will 'under-supply for sure this year', 'probably under-supply next year', and hopes to be in a good position by 2028.
4 to 6 increase in CPU requirements; more than double the output there next year

MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

THE CAPITAL RAISE IS A SUBSTRATE-AND-FAB SPENDING EVENT: Zinsner explained the August equity raise as 'the capital raise precedes capital investment' - 2026 CapEx has already been upticked 'by a couple of billion dollars from $18 billion to $20 billion', next year's will be significantly higher, and 'substrates are really constrained and we're going to need to make investments associated with substrates as well next year, given the significant demand.' Committing to 14A high-volume manufacturing in 2028 means placing long-lead supplier orders now, which was one of the biggest drivers of the raise. On footprint: Ireland's shell is being equipped now; Fab 52 in Arizona is running Intel 18A and Fab 62 is almost ready, with next year's investment accelerating its equipping; Oregon stays the pilot line but will also run volume Intel 14A as 18A is pushed into Arizona; Ohio shells are in progress with the ability to have 'eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio', mod one being built as fast as possible. Zinsner said 2027 CapEx is not locked - the businesses gave him a number and 'I've told them no', sending them back for more efficiency before he guides.
from $18 billion to $20 billion; eight mods, or there is two mods per fab, so four fabs in Ohio

Q2 FY2027 (call 08-25, quarter ended 07-26-2026): RECORD revenue $342M (+17% QoQ, +33% YoY) — 10th consecutive quarter of sequential growth; adj EPS $0.71 (+39% QoQ, +73% YoY, more than 2x the revenue growth rate); adj GM 54.5% (+150bps QoQ) with SEMICONDUCTOR-PRODUCTS GM 62.8% (+210bps QoQ) on 1.6T FiberEdge/CopperEdge and LoRa mix; adj EBITDA $91M (26.6% margin); FCF $61M (+119% QoQ). By end market: Infrastructure $124M (+25% QoQ, +69% YoY), Industrial $179M (+16% QoQ, +25% YoY — LoRa a record $58M, +31% QoQ / +58% YoY; IoT systems & connectivity $98M), High-end consumer $39M (+2% QoQ, -5% YoY; TVS resilient despite MEMORY-CONSTRAINED PRICING across the industry). Cellular module business signed for divestiture and moved to HELD FOR SALE (close expected Q4 FY2027, EPS-neutral on non-GAAP): ex-modules adj GM was 59.7%, i.e. the sale is a STRUCTURAL +520bps gross-margin step-up; CFO calls ~64% the post-divestiture starting point.
Record $342M (+33% YoY); adj EPS $0.71 (+73% YoY); adj GM 54.5% → 59.7% ex-modules

SUPPLY POSTURE: above-seasonal growth for NINE straight quarters with a tenth guided. Inventory rose $83M sequentially building strategic die bank, exiting fiscal Q3 with RECORD balance-sheet inventory plus increased distributor inventory - yet days declined to 156 and channel weeks fell BELOW the six-to-seven week target. No restocking activity seen: customers continue to run very lean and most of the business is still shipping well below historical consumption levels. Industry-wide there are 'some soft spots and lead times have started to extend,' but ADI's own lead times are being kept in check. Capacity is being added by installing new tools in available space plus sourcing more external wafers, with scenario planning underway for capacity beyond current plans and joint long-view planning with front-end and back-end partners across nodes from ~6 micrometer down to 5nm/3nm. FY2026 CapEx still expected within the 4%-6% of revenue long-term model.
Inventory days 156; channel weeks below 6-7 target; 9 straight above-seasonal quarters; CapEx 4-6% of revenue

LINE-LEVEL CAPACITY UNIT AND UTILIZATION (the ~200,000/month-now to 650,000/month-by-end-2026 path was already given on the Q2 FY2026 earnings call; new here is what one production 'line' is and how hard it runs): CFO/CSO Stefan Murry said AOI plans production in blocks of '100,000 units per month capacity' (what he would call a line), run essentially 24/7 apart from maintenance downtime because the transceiver process is automated. Asked whether AOI is at about 200,000 units now heading to 650,000 by year end, he confirmed: 'Probably a little more than 200,000. We were 200,000 kind of at the end of last quarter', and AOI is 'on that pathway between 200 and 650'.
100,000 units per month capacity; Probably a little more than 200,000; on that pathway between 200 and 650

SOLD OUT AND TURNING CUSTOMERS AWAY: Murry said that when another large data center customer asks for units today AOI has to answer that it is 'sold out at least through second half of next year and beyond'. Some large data center customers have already approached AOI ('some have') and it cannot take them without over-committing against existing customers; the only way in may be CPO or another newer technology further out. He confirmed the monthly data center transceiver target put to him is a REVENUE expectation, not merely a capacity figure, and said AOI could do more revenue than that if it had more capacity - 'the demand is not the limiting factor', capacity and to some extent supply chain are. Best case long-term share is 'somewhere around 20% market share'. Several LTAs are on the table but AOI is deliberately cautious: an LTA that locks up too much capacity for one customer could scare away other customers it wants later.
sold out at least through second half of next year and beyond; somewhere around 20% market share

WHERE THE 800G RAMP IS PHYSICALLY COMING FROM: Murry said 'two major hyperscale customers' are both buying meaningful 800G quantities with several smaller customers either buying or about to start. The step up from 'a few million dollars in 800G sales a quarter' to the Q3/Q4 projection comes MAINLY OUT OF THE TAIWAN PLANT - that is the capacity added this year. The Houston/US real estate starts only its very first increment later this year and is really a 2027 and into 2028 contributor.
two major hyperscale customers; a few million dollars in 800G sales a quarter

LASER FAB FOOTPRINT AND THE US PREMIUM: Murry said 'the lasers are only made here in the U.S.' in the Sugar Land facility, that AOI intends to add further laser production in the Houston area but does NOT intend to put laser production overseas, and that the added laser capacity lands mostly in the latter half of next year aimed at CPO/NPO devices. Asked whether customers pay up for that, he said flatly they are 'willing to pay a premium for U.S. production' - driven by the non-zero possibility of a ban on Chinese-sourced optics, which customers say would kill their ability to build new US data centers.
the lasers are only made here in the U.S.; willing to pay a premium for U.S. production

MEMORY SHORTAGE IS DRIVING THE 100G DECLINE (the Q2 FY2026 call already attributed the 100G weakness to the memory shortage; new here is the customer's allocation mechanism and the expedite-fee timing): Murry explained the unexpected margin headwind as 'one of our customers was unable to secure enough memory to meet all of their build-out needs', so that customer is reallocating the memory it can get to higher-speed nodes (800G, 1.6T) and deploying relatively fewer 100G links for the next few quarters - which hits AOI's high-margin 100G business. On expedite fees, he said the 1.6T volume came up faster than AOI's SUPPLIERS had planned for (they had discounted AOI's forecast and are now tight on capacity), but that this irons itself out over the next few months and should not be much of a factor beyond Q4.
one of our customers was unable to secure enough memory to meet all of their build-out needs

WAFER SIZE AND SUBSTRATE SUPPLY: AOI runs lasers on four-inch wafers today; all fab equipment bought in the last year or two can go to six-inch and AOI will switch only when six-inch is cheaper per laser than four-inch and six-inch substrate availability exists - no date is set in stone. On substrates, Murry said AOI feels good about availability through next year, through 2027, and is actively working with a number of vendors to secure 2028-and-beyond capacity; substrate pricing 'has gone up a little bit' but is not a dramatic margin impact, and laser yields still have room to improve, which can offset the higher substrate cost.
We are a four-inch right now; pricing has gone up a little bit

CEO Seamus Grady walked the capacity ladder to a single consolidated number: capacity right now is about $5.8 billion (the $5.3 billion Q4 exit run rate plus the Pinehurst office-to-manufacturing conversion); Building 10 when fully available adds about $3.5 billion at the high end; Nava, the new factory in Nava Nakorn, adds about $250 million; and the newly acquired Santa Clara operation adds about another $250 million - which gets to $9.8 billion of capacity in calendar Q1, early in the March quarter, an 85% increase versus where the year ended. AI / HBM framing in the half-year report (2026-08-14): the memory market is leading semiconductor growth on AI and big-data demand, and the equipment market is expected to keep growing over the medium-to-long term on the aggressive DRAM-centric investment memory makers are making to break the HBM SHORTAGE caused by the explosive expansion of AI end-markets. 2022-2024 is described as a harsh down-cycle (memory price collapse, utilisation drop); 2025-2030 is framed as a structural growth phase driven by generative-AI infrastructure build-out, led by HBM and sub-2nm foundry rather than commodity products. The AI-accelerator and HBM demand surge is forcing the equipment market onto a single high-end track where marginal technology or adequate tools have no place; foreign vendors from the US, Japan and Netherlands still hold the largest shares but Korean localisation is rising and the company's tools are now in mass-production lines of major customers at home and abroad, with overseas sales rising (China semiconductor revenue KRW 63,346M in H1 2026 vs KRW 42,017M in H1 2025). Company cannot estimate market share because device makers' total orders are not observable.
HBM shortage-driven DRAM capex cited as multi-year equipment driver; 2025-2030 structural growth phase (HBM, sub-2nm foundry)

On NAND supply: 'we still able to get supply, but unfortunately supply not enough to what we need... We have supply, but supply still not enough what we need.' Phison met every NAND supplier at FMS last week and pitched that its purchases feed its own AI data-platform systems, not just module resale; it will not disclose how many LTAs it holds so competitors cannot ask for the same amounts. CEO expects the NAND shortage to continue into next year and beyond ('many year'); a top NAND-maker executive told him a new fab takes 4 years from investment to production, not 2. Downgrade-grade NAND supply is also shrinking structurally: 3D NAND yields now run 90-plus percent, with some wafers at 95% good die, so the cheap downgrade bin that used to feed consumer products is disappearing.
new NAND fab: 4 years investment-to-production; 3D NAND yields 90%+ (some wafers 95%)

NAND pricing/margin view: back in March the CEO said NAND makers' gross margin reaching a floor of 80% was easy and 85% might happen; now he says 90% gross margin may happen in 2026, but warns that is unhealthy for the industry ('if you ask component for 90% gross margin, industry potentially will be killed - you can see the IoT, you can see the consumer die'). Demand is too strong, so price will keep rising but at a decelerating rate toward saturation, at which point suppliers start choosing whom to ship. On demand structure: systems have cut DRAM content ('a lot of systems, they cut half of the DRAM') but nobody cuts storage - inference needs storage, 'storage is money' - and aiDAPTIV uses flash to complement DRAM.
NAND-maker gross margin: 80% floor easy, 85% may happen, 90% possible in 2026 (CEO view)

Inventory and funding: in June-July Phison spent more than $450 million of cash buying NAND wafers from Shenzhen module houses that were dumping consumer-heavy inventory at prices well below NAND-maker contract prices ('don't take this as price decrease - the NAND guys are not going to decline their price'). Inventory of roughly 90 billion (NT$, book value) is carried at cost and never revalued upward, only written down. Balance sheet: the large bank debt outstanding at end-March was almost fully repaid by July ('now we have no debt'); the $800 million ECB raised earlier has already been deployed into NAND ('already turned one and a half times'); if business keeps growing strongly, new fundraising may be needed in the second half of next year.
$450M+ NAND wafer purchases in June-July; inventory ~90 billion NT (book value); $800M ECB deployed

Chromebooks face the most severe component shortage and unfavourable supply terms because of their low ASP, staying below 10% of notebook shipments even in the seasonal education peak; brand customers are raising retail prices, further weakening demand, so H2 shipments will be below H1.

manufacturing capacity 4 times above 1H 2025; more than 10x increase in 2026

Q4 $2.05B, DC +66% YoY; FY27 booked out, orders into CY2028, LTAs to end of decade

800G is NOT rolling over as 1.6T ramps — Coherent expects 800G revenue to CONTINUE GROWING YEAR-OVER-YEAR through calendar 2026 alongside the rapid 1.6T ramp. Q4 data center revenue +24% QoQ and +66% YoY. Indium phosphide is the binding constraint across the portfolio (assembly and test capacity is available); June-quarter InP laser output — the lasers that feed both 800G and 1.6T transceivers — was up about 80% YoY, and internal InP capacity doubles YoY by the end of the September quarter, one quarter ahead of plan.
800G still growing YoY through CY2026; InP laser output +80% YoY; InP is the constraint

Both transceiver tiers grow together: 800G revenue continues rising year-over-year through calendar 2026 while 1.6T ramps rapidly into 2027 as adoption broadens. Q4 data center revenue +24% QoQ, +66% YoY, the third consecutive quarter of double-digit sequential growth. Supply, not demand, is the limiter — indium phosphide capacity is the primary constraint (assembly and test have headroom), with internal InP output doubling YoY by the end of the September quarter and more than doubling again by end of calendar 2027.
800G + 1.6T both growing; DC revenue +66% YoY; InP the primary constraint

INDIUM PHOSPHIDE IS THE PRIMARY CONSTRAINT on the whole business — 'we're not constrained in assembly and test capacity right now... we're really just constrained by the ramp of the indium phosphide production.' Internal InP output capacity doubles YoY by the end of the current quarter, ONE QUARTER AHEAD of the original plan, and is on track to MORE THAN DOUBLE AGAIN by the end of calendar 2027; substrates and other critical inputs for that ramp are already secured, and capacity beyond 2027 is being planned. Concrete measure: Coherent produced about 80% MORE indium phosphide lasers in the June quarter than a year earlier — those lasers feed 800G and 1.6T transceiver shipments in the current quarter, so management expects data-center revenue growth this quarter to EXCEED 80% YoY. Six-inch lines in TEXAS and SWEDEN are producing EMLs, CW lasers and photodiodes with yields that exceed the 3-inch lines across all three device types; a third 6-inch location in ZURICH starts in the first half of calendar 2027. Six-inch economics: 4x the output per wafer at half the cost.
InP output 2x YoY (a quarter early), 2x again by end-CY2027; June-qtr lasers +80% YoY; 6-inch = 4x output at half the cost

Build-cost economics disclosed for the first time at this level of detail. Abdel gave an 'indicative range' of build cost of '$10,000-$20,000' depending on geography and project type, and said power connection has gone from free to a major line item: 'Costs us tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site now. It used to cost us nothing.' He is seeing cost inflation in heavily built markets - electricians 'are making $150 an hour these days' - while cost 'definitely moderated on the manufacturing side of the equation'. The response is to shift work offsite: more prefabrication to minimise onsite labour.
build cost indicative range $10,000-$20,000; tens of millions of USD to deliver power to a site; electricians making $150 an hour

The two binding bottlenecks are energy and trades labour, not demand. Abdel: 'Electricians in many locations are very constrained. There's not enough of them' - electricians and plumbers are 'probably being the most acute' trades. Example given: the greater Chicago metro area has '15 gigawatt' of planned data-center expansions on the docket 'with another 15 that's at least marketed to be planned', and 'there is just not enough electricians'. On power he said generation is 'the tertiary issue' - distribution and transmission are the bottlenecks - and that a site requested the old way 'could be 8 years before you get that power'; Equinix therefore now secures the utility conversation and line of sight to power BEFORE taking down land.
Chicago metro 15 gigawatt of planned expansions plus another 15 marketed; up to 8 years for power under the old approach

Component procurement scaled ahead of the FY2027 ramp: closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built in anticipation of higher revenue; the $5.6B June equity raise is described as fully supporting component supply and business needs. Generation-transition risk on memory and other components is managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems that stay compatible across product lines and generations - with management noting that with prices rising so fast, older inventory has often been resold favorably.

Record demand and de-concentrating customer base: over $60B of NEW ORDERS booked in Q4 FY2026 (~70% pure AI, ~30% CPU / CPU-based AI / edge AI), taking order book and backlog to record levels entering FY2027. $60B+ new orders in Q4 (70% pure AI); 9 customers >$1B vs 4; top customer 28%

Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

It is now further expanding manufacturing capacity, system integration capability, the sales organisation and customer support infrastructure to support substantially higher annual revenue levels. Inventory was flat in Q2 but is expected to grow in coming quarters to support forecast revenue growth.

component lead times ~four months -> six months

Centrus HALEU for up to five Aurora powerhouses from 2029; plutonium bridge fuel up to ~2 GW

Per SoftBank's Q1 review and Arm CFO Jason Child: Arm Q1 revenue hit a record $1.3 billion, +22% YoY, with fully diluted EPS +29% YoY (record for a first quarter); Q2 guidance midpoints $1.38 billion revenue and $0.47 EPS, both above analyst consensus.
