Arm Q1 revenue record $1.3 billion +22% YoY; EPS +29%; Q2 guide $1.38 billion / $0.47; AGI CPU orders more than $2 billion vs ~$1 billion initial guide

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manufacturing sites missed: (1) Houston, USA — a fully automated enclosure plant with 15 GWh/year capacity that Fluence off-takes, run by the SAME contract manufacturer that operates its main Vietnam enclosure facility. Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a utility-interconnection delay (the plant has been running on generators, preventing parallel commissioning work); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected within weeks, FULL production in fiscal Q1 2027. (2) One of two new facilities in China — initial production of Smartstack components (the 'pods' that sit on the skids) failed Fluence's testing and required rework; corrections are implemented, shipping has resumed and the site reached full production in Q4. Management put a hedge and a contingency in the plan and blew through both. Organizational response: Roman Loosen (Chief Enterprise Operations Officer, 20+ years at Siemens) takes over supply chain and manufacturing and Peter Williams moves to product, both reporting to the CEO; framed as an EXECUTION/process-scaling fix, not a change of suppliers. Once Houston is fully ramped, Fluence expects domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog.
Houston 15 GWh/yr, full production fiscal Q1 2027; China site reworked, full production in Q4; ~$400M of FY26 revenue pushed to FY27

SOURCING: Fluence signed a long-term battery-cell agreement with an INTERNATIONAL supplier that covers not just supply but technology-roadmap alignment on how cells behave inside Fluence's modules — securing long-term volume and attractive pricing for FY2027-28 and letting it price future orders with more confidence, at the cost of a $15M charge on one in-flight project supplied by the same counterparty. Explicitly NOT related to AESC (the AESC review, run earlier in the year, drove some strategic expense but produced no announcement); Fluence says it is spending a lot of time talking to battery capacity across the market and sees an opportunity to work more closely with U.S. battery manufacturers. On inverters: Fluence uses ONLY non-Chinese inverters in the U.S. — mostly U.S.-made, some imported from Europe — so it expects zero impact from the FCC's inverter restrictions; in Europe it still uses a mix of Chinese and non-Chinese and is working toward a fully European solution ahead of expected European restrictions.
Long-term cell supply + tech-roadmap agreement (int'l supplier, not AESC), $15M charge; 100% non-Chinese inverters in the U.S.

Investment timing has advanced about two years versus the WFE view at the start of the year; suppliers are also preparing capacity and are not currently a bottleneck.
Utilization 70%-80% H1, over 80% H2; lead time around eight months; monthly unit capacity targeted at 2.5 times the March 2025 level in 10 years

Indium phosphide is the key medium-term lever. 200-GIG PHOTODETECTORS are ramping in volume production and becoming a meaningful contributor to Data Center growth; 400-gig photodetectors are in the hands of perhaps a dozen customers with very positive feedback. The 75-MILLIWATT CW LASER qualification continues: MACOM is well into HTOL testing (typically 5,000 hours) with data described as exceptional, is gaining confidence but cannot yet declare success, and is developing plans for a POTENTIAL START TO PRODUCTION IN LATE CALENDAR 2027, scoping modest capex and fab space for a rapid high-volume ramp for a few strategic customers. CEO Steve Daly called bringing a CW laser into production in 2028 'a watershed moment' that could be a very large revenue contributor. Separately, demand for MACOM's 25G DFB lasers (100G QSFP, CWDM4, LR4) is rising with urgency because of a GENERAL SUPPLY SHORTAGE OF INDIUM PHOSPHIDE DFB LASERS. MACOM expects to gain meaningful indium phosphide market share over the next three years; its Ann Arbor, Michigan facility has built photodiodes for over a decade and grows its own epitaxy by MBE.
200G PDs ramping in volume; 400G PDs at ~a dozen customers; 75mW CW laser potential production start late calendar 2027

Capacity and lead times: utilisation at the RTP, North Carolina and Lowell, Massachusetts fabs continues to increase even as capacity is added, and utilisation rates are now IMPACTING LEAD TIMES - MACOM is quoting LONGER LEAD TIMES for internally manufactured products. New capacity is being added across operations through the remainder of fiscal 2026 and into fiscal 2027, and management notes new-capacity capex is typically installed and online in less than one year per project. Fiscal 2026 capex is estimated at $60-65 million (versus $22.4 million in fiscal 2024 and $42.6 million in fiscal 2025), with fiscal 2027 capex expected to be similar at roughly $60 million including infrastructure to support a laser ramp. The Massachusetts fab mix is now a combination of Telecom, Defense and Data Center as indium phosphide ramps.
FY2026 capex $60M-$65M, FY2027 similar ~$60M; longer lead times being quoted on internally manufactured products

On the proposed U.S. ban on Chinese transceiver module makers, CEO Steve Daly said MACOM's Data Center growth is driven by U.S. hyperscalers plus U.S. enterprise and compute OEMs, and that those end users are typically directly involved in selecting chips for their hardware. If hyperscalers have to shift share between transceiver companies because of new regulations, 'we would expect to follow that business to those other manufacturers' - a customer mix shift rather than a demand loss, since MACOM has relationships with most transceiver companies in the industry. MACOM has NO MANUFACTURING IN CHINA, only about 85 employees there in application sales and logistics supporting Scandinavian telecom design centres and the optical industry, and the vast majority of what it sells into China is exported back out inside systems typically headed to the U.S.
No manufacturing in China; ~85 employees there in sales/logistics

Lead times are stretching beyond the prior four-to-eight-week range as constraints spread across substrates, foundry nodes, subcontracted assembly and test. Expedite requests increased sharply and many orders placed inside lead time could not be supported; management said AI demand is crowding out advanced packaging and substrate capacity.
foundry, substrate, advanced-packaging and OSAT constraints; unsupported expedite demand

On overinvestment concerns in AI data centers: 'we do have a very clear view on demand and supply imbalance. The supply is very much short, and that is why this project is announced one after another, which I believe is a healthy situation' - without securing computing power, AI technology and services would slow; SoftBank sees the Stargate Project as having set the fire in the market and does not view it as a bubble.

NEW-BUILD ECONOMICS GAP: ERCOT year-to-date wholesale power has averaged $30/MWh (same as last year) versus the ~$90/MWh area cited for new-build contracting — '30 is not going to get new stuff built.' The price of generation EQUIPMENT 'has doubled, if not tripled' in some cases, so what was an acceptable build price a year or two ago no longer is. In PJM the $555/MW-day RPB cap 'might get some things built' but a spread around it will be needed for certain projects. Large-load customers are willing to contract with EXISTING assets at a PREMIUM because it is still a discount to new build; co-location can beat even an islanded new build on speed.
ERCOT YTD $30/MWh vs ~$90 new build; equipment costs 2-3x; PJM RPB cap $555/MW-day

On our remaining 830 MW of approved capacity at Helios Two (energization slated for late 2028), conversations continue to advance across hyperscalers, Neoclouds, some of the labs themselves, and some new entrants; new guarantee and lease wrap structures are being formalized. We've already placed deposits and issued purchase orders on more than $180 million of long-lead electrical equipment, including main power transformers and switchgear. West's Pitchfork switching station is under construction to support energization of this 830 MW.
830 MW approved at Helios Two unleased, late-2028 energization; >$180M long-lead electrical equipment ordered

Governor Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to conduct a comprehensive audit of all data center projects seeking grid interconnection; we no longer expect communication on Batch Zero classification in the coming days. Forward market demand for power and compute is stronger today than it's ever been, while forward market supply of new projects is very quickly being constrained by both physical delivery and political headwinds. Leases for power at this scale are increasingly being signed well ahead of energization.

Full-year FY2026 forecast raised: revenue from JPY 500 billion to JPY 550 billion (+10%), electronics from JPY 350 billion to JPY 375 billion (+14%); operating profit from JPY 90 billion to JPY 127 billion (+41%, operating margin expectation raised from 18% to 23%), electronics OP from JPY 75 billion to JPY 110 billion; net profit raised to JPY 84 billion. Biggest driver: ASP and product mix with a positive impact of JPY 26.5 billion (majority is ASP - the planned quarterly price-reduction curve became less steep or prices were not reduced at all, plus general substrate price increases in an industry-wide supply shortage; not concentrated in a particular customer - GPU, CPU, switching IC and PC ASPs rising across the board). Revenue growth expected in all sub-segments: AI server, switching IC, and general-purpose server/PC.
FY revenue guide JPY 550 billion (from JPY 500 billion); OP JPY 127 billion (from JPY 90 billion, +41%); ASP/mix impact +JPY 26.5 billion

Supply-demand: 'The situation where demand exceeds the industry supply capacity is expected to continue' - substrates are getting larger and more difficult toward next fiscal year and the one after, AI server demand keeps rising, and current selling prices are expected to at least hold at present levels. Customers accepted fewer price cuts, and in some cases none, because of industry-wide shortages. Glass cloth and CCL cost increases are passed through to ASP in a timely manner. Utilization: apart from Intel Cell 5, almost everything was at full capacity utilization; sourcing for the revised FY2026 plan is already secured, though industry-wide competition for materials and equipment could constrain material supply in coming years.
Demand exceeds industry supply capacity; near-full utilization except Intel Cell 5; prices expected to at least hold

Glass cloth: procurement risks flagged at the beginning of the year have been mitigated. The number of glass cloth suppliers has increased - previously two companies in Japan and Taiwan, now a third and fourth supplier are visible, giving four glass cloth suppliers with visibility for use in mass production; the Japanese glass cloth supplier is increasing capacity, and the tight glass cloth supply situation is expected to simmer down. Ibiden believes it is in an advantageous position in the industry for glass cloth supply. Glass core substrate: joint development continuing (glass core and component-embedding structures pursued as two separate options with their own roadmaps, possibly narrowing to one later).
Four glass cloth suppliers now visible for mass production (was two); Japanese supplier adding capacity

Demand for AI power supply solutions continues to exceed available supply — the business is operating on a first come, first served basis; order backlog rose noticeably quarter-over-quarter; delivery times are increasing across the industry
order backlog nearly EUR 30 billion at the end of June

Several leading AI data center customers have entered into multi-year capacity reservation agreements or are in negotiations; the agreements include certain advance payments, cover customers along the value chain from Asia and the U.S., and prices are reviewed and redetermined regularly
cumulative revenue volume in the high single-digit billion EUR range

Demand indicators are unusually strong for K&S: utilisation rates improved sequentially in ALL regions and ALL end markets, with China utilisation over 95% and both memory and general semiconductor end markets around 90%. Management is seeing inbound purchase orders extending into fiscal Q2 - explicitly noting 'usually, that doesn't happen for us; we usually don't have purchase orders that go out that far' - and customers in China continuing to build factories. On that basis management is confident the traditional business stays strong through the FIRST HALF OF FISCAL 2027, with more colour on the second half promised on the November call. Management declined to project a return to the $1.5 billion annual levels of 2021-2022, calling those pandemic-driven extremes a very high bar.
China utilisation >95%; memory and general semi end markets ~90%; purchase orders extending into fiscal Q2

Capacity: the Singapore capital expansion is progressing well and remains on track for completion by the FIRST FISCAL HALF OF 2027, supporting Advanced Solutions growth over coming years. For the traditional wire bonding business, K&S has increased capacity FOURFOLD compared with about two quarters ago through its flexible manufacturing model. Management said it is explicitly focused on not losing market share because of capacity constraints, noted K&S has supported $400 million quarters before, and did not see a $450 million quarterly run rate at this point while committing to ramp further if needed.
Wire bonding capacity increased fourfold versus ~two quarters ago; Singapore expansion completing in H1 fiscal 2027

Capacity build-out on two fronts. MKS is DOUBLING the capacity of its Guangzhou chemistry equipment factory, which comes ONLINE IN Q3 2027; in the meantime it has turned the Germany factory back on - previously running at a low level, now much busier - and keeps eking out space in the existing Guangzhou plant, so it is 'bursting at the seams' but has been able to take every order. On the semiconductor side the new Malaysia (Penang) supercenter opened in Q2 with first revenue shipments already made; it was not needed for 2026 demand and is ramping for 2027 and beyond, and can be expanded at MKS's option. Management RAISED the WFE level it believes it can support once Penang is filled out to the $200-250 BILLION range, an increase from the $180-200 billion cited last quarter. Start-up costs run through cost of goods at 50-80 basis points of gross margin per quarter for at least the next couple of quarters and are expected to be self-liquidating.
Guangzhou chemistry equipment capacity doubling, online Q3 2027; supportable WFE raised to $200B-$250B (from $180B-$200B); 50-80bps quarterly gross-margin drag from start-up costs

Specialty Industrial revenue was $313 million, up 8% sequentially and 14% year over year - the highest level since 2023 - driven by DATACOM (specifically communications testing for AI data centers) and DEFENSE, both expected to stay strong in Q3. Automotive is bouncing along with no degradation or material improvement, and industrial is seeing incremental improvement of a smaller magnitude. Separately, services revenue reached one of the highest levels ever, which management attributes to very high utilisation at semiconductor customers whose fabs have been running hot for a couple of years; management treats this as a new elevated baseline for the foreseeable future.
Specialty Industrial $313M (+8% QoQ, +14% YoY), highest since 2023

Inventory drawdown on both sides: balance-sheet inventory decreased by $5 million and days on hand fell by 27 days to 265 days at quarter end, with a further reduction in inventory days expected in the second half. Channel inventory also declined, with weeks on hand improving by more than a week and a half to 7.3 weeks, back inside the seven-to-eight-week target range after starting the year above nine weeks. Management expects some level of sell-in in Q3 while still aiming to stay around eight weeks.
Channel inventory 7.3 weeks (target 7-8); DOH 265 days, down 27 days

Supply-chain differentiation: management describes a 'unique supply chain structure' whose ability to supply and to keep lead times 'very competitive' is an opportunity to take share while competitors run into supply issues. A hyperscaler met with during the week of the call raised the same point unprompted. No specific capacity or wafer figures were given.

PJM fundamentals: 'nearly 50% increase in West Hub sparks since last year'; 2028 PPL spark spreads up 28% and ADHUB up 27% versus July 2025 pricing; long-term hyperscaler PPAs were recently discussed at prices in the $80 per MWh range and forward wholesale energy plus capacity is now approaching or exceeding those levels; the last three base residual capacity auctions cleared at the price cap with uncapped prices that would have settled in excess of $500 a MWd; bilateral capacity bids at the cap seen for the early 2030s. PPL basis widened from ~$9 per megawatt hour historically to approximately $20 per MWh on transmission outages — every $1 improvement in basis equals approximately $1 of adjusted FCF per share.
West Hub sparks +~50% YoY; 2028 PPL sparks +28%; capacity auctions clearing at cap (uncapped >$500/MWd)

WULF Compute (Lake Mariner): Approximately $2.3 billion of project capital expenditures have been completed, with approximately $1.7 billion remaining. Approximately 2/3 of the remaining expenditures are committed. We currently estimate total project costs at approximately $9.1 million per megawatt within that original guidance range ($8 million-$10 million per critical IT megawatt) and modestly above the approximately $8.6 million per megawatt financed in October 2025. Electrical labor remains highly constrained; we scaled the workforce to support approximately 1,000 electricians at peak.
$2.3B capex completed, ~$1.7B remaining; ~$9.1M per critical IT MW (up from ~$8.6M at financing)

Order book at multi-decade highs: Q2 book-to-bill was 1.32, with semiconductors at 1.23 and passives at 1.40, and Q2 was a record high for resistor and inductor bookings. Total backlog grew 18% to $1.9 BILLION, equal to 6.1 months. In the Americas, book-to-bill was 1.5 and orders for passives reached the highest level seen in MORE THAN 20 YEARS. Customers are extending visibility to secure supply - many forecasting six months out to replenish their own inventories, and AI-driven demand has led numerous customers to place orders BEYOND 52 WEEKS to hold a place in Vishay's production loading. Some automotive customers are providing 12-to-18-month forecasts.
Book-to-bill 1.32 (semis 1.23, passives 1.40); backlog +18% to $1.9B (6.1 months); Americas book-to-bill 1.5; AI customers ordering beyond 52 weeks

Component supply is tightening and pricing is rising. Industry lead times are stretching and customers are concerned about availability and assurance of supply. Vishay began announcing price increases in Q4 2025 tied to rising metals, materials and logistics costs and continued through Q1 and Q2; ABOUT ONE THIRD of running part numbers now have announced price increases, some of which landed in Q2 results. CEO Joel Smejkal said the increases are real rather than 'paper' and that Vishay reprices the backlog quickly so customers cannot pull orders ahead of them. On whether this is double ordering: management says it is still fairly rational - point-of-sale consumption is growing, distribution inventory FELL to 18 weeks from 20 weeks, and distributors have been unable to replenish despite wanting to. Customers are also increasingly requesting WESTERN supply of electronic components, which suits Vishay's footprint. Management describes the industry as early in the upcycle.
~1/3 of running part numbers have announced price increases; distribution inventory down to 18 weeks from 20

Capacity build-out, funded by $900 million invested during the trough years plus a new equity raise. Full-year 2026 capex is $400-440 million with about half earmarked for the 12-inch fab in Germany (Itzehoe): all equipment is assembled, installation completes in Q3, engineering wafers start toward the end of the year and NON-AUTOMOTIVE PRODUCTION REMAINS ON TRACK FOR MID-2027. At the Newport fab, nine of ten automotive customer audits are complete with PCN program approvals expected monthly through year end, which will raise Newport utilisation and free capacity at the Itzehoe 8-inch fab. Vishay is also ramping production at two foundries in KOREA plus another in CHINA from Q3, explicitly to add wafer capacity for AI MOSFETs and diodes in the later part of the year, and is working to add dedicated in-house back-end capacity to cut dependence on outside subcontractors. Q2 capex was $95 million including approximately $66 million for the German fab.
FY2026 capex $400M-$440M (~half for the 12-inch German fab); Q2 capex $95M incl. ~$66M for Germany; 2 Korean foundries + 1 China foundry ramping in Q3; German fab non-auto production mid-2027

Lead times extending: gas prime (large engines) sold out to the back half of 2028 and into 2029, turbines 'a little bit farther than that', diesel gensets 'well into 2028' with some customers moving down to the smaller C32 platform for availability; far-dated orders carry price escalators tied to economic indicators. 'No one is slowing down at the moment. In fact, if we can get more units out, they're asking us to give them more units.'
gas prime lead times to late 2028/2029; diesel gensets into 2028

Black Pearl: at the request of our tenant, we executed an amendment to the lease that accelerated the development timeline of initial capacity. The first data center capacity at Black Pearl was delivered in August, two full months ahead of the original schedule, and rent has commenced at the site. We've secured approximately 96% of the equipment required across both phase I and phase II.
First Black Pearl capacity delivered 2 months early, rent commenced; 96% of phase I+II equipment secured

Build-cost inflation: we definitely see inflation on labor and equipment across the board. As we build budgets for the next build, I would expect our budgeting to go up, and that probably translates into a higher cost per megawatt (analyst-cited historical range $9 million-$11 million per megawatt). We're running at the contingency level given that inflation. At some of our sites we put a cap on the CapEx that we have exposure to and pass this risk to the tenant.
cost per MW expected to creep higher from the $9M-$11M/MW range; running at contingency level

Capacity: 2026 power generation growth 'will continue to be constrained by capacity'; 20 GW of incremental capacity announced at the May Analyst Day across plants and supply chain — some online in 2027, a bigger step-up in 2028, phasing through 2030; large gensets are 'basically at capacity' so customers are taking smaller gensets; new orders now selling out into the second half of 2028 with 'absolutely no pausing or blinking in demand'.
20 GW incremental capacity by 2030; large gensets sold out into 2H 2028

Procurement: the first Building 1 on each campus are fully contracted. 100% of long lead time bindings are contracted. GC subcontractors pricing is fixed, and that aligns with the financings that we've done. Building 2 was cheaper than Building 1. Now, as we're finalizing Building 3, we expect it to be cheaper than Building 2. We actually haven't seen a big impact when it comes to lead times, capacity and allocation and queues - we focus on building partnerships, integrating vendors' equipment into a skidded design.
100% of long-lead equipment contracted for Building 1 at each campus; cost per building falling B1 -> B2 -> B3

Equipment position: the 1.2 GW project is 'the first 1.2 GW of the 5.4 GW of turbine and EPC capacity we've secured through 2032' via GE Vernova and Kiewit; broader development pipeline is more than twice the 5.4 GW secured, 'with every turbine slot tied to an active customer discussion'; under the GE Vernova/Kiewit structure another 1.2 GW block can come online serially each year after the 2029 COD; plus about 2 GW of uprate opportunities across the PJM fleet (less than half economic at the $555/MW-day cap, all 2,000 MW in bilateral talks).
5.4 GW turbine + EPC capacity secured through 2032; pipeline >2x that; ~2 GW PJM uprates

Capacity build-out: Jacintoport expansion adds 335,000 sq ft (completion in the next month or two, 'well in excess of $100 million of incremental annualized revenue' when fully utilized); 50,000 sq ft Houston-area lease (April) and 30,000 sq ft near Ohio; board authorized a ~300,000 sq ft leased manufacturing facility available late fiscal Q2 / early Q3 2027 supported by an $8 million Moseley fabrication investment; a greenfield owned 250,000-300,000 sq ft factory requiring $70 million-$100 million remains under evaluation. Total footprint up over 20% by end of fiscal 2026 vs fiscal 2025.
Jacintoport +335,000 sq ft (>$100M annualized revenue when fully utilized); ~300,000 sq ft lease facility for fiscal 2027; greenfield option $70M-$100M; footprint +20%

Capacity: approximately $600 million of growth investments deployed since 2022 under the local-for-local model, mostly quick modular expansions in step with customer roadmaps; capex $90 million in the quarter, elevated for the full year, returning to the 6% of net sales range longer term. Management says growth is faster than expected but it can bring capacity online quickly and is well prepared for 2027 and 2028; no near-term risk to supply or output from the ~$20 million logistics/energy cost pressure, which is being offset by targeted pricing.
~$600 million growth investment since 2022; capex $90 million in Q2; ~$20 million cost headwind

CEC (electrical) revenue +140% YoY; CEC combined backlog rose $1.7 billion since year-end 2025 to about $2.4 billion, and 'CEC is now getting the second buildings on data centers that they're at'. CEC capacity filled in about 90 days after acquisition; Q2 adjusted margin 11.4% vs upper-20s for site development, with 300-500 basis points of CEC margin improvement targeted over 12-18 months. 'If we had 1,000 or 2,000 more electricians, we'd be growing it even faster.'
CEC revenue +140% YoY; CEC combined backlog ~$2.4B (+$1.7B since year-end 2025); CEC adj. margin 11.4%

Hyperscaler demand visibility: 'What we are seeing just from our top hyperscalers, the amount of work that is coming, we have to add capacity significantly faster just to keep up with them.' Customers are purchasing incremental land adjacent to existing campuses; projects that were three years are now five to eight to 12 years, none of which is in future-phase numbers. Texas 'is going to be bigger in the next three years than any other market related to data centers'. Electricians remain the tightest resource; no schedule delays from data-center moratorium politics seen.

Notebook H1 beat expectations as brand customers pulled in orders ahead of memory price hikes, but H2 notebook units are guided down 10-20% (around 15% half-on-half) as the pull-forward ends and PCs get too expensive; revenue may not fall as much because per-unit ASP rises with memory content. AI server demand is rigid - customers keep buying even as memory prices rise - whereas PCs and phones see replacement cycles stretch. High leverage across the industry is described as a norm driven by the high material share and by customers pre-buying components against memory shortage; Wistron discusses buy-and-sell versus consignment per customer, with both options on the table.
H2 notebook shipments down 10 to 20% (about 15% half-on-half)

Capacity: Ichor has the capacity today to support $500 million in quarterly revenue ($2 billion annually within the current footprint); with targeted investments (a little more clean room space being executed in the second half of 2026, plus machining capacity) it can expand capacity within the existing footprint upwards of $3 billion annually, more than double the current run rate. Management says neither demand nor manufacturing capacity is the growth constraint today; it is gearing up for a significant 2027 but is not guiding $3 billion.
capacity $500 million per quarter today; up to ~$3 billion annual within existing footprint after investment

Isolated part shortages late in the quarter (flow control is the supplier category that keeps the CEO up at night) kept Ichor from recognizing its full revenue forecast by the June 26th quarter end; the revenue shipped literally days after the quarter, and Ichor surpassed $300 million in revenue for the 13 weeks ending July 3rd. Customers are placing POs out six months ahead, which is abnormal, and product qualifications are going faster than normal because customers need to de-risk their supply chain.
revenue surpassed $300 million for the 13 weeks ending July 3rd; customer POs placed six months ahead

Weldment business is seeing significant growth and recovery after a period of being brought down; Ichor has increased weldment capacity with additional capacity coming online in the second half; chemical delivery, gas delivery and weldments are all executing to what customers need.

Capacity roadmap: built an additional 26,000 sq ft of clean room space in Malaysia and is increasing capacity within the current footprint in Singapore and the Czech Republic; $3.5 billion capacity ready by end of 2026, matching the current run rate; $4 billion annualized revenue run rate (equivalent to $200 billion WFE) in the first half of 2027. Evaluating a new Southeast Asia expansion (greenfield) to support a $5 billion run rate / $250 billion WFE: capacity beyond $4 billion added in the first half of 2028 and a $5 billion run rate in the second half of 2028.
26,000 sq ft clean room added in Malaysia; $3.5 billion capacity by YE2026; $4 billion run rate 1H 2027; $5 billion run rate 2H 2028

Customers are sharing unprecedented visibility, extending forecasts and giving longer planning horizons; they are booking into the back half of 2027 and some into 2028 (analyst framing) and, being constrained on internal capacity, intend to focus on final test and final integration and overflow subsystem build to partners like UCT, which historically drives Products outgrowth in an upturn.

No component shortages or delivery pushouts in Q2 (a competitor reported some): the UCT ramp-readiness campaign secured most critical components well ahead; management expects continued double-digit industry growth quarter by quarter to keep pressure on the WFE supply chain and to produce excursions that must be proactively managed.

Pre-payments rose notably in Q2 because GUC pre-buys materials for large CSP turnkey programs - besides CoWoS it must secure HBM stacks and substrate ahead of the build so everything (substrate, HBM, the SoC from TSMC) arrives together for packaging. GUC sells the customer the finished CoWoS package with HBM inside; if HBM prices rise the chip price rises with it, so the cost risk sits with the customer, not GUC. Management cited HBM pricing going from about 240 at the start of the year to 700 and up to 900 (as spoken; unit not stated), fully passed through. Whether HBM procurement flows through GUC's own P&L or is booked as a service fee is still being worked out case by case at this early stage.
HBM price cited from ~240 early in the year to 700-900 (as spoken), passed through to customers

NAND market view: growth in AI demand is driving the NAND market with data centers and enterprise applications leading; agentic AI applications are a key growth driver, impacting even demand for traditional servers. Smartphone NAND demand expected flat vs calendar 2025 (low-priced model shipments declining, high-end steady with rising storage capacity); PC shipments to decrease on rising BOM costs (NAND slightly down). Calendar 2026 NAND market bit growth anticipated in the high teens percentage range, in line with Kioxia's own bit growth; for calendar 2027 demand is forecast to EXCEED supply. QLC NAND SSD replacing nearline HDD in data centers is an opportunity, though the transition may be slower than expected while the market is skewed toward high-end pricing.
CY2026 NAND bit growth high teens %; CY2027 demand to exceed supply

2026 capex revised up to TWD 18 billion from TWD 13 billion (about 30% land and buildings, 70% equipment, R&D, automation and production testing; includes the planned U.S./Texas expansion); Kaohsiung Plant Phase 2 and the Quang Ninh plant in Vietnam start mass production in Q3 and Q4. Non-China production capacity grew 162% in 2026 vs 2025 and is forecast to grow another 63% in 2027, reaching a 60% share of total capacity by end of 2026 and 70% next year. Strategic material stocking (inventory up TWD 11.2 billion QoQ) covers critical parts for H2 amid shortages, with cost increases passed on to customers who are willing to accept them to secure materials.
capex TWD 18 billion (from TWD 13 billion); non-China capacity +162% in 2026, +63% forecast for 2027; inventory up TWD 11.2 billion QoQ

Board approved a discretionary $5 billion U.S. financing budget to secure supply chain capacity and fuel expansion from AI ASIC chips to full-scale systems and platforms, including flexibility to support key suppliers' expansion; supply chain capacity across foundry, substrate and memory seen as sufficient for the 2026 and 2027 revenue targets.

Data center: demand from the major NPU customers has been very strong, and Renesas memory interface has been growing strongly and continuously alongside; digital power also strong - both infrastructure lines exceeded guidance, and ASIC customer demand is strong on top of the historical GPU customer group. Supply remains the constraint: 'Everywhere you look, everything seems very tight' - WOI numbers show continuous tightness with no breakthrough; Renesas is working on a step-function type supply increase from the end of this year into next year, which would let revenue grow on supply capability. Position: 'As of now, I think we are in a very good position... In order to maintain our good position, we have to do a very strong execution' - digital power spans several ASIC customers and CPU customers with share shifting by product generation.
NPU-driven memory interface and digital power very strong; supply very tight; step-function supply increase targeted from the end of this year and next year

Kumamoto earthquake impact limited: Nishiki back-end factory has resumed full production; Kawashiri front-end factory (about 13% of company-wide sales) expected to resume production on August 5 with about three weeks to full operation - wafer testing already resumed, pure-water and facility repairs under way. Die bank and inventory had been secured beforehand; shake was smaller than the 2016 quake and countermeasures (anti-seismic equipment mounting, BCP inventory) sped recovery. J-OSAT partner in Kyushu also impacted but outlook limited; customer supply chains being monitored. Separately, the Takasaki 6-inch front-end factory will be gradually closed (6-inch equipment maintenance/parts no longer supportable industry-wide), production migrating to 8-inch plus; employment maintained and the site shifts toward R&D.
Kawashiri plant (13% of sales) restart August 5, ~3 weeks to full operation; Takasaki 6-inch plant to close gradually

Q2 outlook (FX-neutral, JPY 150/USD assumption) - sales in all segments expected to exceed beginning-of-year projections: Passive Components +2%-5% (automotive inductive devices plus AI server products such as aluminum electrolytic capacitors), Sensors +3%-6% (ICT seasonality: magnetic sensors, MEMS microphones), Magnetic Application +6%-8% (head volume +10%, suspension assemblies ~+6%, including captive-designated volume), Energy +9%-12% (smartphone production to peak in Q2; small battery volume ~+10%, mid-sized industrial batteries growing). Full-year FY2027 forecast maintained at beginning-of-year levels while Q1 significantly exceeded projections; memory supply tightness and higher memory prices remain the drag on ICT-related production.
Q2 segment growth guides: passives +2-5%, sensors +3-6%, magnetic +6-8%, energy +9-12%; full-year forecast unchanged

Strong AI server demand is producing pull-in requests for delivery and additional orders from customers, and price revisions are being negotiated with multiple customers - applied to existing models as well - with considerable impact expected in the fourth quarter of FY2027. Management aims for gross profit margin of 50% or more within around two years (could be reached in the early stage of next fiscal year) and maintains the 35% operating margin mid-term target. On capacity: the new Miyagi innovative production center (smart fab, completion next summer) can increase capacity by 3 times, and the timing is being accelerated to meet market growth; Tokyo Electron delivers 4,000 to 6,000 units per year and is working to cut equipment startup time by half. The July 28 Kumamoto earthquake closed coater developer, cleaning and bonding system sites in Koshi City, but all employees are safe, no building damage was identified, full operation was expected early the following week, and impacts on business performance are minor - etch systems, deposition systems and probers made outside Kumamoto are unaffected. Epsira (announced December 2025) is the digital infrastructure to raise field productivity, and Tokyo Electron announced expansion of its collaboration with NVIDIA this month to develop solutions for agentic AI and robotics.
Gross margin target 50% or more within around two years; Miyagi smart fab to lift capacity by 3 times; 4,000 to 6,000 units delivered per year; Kumamoto earthquake impact minor

The limiting factor is ramp rate, not capacity — how fast AIXTRON and its suppliers can hire and train people; output ramping 3X within the year (EUR 59 million Q1 to over EUR 200 million implied in Q4); customer advance payments fund the ramp
advance payments EUR 197 million at end of June, around 43% of the equipment order backlog, more than EUR 150 million above year-end 2025

Record ATM (OSAT) revenue NTD 126.1B (+12% QoQ, +36% YoY) with ATM gross margin 27.3% and operating margin 15.7%; full-year 2026 ATM revenue expected to grow ~35%. Capacity is the binding constraint — blended utilization 80-85% but 'generally very close to being full', with near-term growth gated by equipment installation and building construction. Q4 2026 ATM gross margin is likely to EXCEED the 30% structural ceiling, after which management will review raising the 26-29% structural margin range upward; pricing environment described as friendly, with material and component cost inflation passed through to customers.
ATM record NTD 126.1B (+36% YoY), GM 27.3%; Q4 GM to break the 30% structural ceiling

LEAP (leading-edge advanced packaging) revenue is tracking ~USD 200M AHEAD of the USD 3.5B 2026 guidance and management is aiming to DOUBLE LEAP revenue in 2027. Full-process CoWoS-like packaging is on track for ~USD 300M in 2026 with substantial growth in 2027 and is expected to be margin-accretive. ASE's fully automated PANEL line (310mm x 310mm) enters production in Q1 2027, complementary to foundry CoWoS and serving the same customer set at similar reticle size and pitch. Capacity — not demand — is the constraint: blended utilization 80-85% but effectively full, with growth gated by equipment installation and building construction (13 greenfield plus 8 brownfield projects underway). FY2026 capex raised USD 2B to ~USD 10.5B, ~70% of equipment capex going to leading edge.
LEAP ~USD 3.7B 2026, DOUBLING in 2027; full-process ~USD 300M; panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027

CAPACITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: blended utilization 80-85%, but 'outside of equipment lines being placed into service, capacities were generally very close to being full' — non-LEAP wire bond and traditional advanced packaging were tight, and wafer sort and final test were running near full. 'Our capability for near-term incremental growth is being gated by our abilities to install capital equipment and build out our buildings and facilities.' Dr. Wu frames HARDWARE INFRASTRUCTURE as the new bottleneck ('we have not experienced this for the last 40 years') and argues packaging is moving up the system-architecture value chain. On the Q3 guide: '12%-13% growth... means we have to add 12%-13% capacity'; all customers are asking for more devices in Q3 and Q4.
utilization 80-85% but effectively full; growth gated by equipment install + building construction

Technology roadmap. PANEL: ASE's fully automated panel line starts PRODUCTION IN Q1 2027 in a 310mm x 310mm form factor — described as COMPLEMENTARY to foundry CoWoS, serving the SAME CUSTOMER SET with identical reticle size and pitch/line-width coverage; adoption depends on capacity, performance and speed of execution. GLASS SUBSTRATE: NOT in production and not within the next 12 months; R&D is evaluating feasibility and economics with substrate suppliers, the foundry and customers. FULL-PROCESS (CoWoS-like): on track for ~USD 300M of revenue in 2026 with aggressive capacity expansion and substantial growth in 2027; margin not yet fully reflected but expected to be margin-accretive. CPO: launching toward the END OF 2026 in initially small volume, yielding benchmark data on bandwidth, system performance and thermal dissipation; more detail promised in two quarters. Bigger reticle sizes drive panel/more-complex CoWoS first, then POWER DELIVERY becomes the next constraint over the following two to three years.
panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027; glass substrate not within 12 months; full-process ~USD 300M 2026; CPO launches late 2026

Helium: headwind of 2% in the quarter, better than the 3% guided, driven by improved volume and pricing in Asia supporting electronic customers; 40% of all helium volume sold in the quarter came from the Texas cavern (more in June) as Qatar-sourced volumes remain very limited and are excluded from the forecast. Air Products has been gaining many new long-term helium volume commitments, especially in electronics and especially in Asia, some tied to new electronics projects starting in one to three years and carrying the same term as its large on-site contracts.
helium headwind 2% (guided 3%); 40% of helium volume from Texas cavern

TURBINE SUPPLY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT AND AEP IS PRE-BUYING IT: an additional three gigawatts of gas-fired turbines secured during the quarter takes total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 gigawatts for deployment through 2031, and AEP is 'leveraging our sizable market position and strategic manufacturer relationships to secure up to 10 gigawatts of incremental turbine capacity through 2035' — an option it is not committed to. CEO Bill Fehrman named the suppliers: 'using our size and scale and our relationships with namely GE Vernova and Mitsubishi to get this equipment locked up... we know that generation is going to be a driving force, and because of that, it's a scarce resource and will become increasingly more valuable.' Roughly half of the 13 GW already sits in the $78 billion plan; the other half rolls into the 2027-2031 plan. The 10 GW option is timed to replace aging coal and gas plants as they retire.

Three gigawatts of turbines added in the quarter, taking total secured turbine capacity to approximately 13 GW through 2031; option on up to 10 GW more through 2035; about half of the 13 GW already inside the $78B plan

STRONGEST JUNE QUARTER EVER — leading-edge silicon demand keeps compounding: FQ3 revenue $109.4B, UP 16% year over year, with iPhone, Mac and Services each setting June-quarter records and double-digit growth IN EVERY GEOGRAPHIC SEGMENT. Gross margin 50.1% — including a favorable ~2-percentage-point impact from TARIFF REFUNDS — and diluted EPS $2.02, up 29%. Installed base of active devices at a new all-time high across all major product categories and regions. AI angle: WWDC26 introduced 'the all-new SIRI AI' alongside the latest software platforms — sustaining Apple's pull on TSMC leading-edge capacity (the prior quarter's constraint was explicitly advanced-node availability, not memory).
FQ3 $109.4B (+16%), best June qtr ever; EPS $2.02 (+29%); GM 50.1% incl ~2pts tariff refunds; Siri AI

CALL-ONLY: THE JUNE-QUARTER SHORTFALL WAS A LEADING-EDGE NODE SHORTAGE, AND IT GETS WORSE IN SEPTEMBER. Cook: June-quarter supply constraints hit 'primarily the Mac, and to a lesser extent, iPhone and iPad', and 'the constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the ADVANCED NODES that our SoCs are produced on'. Root cause is 'not a regular supply issue - it's a DEMAND FORECAST issue' (iPhone +22% and Mac +29% ran ahead of Apple's own high expectations). 'We are seeing LESS FLEXIBILITY in the supply chain than normal... we've been pulling supply ahead. At some point, there's a limit to that.' For the September quarter the supply-constraint impact 'increases SIGNIFICANTLY sequentially' and now spans iPhone, Mac AND iPad - 'we've got a quarter that we're going to be scrambling on the supply side'. Asked whether adding a second US fab operator would help, Cook rejected the premise: 'this isn't a partner or supplier issue.'
Sept-qtr constraint impact up SIGNIFICANTLY QoQ; iPhone + Mac + iPad all constrained

CALL-ONLY: MEMORY IS NOW THE ENTIRE MARGIN STORY, QUANTIFIED. CFO Parekh's bridge: total-company GM 49.3% (Mar qtr) -> 48.1% (Jun qtr, ex-tariff-refund) = -120bps, and 'MORE THAN 100% of that can be explained by the MEMORY COST change' - FX 'was a factor' but 'the main driver was really the memory cost impact'. The same holds into the September guide: 48.1% -> 46.5% midpoint (ex-refund) = -160bps, again more than fully explained by memory, with partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix. Reported June-quarter GM was 50.1% INCLUDING ~2pts of tariff refunds (products GM 40.1%, +140bps QoQ including >2.5pts of refunds; services GM 75.6%, -110bps on mix). September guide: revenue +9-11% YoY (FX -2.5pts sequential + rising supply constraints), iPhone mid-teens, GM 47-48% incl. ~1pt refunds, opex $19.1-19.4B, tax ~16.5%.
Jun GM 48.1% ex-refund (-120bps, >100% memory-driven); Sep guide GM 47-48%, rev +9-11%

CALL-ONLY: MAC IS BEING BOUGHT AS AI COMPUTE. Mac $10.4B (+29% YoY, June-quarter record) 'despite significant supply constraints', with customers 'using MAC MINI as a powerful platform for AGENTIC AI' and 'deploying CLUSTERS OF MAC STUDIO systems to RUN FRONTIER-CLASS MODELS LOCALLY'; the stated differentiator is 'massive UNIFIED MEMORY BANDWIDTH' plus power-efficient performance and on-device inference. Enterprise pull is explicit - Disney moving creative AI workflows on-device 'to reduce overall CLOUD TOKEN COSTS' and keep IP secure; Credit Agricole on MacBook Pro. On capital intensity for Siri AI, Cook: Apple runs a HYBRID model - 'we use some THIRD-PARTY CLOUD, and we do OUR OWN DATA CENTERS. There will be a mix' - and AI spend is rising both in OpEx (opex $19.1B, +23% YoY on R&D) and 'other locations on the P&L other than OpEx, like COGS'. Siri AI (WWDC26) is in developer + public beta; EU launch still unresolved with the Commission (Mac exempt from those rules), China approved only for the original Apple Intelligence features so far.
Mac $10.4B (+29%); Mac Studio clusters run frontier models locally; hybrid own-DC + 3rd-party cloud

Component supply is tight across the board: lead times are stretching and MOSFETs in particular are short, though Delta's purchasing scale and supplier relationships keep demand largely fulfilled. Memory was the hardest hit - one business unit could not secure memory volumes at workable prices, so it switched designs to second sources and expects H2 shipments to normalize and catch up the backlog without a loss. Management does not expect power semiconductors to repeat memory's shortage dynamics - the two situations differ a lot - but notes power-semi supply is cyclical because capacity investment takes long. On wide-bandgap devices (silicon carbide, gallium nitride) Delta works early and closely with the most important suppliers, keeps talking with them continuously and gets early access to new products, but will not disclose any agreements; it is also broadening its supply chain, including Taiwanese supplier options. Supplier price increases will be negotiated and passed to customers where the business model allows, with a timing lag.

Component shortages were the quarter's defining constraint. Critical suppliers 'essentially shut a lot of us down with a hard stop' and the shortages hit faster and lasted longer than anticipated; Modine had previously flagged four suppliers as potential vulnerabilities in its risk-management process. Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.
450-550 bps Data Center margin impact from excess labour/overhead absorption; 150 bps warranty variance; four suppliers flagged as vulnerable; June margin back to normal

Structural response to the shortage: Modine is actively negotiating long-term agreements with its critical component suppliers covering FY 2028 and FY 2029 and expects them in place soon, its existing suppliers are expanding capacity to meet market demand, and in one instance Modine is considering vertical integration. Management noted it has doubled supply-chain spend year after year as the business has grown, and has brought in senior operations talent at plant level to negotiate these long-term contracts and dynamically rebalance launch schedules against available component capacity.
supplier LTAs targeted for FY2028 and FY2029; vertical integration under consideration in one case

Capacity ceiling stated: with the capex already deployed and the facilities and rooftops it has in place today, Modine believes the range is 'right around $4 billion' of revenue it can support over time. Going beyond that would require a different level of capex outlay, or a combination of an incremental facility, more efficiency on existing lines, and leveraging the supply chain to produce overflow capacity; design work is moving toward a more modular systems approach in the factory to add flexibility. The remaining chiller lines in Grenada, Jefferson City and the Dallas area are expected to be up and established at some level of efficiency by the end of the fiscal year. Coils production has been consolidated into Grenada and Juarez to allow the Grenada chiller lines to expand while preserving coil capacity for data-center customers; Heat Transfer Solutions sales improved 7%, or $11 million, on strong North America coil volume supporting data-center customers.
~$4 billion of revenue capacity on current capex and footprint; Grenada, Jefferson City and Dallas chiller lines running by end of fiscal 2027; coil sales +7% / $11M on data-center demand

Modine's 10-Q: Data Centers segment operating income was $46.3 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026 versus $34.7 million a year earlier. Data Centers cost of sales rose $149.3 million, or 116 percent, on higher sales volume, approximately $16.0 million of higher material costs, expenses of the rapid U.S. manufacturing capacity expansion, and supplier capacity constraints for certain key components that temporarily disrupted production schedules; Modine is working with current partners and qualifying additional suppliers to secure supply. Data Centers capital expenditures were $30.9 million versus $7.1 million, driven by investments to increase production capacity.

Data Centers operating income $46.3 million vs $34.7 million; Data Centers cost of sales +$149.3 million (+116 percent), material costs +~$16.0 million; Data Centers capex $30.9 million vs $7.1 million

Multilayer circuit board materials (MEGTRON): responding to strong demand, Panasonic is strengthening the supply chain including MULTI-SOURCING of key raw materials like glass cloth, in addition to building new production plants - capacity expansion for circuit board materials at Ayutthaya and Sukhothai sites; management concedes production capacity expansion was the challenge and 'we converted the phase completely'. For conductive polymer capacitors, plans to expand capacity at manufacturing sites are being accelerated; capex for capacitors and electronic materials being implemented EARLIER than the original plan because demand is growing faster than anticipated. Competitive backdrop: Taiwanese players are aggressively expanding capacity in circuit-board materials and capacitors; Panasonic cites high product capability (technical leadership in MEGTRON and capacitors). Supercapacitors attracting increased attention on surging AI server power consumption - mass production of devices for external customers to start at the Chitose plant during FY2027.
MEGTRON capacity expansion at Ayutthaya/Sukhothai + glass cloth multi-sourcing; capacitor capex pulled forward; Chitose supercapacitor mass production in FY2027

Raw materials and pricing: raw material/logistics prices a negative JPY 37 billion in Q1 (copper, resin and memory price hikes) and a negative JPY 66 billion expected for the full year - 'difficult to find the materials of which prices are not increasing': oil-linked resin, memories, metals (copper, silver), and device-specific tantalum and glass cloth, across essentially all segments. Price revisions/rationalization a positive JPY 54 billion in Q1 and JPY 59.6 billion expected full-year: Panasonic is raising prices not only to pass through material costs but also to lift unit prices and margins in high-demand AI-related materials and peripherals where supply is tight.
Raw material headwind JPY 66 billion FY (copper/resin/memory/tantalum/glass cloth); price revisions +JPY 59.6 billion FY

Craft labour is NOT the binding constraint today - Duke Austin: 'We're nowhere near capacity.' More than 85,000 employees; roughly 15,500 people added over the past year, well over 7,000 of them organic with a significant portion in Q2; Quanta spends about $250 million a year on training. It takes about four years to make a craftsman and a journeyman, and he sees no oversupply of craft-skilled labour in the near future. Labour is fungible across segments - electricians and underground crews move between data-center work, industrial and gas compression work and T&D - which is where the acquisition synergies show up. Customers are securing craft as far out as their five- to seven-year capital plans, with 'decade-plus type arrangements out there'. Margin follows that utilisation: the electric segment can operate at 10% to 12% on the utility side, with 12% the utmost 'when you stack in large transmission and all aspects at once', and Duke sees room for further margin improvement in the second half.
85,000+ employees, +15,500 over the year (>7,000 organic); ~$250M/yr training; 'nowhere near capacity'; electric segment margin range 10%-12% on the utility side

VERTICAL INTEGRATION INTO CRITICAL-PATH EQUIPMENT. Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' The rule he states: 'Anywhere there's a critical path that we think we can invest capital to move it forward, that's what you've seen us do... we're taking advantage of areas where there's underinvestment', and those vertical supply-chain investments are 'showing up in synergies'. He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Done collaboratively with the client it takes total installed cost down significantly and de-risks logistics; the Phalcon acquisition puts that capacity in the Northeast, close to where the work is.
HICO high-voltage breaker JV plus owned transformer and utility-pole manufacturing; fabrication footprint ~seven million sq ft, +0.5 million sq ft from the recent acquisitions

WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.
no specific figure (engine orders placed today carry a five- to six-year lead time; substation interconnection queue is the constraint)

Supply chain: SPX engineers its own fans, gear reducers and heat exchangers, giving it flexibility to build in-house or use third parties; before taking any large data-center order its supply chain team scrubs every bill-of-material item to validate it can deliver, having watched competitors fall down on supply chain. Management notes some customer concentration among a small number of hyperscalers.

Inventories at chip manufacturers in memory and logic had largely normalised, and Siltronic now sees indications that memory players are starting to rebuild wafer safety stocks, most likely to secure supply in an environment of strong AI-driven demand and tightening wafer availability; management called this safety-stock rebuilding a potential additional upside to wafer demand.

CEO Michael Heckmeier: customers are approaching Siltronic to manifest and confirm midterm demand, particularly in the memory space, where customers want to talk about volume developments two to three years out and discussions about new long-term agreements are starting; Siltronic engages but repeats that prices must come up to justify further investment.

300-millimeter demand recovery is becoming increasingly evident: new and smaller customers are approaching Siltronic and some existing customers are looking for upside volumes above their long-term agreement levels, which helped drive the Q2 sales improvement and the raised full-year sales guidance; management says it stays very careful and selective about whom it gives which volumes because the price level is still too low.

Balance sheet at end-June: total assets EUR 4.9 billion versus EUR 4.8 billion at year-end 2025, fixed assets down EUR 93 million as depreciation exceeded capex, cash and securities up to EUR 650 million on the capital increase, equity EUR 2.2 billion for an equity ratio of 45% versus 43% at year-end 2025, net financial debt down to EUR 692 million, plus an undrawn syndicated loan facility of EUR 127 million. Inventories rose on a targeted build to support improving demand and prepare for higher shipment volumes.
total assets EUR 4.9 billion; cash and securities EUR 650 million; equity EUR 2.2 billion; equity ratio 45%; net financial debt EUR 692 million; undrawn facility EUR 127 million

Utilisation is strong, particularly in the legacy fabs, and overall industry utilisation looks very high; equipment is still flowing into FabNext so capacity and output are still growing there, which is also why capex still runs ahead of the cash number. Lead times for further brownfield equipment are 18-24 months and Siltronic is in close contact with its major suppliers but has not triggered any future capex; no new greenfield fab will be announced anytime soon.

300-millimeter pricing: positive price developments are visible on low volumes in the non-LTA space, but spot pricing is still below the LTA price level and clearly below the reinvest level. CEO Michael Heckmeier: 'We always said prices need to come up and to cross the reinvest level. That holds true unchangeably.' Siltronic still expects an overall negative price impact for 2026 and will not commit to further brownfield investment or new long-term agreements until prices cross the reinvest level.

Around two-thirds of Siltronic's business is under long-term agreements, the majority of that in 300-millimeter, with one-third outside LTAs. Management sees no LTA cliff or major LTA change in 2027 or 2028; the major LTAs signed around 2020-2021 to underwrite FabNext run far beyond three years and some run until 2030, while a portfolio of shorter one-to-three-year agreements rolls over and could be renegotiated under better commercial terms in 2027 and 2028 if pricing improves.
around two-thirds of business under LTAs (majority 300mm); some LTAs run until 2030; no LTA cliff in 2027 or 2028

2026 wafer area consumption is still expected to grow by around 7% before inventory effects, unchanged from the Q1 view, but the mix outside servers weakened: smartphones now seen down around 11% and PCs down around 10%, automotive broadly unchanged at moderate growth of around 3%, and industrial applications up around 13% from a relatively low base including demand from data-center infrastructure.
wafer area consumption +7% in 2026; smartphones -11%; PCs -10%; automotive +3%; industrial +13%

On the wafer supply-demand balance, CEO Michael Heckmeier said there still seems to be a bit more wafer supply than demand, but that this could change pretty soon in the next quarters, with the price pattern the true indicator; a broad, meaningful wafer price increase has not happened yet, only small volumes here and there, and he argued a very significant price increase must come to the wafer industry to rebalance value creation across the chain.

Recent news flow from a competitor could create another smaller shortage in certain 200-millimeter products; some customers have approached Siltronic to fill that demand and some have even started discussions about 200-millimeter long-term agreements. Siltronic receives 200-millimeter requests from all over the globe including China, where customers want advanced specifications from the established supply base. Siltronic is restaffing lines it had been running on a cost- and cash-optimised basis to follow the demand.

GENERATION BUILDOUT FOR AI LOAD - 10 GW APPROVED AND GEORGIA ALREADY OVERSUBSCRIBED. Over the past several years Southern has secured regulatory approvals for 10 GW of new company-owned generation resources, including thermal, battery and solar, as well as hundreds of miles of new transmission lines. The first two of several battery sites are in service, and work on three combustion turbines at Plant Yates is advancing toward completion in the coming quarters. Poroch said the company is 'about 1 GW or 2 away from... selling out the capacity that we had approved in Georgia last year', and Womack added that 'the OpenAI contract in Georgia pushes us beyond our recently approved capacity by right around 1 GW' - i.e. the signed AI load has already outrun approved supply.
10 GW of new company-owned generation approved (thermal/battery/solar) + hundreds of miles of transmission; Georgia capacity ~1 GW oversubscribed after the OpenAI contract

NEW NUCLEAR: HYPERSCALERS BEING ASKED TO SHARE AP1000 COST-OVERRUN RISK. Womack said the country needs more nuclear units in operation particularly in the mid-2030s, credited the administration for regulatory actions and for convening groups around long-lead-time items, but stated plainly that 'Southern Company is not going to be next' on a new nuclear build. Asked whether hyperscalers are willing to absorb cost overruns above budgeted amounts for AP1000s, he said he did not want to get ahead of a firm conclusion but 'yes, we are having conversations with them in terms of what role they can play.'

Thailand ramp and inventory: Thailand plant phase 2 mass production slipped about two months on equipment-delivery delays, but phase-1 experience shortened the ramp curve - it began contributing shipments in July 2026, ramps through August, should help Q3 results and reach full output by Q4 2026. Inventory stands at NT$100 hundred million with turnover days down to 90 despite much higher revenue; management says inventory must keep rising as new capacity opens.
Thailand phase 2 contributing from July 2026, full output by Q4; inventory NT$100 hundred million, 90 turnover days

Management says demand is outstripping supply across the electrical value chain: 'the constraint is power and labor' - power is the ultimate largest governor of data center construction, followed by construction labor, with a variety of in-front-of-the-meter and behind-the-meter power solutions being worked; Wesco says it is not yet seeing data center demand crowd out its own non-residential construction business, which grew high-single-digit

Pricing on electrical gear is back to business as usual: an approximately 3% overall price benefit in the quarter split CSS +1%, EES +5% (about a point of that commodity driven) and UBS +3%; supplier partners are being 'very measured' about price with nothing out of the ordinary to highlight
price +~3% overall; CSS +1%, EES +5% (~1pt commodity), UBS +3%

Capacity utilization at 60% at the end of Q2, targeting a gradual increase toward 85%-90%; enough capacity in hand for the next two to three years under current growth projections; watching wafer supply tension closely — high demand for SOI wafers and 200 millimeter wafers, with any input price increases to be propagated to customers case by case

Supply chain and EPC capacity lock-in: over the past 3 to 4 years Xcel shifted to being a 'partner of choice' with its Tier 1 suppliers and EPC partners across a 5-plus year portfolio of nearly 13 gigawatts of new renewable generation and battery storage, over 3 gigawatts of new natural gas generation and nearly 2,000 high-voltage transmission line miles. Management said these partnerships 'help ensure that we have access to the labor and equipment capacity that we need to deliver with certainty for our customers well into the 2030s', supported by standardized repeatable designs and one consolidated project execution organization. Van Abel separately framed the build as 15-plus gigawatts of new generation.
nearly 13 GW renewables + storage, over 3 GW new natural gas, nearly 2,000 high-voltage transmission line miles under multi-year supplier/EPC agreements

Q3 2026 revenue guided to $630 million to $690 million, at midpoint up 4.8% QoQ and 46.3% YoY, exceeding market consensus despite longer lead times for certain materials; Q3 bookings expected to grow a high single-digit percentage sequentially, mainly driven by TCB and photonics; group gross margin expected to stay above 40% through Q3 and about three quarters out; full-year 2026 revenue growth expected across both SEMI and SMT.
Q3 revenue $630 million to $690 million (midpoint +4.8% QoQ, +46.3% YoY); group gross margin above 40%

Given the recent surge in demand, Advantest is accelerating capacity expansion efforts and pulling forward its original plans - going beyond increasing production volumes to strengthening the entire supply chain, deepening collaboration with production partners, securing critical components, maintaining quality, and ensuring timely delivery to customers.
Capacity expansion accelerated and original plans pulled forward; no specific figure

Generation equipment secured: 'about 7.5 GW of plant island equipment' (gas turbine power islands under contract with exclusivity), which is the low end of the 10 to 17 GW opportunity; no additional turbines added since Investor Day but the company is 'staying ahead' as the front end of the funnel fills. Cottonwood plant acquisition pending as the most economic option for near-term industrial (steel, LNG, petrochemical) load; a new plant would not be available until the early part of the next decade.
7.5 GW plant island equipment contracted (10-17 GW opportunity)

Capacity build-out for the back-half CPI ramp: Q1 net capex was $235 million (approximately 3% of revenue) and FY2027 capex is guided to $1.5-$1.6 billion, described as 'pretty significant investment in terms of facilities, cooling infrastructure, manufacturing infrastructure', most of it serving the FY2027 and FY2028 acceleration. CEO on constraints: 'Don't see any significant constraints per se other than putting the capacity investments in place and making sure those factories are ramped up' — the investments 'have been going on for a bit', not started 90 days ago.
Q1 capex $235M (~3% of revenue); FY27 capex $1.5-1.6B for CPI facilities/cooling capacity

High-voltage transition update: 'first is on 400 volt, which is kind of the immediate programs that we are working on, followed by 800 volt. We feel very good about the progress on those programs. Don't see any major limitations, at least to the guide we have given for 2027 and 2028', with solid-state transformer technology 'that is going to be coming our way' after that. CEO: 'Flex is kind of the leader in this transition on the embedded power side'. On components: 'there's lots of conversations about component constraints and all of that, we have planned all of that in the guide we have given.
