Company-wide: Q2 net sales EUR 9.3B above guidance, FY2026 raised to EUR 43-45B; ~65 Low-NA EUV systems shipping in 2026 with 2027 Low-NA EUV nearly sold out and capacity being raised ~30%.
FY26 memory system sales +>75%; memory 49% of Q2 systems; 1c/1b add EUV layers

CAPACITY EXPANSION on multi-year customer visibility: order momentum 'extremely strong' through H1 with backlog increasing across a broad mix of customers. For 2027 ASML is now CLOSE TO FULLY COVERED WITH ORDERS FOR LOW-NA EUV and is planning to increase Low-NA EUV capacity by ~30%; for 2028 it has ALREADY RECEIVED A SIGNIFICANT NUMBER of Low-NA EUV orders (~two years in advance, a situation 'we haven't enjoyed in many years') and is investigating a FURTHER 30% increase (toward ~110 units). Immersion capacity to rise 30% in 2027 with a potential further 30% for 2028 under investigation. All of these increases are achievable WITHIN THE EXISTING CLEANROOM FOOTPRINT by optimizing existing space — no new cleanroom required. Pricing: value-based pricing gives 'more flexibility for pricing than what you would have seen in the past', though long order lead times delay the effect. Next Capital Markets Day 06-10-2027.
2027 Low-NA EUV nearly sold out, capacity +30%; 2028 +30% under study (~110 units)

OPTICAL IS NOW AEHR'S SECOND PILLAR: optical device test and burn-in for DATA CENTER INFRASTRUCTURE TRANSCEIVERS, CHIP-TO-CHIP I/O and hard disk drives accounted for approximately 20% OF FISCAL 2026 REVENUE, alongside AI accelerators/CPUs/network processors at ~71% — and management expects BOTH markets to grow significantly in fiscal 2027. Silicon photonics is named as one of the two focus areas (with AI accelerators) that together drove the majority of fourth-quarter revenue. Company-wide: record quarterly bookings, record effective backlog over $100M, and FY2027 revenue guided to $130-150M (2.6x-3x fiscal 2026) with 18-22% non-GAAP pretax margin and no capacity constraint at that level. Two years ago over 95% of Aehr's revenue was EV silicon carbide; today almost 95% comes from other markets.
Optical/data-centre device burn-in ~20% of FY26 revenue; silicon photonics a named growth driver

LEAD AI-PROCESSOR CUSTOMER SCALING: Aehr's lead AI-processor wafer-level burn-in customer is 'significantly ramping their products', driving increased forecast capacity needs for FOX systems and proprietary WaferPak full-wafer contactors; over the past year that customer ordered fully automated WAFERPAK ALIGNERS to integrate with its installed base, DOUBLED its systems from Aehr, and is forecasting significant increases in WAFER ALLOCATION FROM ITS FOUNDRY (previously a constraint on its growth). Critically, the customer MOVED ALL PRODUCTION BURN-IN SCREENING TO WAFER-LEVEL BURN-IN on Aehr's system and NO LONGER PERFORMS ANY SYSTEM-LEVEL SCREENING of those products — Aehr is described as 'a critical supplier'. Technology advantage cited: the WaferPak contactor manages INDIVIDUAL DIE TEMPERATURES, giving significantly better thermal management than conventional package-level approaches; systems process up to a quarter of a wafer at a time with as many as NINE WAFERS TESTED IN PARALLEL.
Lead AI customer doubled systems, moved ALL production burn-in to wafer level; 9 wafers in parallel

Supply tightness expected to persist over the next several quarters; DDR4/LPDDR4 supply is restricted — customers cannot get sufficient supply from other suppliers, and Nanya cannot support double-booking or pull-in requests; multi-year LTAs aligning supply and demand beyond 2028 (fixed volume+price renewed at term end, or committed volume with mostly quarterly market-based pricing)

Q3 FY2026: AI-server input constraints persist - HBM in high demand with lead times extending; high-end high-density-interconnect PCBs in high demand; DDR4-and-below memory faces some shortages while DDR5 capacity is 'decent'; hyperscalers secure more than their fair share of constrained components. Jabil manages via access, allocation and long-term commitments rather than transactional pricing. Networking & communications grew >50% YoY (India ramp ~2x, InfiniBand/Ethernet) and capital/test-equipment demand was 'through the roof' on rapid chip-technology evolution (wafer-fab equipment recovering). Jabil contract-manufactures AI server/GPU PCBs populated with MLCCs and high-density interconnect.
HBM lead times extending; high-density-interconnect PCBs in high demand; DDR4 shortages, DDR5 decent

Supply-chain constraints are ALREADY BUILT INTO the preliminary FY2027 AI growth outlook — 'we're aware of where the shortages are... the numbers we talked about definitely have that built in'. Management is relatively relaxed on the AI side specifically because large Intelligent Infrastructure customers 'do manage to get their fair share and then some' of constrained components ('I don't lose that much sleep over it from the Intelligent Infrastructure standpoint'). The nature of supplier engagement has shifted: 'it's not transactional, it's not about pricing — it's about strategy, it's about access, it's about allocation, long-term commitments.'
FY27 outlook has shortages built in; AI customers get 'fair share and then some'

China substrate export licence still pending: VPEC has not yet received the export permit for substrates affected by China's export controls, but two weeks ago it was notified to file supplementary documents (routine paperwork) and completed the filing last week - management likens the situation to finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel.

Capacity: Kulim (Malaysia) plant 1 successfully running high volume production of advanced substrates, with the next generation of larger advanced substrates under development; new customer-financed capacity expansion for AI-related substrates announced in Chongqing under a long-term contract (accretive from the start, high double-digit EUR million bottom-line impact); Leoben and Fehring in Austria being rebuilt for embedding of high-power electronics (partly single source) with revenue impact from the second half of the year; Shanghai focused on accelerator cards, co-packaged optics and embedded optics. T-glass shortage managed by expanding allocation from existing suppliers and qualifying new ones, though some effects remain on finished product availability; inflationary input cost increases (an ABF price increase was flagged by an analyst) are passed through to customers with a delay of a couple of months.

Momentum remains very strong and management is optimistic 2026 revenue keeps setting records, with the second half stronger than the first. In DIY motherboards and graphics cards, memory price hikes and CPU shortages have buyers waiting - ASPs are rising while mid-range unit volumes dip, but high-end demand is intact; the demand is seen as delayed rather than lost, and the H2 peak season is still expected, helped by added AI-compute demand, even as research firms forecast global PC shipments to fall this year. Full-year capex is estimated around NT$25-27 hundred million (Q1: NT$4.8 hundred million), mostly office building and production equipment.
2026 capex about NT$25-27 hundred million (Q1 NT$4.8 hundred million)

SIPHO RAMP: silicon photonics revenue grew 3x year-over-year in Q1 and led the quarter (SiGe +24%, RF SOI +12%, power management +10%, imagers +9% YoY). SiPho production is ramping in FOUR fabs at once - Fab 2 Migdal Haemek, Fab 3 Newport Beach, Fab 9 San Antonio and Fab 7 Uozu (300 mm) - with FIRST-FLOW SiPho revenue shipments from both Fab 2 and Fab 7 in Q1 (Fab 7's first SiPho wafers at 95% yield). 200 Gbps products in a strong ramp for multiple customers. The expansion is on track to grow SiPho capacity FIVE TIMES from the Q4 2025 wafer-shipment base by the end of 2026; in 2027 the focus turns to additional 300 mm capacity in Uozu.
SiPho revenue 3x year-over-year; Fab 7 first SiPho wafers 95% yield; SiPho capacity five times Q4 2025 base by end of 2026

CONTRACTED SIPHO DEMAND: long-term photonics customer commitments contractually represent $1.3 billion revenue in 2027 (wafers DELIVERED in 2027), with 'significantly larger valued contracts for 2028', backed by approximately $290 million of prepayments already received from the largest SiPho customers (booked as customer advances and in Q1 operating cash flow). CEO: the $1.3 billion is not those customers' full demand and excludes the broader base of 'more than 50 active SiPho customers'; SiPho was 'somewhere about $230 million' in 2025, and Tower is 'forecasting substantially higher' than $1.3 billion for 2027 SiPho.
$1.3 billion revenue in 2027 contracted; approximately $290 million in prepayments; more than 50 active SiPho customers

CAPACITY / CAPEX AND JAPAN 300MM: the $920 million SiGe + SiPho capacity plan (8-inch fabs in Israel, Newport Beach, Texas plus the 12-inch Uozu fab) is on track - approximately 40% already paid, the remaining 60% to be paid through 2026 and 2027. The TPSCo restructuring moves Tower to FULL OWNERSHIP of 300 mm Fab 7 (Uozu), already profitable at present volumes; with adjacent land Tower expects to scale up to four times current levels (grant-dependent). CEO timeline: METI approval expected very short term, then permits and roughly a year and a half from ground-breaking to tool-in - best case first half of 2028 for that capacity. As an interim step, Tower will place a specific set of tools in the shut-down Arai factory (owned by Nuvoton Winbond) to meet 2027 customer demand; a first phase of Fab 7 SiPho capital spending is approved but not yet quantified (numbers expected within two, three quarters). Separately, a long-term supply agreement with Nuvoton for Fab 5 Tonami keeps 200 mm customers supplied.
$920 million investment plan, approximately 40% paid, remaining 60% throughout 2026 and 2027; Japan 300 mm up to four times current levels, best case first half of 2028

MODULATOR / LASER ROADMAP AND INP CONSTRAINT: demonstrated an all-silicon 400 Gb per lane Mach-Zehnder modulator with Coherent (Coherent's design on Tower's platform); with OpenLight, a heterogeneously integrated 400 Gb per lane InP electro-absorption modulator on PH18DA; moving thin-film lithium niobate toward high volume manufacturing (both side-by-side and chiplet-on-PIC forms, with different customers); organic-polymer modulator partnerships with Lightwave Logic and NLM Photonics. CEO's personal view: TFLN 'will come in fairly strong for one generation' before the industry moves to indium phosphide, which wins on form factor at many channels; integrated lasers are no less reliable than discrete ones, and Tower is agnostic to external vs integrated lasers. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE IS CONSTRAINED - 'the starting material is the constraint' - but Tower says its supply-chain plans position it to meet demand as the integrated InP laser ramps this year.
400 Gb per lane modulators (silicon with Coherent; InP with OpenLight); InP starting material constrained

FAB UTILIZATION AND RF SOI: Q1 utilization - Fab 2 around 60% (SiPho and SiGe qualifications continuing), Fab 3 80% (slightly constrained while adding newer SiPho/SiGe processes; expected to rise in Q2), Fab 5 75%, Fab 9 80%, Fab 7 fully utilized, well above the 85% utilization model. 200 mm RF SOI capacity is being repurposed for higher-margin SiPho and SiGe as RF SOI moves to 300 mm; the CEO expects full-year 2026 RF SOI down vs 2025, then record 300 mm RF SOI growth in 2027 and 2028 on design wins for phones first launching in 2028.
Fab 2 around 60%, Fab 3 80%, Fab 5 75%, Fab 9 80%, Fab 7 fully utilized, well above 85% utilization model

Board-level components are the shortage zone: power ICs are short, and passives (MLCC-type components) and PCB also show shortages, driven by overall market demand rather than any single product, so Inventec is pre-buying materials. Memory, hard drives and SSD are customer-controlled buy-and-sell items, so customers bear those materials while Inventec is responsible for board-level components.

Capacity and cost dynamics: Legrand has scaled with US data-center demand WITHOUT materially changing its CapEx-to-sales ratio of about 2% — 'data center is not a CapEx-intensive industry' for Legrand — absorbing ramp inefficiencies (air freight, subcontracting, overtime) without significant P&L impact. Gross margin down 190 basis points as pricing of +2.3% did not yet compensate inflation of +4.2% on raw materials/components and +3% on personnel cost (half of the ~4% purchase-price increase is tariff effect); gap expected to ease through the year. Four acquisitions announced so far in 2026, all in data centers and energy transition, representing combined annual revenue of around EUR 275 million.
CapEx ~2% of sales maintained; pricing +2.3% vs raw-material inflation +4.2%; four 2026 acquisitions ~EUR 275 million combined revenue

Strong 300mm wafer demand from leading-edge DRAM for AI data centers is a core part of SUMCO's outlook; memory makers' supply constraints are so tight they are curbing wafer demand from NON-leading-edge logic customers (memory shortage spillover). Long-term contract prices maintained.
leading-edge DRAM wafer demand strong; memory shortage spillover

Wafer market outlook: semiconductor market sees continued strong AI growth and only gradual recovery elsewhere. 300mm demand strong for leading-edge logic and DRAM in AI data centers with a projected NAND uptick ahead; recovery in non-leading-edge logic is gradual and partly TEMPERED BY MEMORY SHORTAGES (memory supply constraints curb non-leading-edge logic demand). 200mm and smaller lacks momentum, inventory-adjustment progress varies by customer.
AI leading-edge strong vs non-AI gradual; memory shortage caps non-leading-edge logic

US transformer market faces severe supply constraints with lead times extended to ~4 YEARS; a major factor is limited availability of grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) and copper — premium GOES is supplied by only a few producers (Nippon Steel, POSCO, Thyssenkrupp), supporting multi-year demand visibility for transformer-core steel into grid/datacenter expansion.
US transformer lead times ~4 years; GOES scarcity

Supply chain readiness: last month NuScale held its annual supplier working group with 37 key supplier partners to align on 2026 demand signals and near-term deployment milestones. The COO said the Houston summit drew 'over 120, 130 people', representing 'well over half of our supplier base'. NuScale is pursuing a deliberate multi-sourcing strategy for critical components to reduce single-source dependence 'in a constrained global market'. Key NuScale Power Module components remain in active production at Doosan Enerbility. The CFO cited long-standing Japanese and Korean supply-chain and equity relationships 'through IHI and through Doosan'. On domestic-content requirements for tax credits, the CCO said large-scale forgings are one area where the industry 'has fell short' on U.S. supply, and that where supply is inadequate it can be compensated from externally, with 'alternatives and ways to get past that'.
37 key supplier partners at the annual supplier working group; over 120, 130 people at the Houston summit

Fuel supply (COO/CEO): NuScale modules run on commercial low-enriched uranium (LEU), which the COO called 'not a risk area. It's not a bottleneck', unlike HALEU. Fuel partner Framatome supplies from multiple sites: Richland, Washington in the U.S., Lingen in Germany, and a facility in France. NuScale is in preliminary fuel design with Framatome and started early so it can support market needs. The COO said: 'we don't see any bottlenecks or any kind of shortcomings there because we got ahead of it early'. Framatome asks to be kept informed on the market and customer base so it can plan capacity.

PJM supply shortage as seen by Exelon management. The CEO said customers paid $32 billion to generators for capacity in PJM over the last two years while supply declined by 1.2 gigawatts, and that Mid-Atlantic residential supply costs rose by up to 80% or more over five years. Exelon's Colette Honorable said PJM reported 811 new generation projects capable of 220 GW applying to interconnect. She noted only 19% of queued projects reach operation, and that 54 GW already cleared are delayed by siting, permitting, and supply chain issues.
$32 billion paid to generators for capacity in PJM; supply declined by 1.2 gigawatts; 54 GW cleared but delayed; only 19% of queued projects reach operation

SPOKANE SPUTTERING-TARGET CAPACITY DOUBLING: Solstice is 'investing $200 million in our Spokane, Washington facility to double our target's capacity, reduce customer lead times'. CEO calls its sputtering targets 'the materials of choice for leading-edge semiconductor nodes used for AI and data center applications' and expects the project to exceed its 'mid-teens percentage IRR' hurdle; it is 'evaluating opportunities to further accelerate similar organic growth investments'.
$200 million to double sputtering-target capacity at Spokane

SOLD OUT AT SPOKANE, EXPANSION BEING PULLED IN: asked whether electronics would become capacity constrained before the expansion starts up, the CEO said 'we're, for lack of a better word, selling everything we can make in our Spokane facility' and are working 'to accelerate the expansion that we're doing, looking at it in a little bit of a modular design'. He said its 'technology in copper manganese is a better technical solution' getting 'broader adoption in the marketplace', expects leading-edge-node growth to continue 'going into the 2030s', and said the TIMs (thermal interface) business is also seeing significant growth and working on expansion. Separately, the CEO said growth capex projects that were originally multi-year (full benefit '2-3 years out') are being pulled in for electronics and defense 'because the demand is so strong', giving returns earlier.

CAPACITY / SUPPLY CHOKE POINTS: thermal handlers are running at a 14 week cycle time, but lead time depends on backlog (CEO: a $30 million order would not all ship in 14 weeks; it is spread over several months). Cohu is meeting suppliers to identify choke points, particularly for its thermal heads, hiring in Malaysia and re-laying out the Malaysia facility for more floor space, and expanding production capacity into 2027. Order shipments ramp in Q3 with some falling into Q4. Capex targeted at about 2% of revenue in 2026.
14 week cycle time on thermal handlers; capex about 2% of revenue in 2026

Trainium2 has ~30% better price-performance than comparable GPUs and is largely SOLD OUT; a consistent majority of Bedrock inference workloads run on Trainium; delivered 4x improvement in Trainium2 token throughput during 2025.
Trainium2 ~30% better price-perf, largely sold out

Capacity limits: Guzzi said growth is 'emphatically not' limited by equipment procurement because 'on data centers, most of the major equipment is being bought by the owners or the owners through the GCs'; the bottleneck is field leadership (foremen, general foremen, project managers). He reported no notable change in craft labor tightness. CFO: 2026 capex of somewhere between $115 million and $125 million, a significant part fitting out or upgrading prefabrication facilities; over three years capex is growing at twice the revenue rate.

Q1 2026: RECORD quarter — revenue, gross margin and operating income all MATERIALLY above prior outlook, revenue growth >100% YoY, record Q1 operating cash flow. Full-year guidance RAISED MATERIALLY (non-GAAP EPS now $1.85-2.25; FY2026 expected best in company history). Manufacturing footprint can deliver 5 GIGAWATTS of product annually — "not order constrained and not capacity constrained": revenue pace decided by how fast customers can deploy. Time-to-power has become "an existential necessity" for AI builders bumping into grid/permits/community bottlenecks.
Record Q1, rev >+100% YoY; FY EPS guide $1.85-2.25; 5GW/yr manufacturing capacity

The 2028 game changer: the biggest GPU vendor's next-generation GPU (2028) disclosed 3D stacking that is FORECAST TO BE HYBRID BONDED - equipment ordered in 2026, installed in 2027, volume production from 2028. BESI raised HB bonder capacity from ~15/month (~180/yr) to 250/YEAR, lead time ~6 months (100nm-accuracy tool), able to satisfy any model from "the big five". Long-term model: EUR 1.5-1.9B revenue in 3-5 years (~2.5-3x current) with the support infrastructure being built now; service revenue (15-16% of sales) to move toward 18-20% as the HB installed base adopts a front-end-style 24/7 support model (~900 defined spare parts, 4-hour availability) - a GROSS-MARGIN TAILWIND. Onshoring: TSMC/Amkor/Micron US advanced-packaging fabs build through 2026-27 with volume production from 2028 - BESI engaged in those programs.
Next-gen GPU 2028 = hybrid bonded (orders 2026); HB capacity to 250/yr; LT model EUR 1.5-1.9B

Data-center power positioning: competing in application-specific sockets — stage-one high-voltage conversion (800V down to 12V/6V) and stage-two VRM / final VCORE multiphase delivery for GPUs — built on 15 years of GaN investment plus advanced BCD nodes manufactured in Texas ('geopolitically dependable'); ASSP design-ins gaining momentum, expected to kick in H2 2026 and into 2027. Beyond ASSPs, an AI rack carries TENS OF THOUSANDS of general-purpose analog parts across many SKUs — TI claims it can fulfill almost every analog socket, and is winning sockets when competitors hit supply shortages.
800V->12/6V stage-1 + VRM stage-2 sockets; tens of thousands of GP analog parts per rack

Kinsus ABF substrate capacity has SOLD OUT (alongside Unimicron and Nan Ya PCB) on escalating AI chip demand; industry ABF quotes expected +5-10% QoQ from Q2 2026, spot prices +30%+; Taiwanese suppliers making AI-chip ABF expansion the primary 2026 capacity goal.
Kinsus ABF sold out; pricing rising

ABF substrate has SOLD OUT at Unimicron, Kinsus and Nan Ya PCB as AI chip demand escalates; ABF quotes expected +5-10% QoQ on average from Q2 2026 while spot prices are up >30%. March 2026 Nan Ya PCB revenue NT$4.29B (+39% YoY), a 36-month high.
ABF sold out; quotes +5-10% QoQ, spot +30%
Landmark commits to significant capacity expansion in 2026 to address light source supply tightness

InP substrate supply constraints (used in both EML and CW lasers, across PD receivers and LD transmitters), under geopolitical tension / export controls by China government; GS expects light source supply to remain tight through 2027
YJ Semi commits to significant capacity expansion in 2026 to address light source supply tightness

Memory is the biggest cost pressure for 2026: at current prices memory has reached about 30% of general-server cost (already factoring the recent sharp hikes; the share could exceed that if prices keep rising - management noted memory may have risen toward 4x), while the share in AI servers is smaller because GPU/ASIC content dominates. Customers held long-term contract prices last year so the 2025 increase felt moderate, but increases turned aggressive recently. Gross margin will be better than Q4 but is not expected to return to prior levels; the absolute profit impact is minimal-to-none because material is passed through - quotes separate material cost from Wiwynn's service fee. CSPs are signing long-term contracts and booking capacity with memory makers, and Wiwynn sees at least one quarter of secured supply with no material shortage for itself.
memory about 30% of general-server cost, already factoring recent hikes

Data storage: customers are adopting Heat-Assisted Magnetic Recording (HAMR), raising capital intensity and CapEx; Veeco is fully booked for system orders for 2026 and has started booking orders into 2027. The first round of orders shipping in 2026 is for front-end fabs, and new orders are now arriving for back-end slider fabs for shipment in 2027 - a function of the number of heads shipping - giving 'legs into '27 and potentially beyond.'
Data storage fully booked for 2026; slider fab orders for 2027 shipment

CEO: DRAM demand keeps rising, driven by AI, but capacity is limited by cleanroom space. Many customers are squeezing in an extra couple of tools, and large tool volumes will come only when the new fabs open. DRAM is expected to be significantly up in 2026 over a lower 2025 base, with momentum into 2027 across all DRAM manufacturers as the cleanroom bottleneck eases. As an example he cited SK hynix's Yongin cluster, '4 mega fabs of 200,000 wafer starts a week', where he expects SK hynix to start taking systems around early 2027 to ramp the fabs. DRAM prices are spiking because supply is very constrained.
SK hynix Yongin cluster (cited as an example): '4 mega fabs of 200,000 wafer starts a week' (as spoken); taking systems early 2027

DRAM, HBM and advanced packaging: DRAM capacity was nearly fully utilized at the end of 2025, and management expects it to stay that way through 2026. More DRAM is shifting from standalone DDR5 into HBM, which adds some content per wafer, though less than a new wafer start would. Management expects tight supply in HBM, DDR5 and advanced packaging to require additional fab capacity heading into 2027. Entegris is gaining traction in DRAM and HBM, particularly with CMP consumables and advanced packaging solutions. The CEO said advanced packaging revenue grew nicely in 2025, to 'roughly a $100 million plus minus', and should keep growing in 2026. Several product lines for advanced packaging are sampling now and more will sample later in the year, so the larger benefit is expected in 2027 and beyond.
advanced packaging revenue roughly $100 million (2025), expected to keep growing in 2026

Helium and rare gases: CFO Matthew White said the two combined were about a one to 2% headwind on 2025 EPS, toward the upper end of that range, and that rare gas 'does feel a little bit better right now, especially with some of the electronics recovery'. CEO Sanjiv Lamba said helium pricing has been high single-digit negative for a few quarters, 'Helium is gonna be long in the medium term at least' (China long on Russian helium), and helium is a low single-digit business for Linde.
helium and rare gas about a one to 2% headwind on 2025 EPS (upper end of range)

Ordering and backlog turned up in Q4 2025: management 'saw a good step up in the ordering patterns', the book-to-bill ratio 'was well in excess of one', and backlog is 'starting to extend out into Q2 2026'; channel inventory stayed at the low end of MPS's range. Bernie Blegen: after a period of very short lead times, MPS is now 'seeing longer ordering patterns because some of our customers are concerned about capacity constraints. Not necessarily with us, but just in general.' He called 'the first half for enterprise data in particular, but for the company, is more secure', with the second half still uncertain, and flagged the need to sort 'real demand' from possible 'double ordering on the part of our customers as they try to secure capacity.' Management expects strength in enterprise data, communications and automotive to extend into Q1 and the rest of the year.
book-to-bill well in excess of one; backlog extending into Q2 2026

Capacity: MPS achieved its milestone of securing more than $4 billion of geographically balanced capacity in 2025 and continues to add supply chain partners. Management said 'we don't have constraints on our capacity side.' Asked about the next three years, Michael Hsing said MPS established a supply management organization at the beginning of last year covering not only silicon but also silicon carbide, gallium nitride materials and module components, with suppliers going through heavy audits; 'We're expanding very fast.'
more than $4 billion of geographically balanced capacity secured

Capacity ramp: around $1.5 billion of announced investments across around two dozen (24) projects to expand Electrical Americas capacity. Half finished construction by mid-2025 and started ramping in the second half (mostly Q4), continuing to ramp in 2026; construction of half of the remaining projects will be largely done by the first half of 2026 with ramp starting at the end of the first half; the last quarter of projects continues through 2026 with production ramp in 2027. Second-half 2025 orders were 41% higher than 2024, so Eaton accelerated the ramp (bringing people and resources in earlier), which pressured Q4 2025 and Q1 2026. CFO: ramp costs hit Electrical Americas margin by about 100 basis points in 2025 and about 130 basis points in 2026, front-end loaded (most in Q1 and Q2), with segment margin still about 30%. CEO modeling cadence: Q1 = guidance, progress in Q2, momentum into Q3, then a stronger pace of backlog liquidation in Q4 and into 2027; tiger teams deployed at critical sites, partner network and supply chain scaled for material availability.
$1.5 billion across 24 projects; ramp margin impact about 100 basis points (2025) and about 130 basis points (2026); last projects ramp in 2027

CALL-ONLY: HYPERSCALER DEMAND AND BUILD SPEED. Asked whether customers could pause builds over bubble concerns, management said: 'Hyperscalers are not talking about a bubble. They are talking about they don't have enough fast enough', and 'many of our contracts have performance bonuses in them for us to go faster'. Also: 'the general feeling in the market is how fast can you go?' Lumen avoids construction delays through scale across the supply chain ('our contracts are very favorable and terms of first off the line priority status') and workforce, and on fiber supply management said 'we've got a very special relationship with Corning' and 'we are doing very well in terms of access to fiber' (the CEO also said Lumen 'expanded our partnership with Corning, ensuring we have priority access to the newest state-of-the-art fiber technology'), and because many deals are 'two existing data center areas where our network has proximity' - overbuilding rather than building for the first time. A large deal with an unnamed cloud company, the first time Lumen had worked with it, went so fast that its head of operations called to say they had 'never experienced this kind of speed before' with a telco. Per the CEO, 'the largest tech companies are choosing Lumen to help construct the supply side of the AI economy'.

Capacity for the applied ramp (CEO Dave Regnery / CFO Chris Kuehn): 'our chiller capacity over the last, you know, two or three years is up over four x', through new builds, lean work and new lines. Management also works with supply-chain partners on their capacity because 'their ability could hinder us if we're not careful' - 'we're in good shape there'. Trane commissions its applied systems with its own field force of over 7,500 technicians globally. Asked about capex, the CFO confirmed the analyst's capex-to-revenue range for the last few years ('You're right, Jeff') and said 'it's been able to support all the capacity expansions we needed to do', and that 'we brought in businesses on air handling or industrial process cooling capacity for data centers' via M&A, which adds capacity inside Trane's four walls. On lead times: no dramatic change for at least twelve months, Trane is 'very competitive on our lead times' and has introduced quick ship programs.
chiller capacity up over four x (last two or three years); over 7,500 technicians

PRODUCTION TEST IS THE FASTER GROWER; REPURPOSED PRODUCTION CAPACITY IS A FRACTION OF WHAT IS NEEDED. Khaykin: lab instruments track 'the r and d CapEx at semis system vendors, and module vendors', production test is 'heavily driven by volume' ('for every tranche of volume, you need to increase capacity'), and field instruments are linked to the number of data centers being built - the higher growth is 'clearly clearly gonna be the production'. On the cycle: 'pretty much every ounce of capacity that was kinda abandoned by service providers when they cut back about three years ago in investment. It's been totally repurposed into the data center. And it's a fraction of what they need', so 'you're gonna see significant growth over the next two years'. Node cadence has compressed: 'We now see the new each technology notes turning over. Every two years. So no longer, let's say, between between a 100 gig and a 400 gig you have six years. You really now have two years between'.
technology nodes turning over every two years (vs six years between a 100 gig and a 400 gig); significant growth over the next two years

Every ALC goes through the same qualification rigor as AECs - Credo runs live traffic through customers' own switches and NICs over every corner, deliberately breaking the link and strengthening it through firmware, so the customer only has to plug it in.

New detail on the pending Claros acquisition: the close is now targeted 'around the beginning of Q4. October timeframe' (tighter than the previously stated before-year-end). Claros' part is an IVR with a 3.3 volt entry, sub 1 volt output, 40 amp per chip, no caps and no inductors, arranged as an IVR array with current sensing — 'if you need 2,000 amps, you put 50 of them. If you need 4,000 amps, you put 100 of them'. Big VPD modules are shipping now, but the tiny IVR chips (Claros, Empower) are 'happening in 2028'; Claros' lead customer is an XPU customer ramping in 2028, so the deal does not change the organic 2026/2027 plan. Management cites ADI's Empower acquisition as the same move.
Claros close targeted around the beginning of Q4 (October); IVR 3.3 volt entry, sub 1 volt output, 40 amp; 2,000 amps, you put 50 of them, 4,000 amps, you put 100 of them; IVR chips happening in 2028

Generation demand mix across the installed base (CRO Boroditsky): older-generation GPUs are not a fallback but properly matched to simpler workloads — 'RAG infrastructure or text prediction or image creation' — and 'we actually have a list of new customers that are looking for any of the older generation chips that come available. So very robust demand for the older ranges.' On new silicon: 'We're seeing that across the Blackwells. We have a very robust level of interest and adoption that continues to be at a multiple of customers to chips that we have available that actually projects out as well to Vera Rubin interest.' The four landmark Q2 wins are already discussing follow-on clusters: 'In some cases, they are looking for additional GB200s. In all cases, they are all talking to us now about their Vera Rubin platform requirements.'
a multiple of customers to chips that we have available

WHY NOVA IS NOT OUTPERFORMING WFE AS USUAL IN 2026 (the '2x WFE' framing was the moderator's, not management's): Kizner said Nova historically outperforms WFE significantly ('2024, we grew by 30%', '2025, we grew by 31%' while WFE did not grow much) but 2026 breaks the pattern because of investment MIX. Three reasons: (1) NAND contributes to WFE but nothing to Nova because the spend is upgrades, not greenfield capacity; (2) heavy DRAM investment, where metrology intensity is lower than logic; (3) most important, the AI customers did NOT transition to Gate-All-Around - they are 'still using the N-1, 3 nm and 5 nm' and are spending on 3 nm capacity expansions in both the U.S. and Taiwan, so the metrology intensity of 2026 spending went down on mix.
2024, we grew by 30%; 2025, we grew by 31%; still using the N-1, 3 nm and 5 nm

2027 SETUP BY END MARKET: Kizner expects the mix to swing back in Nova's favour in 2027 - NAND capacity additions would be 'coming from zero to business' for Nova since it is positioned with all the key NAND customers (he called this the longest NAND down cycle, with upgrades-only spend that Nova does not benefit from, and hopes for greenfield in 2027); DRAM stays a significant driver on capacity expansion but with NO metrology-intensity increase until the industry moves to 4F², which he placed in '2028 and going forward'; and logic mix shifts 'much more towards the 2 nm and the Gate-All-Around, and less on the 3 nm', pushing metrology intensity up.
it will happen in 2028 and going forward

HYBRID BONDING IS THE PACKAGING SHARE PRIZE - TIMING GIVEN: Kizner said the main advanced-packaging share-gain opportunity ahead is hybrid bonding, which brings front-end capability into the back end: copper-to-copper bonding requires wafer-to-wafer and die warpage control, CMP uniformity and flatness control, all of which raise metrology intensity and pull in both Nova's dimensional and materials metrology portfolios. The work right now is QUALIFICATIONS - high-volume manufacturing 'capacity is not big story in 2027', it comes later. He added that Nova's materials metrology is not yet exposed to advanced packaging at all and that early customer discussions to apply it there are another growth engine on top of the ancosys and Sentronics acquisitions and the PRISM front-end tools already deployed into packaging.
the capacity is not big story in 2027

Four-franchise data-center strategy laid out with named customers for the first time: (1) custom silicon - Amazon plus one other undisclosed global hyperscaler, working on 'their main AI accelerators', not ancillary custom chips; (2) AI accelerator built on High Bandwidth Compute (stacking compute and memory) aimed at memory-bandwidth-constrained inference decode, with Humane announced as an AI accelerator customer; (3) CPU, with Meta as the first data-center silicon customer, contributing 'late in 2028, going into 2029'; (4) connectivity - the acquired Alphawave SerDes is integrated into the custom-silicon engagements and Alphawave optical connectivity products are part of the Amazon agreement. Palkhiwala frames the accelerator market as disaggregating (GPU vs XPU, training vs inference, prefill vs decode), with Qualcomm starting at decode and extending across inference.

SERVER-CPU TAM RE-SIZED SINCE THE META AGREEMENT WAS SIGNED: Palkhiwala says 'when we signed our agreement with Meta, the size of the CPU market was a lot less than it's perceived to be today. The CPU TAM obviously has tripled since then', and is now 'over $200 billion a year', with 'about half of that market transitioning over to Arm architecture', where Qualcomm claims performance-per-watt and performance-per-area leadership. Asked to bridge to a longer-term share target, he answered that Qualcomm's longer-term forecast is not tied to the CPU engagement alone but rests on all four franchises - CPU, AI accelerator, custom chip and connectivity.
CPU TAM tripled to over $200 billion a year; about half of that market transitioning over to Arm architecture

First explicit 800V DC RAMP timing, more granular than the May Investor Day or the July call: CEO Gio Albertazzi says Vertiv will start to see an acceleration in everything sidecar happening in 2027, probably second half of 2027, while a fully native end-to-end 800 volt DC powertrain would probably be commercially back end of 2027, volumes 2028. He stresses the future is multi-architecture rather than one winning standard - 800V DC either at the individual pod with a sidecar or as a native end-to-end architecture across the whole data hall - and says Vertiv is delivering nicely on the timelines shared in May with customer validations ongoing and some products already in the offering cycle. CFO Craig Chamberlin adds that 800V is a content-per-megawatt opportunity in every architecture variant (sidecar, pod level, or built into the data centre), and Albertazzi notes the powertrain is getting more complex simply because required performance is rising, which favours Vertiv on content and know-how.
sidecar acceleration in 2027, probably second half of 2027; native end-to-end 800 volt DC powertrain commercially back end of 2027, volumes 2028

H1 2026: the InP substrate diameter mix, from the epiwafer maker's own view - "3-inch is still very dominant. Then it's 4-inch with almost half of the volume driven by 4-inch, and only then comes 6-inch as the fastest-growing sort of diameter, and it's scaling right now." 6-inch maturity and line yields still need to improve and "we are not seeing truly the really demand on 6-inch yet". Management clarified that IQE's tool conversions are material conversions (Gallium Arsenide to Indium Phosphide), which "doesn't necessarily come with a dimension conversion"; IQE can support 3-inch, 4-inch and 6-inch. Tightness across the three diameters is hard to rank because "there is different types of substrates too".
InP substrate volume mix: 3-inch dominant, 4-inch almost half of volume, 6-inch fastest growing but least mature

H1 2026: capacity is being added by converting existing tooling in the second half "to increase capacity to meet the strong demand for Indium Phosphide", and every conversion is gated on a signed customer commitment - "we will also not expand capacity without a clear customer commitment and a clear visibility on what value is going to be driven with that expansion" and "we are still not converting tools without customer commitments and secured demand on these tools". Conversion cost is "definitely insignificant compared to the cost of a new reactor"; the real cost is the downtime of the tool. Customer prepayments are "definitely a mechanism for us to fund our growth", following what "some of our players in the same ecosystem" already do. Newport still has "ample clean room space to add capacity" so IQE "can scale up rather quickly compared to others because we already have the infrastructure to house these reactors".

AI portfolio catalysts: WaveLogic 6 Extreme — after 18 months still the ONLY 1.6 Tb high-performance modem on the market — with a ramp already exceeding WaveLogic 5 Extreme and output doubled. RLS holds roughly 70% market share in disaggregated optical line systems; next-generation RLS HYPER-RAIL (co-created with the hyperscalers for scale-across / distributed AI training over greater distances) is on track for initial customer standardization by the end of calendar 2026 and will ramp to SEVERAL HUNDRED MILLION DOLLARS of revenue in 2027 (could be faster with more components), with economics a step function above RLS and accretive to corporate average margins. Interconnects: Q3 800 ZR pluggable shipments MORE THAN TWICE the previous quarter's volume; strong market receptivity to Nitro, the linear redriver for active copper cable solutions; VESTA, the open co-packaged optics (CPX) solution, received SAMPLE ORDERS FROM SEVERAL ANCHOR CUSTOMERS in the ecosystem — CPX revenue expected to begin in 2027 and ramp into 2028. Coherent moving inside the data center is viewed as inevitable with the right general-market intercept at 3.2 Tb; OCS is welcomed as driving coherent adoption inside the data center faster (no comment on Ciena entering the OCS market itself). The major-hyperscaler WaveLogic 6 Extreme win announced last quarter — DSP, drivers, TIAs and coherent expertise in a complete module deployed across the customer's own global optical platform, a significant takeaway from a component competitor — is one of two bespoke performance-optics consumption-model relationships. TAM expected to effectively double from approximately $25 billion today to approximately $50 billion by 2029; scale-across is a major demand driver, almost entirely North American/US-based and just beginning, with asynchronous training and inference traffic still ahead.

Hyper-Rail standardization by end-2026, several hundred million dollars of revenue in 2027; 800 ZR plug shipments more than twice QoQ; Vesta CPX sample orders, revenue from 2027; TAM ~$25B to ~$50B by 2029
Hock Tan stated Broadcom is now shipping the TPU v8i ahead of the MediaTek version v8t, which in fact was initiated earlier
Dell became the first to ship rack systems engineered on the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, which it cites as proof of its rack-scale engineering and deployment capability.

18G PowerEdge begins shipping next month at consolidation rates of 12-14 legacy servers per new 18G server, versus six-to-eight-to-one on 17G. Dell still has 1.2 million assets that are 14G or older in the install base that have to be upgraded, with security, resiliency and new requirements such as post-quantum cryptography acting as the forcing function.
18G ships next month; 12-14 old servers consolidated per new 18G server; 1.2 million assets still 14G or older

CEO Gary Dickerson quantified where advanced packaging goes next: an advanced package next year will have over 300 chips in the package, over 500 billion transistors and over 2,000 miles of wiring, and how those compute components are connected and how the data is moved has an enormous impact on performance, power and cost. He frames multi-chip connectivity as one of the most important innovations in the industry, alongside memory stacking for higher speed and lower power.
advanced package next year: over 300 chips in the package, over 500 billion transistors, over 2,000 miles of wiring

→ NVIDIA: IREN's Horizon 1 achieved NVIDIA EXEMPLAR CLOUD STATUS ON GB300 NVL72, and its Mirantis software business was named an INAUGURAL NVIDIA-CERTIFIED HYPERVISOR, which IREN says makes it the only neocloud with a certified hypervisor from NVIDIA - validation at both the hardware and software layers. IREN's next-generation data center design, built for successive GPU generations and evolving cooling including 800-VOLT DC, was developed in collaboration with NVIDIA, and IREN expects to use NVIDIA MaxLPS power smoothing and the NVIDIA DSX reference architecture to run more compute inside the same electrical envelope. Separately, the NVIDIA cloud contract is expected to contribute $700 million of ARR ramping in 2027, which is excluded from the $4 billion of 2026 contracted ARR.
value: $700M of ARR associated with the NVIDIA cloud contract, ramping in 2027

Memory content per humanoid robot quantified as the next demand wave after data center and edge: 'Each humanoid is going to have hundreds of gigabytes of DRAM content and terabytes of SSD NAND content. They are going to be massive drivers of growth in demand for both DRAM and NAND.' Management expects robotics to start in factory-automation settings and become a massive growth driver in the latter part of this decade and into the 2030s, a wave that compounds on top of data center demand rather than replacing it.
hundreds of gigabytes of DRAM content and terabytes of SSD NAND content per humanoid

Sadana on NAND process complexity: 'We are piling up these layers over 200 layers, over 300 layers, over 400 layers, and then being able to do these devices. The process complexity of that is just enormous.' No dates were given for the layer steps.
over 200 layers, over 300 layers, over 400 layers

Node-capability roadmap by site, more granular than the Q3 call. Boise is the U.S. high-end facility and 'can produce masks down to seven nanometers' today, with little revenue at 7 nanometers so far, and 'with the same equipment, we are advancing our capabilities to actually go down to four' - not ready and no revenue presented today. Allen, Texas is being taken from 180 nanometers and 130 nanometers up to 65 nanometers and 'we should be up and running in the next month or two'; production then shifts out of Boise to Texas, freeing Boise to capture more 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometer business. Korea is the other upgrade: the bulk of that facility's business today is about 40 nanometers, the expansion to 8 nanometers is expected 'in about a year from now', and Photronics expects significantly greater 8 and 10 nanometer business there 'largely because of customers that are very close to that facility'. The U.S. is 17%-19% of revenue today and is expected to be a higher share of total revenue in fiscal 2027.

Boise down to seven nanometers today, advancing toward four; Allen, Texas from 180 and 130 nanometers to 65 nanometers up and running in the next month or two, freeing Boise for 7, 10, 14 and 22 nanometers; Korea about 40 nanometers today to 8 nanometers in about a year; U.S. 17%, 18%, 19% of revenue rising in fiscal 2027

Mechanism behind the better-than-expected July quarter, which the Q3 call did not spell out. April-quarter push-outs came from customers being unable to capture memory and from Asian fabs at unusually high utilization telling chip designs 'You have to delay your design because we don't have the capacity for it'. Through the July quarter those designs started to be released because the same fabs 'added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range', and in some cases told a customer with a 40 nanometer design 'if you move that chip design to 28 nanometers or 22 nanometers, I will then manufacture it for you' - i.e. the capacity shortage is actively forcing node migration, which is the ASP-positive trend Photronics benefits from. On the display side Korea is strong on high-end consumer electronics launching this fall while China has pulled back because low-end consumer electronics cannot capture memory; Moreau relayed that the memory companies are talking about 'another 2, 3, 4 years before supply and demand comes into equilibrium'.
fabs added capacity in the 14-nanometer, 22-nanometer, 28-nanometer range and pushed 40 nanometer designs to 28 or 22 nanometers; memory supply and demand equilibrium another 2, 3, 4 years away

Automotive framed with numbers the call did not give: 'We expect automotive to grow about 6% or so year-on-year' against a flat-to-slightly-down SAAR, and over the last five years (end of 2019 to beginning of 2026) onsemi's automotive revenue grew 72%, 'a 9.5% CAGR over a five-year period.' New content drivers: plug-in hybrids are moving from IGBT/silicon power to silicon carbide as OEMs push 100-mile range - 'we have already have two design in China and North America for a plug-in hybrid with silicon carbide' - and the zonal/software-defined-vehicle architecture products (10BASE-T1S Ethernet, smart power at every zone) start ramping this year.
automotive ~6% year-on-year; 72% growth over five years (9.5% CAGR); two plug-in hybrid silicon carbide designs (China and North America)

Scale-across demand driver: because data centers are power constrained, large AI workloads 'are being forced to be spread across multiple data centers because there’s just not enough power in one data center to process these large workloads', which drives demand for very high bandwidth connections between data centers. Parthasarathi split that opportunity into two functional blocks Coherent serves - data center interconnect (DCI) transceivers at the edge of the data center, and optical transport equipment (amplification, signal conditioning, fiber and signal health monitoring) sitting between the data centers - with bandwidth first and energy efficiency second as the metrics customers buy on.

CEO expects large hyperscaler order commitments for DirectFlash to extend into calendar 2028, powering tens of exabytes of capacity — a multiple of this year's expectations; committed order volumes for FY2027 and FY2028 continue to grow. Hyperscale revenue was minimal in Q2, with the majority expected in H2 FY2027 at 75%-85% margins; the hyperscale contribution in guidance was 'mostly baked in' and on track. In hyperscale, DirectFlash is mainly replacing SSDs for now (HDD replacement once pricing comes back into line); the CTO cited 5 times more reliability on a component basis versus SSDs and 2, 3, 5 times the density.
hyperscaler order commitments into calendar 2028, tens of exabytes; hyperscale margins 75%-85%

MEMORY PRICING IS KILLING CLIENT DEMAND, AND INTEL DELIBERATELY REDIRECTED THAT CAPACITY TO DATA CENTER: Zinsner said Intel made a conscious decision at the beginning of the year, seeing that memory pricing would 'start to destroy some of the demand on the client side' - it focused client CPU capacity on big-core products, yielded small-core parts to others, and shifted as much supply as possible to data center on the strength of long-term agreements with data-center customers. Intel 3 cannot flex (Meteor Lake was the only client product in Ireland and is rolling off as Panther Lake ramps), so more Granite Rapids output has to come from new capacity, throughput and yields; but moving client off Intel 7 onto Intel 18A frees Intel 7 capacity that is being used to supply the data-center market. He called the client weakness 'probably the best thing we could have, given the data center demand', and expects the memory hangover to persist into next year before snapping back through 2027.

INTEL 14A: 0.9 PDK IN OCTOBER, RISK PRODUCTION 2027, HIGH-VOLUME 2028: Zinsner said Intel is within two months of the 14A 0.9 PDK, so 'you can pretty much now expect us to land in October with that 0.9 PDK', and the remaining step from 0.9 to 1.0 is much smaller than 0.5 to 0.9. Defect density on Intel 14A is tracking better than the target curve and is coming down faster than any previous node - 'we haven't seen this performance since 22 nanometer, which is arguably one of the best nodes Intel's ever put out' - while 18A yields are beating internal milestones. Demand side: internal product teams, 'probably the most cynical bunch out of anybody', are now designing products on Intel 14A, and external foundry engagements have increased enough that Lip-Bu Tan and the team meet customers weekly and the conversation has moved from data to 'how much capacity can I get? What does that supply look like?'. That sequence forces risk production in 2027 ahead of high-volume manufacturing in 2028.
0.9 PDK in October; risk production in 2027; high volume production in 2028; 22 nanometer

DATA-CENTER VOLTAGE STEP-UP IN ONE YEAR - CONTENT MIX MOVING TO POWELL'S HIGH END: 'If I was sitting here last year talking specifically about data centers, it was 5,000 and 15,000 volt. Now it's 38,000 volt. They need more power.' 38,000 volts is the top of Powell's medium-voltage range ('that's where we stop') and Metcalf says 'We can't build it fast enough.' He adds 'I think the power equation hasn't yet been solved ... these things need so much power, and there's not enough power to feed all of them.' Powell remains outside the data center only ('we do not do anything on the inside'), supplying switchgear inside power control rooms / e-houses that step power into the site. On cycle length, management's working assumption is three to five years of this demand with no let-up visible today, and revamps of today's data centers in about five years are viewed as a future services opportunity.
data-center orders moved from 5,000 and 15,000 volt last year to 38,000 volt today

800G -> 3.2T TRANSITION: as customers increase the number of optical lanes, signal bandwidth, or both, to accelerate network speeds from 800 Gb to 3.2 Tbps, ADI expects to benefit THREEFOLD - unit growth in pluggables and coherent light modules, INCREASING BOM CONTENT per module, and GREATER SHARE as these transitions unfold.

POWER franchise detail: customers are pushing for greater than 98% conversion efficiency, multi-kilowatt delivery with peak power up to 2x rated load, plus protection, telemetry and fault recording. Significant design uptick for ADI protection and 800V-to-intermediate conversion technology delivering 20 kW at industry-leading power density exceeding 2.5 kW per cubic inch, as the industry transitions to 800V DC power distribution. At the intermediate-to-core conversion layer - called ONE OF THE FASTEST AND LARGEST GROWING ANALOG OPPORTUNITIES IN THE AI ERA - ADI combines advanced power conversion, intelligent system control and real-time telemetry for next-generation processors operating at 6,000 A and sub-1V. Framing on efficiency: a 97% converter loses roughly 50% more energy as heat than a 98% one, compounding into cooling infrastructure and opex.
800V->intermediate: 20 kW at >2.5 kW/cubic inch; core rails 6,000 A at sub-1V; >98% efficiency

2030 SAM RESET: ADI's current assessment is that its 2030 data center AND energy SAM has MORE THAN DOUBLED versus what it envisioned just one year ago - driven not simply by higher AI infrastructure CapEx but by new markets and architectures requiring ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE MORE ANALOG CONTENT delivered via higher-value solutions. Supporting math from the call: ~100 GW equivalent of data center infrastructure is expected to be built between now and 2031, with EACH GIGAWATT generating a $1B-$1.5B analog SAM. Runway seen extending to at least 2030 for strong double-digit data center growth; the ~$0.5B energy business is expected to DOUBLE by the end of the decade. ADI is contemplating long-term company growth above the 5%-7% model set at its 2021 investor day.
2030 DC+energy SAM >2x prior view; ~100GW to 2031 at $1-1.5B analog SAM per GW; energy to 2x by 2030

SCALE-UP LASER CONTENT - THE INDUSTRY CAPACITY GAP QUANTIFIED: Murry agreed scale-up optics is 'an order of magnitude-ish increase' in the NUMBER of lasers per rack versus scale-out, and added the die itself is 'five or six times larger size per laser', so the wafer real estate the industry must process rises enormously. He said there is not enough capacity in the industry right now to come close to meeting scale-up demand, let alone scale-out - which is why AOI and its competitors are all investing in laser fabs. He called the AI shift in optics the most impactful game changer he has seen in 30 years in the business.
an order of magnitude-ish increase; five or six times larger size per laser

LRO READY, LPO NOT FULLY PRODUCTIZED, CUSTOMERS STILL BUY FULL DSP: Murry said 'we do have LRO products for sure. We have some designs on LPO. I wouldn’t say they’re productized completely at this point.' The production process is built to switch readily between types, though moving away from DSPs depends on sourcing the replacement components, and 'customers by and large, are still demanding full DSP solutions at this point.'

HPC program with Amazon Web Services is performing ahead of expectations with good sequential growth as a number of programs with the major hyperscaler continue to ramp. Fabrinet is in the process of ramping the customer's NEXT GENERATION silicon platform and is installing additional capacity to support both the technology transition and additional products it will manufacture. The products are follow-on products from previous-generation programs plus newly won additional products. HPC will no longer be broken out separately - it is now reported inside the data center category alongside Datacom and DCI.

→ Amazon: Amazon was a 10%+ customer at 11% of fiscal 2026 revenue. Fabrinet confirmed the HPC program is with Amazon Web Services, is performing ahead of expectations with good sequential growth, and is now ramping the customer's NEXT GENERATION silicon platform, with additional capacity being installed for both the technology transition and newly won follow-on products. HPC is now reported inside the data center category rather than broken out.

1.6T TEST ECONOMICS THE CALL DID NOT SIZE: CEO Oleg Khaykin said a 1.6T tester carries 'about 50% price increase' over an 800G box, 'because the components are much more expensive', comparing it to TSMC raising price per wafer 'about 1.5x' each node. Viavi has sold 1.6T equipment 'for over a year, mainly to the developers' (system, module and silicon vendors); production started 'beginning of this year' and adoption is 'maybe third inning for 1.6T, second, third inning, depending on who you are talking to'. The box is backward compatible - one 1.6T tester can test four 400G modules, two 800G or a 1.6T - so cost per bit falls even though cost per box rises, and one high-performance tester can service multiple production lines at once. Content per test is also rising: 400G was laser/dispersion/power in-out, 800G adds precise laser and insertion-loss measurement, and 'as you go to 1.6T, it is a whole new ballgame... a lot more functional test on the line'. On share, of the top 5 transceiver manufacturers Viavi works with all of them, engagement is 'very high with probably 4 out of 5', and with numbers 1, 2 and 3 'we are very much in all of their labs'.
1.6T tester about 50% price increase versus 800G (TSMC node analogy about 1.5x); engagement very high with 4 out of 5 of the top 5 transceiver makers

N3 AI accelerator entered mass production and began shipping in June; even with a month's revenue contribution it drove QoQ revenue growth up more than 80%, and July revenue reached a record high for the company. 3-nanometer/2-nanometer process node revenue contribution grew to 47% in Q2 from 21% in Q1, and North America region revenue contribution rose to 51% from 23%.
3nm/2nm node revenue contribution 47% in Q2 (from 21% in Q1); North America 51% of revenue (from 23%)

Next-generation N2 accelerator reached a major milestone and entered the final implementation phase: heterogeneous chiplet design requiring multiple tape-outs, on track for tape-out by the end of this year with production by the end of next year. Die size stays four-reticle at 800 millimeter square, but pricing will be much more expensive than N3 and shipment volume higher. Management compared the serviceable market scale to $80 billion, $100 billion (referencing TPU).
N2 tape-out by end of this year (2026), production by end of next year (2027); four-reticle, 800 millimeter square die; market scale reference $80 billion, $100 billion

→ Amazon: The N3 AI accelerator program (identified by analysts on the call as Trainium 3) entered mass production in late May and began shipping in June, driving QoQ revenue growth up more than 80% with only one month of contribution; July revenue reached a company record. Full-year N3 contribution guidance unchanged (orders for this year almost all placed given long lead times), but management sees a chance to revise up next year's shipment and revenue assumptions.

→ Amazon: For the next-generation N2 accelerator Alchip is the sole design partner: compute die, I/O die and final 2.5D packaging integration are all done by Alchip. The heterogeneous chiplet design requires multiple tape-outs (including a possible interposer tape-out), targeted by the end of this year with production by the end of next year; pricing and shipment volume are both expected to be higher than N3. The end customer is receiving very good wafer and packaging capacity support from TSMC, expected to continue for N2 capacity in 2027, 2028.

H1 2026 half-year report (DART, filed 08-14-2026): the Electro-Materials BG, the copper-clad-laminate business, generated segment revenue of KRW 1,293,352M against KRW 879,071M in the year-earlier half, roughly 47% growth, and segment operating profit of KRW 386,913M against KRW 252,313M, a margin near 30%. On 12.1% of group revenue the unit produced 43.2% of group operating profit. Segment net profit was KRW 317,353M and segment assets rose to KRW 1,948,103M from KRW 1,398,847M at the end of 2025. External CCL revenue was KRW 1,293,293M, split KRW 858,904M export and KRW 434,389M domestic; by region the unit billed KRW 859,057M into Asia and KRW 438,836M domestically. The company describes its CCL as a core material for AI accelerators, semiconductors, communications equipment and smartphones, with the main products being NetworkBoard (NWB) CCL for AI accelerators and data centers, package (PKG) CCL for semiconductors, halogen-free CCL for optical modules and flexible CCL for smartphones.

Electro-Materials segment H1 revenue KRW 1,293,352M vs KRW 879,071M; segment operating profit KRW 386,913M vs KRW 252,313M; 43.21% of group operating profit on 12.09% of group revenue; segment assets KRW 1,948,103M vs KRW 1,398,847M

CCL capacity investment: KRW 88,085M was spent on CCL machinery in H1 2026 after KRW 89,663M in 2025 and KRW 38,699M in 2024. The forward plan commits KRW 755,135M to CCL equipment, of which KRW 299,531M falls in 2026, KRW 287,030M in 2027 and KRW 168,575M in 2028; including the electrical-materials and flexible lines and IT infrastructure the total planned programme is KRW 824,188M. A new overseas laminate plant is being added: Doosan Electro-Materials (Thailand) Co., Ltd. was incorporated on 04-27-2026 and is held 99.99% through the Singapore holding company; the 03-31-2026 board approved a capital increase into Doosan Electro-Materials Singapore of KRW 29,510M and a payment guarantee for the Thai company, and the parent has since guaranteed USD 110,000 thousand of facility funding from the Export-Import Bank of Korea running June 2026 to June 2031 at 4.78%. The Vietnamese laminate plant continues to draw parent loans totalling USD 24,500 thousand at 4.60%.

H1 CCL capex KRW 88,085M; planned CCL programme KRW 755,135M (KRW 299,531M in 2026, KRW 287,030M in 2027, KRW 168,575M in 2028); Thailand plant guaranteed USD 110,000 thousand of Eximbank facility funding; KRW 29,510M capital increase into the Singapore holding company

Market position and mix shift: the company estimates its Q2 2026 global CCL share at 30% in package CCL, 22% in flexible CCL (single and double sided) and 16% in halogen-free CCL. The sales strategy has moved away from commodity grades toward high-function products, specifically NWB CCL for AI accelerators and data centers, PKG CCL for semiconductors and halogen-free CCL for optical modules, sold into the global market, and 2026 targets a higher weighting of high-value products together with supply diversification to global customers beyond Samsung. Submarine plant 2 total investment about KRW 7,200 hundred million (phase 1 KRW 4,972 hundred million); HVDC test centre about 7,000 square metres completed January 2026; 320kV HVDC 3000 square millimetre KEMA certifications

Demand outlook (section II-7): the filing states that growth in AI and data centres is raising electricity demand and expanding transmission, distribution and substation investment, citing the IEA estimate that global data centres consumed about 415TWh in 2024, roughly 1.5% of world electricity, after about 12% annual growth over five years, and arguing that this raises the need to relieve grid bottlenecks and add interconnection equipment, lifting demand for extra-high-voltage cable and transmission and distribution infrastructure. Korea's 11th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand projects power demand growing about 1.8% a year to 129.3GW by 2038 with renewables at 29.2%, driven by advanced industry, data centres and electrification. The company sizes the global submarine cable market at about KRW 6.5 trillion in 2024 rising to about KRW 24.9 trillion by 2030, an oligopoly led by Prysmian, Nexans and NKT.

Global data-center power consumption about 415TWh in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity, about 12% annual growth); Korean demand to 129.3GW by 2038 at about 1.8% a year; submarine cable market KRW 6.5 trillion (2024) to KRW 24.9 trillion (2030)

Q3 server revenue should grow QoQ on the GB series plus B200/B300 and storage & compute servers as customers' AI infrastructure build-out continues, partly offset in computing by notebook CPU/memory price hikes and shortages. GB300's life cycle extends into next year - it will not stop when Vera Rubin comes out - so Pegatron is racing to lock in GB300 material allocations for H1 2027 business on top of orders already received and expected Q3/Q4 business; factories have been extremely busy since July-August, with delivery timed to when each customer's infrastructure is ready. CoreWeave was the FIRST CLOUD PROVIDER TO BRING UP AND VALIDATE NVIDIA'S VERA RUBIN NVL72, using its software-defined liquid cooling and rack management. CEO Mike Intrator said Vera Rubin 'is a generation that is seeing the margin expansion right from the start,' that demand for the platform is enormous, and that much of the 5-10 percentage point contribution-margin step-up on Q2-signed contracts is coming in the Vera Rubin SKU. Pricing and margins for Blackwell and Vera Rubin SKUs are setting new highs. The first named Vera Rubin end customer is CATERPILLAR, which will use the platform on CoreWeave's cloud as its 'data factory' to train specialized models for autonomous construction equipment - physical AI training and inference at industrial scale.
First cloud provider to validate Vera Rubin NVL72; Vera Rubin driving much of the 5-10 point contribution-margin step-up

A100 contract signed extending into 2029 (SKU introduced in 2020); largely sold out of prior-generation GPUs

shipping GB200 NVL72 / HGX B200 / B200 NVL4 / RTX 6000 Pro in volume

first-to-market target for Rubin / Vera Rubin NVL72 / Rubin HGX / Vera CPU

The HBM4 transition is a direct order driver: CEO Rafi Amit said 'the industry transition to HBM4 together with continued capacity expansion has resulted in significant orders from MULTIPLE LEADING HBM MANUFACTURERS.' In parallel, ongoing expansion of 2.5D and 3D IC packaging capacity is producing large multi-system orders from leading foundries, IDMs and OSATs. → Siemens: Siemens highlighted its collaboration with Infineon: integrating Infineon silicon carbide power modules into Siemens' latest solid-state circuit breakers — described as a critical enabler for safe and reliable distribution of DC power on the road to 800-volt DC data-center architecture.

Growth catalysts: GAA sales were about JPY 5 billion in Q1 and are expected at over JPY 20 billion for FY March 2027. Advanced packaging revenue, JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026, is now expected at JPY 15 billion in FY March 2027 (Q1 was JPY 4.5 billion) - a significant upward revision from the JPY 6 billion prior plan, driven by both rising customer CapEx and additional POR wins for its film deposition technology. In DRAM, the D1C transition is complete and D1D is progressing. NAND sales could approach record highs, and DRAM plus NAND plus advanced packaging support growth above WFE (targeting more than a 20% sales increase).
GAA JPY 5 billion in Q1, over JPY 20 billion FY March 2027; advanced packaging raised to JPY 15 billion FY March 2027 from JPY 6 billion in FY March 2026

800-volt DC roadmap: Siemens is shaping the path to 800V direct-current architecture required for high rack density in AI factories — adoption expected to progress IN STAGES over the next four to five years with hybrid architectures dominating early phases; AC and DC to coexist in brownfield retrofits and greenfield builds; FIRST PILOTS EXPECTED IN 2027. Siemens is helping major data-center providers design, test and deploy DC power distribution. Developed a reference architecture together with NVIDIA, nVent and Fluence across compute, cooling, power and control systems for the latest NVIDIA DGX Vera Rubin platform (goal: maximizing tokens per watt); modular automation framework with ready-to-use Simatic libraries — Siemens PLCs already automating critical OT infrastructure in several megawatt-scale data centers; collaborating with Infineon to integrate silicon carbide power modules into its latest solid-state circuit breakers for safe DC power distribution.
800V DC adoption staged over four to five years; first pilots 2027; NVIDIA/nVent/Fluence reference architecture for DGX Vera Rubin

→ NVIDIA: Siemens developed a reference architecture together with NVIDIA, nVent and Fluence across compute, cooling, power and control systems for the latest NVIDIA DGX Vera Rubin platform — goal: maximizing tokens per watt and ensuring predictable, scalable operations; Siemens built a modular, scalable automation framework on it with ready-to-use Simatic libraries.

BOYD RAISED AND THE 800V PLAYBOOK: Boyd (liquid cooling — COLD PLATES + CDUs) raised to $1.8B FY2026 revenue, up from the ~$1.7B+ trajectory flagged in Q1 ($1.5B lands in Eaton's books; Boyd did $1.1B in 2025); Q2 $432M was 20% ABOVE plan; wins on being the DESIGN PARTNER embedded in chip providers' roadmaps (first look/first bid), aerospace-grade quality at scale (smaller rivals showing 'quality issues from the get-go'), and it hands Eaton an early strategic read into chip development; joins organic growth in 2027. 800V DC: content ~$3.4M PER MW CONFIRMED 'the right number'; the customer objective is TOKENS PER MEGAWATT (~5% efficiency gain from DC conversion — 'when there's so much money involved, this is going to happen'). Eaton frames FOUR technical blocks required to win 800V — (1) medium-voltage SOLID-STATE TRANSFORMER (Resilient Power, 'clearly ahead' per hyperscaler and chip-maker feedback), (2) DC BREAKER technology, (3) power electronics/power quality (UPS), (4) COOLING (Boyd) — plus a service network that arrives 'in an hour, not days'; players missing blocks 'will have a really hard time.' Prefab/modular (Fibrebond): electrician/plumber scarcity pushes modular builds, and 800V's simpler architecture INCREASES the modular opportunity, extending Eaton from gray space into white space.
Boyd raised to $1.8B FY26 (Q2 +20% vs plan); $3.4M/MW confirmed; 800V = 4 blocks (SST/DC breaker/UPS/cooling) + service; modular expands with 800V

Advanced Solutions, which includes the Fluxless Thermo-Compression (FTC) bonding platform, recognised revenue 20% ABOVE last quarter's record. K&S is maintaining its target of OVER $100 MILLION in Advanced Solutions revenue for fiscal 2026, and for fiscal 2027 Lester Wong guided TCB revenue to a range of $150 MILLION TO $200 MILLION - significant sequential growth. The company remains closely engaged with a broad base of IDM, OSAT and foundry customers as heterogeneous packaging goes mainstream, with particular confidence in heterogeneous integration around logic for Fluxless TCB.
Advanced Solutions revenue 20% above prior record; >$100M Advanced Solutions target for FY2026; TCB guided to $150M-$200M in FY2027

Beyond thermocompression, K&S accelerated its HYBRID BONDING program over the last year and says its hybrid bonder has unique features not currently in the market; it PLANS TO DELIVER A HYBRID BONDING TOOL TO A CUSTOMER IN THE FIRST HALF OF FISCAL 2027. It is also investing significantly in a PANEL-level project, seeing a lot of interest from IDMs, foundries and OSATs because panel geometry allows many more dies on a rectangle than a circle; specific panel applications are still being scoped with customers. Management frames FTC, vertical wire, direct copper-to-copper, hybrid and panel-based architectures as the emerging packaging set that will be critically necessary across a much wider array of semiconductor production, and stresses the industry is still in the relatively early stages of this More-than-Moore advanced packaging transition.
Hybrid bonding tool to be delivered to a customer in H1 FY2027

NAND is turning: MKS saw increased momentum in NAND UPGRADE activity in Q2 and expects it to continue, possibly better. RF power is the LARGEST PART OF THE BILL OF MATERIALS in such an upgrade, which is why MKS benefits disproportionately from upgrades. Announced NAND GREENFIELD fabs are expected to come in towards the END OF 2027 AND BEGINNING OF 2028, which would be even better because MKS would supply the rest of its semiconductor portfolio around a brand-new tool; NAND should become a bigger percentage of semi revenue in 2028. Until then the mix stays largely logic and DRAM driven.
NAND greenfield fabs expected end-2027 into 2028; NAND to become a bigger share of semi revenue in 2028

Demonstrated 2,200 volt PowiGaN technology, extending PowiGaN into application spaces traditionally served by silicon carbide and using the same proven architecture as the prior 750, 900, 1,250 and 1,700 volt nodes, with eight years of demonstrated field reliability and 1,500 volt architectures already in view. Positioned as a single-platform alternative to complex stacked-device approaches so data-center customers can adopt GaN today without being forced to change technologies on next-gen designs. Timing: it is a technology demonstration, not a launched product; data-center products would sit on the 1,500 volt roadmap, 'several years' out — 'the next couple of years before we see anything meaningful there', not the next couple of quarters.
2,200 volt PowiGaN demonstrated; products several years out (1,500 volt roadmap)

Data-center engagement runs on two tracks. (1) Main power path to the GPU — the biggest component of the projected billion-dollar data-center SAM — being developed with customers around Power Integrations' 1,250 volt GaN as a high-density alternative to stacked 650 volt designs; this track is earlier, still requires work with customers, and depends on when the 800 volt systems deploy. (2) Auxiliary power in and around the rack — switch trays, power sidecars and other high-voltage sockets — where there is 'a healthy roster of design-ins and a strong pipeline of ongoing design activity' with 1,700 volt products for 800 volt data centers, addressable with products in hand today and pointing to revenue in 2028. Broad range of ongoing customer engagements addressing 800 volt data centers; recent hyperscaler discussions confirm power remains a major challenge.
Aux-power design-ins could be revenue in 2028; main GPU power path further out

Battery energy storage: already shipping SCALE-2 gate-driver boards into battery storage systems used alongside renewable installations, and won an important new customer in Q2 — a utility-scale design at a top supplier of batteries for energy storage systems and EVs (customer not named). Rising power demands are pushing storage toward higher-voltage architectures and greater silicon-carbide adoption, which requires more advanced gate drivers. A number of customer engagements are underway for battery storage specifically targeting AI data centers, described as another element of the projected billion-dollar data-center SAM in 2030. Deployments of battery storage are expected to grow at a double-digit CAGR through 2035.
One new utility-scale gate-driver design win; billion-dollar data-center SAM in 2030

→ NVIDIA: In June, Power Integrations published two reference designs targeting NVIDIA 800 volt racks using its 1,700 volt InnoMux products. These auxiliary supplies sit on the compute tray in a native 800 volt system, powering components such as MCUs, gate drivers and op-amps, and deliver space savings of about 30% compared to discrete silicon carbide designs. Alongside the aux track, the main power path to the GPU is being developed with 1,250 volt GaN as a high-density alternative to stacked 650 volt designs. Aux-power design-ins point to revenue in 2028; the main power path depends on when the 800 volt systems deploy.
units: two reference designs; 1,700 volt InnoMux aux supplies on the compute tray; about 30% space saving vs discrete silicon carbide

Drug-design efficiency: candidates are being advanced with roughly 330 synthesized compounds over about 1.5 years versus an industry benchmark of roughly 2,500 compounds over four years. REC-7735 was designed in 10 months using 242 compounds across 13 cycles and is nearly 130x selective over wild type.
~330 compounds / 1.5 years vs ~2,500 / 4 years; REC-7735: 242 compounds, 13 cycles, 10 months

Advanced nodes portfolio grew more than 20% in Q2 (Investor Day plan was ~7%): continued growth at three nanometer, emerging activity at two nanometer, really strong pull for 2 nm and 18A, and successful scale-up of HBM3/HBM4 on the memory side; advanced nodes were about 40% of the portfolio exiting the first half versus the 45%-50% Investor Day target, which Qnity expects to reach early.
advanced nodes +20% YoY; ~40% of portfolio vs 45%-50% target
