New advanced packaging architectures (panel-level packaging, larger package formats, tighter lines and spaces on high-layer-count boards and IC substrates) all mean more material complexity and more material intensity, with fewer suppliers able to qualify; Qnity has incumbency with the same customers that commercialized the existing advanced packaging formats and expects more content per package as formats grow. Customer capacity expansions in advanced packaging underpin the durability of ICS growth.

AMD's new MI450 series is on schedule and Wistron, as AMD's main component-level supporter, sees AMD's customer forecasts growing (citing Lisa Su's optimism). Beyond components, Wistron has already taken rack/system orders for MI450 from customers ('yes'), on schedule to ship together with AMD's product ramp in H2 2026; whether Wistron builds components or full AMD systems is decided by the customer, across enterprise and CSP.

VR (Vera Rubin) is already in mass production - management confirmed it, citing Jensen - and the generation handover has caused no Q3 air pocket: some customers still prefer GB300 so GB300 volume persists, while others are moving to VR, leaving Q3 looking quite good. Wistron expects to keep a reasonable margin after the VR launch despite the higher rack price, with OP margin 'no worse than GB300' and the trend holding into H1 2027 when VR volume ramps; some new customers are starting directly on VR. Wistron is also working on the pure Vera CPU racks and switch/storage racks NVIDIA announced alongside VR, has already received orders for the new products, and will ship them in H2 2026.
→ AMD: MI450 series is on schedule; Wistron is AMD's main component-level supporter and has additionally received customer orders for MI450 rack systems, shipping when AMD's product ramps in H2 2026.

→ NVIDIA: Vera Rubin is already in mass production and Wistron ships as NVIDIA's component-level partner; Wistron has also received orders for NVIDIA's new Vera-based products (pure Vera CPU racks, switch and storage racks), shipping in H2 2026, and NVIDIA develops these new products with its small set of ODM partners.

The new Turing design center began trial operation in Q2 running small and mid-size projects and is expected to be in full use in H2; it adds some depreciation/R&D cost but is aimed squarely at 3nm, 2nm and even more advanced process work plus advanced packaging. The R&D roadmap already includes CPO, IVR (integrated voltage regulator), next-generation UCIe die-to-die, and N2-on-N2 advanced-process development; opex should grow only modestly versus a clearly larger revenue increase next year.

Capacity and technology roadmap: multi-site production at Yokkaichi (one of the world's largest flash memory bases, leading-edge R&D) and Kitakami; the K2 fab at Kitakami began operation in September 2025 and began production of the 10th generation BiCS FLASH this year. Capex plan: average JPY 470 billion annually from FY2026 to FY2028 (JPY 450 billion this year), flexible to market change and fully covered by cash flow. R&D about JPY 200 billion for the full year, concentrated on BiCS 10/BiCS 11 and AI inference SSDs (super high IOPS SSD for inference servers); UFS 5.0 new high-speed standard for edge AI / on-device AI announced. Strategy: not pursuing market share through aggressive investment - pursuing quality and profitability via higher sequential speed, energy efficiency and product quality.
Capex average JPY 470 billion/year FY2026-FY2028 (JPY 450 billion this year); R&D ~JPY 200 billion; BiCS10 in production at Kitakami K2, BiCS11 and AI inference SSD in development

AI data center applications drive the WFE market: sales to AI data center are expected to grow by five times or more in the five years from calendar 2023 through calendar 2027, spanning not only GPU and HBM but also DDR, CPU and 3D NAND. Technology transitions expected within two years: logic scaling from the 3 nanometer mainstream toward 2 nanometer with backside PDN adoption, DRAM evolving to the 1D node (1C to 1D transition), HBM stacked DRAM count rising from 12 to 16, and NAND evolving to 300 layers and further to 400 layers. Agentic AI is the driver of the overall WFE market; CY2026 WFE application mix is about 60% logic and 40% memory, versus 65%/35% last year.
AI data center WFE sales to grow five times or more CY2023-CY2027; HBM stacks from 12 to 16; NAND to 300 then 400 layers; logic mainstream 3 nanometer moving to 2 nanometer

Power electronics stable at a low level: SiC installed base underutilized, GaN utilization around 60%-70% and gradually increasing; GaN has a strong opportunity in AI data centers for 800-volt DC to DC conversion, with SiC coming first at the high-voltage entry point and GaN following with a delay; mid-term view of a GaN market 3X-ing to around EUR 450 million of tool revenue fully holds; AIXTRON systems (G5+ and G10-GaN) are the tools of record across the GaN power market, so customers are expected to arrive with multi-dozen tool orders when the wave starts
GaN installed-base utilization around 60%-70%; mid-term GaN tool revenue view around EUR 450 million

HVDC ramp: plus/minus 400V and 800V systems start mass production in Q3 2026, but Q4 shipments and full-year volume stay limited - larger volume comes next year. The plus/minus 400V architecture is being pushed more aggressively and ships more this year; 800V is driven mainly by NVIDIA and depends on when data-center operators adopt that power architecture - NVIDIA's Blackwell shipments are still much larger than Rubin, and part of the Rubin lineup can still run on low voltage. On the 110kW power shelf and other new product cycles Delta believes its market share remains high because it engages customers earliest, and the fast generational churn of AI power architecture favors its engineering resources; it declined to quantify share for the Rubin-linked 110kW PSU but asserts market leadership. A solid-state transformer (an energy gateway, not a one-for-one transformer replacement) has its first trial customers in smaller data centers, and a first small fuel-cell line starts by year-end with the first volume line planned next year, with units at Taipower and another test site performing well.
HVDC plus/minus 400V and 800V mass production from Q3, limited volume this year, ramp next year; 110kW power shelf share seen high

Liquid cooling keeps scaling: liquid-cooling products were about 10% of group revenue last year and will exceed 12% this year (an analyst cited about US$1.6 billion of Liquid-to-Air contribution last year). Management expects Liquid-to-Air to persist considerably longer than the market's assumption that Liquid-to-Liquid fully takes over around 2028.
liquid cooling about 10% of revenue last year, above 12% this year; Liquid-to-Air about US$1.6B contribution last year

Technology read-through on evolving cooling architectures: asked whether higher inlet fluid temperature specs for future GPU designs reduce chiller demand, management said demand is improving and increasing for Modine because of its free-cooling technology — a higher inlet temperature lets the unit run in free-cooling mode more of the time, driving further efficiency and reducing data-center power consumption, while the chiller and refrigerant cycle stay in place as the 'insurance policy' for temperatures above that band. Chillers support both facility cooling and incorporation into direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems — similar models and SKUs sit on the same data-center rooftop doing both — so Modine cannot split its order book between the two. The enhanced three-megawatt chiller is being introduced to customers and will raise output per line versus the 2 MW unit.
3 MW chiller launching (vs 2 MW today); higher GPU inlet temperatures increase free-cooling/chiller demand

BBU content growth with next-generation accelerators: asked about NVIDIA Rubin production starting and per-rack battery cell capacity possibly rising from 80 W to 120 W, management said the Rubin percentage will not be so high yet but Panasonic's portion will increase including capacity, and as the BBU solution evolves the unit price would go up - required output changes and the total solution expands ('it's not replacing PBU, but it's PBU plus CPU'); non-GPU demand (TPU, ASIC, including CPU racks for inference) is also expanding and is part of the JPY 550 billion full-year picture.
Per-rack battery cell capacity discussion 80 W to 120 W with Rubin; unit price to rise as BBU solution evolves

Market shift toward SPX solutions: as more liquid cooling goes under the roof, dry cooling appears to be the most favored heat-rejection solution, with adiabatic and cooling towers also in demand; SPX sees significantly increasing demand from existing hyperscalers and had nice wins with colos and neoclouds. Hyperscalers give visibility several years forward because they need SPX's product to turn the data center on and send teams of 10 people into SPX facilities for two weeks at a time.

EMIB-T advanced packaging: Unimicron is one of three substrate makers (alongside two Japanese peers) qualified on the EMIB-T platform; first-phase yield target is 50%, with the customer contractually protecting supplier profitability below that yield and volume production starting next year (2027). Key EMIB-T equipment is centrally allocated among the three suppliers and second/third equipment sources are being qualified; EMIB-T-related investment is less than 10% of the raised capex and platform-dedicated equipment only 10% to 15% to 20% of that, since much of the new capacity is general FC-BGA for CPU-based inference designs that need no interposer. Management notes hyperscaler customers moving toward chiplet-style in-house designs are qualifying substrate suppliers directly and pre-booking capacity. Glass-core substrates: no volume production expected before 2029-2030, though R&D programs run with three customers, each customised. Mid-to-long-term gross-margin ambition is 50 to 60%.
EMIB-T first-phase yield target 50%, volume production 2027; EMIB-T investment under 10% of capex (dedicated equipment 10-15-20% of that); glass-core substrate volume not before 2029-2030

Ahead of schedule and currently billing for 437 MW of capacity. Billing began on 437 MW in mid-July, nearly 200 MW more than at the end of the first quarter, after substantially completing four of the five CoreWeave campuses ahead of the end-of-summer target. Management stresses that delivering hundreds of megawatts of high-density infrastructure 'requires far more than access to power' - it requires an integrated development and operating platform - and that the AMD sites are not greenfield: equipment is secured, contractors are on site across the five campuses, and at Pecos the building shell is essentially complete.
437 MW billable, nearly 200 MW more than at the end of Q1

The Bitcoin-mining-to-AI conversion is nearly complete: Core Scientific ended June with nearly 30% fewer miners online than at the end of the first quarter and is now self-mining at only two sites, running that business primarily to offset contractual power costs during the wind-down, which continues over the remainder of the year so that 2027 starts with a clean sheet of paper. Having spent the past year converting existing power capacity from Bitcoin mining to high-density colocation, the next phase complements that with selective acquisition of powered land and development of new sites: a new site pipeline of more than 2 GW of potential incremental power has been identified, with initial capacity potentially available from late 2028 through 2030, and management hopes to bring a new site to market by year-end. The Hunt County, Texas acquisition earlier this year is representative of that pipeline.
nearly 30% fewer miners online QoQ, self-mining at two sites; >2 GW new-site pipeline (late 2028-2030)

→ CoreWeave: Four of the five CoreWeave campuses were substantially completed ahead of the end-of-summer target, taking the program to 437 billable megawatts - nearly 200 MW more than at the end of the first quarter - and driving GAAP colocation revenue to $137 million. Dalton Phase II, the fifth and final campus and the last 150 MW of the CoreWeave build-out, begins delivering at the end of 2026 and is on track for full completion in early 2027. The relationship began as a 16 MW lease at the Auburn campus in 2024 and has since expanded to 590 MW of total contracted capacity; revenue is recognized straight-line over the 12-year lease terms, pulling contractual escalators forward. Auburn and Dalton become fully leased once the AMD-credit-supported neocloud leases are added.
units: 437 MW billable of 590 MW contracted; 150 MW remaining at Dalton Phase II; value: $137 million GAAP colocation revenue in the quarter

Advanced packaging (quantified as several hundred million dollars of revenue) is performing quite well with share gain in the IC substrate / package substrate part of circuitry, strong high-end paste and wafer-level packaging; Element is establishing processes of record for the transition from CoWoS to CoPoS and other emerging technologies expected to ramp about 18 months from now, and expects the advanced packaging business to accelerate into 2027 and 2028.
advanced packaging several hundred million dollars of revenue; CoWoS-to-CoPoS ramp ~18 months out

Product content for higher-capacity data centers: 'We're adapting some of our products for those applications ... our new Pin & Sleeve devices that are going to higher amperage to the 800 volt infrastructure.' Modular/factory-built trend: PCX power skids for data centers and System Control substation control houses built in a factory setting, DMC crimp connectors replacing field welds on busbar.
new Pin & Sleeve devices for 800 V data-center infrastructure

The next product wave is not yet in revenue: NXP's S32N 5-nanometer processor and S32K5 16-nanometer zonal-controller products remain in the design-win phase, while management said physical-AI deployments have not begun in earnest. Their future ramps underpin management's constructive 2027 outlook.
S32N 5nm and S32K5 16nm not yet ramping; physical-AI deployments still early

Fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) for AI: chairman confirms PTI is an AMD AI-chip supply-chain partner providing fan-out PLP solutions and is actively pursuing more AMD AI-chip applications; despite equipment-delivery delays, installation issues and doing new-product qualification in parallel, the program is on schedule and PTI is confident of volume production before the middle of next year, which would make it the world's first company to mass-produce fan-out PLP for AI applications. The former-AUO fab conversion is going smoothly: floor 1 for middle-end/RDL processing, floor 2 for chip-on-panel and mounting packages onto ABF substrates; the G7 panel equipment supporting the AMD program is fully installed and in qualification, with automation being added. PTI showed an engineering sample of a 5x-reticle-size AI package (one reticle = 26x33mm) - it says only TSMC otherwise has this capability - and notes a G7 panel fits about 45 such large AI packages versus 8 to 9 on a wafer, positioning panel output as a complement to foundry wafer-based advanced packaging. FOPLP equipment lead times run about a year plus installation; management estimates a new entrant would need roughly three years from ordering to customer qualification (PTI started fan-out panel work in 2015). In high-end flip-chip BGA, PTI already mass-produces large FC-BGA/MCM and will move a large one-reticle-size chip package into volume production in Q3.
AMD fan-out PLP volume production before mid-2027 (target: world's first FOPLP for AI); 5x reticle-size panel packages, ~45 per G7 panel vs 8-9 per wafer; FOPLP equipment lead time ~1 year

Optical/CPO roadmap: the Broadcom cooperation has brought PTI into optical communications - it will build Optical Engines using its panel fan-out technology, with small-volume production of the first OBO and OSFP versions starting around end-2026; integrating the Optical Engine into a switch (a CPO switch) is targeted to start shipping in H2 2027, and integration of the Optical Engine into AI chips is expected around 2028 or later once designs mature (engineering simulations already completed). Separately, TSV interconnection for DRAM co-developed with a partner has completed DDR-5 trial production and moves to volume production and shipments in Q4 2026 - a foundation for future HBM manufacturing that management expects to start shifting DRAM packaging from 30-year-old wire-bond formats toward advanced packaging, with a meaningful revenue and margin contribution from next year.
Optical Engine small-volume production from end-2026 (OBO, OSFP); CPO switch shipments from H2 2027; AI-chip integration ~2028; TSV-based DDR-5 DRAM volume production from Q4 2026

→ AMD: Chairman: PTI has become a supply-chain partner for AMD AI chips and will provide AMD fan-out PLP (panel-level packaging) solutions, and is actively pursuing additional AMD AI-chip applications. Despite equipment-delivery delays and parallel qualification, the AMD program is on schedule; PTI is confident of volume production before the middle of next year at the converted former-AUO fab, where the G7 panel equipment supporting AMD is installed and in qualification - which would make PTI the first company globally to mass-produce fan-out PLP for AI applications.

→ Broadcom: PTI and Broadcom will form a joint venture in Singapore - a major milestone making PTI a strategic and preferred partner of Broadcom. Built on PTI's fan-out PLP AI packaging experience, the JV will co-develop and produce additive-process fine-line-width redistribution-layer (RDL) packaging directly on advanced substrates (fan-out based), and will serve Broadcom exclusively without affecting PTI's fan-out PLP work for existing and future customers. An NDA is signed and the deal awaits Taiwan investment-authority approval, after which details will be disclosed; the JV funding goes in staged installments and does not raise PTI's NT$500 hundred million capex. The cooperation also brought PTI into the optical-communications field (Optical Engine, CPO switch roadmap).

Skyworks is engaged with leading data-center customers on the transition to 400V and 800V HVDC architectures. Rising rack density is driving demand for its advanced power-delivery solutions alongside its precision timing portfolio, and AI data center is the company's fastest-growing business at more than 50% annual growth.
400V/800V HVDC power transition; AI data-center growth >50%

Bookings in the third quarter were strong with book-to-bill better than 1.1; Sanmina continued to secure more customer orders for the next-generation accelerated compute business in Q3 (after securing orders with both hyperscale and OEM customers last quarter), expanding its overall customer base, while the legacy accelerated compute platform at ZT Systems has gone to zero.

Sanmina's ZT Systems business (the acquisition announced in May 2025 that created its partnership with AMD) is working in very close collaboration with AMD and joint customers to support almost all pre-production activities for the next-generation accelerated compute program; these non-recurring engineering services carry little revenue but a lot of labor charges and drove the non-GAAP operating margin beat to 8.0%, though longer-term margin is still expected in the 6%-7% range.
non-GAAP operating margin 8.0% (+230 bps YoY); long-term 6%-7%

Q4 FY2026 outlook: revenue $3.3 billion-$3.6 billion (core Sanmina $2.5 billion-$2.6 billion, ZT Systems $0.8 billion-$1.0 billion) and non-GAAP operating margin 7.5%-8.0%; the ZT range is below the prior implied guidance entirely because of a few legacy programs, and the new next-generation accelerated compute program is not included in the Q4 outlook due to revenue recognition timing — it is expected to begin contributing revenue in Q1 fiscal 2027 and ramp over time.
Q4 revenue $3.3 billion-$3.6 billion; ZT Systems $0.8 billion-$1.0 billion; op margin 7.5%-8.0%

→ AMD: ZT Systems is working in very close collaboration with AMD and joint customers to support almost all pre-production activities for the next-generation accelerated compute program; orders have been secured with both hyperscale and OEM customers, with more added in Q3; production revenue is expected to begin in Q1 fiscal 2027 and ramp over time through fiscal 2027 into fiscal 2028.

→ AMD: The ZT Systems partnership with AMD dates from the ZT Systems deal announced in May 2025; the business was expected at a $5 billion-$6 billion annualized run rate in its first year, and AMD 'continues to add more customers', which management says broadens Sanmina's addressable market for AMD Helios production even though share is hard to gauge.
value: ZT Systems run rate $5 billion-$6 billion (FY2026)

HBM hybrid bonding at a decision point: evaluations ongoing at one of the three memory companies with another starting its evaluation; all three are preparing to adopt hybrid bonding at some point because the device performs significantly better and produces far less heat; H2 2026 will clarify which HBM applications (HBM4E or even HBM3) adopt the technology and at what scale; the JEDEC height relaxation does not change that characteristic

Photonic SOI addresses pluggable transceivers, near package optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO); most current revenue and growth comes from scale-out, mostly pluggables, with NPO taking share and CPO expected to ramp on scale-out at the end of the year; scale-up is starting with pluggables and will move to CPO; roughly the same Photonic SOI content in all these architectures

Electrification: $2.7B of data-center orders in Q2 — >$5B in H1 2026, MORE THAN DOUBLE full-year 2025 (of ~$14B total H1 orders); segment orders +66% to $6.3B (~1.7x revenue); equipment backlog $41B (+69% / +$17B YoY; air-insulated switchgear alone ~$5B, shipments 9,000 -> ~10,500 units this year); North America equipment orders ~4x YoY (now largest region, incl. Prolec ~$900M revenue in Q2); revenue +68% reported / +29% organic; EBITDA margin 18.4% (+700bps). NEW AI-datacenter products: first 5 MW SOLID-STATE TRANSFORMER (indoor) prototype delivering to a hyperscaler (R&D-shared) later in 2026, 6 MW outdoor SST started with a DIFFERENT hyperscaler — SST orders '27+, gated by how fast AI factories shift to 800V DC; medium-voltage UPS 'stability block' could book orders even sooner (possibly H2 2026). Data-center scope today ~$300M/GW; with SST + MV-UPS entitlement is 2-3x that, expected in 2027 orders. Integrated Electrification+aeroderivative solutions seen adding up to $500M orders/year.
H1 DC orders >$5B (2x FY25); SST 5MW to hyperscaler 2026; scope $300M/GW -> 2-3x

AI chip roadmap: an upgraded AI chip that is a 'moderate improvement over AI4' probably reaches production around the middle of next year, and AI5 is hopefully in VOLUME PRODUCTION around the middle of next year, going INITIALLY INTO OPTIMUS. Musk: 'Tesla chip team is really doing great work... I think it's going to be the best edge computing chip in the world.' Tesla also intends to upgrade essentially every camera-equipped car below Hardware 4 to the next-generation AI board so they can run FSD v15 and later versions.
no specific figure (both chips targeted for production around the middle of next year)

800V DC data centers: 'We have ZERO order in the backlog for 800 volt DC data centers. Nobody has, because there is waiting for the availability of components from NVIDIA and the like.' Commercial impact seen from late 2027 or 2028 onwards; ABB building the complete 800V DC portfolio now — already a leading player in DC switches, breakers and components, expects the new architecture to shift more content to medium voltage, boosting its medium-voltage UPS. Heavy R&D allocation plus the announced acquisition of Advantics (France — DC technology, silicon carbide technology, joining Electrification for DC and data center). Dedicated DC-topic webcast announced for September 24.
Zero 800V DC orders in backlog industry-wide; commercial opportunity late 2027/2028; Advantics acquisition adds DC/SiC technology

The June 2026 presentation says data center TAM is shifting to liquid cooling: to date a vast majority of the TAM for the thermal management equipment BASX provides to data centers is cloud compute data centers cooled by air-side equipment, and by 2028 AAON anticipates the split to be 60% liquid and 40% air-cooled.
by 2028 anticipated split 60% liquid / 40% air-cooled (AAON estimate)

Backlog mix: CEO said the backlog is approximately 79% natural gas projects, 13% renewable and 8% industrial, and that with current demand for natural gas-fired facilities, complex combined cycle projects are expected to represent the majority of backlog for the near and midterm; renewable demand 'has softened' but Argan will keep renewable capabilities. Current backlog includes four gas-fired power plants in the United States totaling over 4.1 GW.
backlog approximately 79% natural gas, 13% renewable, 8% industrial; four gas-fired plants totaling over 4.1 GW

Long-haul / middle-mile data-center fiber: CEO says the $20 billion long-haul middle-mile opportunity set first cited about five quarters ago 'has certainly grown' (updated internally, not published). A customer is discussing hyperscaler routes with up to 7,500-10,000 fiber strands per route, versus the 864 or 1728 count fiber being placed today, which he calls 'a decade plus long build'. The work is 'still in early innings': programs take 'a year-ish' from announcement to start, calendar 2027 comes online and calendar 2028 is 'that fast and furious year'; Dycom believes it was 'first on the field' and keeps winning more.
$20 billion opportunity set (grown, not updated publicly); routes up to 7,500-10,000 fiber strands vs 864 or 1728 count fiber today; ramp calendar 2027, especially calendar 2028

Next-generation substrate roadmap: significantly bigger substrates integrating more chips - up to more than 40 chiplet structures on one board-like substrate the size of a laptop, with silicon-based communication structures inside so chips talk to each other like one big chip; energy supply for these super structures up to 40 kilowatts at around 0.7-0.8 volt, driving embedded high-power electronics (miniaturized silicon carbide transformers embedded in PCBs on accelerator cards); glass cores and embedded optical connections also on the roadmap, co-developed on long-term roadmaps with hyperscalers and chip producers.

Development of the next-generation Vera Rubin series is already underway in step with NVIDIA's GPU roadmap; Gigabyte expects to be time-to-market leading, with mass production currently expected to start in the second half of 2026 - final timing per NVIDIA's official announcement. Rubin platforms are positioned for next-generation training and inference and for higher-density, higher-efficiency AI infrastructure.
Vera Rubin products expected to start mass production in H2 2026 (timing per NVIDIA)

FORM-FACTOR TRANSITIONS (CEO): pluggables stay dominant 'at least through the 2030', with Arista-led XPO (extra dense pluggable optics) and NEAR-PACKAGE OPTICS (NPO) emerging next and CPO 'several years down the road'; Tower SiPho was in leading XPO and NPO demos at OFC, has 'multiple design wins' in NPO with 'reasonable volume' shipping in 2026, 2027 and 'strong demand for NPO products in 2027'; NPO is expected to precede a significant CPO ramp for its primary customers. Citing a LightCounting report: SiPho ports go from 30 million (2025) to 137 million (2028) while total ports go from 90 million to 205. CPO investments: in-house 200 mm and 300 mm hybrid bonding with Through-Silicon Vias (SiPho-to-EIC), laser sources incl. DWDM, and compact modulators. Optical circuit switches: partnerships with Salience Labs and Oriole Networks to manufacture SiPho OCS on PH18DA with integrated InP amplifiers; partner Scintil Photonics launched heterogeneously integrated DWDM laser sources for NPO/CPO.
SiPho ports 30 million (2025) to 137 million (2028) per LightCounting; NPO volume shipping 2026, 2027

MODULATOR / LASER ROADMAP AND INP CONSTRAINT: demonstrated an all-silicon 400 Gb per lane Mach-Zehnder modulator with Coherent (Coherent's design on Tower's platform); with OpenLight, a heterogeneously integrated 400 Gb per lane InP electro-absorption modulator on PH18DA; moving thin-film lithium niobate toward high volume manufacturing (both side-by-side and chiplet-on-PIC forms, with different customers); organic-polymer modulator partnerships with Lightwave Logic and NLM Photonics. CEO's personal view: TFLN 'will come in fairly strong for one generation' before the industry moves to indium phosphide, which wins on form factor at many channels; integrated lasers are no less reliable than discrete ones, and Tower is agnostic to external vs integrated lasers. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE IS CONSTRAINED - 'the starting material is the constraint' - but Tower says its supply-chain plans position it to meet demand as the integrated InP laser ramps this year.
400 Gb per lane modulators (silicon with Coherent; InP with OpenLight); InP starting material constrained

SIGE ATTACH AND POWER FOR AI RACKS: the SiGe platform sees 'unprecedented demand' for optical-transceiver drivers and TIAs and for active copper cables as a short-reach scale-up alternative to optics; SiGe units go 'pretty much' hand in hand with SiPho units as ports grow, though SiGe revenue grows slower and SiPho earns the higher margin. Power management: Gen3 BCD platform (on-resistance below 1.5 milliohm millimeter squared above 10 V; lead customers saw a 15% reduction in power conversion losses) targets smart power stages and point-of-load converters as AI data center racks move to 800 V DC; 200 mm BCD pricing increased by 13% (a value reset, not a capacity-driven hike, per the CEO).
SiGe +24% year-over-year; 200 mm BCD pricing increased by 13%; 15% reduction in power conversion losses

AI power content expanding: designing 800V power management for data centers; high-voltage MOSFETs used in AI power applications (strong quick-turn Asia demand); customers increasingly adding Vishay passives in AI power-management solutions — polymer capacitors, power inductors and current-sense resistors. Next-gen design focus on server power, optical communication modules and high-bandwidth network switches (incl. 800G/1.6T AI optical switches). SiC strategy: released 750V Gen2 planar MOSFETs, standing up an 8-inch SiC wafer fab at Newport; SK Key Foundry releasing products in Q3 to add AI-application capacity.
800V DC power mgmt; HV MOSFETs + polymer caps/inductors/current-sense for AI power

AMD's MI450 series is in NPI stage at Inventec alongside the NVIDIA next-gen program, with mass production expected around H2 2026 per market schedules. Inventec's initial role on MI450 is board-level provider in the initial stage, with the option to go for the full rack later if the opportunity arises; the collaboration model with former partner ZT on MI450 was left open.

Next-generation GPU server products for both NVIDIA (Rubin) and AMD (MI series) are in NPI stage at Inventec, which will match both vendors' mass-production schedules - external expectations put volume production in H2 2026 to year-end. Both L6 board-level and L10 system-level are planned, with L6 the initial focus.

800V DC architecture stance unchanged: 'We believe it's gonna come. We believe that it's gonna be more progressive than some of you expect' — Legrand sees itself well-positioned for both hybrid architectures and full DC, viewing the shift as an opportunity (more data centers, higher density, more energy efficient) rather than a threat. More detail promised at the capital markets day in Singapore on September 29, 2026, with a particular focus on data centers. In UPS, Legrand is a small player (industrial and increasingly data-center use); not a significant inverter player.

Lease terms and hardware evolution (CTO Khan): TeraWulf's initial contracts were 10 years (among the earlier contracts signed), while more recently the term has been 15 years, which has become well accepted in the market; with a tenant in place for 15 years, hardware changes will occur and contracts must align on how those transitions are handled. The design finalized with Fluidstack and Google toward the end of last year has gone through a couple of iterations as vendors evolve their hardware; TeraWulf works with AMD, NVIDIA and Google TPU hardware. Counterparty creditworthiness remains paramount, and CFO Fleury said the economic focus is NOI yield over cost to build aligned with the counterparty's credit support.
initial contracts 10 years; more recent market term 15 years

Mining wind-down and Abernathy (management): CFO Fleury said Bitcoin mining runs at somewhere between 5 and 6 exahash, will get no significant new investment, and TeraWulf will likely be out of that business by the next halving, with miners coming offline as buildings and power feeds are repositioned for HPC leasing; Q1 impairment included $8.9 million for shutting a mining facility to support HPC operations. CTO Khan said the Abernathy, Texas joint venture is being delivered under a lump-sum EPC agreement with Hypertec, with Fluidstack leading development and construction, and deployment sequencing and delivery timing are still being finalized with the ultimate compute end user.
5-6 exahash mining range for the year

Power / silicon carbide: shipments moderated sequentially but bookings strengthened and customer engagement on capacity plans rose; at SEMICON China focus was on super junction development, high energy implant, channeling and the transition to 200 mm. Rising SiC penetration and content per EV (800 V systems: traction inverter, DC-DC, onboard charging, AC compressor) and use in white goods. In AI data centers management sees both materials: gallium nitride inside the rack as it moves to 800 V, silicon carbide as power steps down from the grid (13 kV or more) toward the rack; data-center SiC is still low volume relative to EVs and its size is TBD.

NVIDIA is Hut 8's design and technology partner on Beacon Point: the facility was redesigned for next-generation chip architecture, lifting IT capacity from 224 to 352 megawatts within the same land and utility footprint (about 300 MW utility became 500 MW utility in a single building) and raising base term contract value by $3.6 billion from $6.2 billion to $9.8 billion. The CEO called it 'one of the most advanced data centers with 0.5 gigawatt capacity in a single building on Earth' and said Hut 8 now has designs for two of the three largest chip offerings in the market.
IT capacity 224 to 352 megawatts; contract value +$3.6 billion (from $6.2 billion to $9.8 billion)

DATA-CENTER REFRIGERANTS GROWING DOUBLE DIGITS; TWO-PHASE DIRECT-TO-CHIP NEXT: CEO said 'we are definitely seeing double-digit growth in refrigerants in data centers' (not quantified; Solstice is 'a step removed' but has 'line of sight' via customers). It has 'multiple projects co-innovating with customers, both on the chip side and at the data center infrastructure side': 'single-phase direct to chip, which is kind of happening now. I think you'll see soon two-phase direct to chip', with immersion cooling explored over 'the next four or five years'. Also working with data centers on reusing waste heat; this co-innovation is driving higher R&D spend.

HFO MIX SHIFT AND MARGIN TURN: CEO said Solstice entered 2026 at 'about a ratio of 60% HFOs, 40% HFCs' and expects to 'approach 70/30' exiting 2026 into 2027. 'Now, approximately four quarters into the R-454B transition', management expects sequential refrigerant margin improvement from Q1 levels, and wants to 'establish ourselves as a strong leader' in data centers with HFOs.

ELECTRONIC MATERIALS ACCELERATING ON SEMICONDUCTOR DEMAND: electronic materials delivered '21% year-on-year revenue growth following 19% year-on-year growth in the fourth quarter of 2025'. CFO: electronic materials net sales rose 21% to $109 million, 'driven by volume growth and robust customer demand across semiconductor applications'; the Electronic & Specialty Materials segment posted $281 million net sales (+7%) and $58 million adjusted EBITDA (20.8% margin). Management ties the growth to 'the ongoing shift to advanced nodes and advanced packaging' and to 'secular trends for AI and data centers'.
electronic materials increased 21% to $109 million (after 19% growth in Q4 2025); ESM segment $281 million, 7% growth

Demand drivers and visibility: technology transitions and strategic capacity expansions, largely in support of AI hyperscaling, favor etch and deposition applications and therefore Ichor; gate-all-around leading-edge logic requires a 30% increase in process steps, a significant tailwind. Ichor has hard PO coverage for about a full quarter and about 6 months of good visibility, with customers signaling growth into 2027; management expects double-digit sequential growth in the second half of 2026 and expects 2027 to be a growth year, with the supply chain as the main gate on revenue growth.
30% increase in process steps for gate-all-around logic; hard PO coverage about a full quarter; about 6 months of visibility

Two-phase liquid cooling: Carrier announced an expanded investment and partnership with ZutaCore, "one of the few guys that has two-phase solutions, which I think is where the puck is going"; on timing the CEO said two-phase is "not 10 years out, and it's not one year out" and probably within the next 5 years or so, while Carrier develops a whole host of single-phase CDUs; after looking at bigger plays it prefers organic development and VC-type investments, maybe with smaller acquisitions over time (in the $ millions, not in the $ billions range).

HBM INSPECTION OUTLOOK RAISED: CEO says Cohu continues to see strong momentum for final inspection of HBM3 and HBM4 and is investing to keep pace with design requirements for next-generation HBM5. Cohu now forecasts Neon HBM platform revenue growing 80% year-over-year to approximately $20 million in 2026 (CFO: the prior $15 million-$20 million HBM range is now at the higher end). In Q1 Cohu secured a significant volume repeat order for Neon inspection from a U.S.-headquartered customer and from a Korean customer (neither named). Inspection and metrology orders were up 64% year-over-year and the inspection business is estimated at approximately $70 million of revenue this year. HBM inspection is counted as about $100 million of the ~$750 million computing opportunity pipeline.
Neon HBM revenue growing 80% to approximately $20 million (2026); inspection revenue approximately $70 million; inspection orders up 64% YoY; HBM inspection pipeline $100 million

COMPUTING PIPELINE AND HPC OUTLOOK RAISED: CEO sees a computing segment opportunity pipeline (a SAM tallied from a targeted list of customers, not a TAM) of approximately $750 million — roughly $650 million in test handlers plus $100 million from HBM inspection — across 12 customers (five in qualification, seven in early engagement). FY2026 high-performance computing revenue outlook raised from $60 million-$85 million to approximately $80 million-$100 million, mostly from the Eclipse handler after a successful Eclipse qualification at one account; HPC systems revenue in the first half of 2026 roughly about $30 million. The five qualifying customers (all Eclipse thermal, a $10 million-$40 million annual spread depending on the customer) represent an incremental $200 million opportunity starting late this year, largely 2027; some qualifications expected to be completed by early Q3; the remaining $450 million-$500 million in engagement should move into qualification later this year or early 2027.
pipeline approximately $750 million (roughly $650 million test handlers + $100 million HBM inspection); FY2026 HPC revenue approximately $80 million-$100 million; $200 million in qualification

Guzzi: versus a year ago the RPO mix has moved 'a little more to GMP', mainly in mechanical, driven by larger scopes 'because of the power requirements and the interact cooling we're doing, which is driven primarily, which we think, by AI data centers', including 'large language model data centers' sited for access to power. Customers start AI data center jobs as GMP while designs evolve, and the CFO said two customers simply prefer GMP work. Management said it takes this work because it drives more margin dollars.

Package-level hyperscale customer (a premier large-scale data center provider, not named) selected Aehr for production burn-in of its next-generation, significantly higher-power AI ASIC with an initial Sonoma production order; that ASIC is expected to move to production later this year at even higher volumes than the current device. Aehr expects a significant near-term follow-on order for the current device, and the customer is forecasting a substantial expansion of Sonoma purchases beginning in the second half of calendar 2026 and continuing into '27, with overlapping ramps. The customer has asked about DFT for a third device to consider wafer-level burn-in on FOX.
Sonoma expansion forecast beginning second half of calendar 2026 into '27

Building on the photonics business acquired from Intel: developing capabilities across co-packaged optics (CPO), near-package optics and co-packaged copper; demonstrating system-integration at OFC 2026 with next-gen optics from 800G to 1.6T plus integrated advanced packaging and the accompanying cooling technologies. Silicon photonics cited as a margin-accretive driver of the Intelligent Infrastructure segment.

LASER ACQUISITION: Semtech acquired HIFU Corporation (name as printed in this transcript), a California-based maker of indium phosphide optoelectronic devices (gain chips and CW laser chips for optical transceivers), with a comprehensive investment plan for the Alhambra, California facility. Combining its InP lasers with Semtech's TIAs and laser drivers raises Semtech's content opportunity 'from high single-digit dollars in an 800G module to about $80 in a 3.2T module'. The fab is vertically integrated (epi growth, multi-step regrowth, wafer processing, internal test; backend packaging via the ecosystem). The gain chip for tunable lasers is in volume production, capacity limited, and should contribute 'roughly about a high-teen level of revenue' in fiscal 2027. The CW laser for transceivers has 42% wall-plug efficiency at room temperature vs a typical about 25%; there is not enough capacity for industry demand, multiple customers asked for samples, and Semtech plans to intercept at 3.2T transceivers (1.6T also supported). Go-to-market: co-optimized chipsets (TIA, laser driver, modulator driver + lasers) with a reference design; 'the major inflection point is 3.2T transceiver modules. It could be earlier than that.' Deal expected to be accretive to non-GAAP EPS within the first year.
content from high single-digit dollars (800G) to about $80 in a 3.2T module; CW laser wall-plug efficiency 42% vs about 25% typical

COPPEREDGE / ACC: Semtech expects to start shipping CopperEdge for the 1.6T ACC hyperscaler deployment this quarter — toward the end of the fiscal quarter, in the April time frame, to the cable manufacturers (its direct customers) — to support a rack-level volume ramp in the middle of the year, with demand accelerating through the year; DAC vs ACC mix still being set in rack-level validation. Semtech co-authored the ACC MSA (12 founding members spanning IC, XPU and cable suppliers with major hyperscalers) and says other hyperscalers are 'lining up to get their racks designed by using ACC'. Copper linear equalizers onboard have multiple customer engagements, with customers defining five or six use cases (switch, merchant GPU board, hyperscaler ASIC board, active backplane); qualification expected within the coming quarters. OFC demos: 1.6T ACCs running live traffic to NVIDIA's 224G SerDes and next-generation 448G per-channel CopperEdge chips.
ACC MSA with 12 founding members; 1.6T ACC shipments start in the April time frame; next-gen 448G per-channel CopperEdge

CEO VIEW ON COPPER VS CPO: 'Copper scale-up is always going to be there, and CPO scale-up is only going to make more sense in multirack systems' (e.g. NVL576 across eight racks, NVL1152); copper scale-up stays mainstream within a rack — 'do not put a terminal value on copper yet'. NPO is a complement to CPO that leverages the whole ecosystem: 'In CPO, we may not have much content in there except for lasers. But in NPO, we will be all over the place—with laser drivers, TIAs, and lasers, and even silicon photonics modulators'.

Media-mix response to NAND inflation: after the price increases, customers are having more discussions about hybrid flash arrays (HFA), Keystone and cloud alternatives; Kurian said it is 'too early' to call it a trend but 'HFAs are starting to see a lot of interest from customers', and NetApp's broad portfolio (unlike all-flash-only competitors) lets it serve price-sensitive workloads.

NVIDIA still leads the GPU market and will remain the larger share of Wiwynn's GPU business, but AMD is re-entering the fight with its next generation and more than one customer has approached Wiwynn about AMD GPU projects; Wiwynn will co-work with AMD from the pilot-build stage, leveraging a similar rack design across customers. The AMD rack is double-wide, also a 72-GPU configuration but with more memory content, so its price should be higher than the GB rack: against an analyst's roughly US$3.58M per GB rack reference, management indicated around US$5M for the AMD rack (with margin rate expected similar to GPU projects). Customers are still deciding how to portfolio their data centres across NVIDIA, AMD and their own ASICs.
GB rack about 358 ten-thousand US dollars per rack (analyst reference); AMD next-gen rack seen around 500 ten-thousand US dollars; 72-GPU double-wide with more memory

2026 outlook: demand remains strong for both AI and general-compute servers, with good growth expected for the full year but the momentum weighted to H2 because of the AI platform transition. AI stays above 50% of revenue (slightly above 2025's roughly half), with ASIC projects still the main AI contributor at roughly nine-tenths of AI volume. General server growth is driven by AI itself - CSPs split workloads such as agentic AI front/back-end services and part of inference onto general compute for TCO - and 2026 general server revenue and shipment units will both exceed 2025 (management suggested roughly 20-30% growth as a reference), with every quarter growing versus last year's H1-weighted pattern. Q1 2026 will certainly grow YoY, while QoQ growth off the record Q4 is challenging.
AI above 50% of 2026 revenue; ASIC about nine-tenths of AI volume; general server revenue and units both above 2025

The previous-generation GB200 GPU project has concluded - its cost structure drove the Q4 gross margin decline - and 2026 GPU efforts shift to developing the new-generation platform with customers and technology partners, with new ASIC and new GPU products both starting to ship in H2 2026. Wiwynn has been pushing customers toward a consignment model for GPU components since GPU projects began and hopes to have a definite answer by the next-generation ramp; it mostly builds to L11 for CSP customers (who handle their own integration), with L12 opportunities limited to sovereign-AI style tenders it pursues selectively after last year's project.

Interconnect IP: more than 40 PCIe design wins in the quarter with HPC and automotive customers, an industry-first demonstration of PCIe 8.0, and a first-to-market 224 gig SerDes on advanced nodes and leading foundries with 10 lifetime wins. Interconnect standards now turn over in about half the historical 3-to-4-year life. Hyperscalers, which lack their own IP teams, want customized IP delivered 'one generation ahead'; Synopsys is in active talks and expects several to become actual business in FY26, with the upside arriving after customer tape-outs.
more than 40 PCIe design wins; 224 gig SerDes 10 lifetime wins

Logic/foundry annealing: LSA is production tool of record at all 3 Tier 1 logic customers; the next-generation NSA (nanosecond annealing) system has 2 evaluations at Tier 1 logic customers, an evaluation system is planned to ship to the third in 2026, and 2 evaluation sign-offs are expected during 2026 with potential pilot line orders shortly after (low thermal budget uses such as contact annealing and 3D device stacking). Annealing SAM is projected at $1.3 billion by 2029 as devices shrink and shallower, more precise anneals are required, and the IBD300 low-resistance metals platform plus ion beam EUV mask blank and pellicle deposition SAM at $500 million by 2029; management expects the semiconductor SAM to expand on investment in gate-all-around, high-bandwidth memory and 3D packaging, with IBD a key enabler of high-NA EUV adoption. In 2026 logic, foundry and memory customers are all increasing capacity for annealing tools.
LSA tool of record at all 3 Tier 1 logic customers; NSA 2 evaluations; annealing SAM $1.3 billion by 2029; ion beam SAM $500 million by 2029

Technology drivers (CEO): industry projections suggest semiconductors could reach $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2027, possibly earlier. Leading-edge fabs are deploying new materials like molybdenum and new structures such as gate-all-around and high-bandwidth memory, raising deposition/etch capex intensity. UCT expects strength around etch and deposition, especially ALD and high-precision etch, to support gate-all-around and backside power distribution logic transitions as well as high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging and greater than 300-layer NAND. A multiyear WFE upturn should follow once wafer fabs address their near-term clean room constraints.
semiconductor market $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2027 (industry projection); greater than 300-layer NAND

Wafer-size transition: Tim Bettles says 'there's already been a big move from 3-inch to 4-inch' and AXT has scaled up its 4-inch business; 'we all know one customer that's really driving 6-inch demand' (customer not named), so AXT is 'looking at adding significant 6-inch capacity' as it doubles capacity through 2026 and beyond. CEO: a major focus of the expansion is more investment in 6-inch InP for 'next-generation EML and silicon photonic-based devices', and customers are deciding how much to switch 'from 3 to 4 and 4 to 6'. Larger sizes normally bring better margins, but 6-inch is 'still a little bit in development stage', with lower margins at first; the product mix is still 'very much geared towards 3-inch and 4-inch'.
big move from 3-inch to 4-inch already made; significant 6-inch capacity to be added as capacity doubles through 2026 and beyond

Asked about possible changes to cooling requirements for next-generation chips, the CFO said the impact on Comfort is 'not at all': 'the new chip stuff—they said, okay, we can use 45-degree water. Still needs pipe. Still needs water.' He added that 45-degree water is not naturally occurring for 99% of the year in 99% of places, and that as long as servers run on electricity they produce heat, so customers will keep needing electricians and pipe fitters; the CEO said the change is 'Far more impactful for the OEMs than for us.'
45-degree water (next-generation chip cooling requirement cited by management)

VPD lead customer (not named on this call) is ramping a Gen 4 factorized power system before transitioning to a Gen 5-based solution with higher current density and performance. The transition is expected to start in the second half of 2026, while Gen 4 production continues to 'ramp at a steep rate to the end of 2026'. According to the CEO, the Gen 4 system is mature, but the customer's next-generation system as a whole 'isn't quite there yet'. By year-end the lead customer will be using 'a significant share of our capacity' on the earlier generation, and the next-generation system adds 'an additional layer of use of capacity' into next year. Other Gen 5 (second-gen) VPD engagements will be selective: over the next couple of weeks, the global FAE team is being trained on Gen 5 VPD demo boards before engaging target hyperscalers and OEM chip companies. One prospect 'alone fill 2 fabs', and an automotive customer has shown interest. The VP of Sales says one very, very large company uses vertical power delivery in very high volume today (increasing year on year); high-volume use by anyone else is 'fairly limited', with others 'all trying to get Gen 1 VPD to work' and none he knows of deploying it in volume yet. The CEO says second-gen VPD with fifth-generation modules has much higher density, needs no stacking and is more efficient.
lead customer Gen 4 -> Gen 5 VPD transition to start in second half of 2026; Gen 4 ramping steeply to end of 2026

Content per accelerator: the VP of Sales puts Vicor's second-gen VPD opportunity at 'somewhere between $200 to $400 per XPU', depending on the XPU's current and number of rails. The CEO added 'Take that with a grain of salt' and clarified it is 'about like a 2,000 amp up to a 4,000 amp type of product'. For context, the CEO said a GPU power-system opportunity a number of years ago was 'about $100 million per year'. 'We are locking into an opportunity that will double that', he said, and a hyperscaler opportunity 'could be another'.
$200 to $400 per XPU; 2,000 amp up to a 4,000 amp product

DC power architecture for data centers (an analyst asked about the shift from 54-volt to 800-volt DC): Duke Austin - 'voltage going to DC, some of the architecture that NVIDIA has put out ... I believe we're in front of that I don't see it changing our TAM at all. You might get more medium voltage type arrangements in there. Still a lot of low voltage type things.' 'We work with NVIDIA and others to make sure that we see where they're going and make sure we have the craft necessary.' Older architecture will still be used and 'both are growing significantly'. Front vs behind the meter: it is better to let the utility take the chips' intermittency, but 'People are trying to go behind the meter simply because you can't get to the meter' because of queue constraints; he expects much off-grid generation to become backup power ('you'll start with 100, 200 max and then back up for a bit and then come on with utility type solutions'). Quanta never left natural gas and is getting involved in plants 'backing up some of the hyperscalers and data centers'.
no specific figure (DC power architecture not expected to change Quanta's TAM; more medium voltage arrangements possible)

2026 logic and industry outlook: management expects Entegris to benefit from node transitions in both logic and memory. Rising demand for two-nanometer devices should meaningfully lift wafer output through 2026, and that node carries both higher content per wafer and strong share for Entegris. Advanced logic fab utilization is already near 100%, and customers are investing aggressively in more capacity. At the most advanced logic node, Entegris has secured strong POR (position of record) positions in CMP consumables, advanced deposition and implant materials, liquid purification and filtration, and wafer handling. The team is now focused on winning incremental share and PORs at subsequent advanced nodes. Separately, the CEO said it takes time to grow two-nanometer and to transition to new nodes such as 1.4 nanometer. Management expects 'middish single-digit' industry MSI (wafer starts) growth in 2026 and strong WFE growth. Fab construction CapEx should grow modestly after last year's high single-digit decline, weighted to the second half, with a bigger acceleration in 2027 as work starts on new fabs. Management flagged ongoing memory shortages as a possible second-half 2026 risk for mainstream end markets; guidance assumes no impact.
middish single-digit industry MSI growth expected in 2026; advanced logic utilization near 100%

NAND: the move from roughly 250 layers to approximately 300 layers is under way. Management expects more than 20% NAND bit growth in 2026, driven mainly by higher-layer, higher-capacity NAND rather than a big increase in wafer starts. Entegris expects a double-digit increase in its NAND content per wafer as customers move to higher layer counts and adopt new materials such as moly and selective etch. It has won strong POR positions in NAND deposition materials, CMP and selective etch. NAND utilization is around 85%, and layer-count increases are absorbing most of the remaining 15% of capacity, with fewer new wafer starts. If demand stays strong, flash makers will likely need to add significant fab capacity, setting up higher NAND MSI growth in 2027. The CEO said Entegris gains from both layer growth and wafer growth, with slightly more from a full wafer start.
more than 20% NAND bit growth expected in 2026; double-digit increase in NAND content per wafer; NAND utilization around 85%

Technology roadmap. PANEL: ASE will have a FULLY AUTOMATED 310x310 panel line in production by the end of this year (manual today, which management says 'doesn't count'), for chiplet sizes too large for the 300-millimeter wafer form; a move to 620x620 depends on volume and technology requirements. FULL PROCESS 2.5D is not new for ASE; management frames it as second-source capacity next to the foundry partner ('We're not competing'), with configurations evolving as the HBM and TPU size grows. CPO / SILICON PHOTONICS: ASE is working with its foundry partner and the end customer on the silicon photonics (CPO) part, managing PIC and EIC together or separately across chip-to-chip, chip-to-packaging and chip-to-rack configurations, and expects 'some early volume on the silicon and the CPO part of it'. The EMS subsidiary USI made a fiberoptic acquisition, EugenLight, as part of piecing together early deployment for the future optical road map ('There is no conflict' with ASE), and EMS is extending into AI server, optical and power solutions. The packaging toolbox also includes next-generation power delivery for the VRM.
fully automated 310x310 panel in production by the end of this year (2026); CPO early volume expected

CEO Andrew Jassy: Trainium3 was recently launched and has just started shipping, with up to 40% more price performance than Trainium2. Demand is very strong, and Amazon expects nearly all of its Trainium3 chip supply to be committed by mid-2026. Trainium4 is still being built and is coming in 2027, with very substantial interest already, and Amazon is already having conversations about Trainium5.
up to 40% more price performance than Trainium2; nearly all supply expected to be committed by mid-2026; Trainium4 coming in 2027

800V DC transition: KR says AI racks will need 800 volts DC ('This switch to 800 volts DC is a necessity and not a choice') because upcoming AI racks will consume almost 100 times more power than traditional CPU racks. Grid, turbine or engine-powered sites will need transformers, rectifiers and power-conditioning gear to convert high-voltage AC, while 'Bloom, and only Bloom, natively produces 800 volts DC today.' 'Starting now, every Bloom server we ship will be 800 volts DC ready', with a removable adapter for legacy AC environments, and Bloom offers to convert previously shipped servers with simple modifications. KR says it also cuts copper use (copper is short in transformers) and efficiency losses.
every Bloom server shipped from now is 800 volts DC ready; AI racks almost 100 times the power of traditional CPU racks

800V data-center power: in 2025 MPS positioned for a further shift to solutions by sampling its 800-volt power solution for data centers. Asked whether 800-volt racks will use GaN or silicon carbide, Michael Hsing said MPS is developing silicon carbide and in the last few years developed its own GaN devices (he mentioned '100 volts'); 'that revenue is not for this year, not for even for next year. So, okay, maybe end of the next year. However, we're the first company to sample it.' Tony Balow: whether GaN or silicon carbide is what is demanded, MPS expects to be well-positioned.
800-volt power solution sampling; revenue 'maybe end of the next year'

Modules and vertical power: MPS had record module revenue in 2025 and is migrating 'from silicon to systems', with customers changing from silicon to modules on MPS's power density. On the packaging innovation to double module current density (raised by an analyst), Michael Hsing said 'We start to sampling those products' and 'expect to have a shipping in this quarter and next quarter', with customers having gone through qualification. On vertical power delivery: 'everybody is going to a vertical power'; Bernie Blegen called it 'the only energy-efficient solution' at high current. On server CPUs, the majority still use 12 volts while some models use 48 volts, and modules are 'the way to go'. Michael Hsing also said MPS is moving into MCUs, data converters and high-speed products.
record module revenue in 2025; higher-density modules shipping this quarter and next quarter

AGENTIC INFERENCE RAISES CPU CONTENT: AI is shifting from training to inference, and that inference is increasingly agent-based: 'persistent, always on, and power constrained'. Agent coordination runs on CPUs, so customers want higher core counts and better power efficiency. Haas said the latest hyperscaler and NVIDIA CPU generations 'have increased the number of cores. And we think that only continues.' He cited four examples. AWS's fifth-generation Graviton has 192 cores, double Graviton4. NVIDIA's Vera has 88 Arm-based cores, up from 72 cores in the 'gray CPU generation' (as transcribed). Microsoft's Cobalt 200 has 132 cores on Neoverse CSS V3, up from 128 in Cobalt 100 on Neoverse N2. Google previewed its second Arm server processor (Axion-powered m4a instances). Integrated platforms raise output per watt: AWS pairs Graviton with Arm-based Nitro DPUs and training accelerators, and NVIDIA pairs GPUs with Arm-based CPUs and BlueField. Over the next three years Haas expects CPUs to take on work GPUs used to do and more custom CPU-based chips to appear. He also sees specific prefill/decode inference solutions continuing to extend.
Graviton 192 cores; Vera 88 cores (vs 72); Cobalt 200 132 cores (vs 128)

→ NVIDIA: NVIDIA's next-generation Vera CPU has 88 Arm-based cores, up from 72 cores in the 'gray CPU generation' (as transcribed). Arm cited it as evidence that agentic inference is pushing CPU core counts higher. Haas said NVIDIA pairs its GPUs with Arm-based 'gray CPUs' (as transcribed) and Arm-based BlueField parts (printed 'blue field GPUs'), 'which has transitioned to Vera, delivering a 6x increase in GPU compute capability over the prior generation' (quoted as transcribed; the sentence is ambiguous).

Data center chiller launches introduced 'earlier this week', at 'the big show that's ongoing as we speak'. The YDAM 'delivers up to 3.5 megawatts of cooling in a compact footprint, providing approximately 20% higher capacity density than competing options and enabling warm water cooling for advanced GPUs'. The YKHT offers 'the industry's widest operating range and supports waterless heat reduction, which can eliminate up to 9 million gallons of cooling tower water annually in typical deployments'. The Smart Ready Chiller provides '10 times the insights over a standard remote connected chiller', which management expects to move more customers into recurring service. JCI also released a new reference guide that 'maps the full thermal chain and outlines scalable high-performance cooling architectures for an emerging class of AI factories'. CEO Joakim Weidemanis said 'We continue to work closely with NVIDIA' and that some of the guides 'is in collaboration with NVIDIA'. An analyst asked about the technology path, noting investor worry over NVIDIA and warm water cooling. The CEO would not comment on future launches but said there is 'a significant roadmap behind that'. He said the new products' effect on orders so far is 'very minor' ('it's more about what's to come') and that he expects them to start lifting orders in the current quarter.
YDAM up to 3.5 megawatts of cooling with approximately 20% higher capacity density; YKHT can eliminate up to 9 million gallons of cooling tower water annually

Data center thermal portfolio, per CEO Joakim Weidemanis. JCI plays in three categories plus controls: chillers; CRAHs (transcribed as 'craws') and air handling units 'through our silent air franchise, which is the leading franchise in air handling'; and CDUs. JCI entered the CDU space 'a couple of quarters ago' and is 'now starting to grow nicely here on the CDU side'. CDU sales today are 'a mix': plenty of business is CDUs only, but JCI sees 'plenty of opportunity for combined offers' with key accounts. As data center thermal architecture evolves, 'the roles that certain devices play today might evolve', which is why JCI added CDUs. Customer mix: JCI historically had a good position with hyperscalers and many large colos in the United States. Growth in Europe and Asia has now become 'very meaningful', and more future growth will come from Asia Pac and Europe, where the mix of hyperscalers and local colos is a little different, so 'our data center business is gonna broaden'. Countries in Southeast Asia and India are looking at data centers, with several emerging players. The CEO saw no material change in how the big hyperscaler and colo players behave. Every other week, large engineering teams from JCI's largest customers, colos and hyperscalers, work with JCI engineers at its JADEC innovation center in Pennsylvania on next-generation designs, and that work feeds the product roadmap.

AI data center: 'we have doubled our data center revenue in the last three quarters, with 50% quarter-over-quarter growth from Q1 to Q2'; Wolfspeed devices are 'already embedded in critical AI data center power systems'. The company is 'actively collaborating with a broad ecosystem of partners to support the industry transition from legacy 400-volt architectures to next-generation 800-volt AI platforms'. AI data centers operate at significantly higher voltages than legacy data centers, and as voltages rise management expects a growing share of the addressable market 'from grid to rack' to be better served by SiC than by silicon.
data center revenue doubled in the last three quarters; 50% quarter-over-quarter growth from Q1 to Q2

DDR5 RCD SHARE AND GENERATION MIX (CEO): Rambus believes it ended 2025 at mid-40% share for DDR5 RCDs, up from the early forties in 2024, the result of a larger design-win footprint at every DDR5 generation; the market grew mid-single digit from 2024 to 2025 while the DDR5 portion rose and DDR4 kept shrinking. DDR5 is still early in its cycle, leaving room to gain share: 'We always said we could be between forty and fifty.' Mix: in Q4 Gen 2 was predominant and Gen 3 was starting to ramp (growing vs Q3); in 2026 Gen 3 is expected to be the predominant version of DDR5; Gen 4 will contribute but with more limited adoption because it is on a different type of core; the big next step is Gen 5, which depends on the introduction of next-generation Intel and AMD platforms. As DIMM speeds rise, customers increasingly want all module chips from the same supplier for interoperability, an indirect positive for Rambus's companion chips.
mid-40% DDR5 RCD share in 2025 (early forties in 2024)

MRDIMM AND SOCAMM2 TIMING (CEO): MRDIMM timing unchanged; the rollout depends on the Intel and AMD platform rollouts (the analyst cited Intel Diamond Rapids and AMD Venice). Rambus expects MRDIMM to ramp towards the very end of 2026, with only the very initial contribution towards the end of the year and the main contribution happening in 2027: 'As far as we're concerned, we are ready.' SOCAMM2: 'On SOCAM two, we have an opportunity for the SPD hub'; Rambus is taking part in defining next-generation SOCAMM chips, where power management could open further opportunities, in line with its strategy of having solutions for every JEDEC standard module on the client and data center side.

New networking win (CEO): Celestica 'secured the design and manufacturing award for the 1.6T networking switch platform with a third hyperscaler customer'; this HPS engagement is expected to ramp production beginning in 2027, with design work already underway. With this hyperscaler Celestica held predominant share on 400G and on 800G; the 1.6T engagement started with a design win and Celestica was also awarded the mass production for the switch. Separately, mass production for the first 1.6T switching programs is expected to begin ramping in the latter part of 2026.
1.6T switch design and manufacturing award with a third hyperscaler; production ramp beginning in 2027

Switch generation cadence (management): Celestica has '10 active 1.6T programs in the pipeline right now'; about five of them start ramping in the back half of 2026 and into 2027, and several of the rest are in development and ramp later in '27 into '28. The gating factor is completing the development cycle as planned, and silicon is on track. 400G remains highly resilient and a strong 2026 contributor, 800G continues to grow, and 1.6T comes on toward the end of 2026: 'the next-generation technology is not necessarily cannibalizing the previous generation.' The 1.6T wins to date are used for both scale-up and scale-in. At 1.6T and 3.2T the engineering complexity is moving engagements toward HPS (design-led) work, and the CFO expects 1.6T programs to be as profitable as past switching programs. Some business Celestica declined to chase on price in 2025 came back in 2026 'because others could not execute on it.'
10 active 1.6T programs; about five ramp in the back half of 2026; 400G, 800G and 1.6T running concurrently

Co-packaged optics and 3.2T (management): customer conversations on co-packaged optics are increasing, but 'in terms of mass adoption, it's going to be more towards 3.2T, which are programs that we're working on in our R&D group. But we haven't seen customers looking for mass adoption of CPO as of yet.' 3.2T switch samples are due probably towards the end of 2026 and work has already started; Celestica has proof-of-concept work on co-packaged optics so it is ready when CPO hits the 3.2T cycle. On scale-up, management sees increasing R&D activity toward fully integrated AI/ML and networking systems supporting both scale-up and scale-out fabrics: 'scale-up will be as much of an opportunity as scale-out.'
3.2T samples towards the end of 2026; CPO mass adoption expected at 3.2T

Next-generation compute (management): Celestica has 'already won the next generation of that program' (the hyperscaler AI/ML compute program ramping through 2026) and expects those programs 'to actually ramp into 2027'. Looking towards 2027, management anticipates strong demand from hyperscaler and digital native customers driven by ramps in next-gen AI/ML compute programs; on the compute side Celestica focuses on HPS and JDM design-oriented work and has 'several projects in the pipeline to improve those engagements on the HPS side'.
next-generation program already won; ramp into 2027

Scale-across and speed transitions (CEO): scale-across data center interconnect is 'one of the most significant near term' drivers of optical demand. 'We've gone through the 400- and 800-gig transition very quickly.' 'we expect that 1.6 and 3.2 will come. And when you look at that scale across is the tailwind for both the technology transitions and the demand. And then, of course, over time, we see scale out increasingly be an opportunity for coherent optics.' Scale-across is also a tailwind for routing ('switching is much more about the data center racks, the spine-leaf architecture'). Later: 'Scale across is an emerging opportunity' and 'over time, as speeds continue to ramp within the data center, there will be more opportunity for coherent optics within the data center.' He described 'a much more mature and larger optical market, driven by the AI infrastructure build-out than we've seen in the past.'
400- and 800-gig transition passed very quickly; 1.6 and 3.2 will come; coherent optics moving toward scale out / inside the data center over time

Data-center architecture and future designs (CEO Dave Regnery, answering analyst questions on recent comments from a data-center partner about chillers and liquid cooling): 'we're working very closely with many influencers in the data center vertical. So think of hyperscalers, think of chip manufacturers, like Nvidia and others. We're helping them design data centers of the future. Or you may have heard them referred to as reference design data centers' - data centers to be built 'maybe two to four years out'. 'I have not seen a reference design or data center of the future that does not include chillers, just to be very clear', with 'a lot of innovation around the thermal management system, specifically around the chiller' in Trane's pipeline. Future data-center farms will build in free cooling: fans keep running through the free-cooling cycle while the compressor side runs less often; because chillers are sized to the thermal load, 'you're still gonna have the same number'. Asked whether HVAC's share of data-center spend is higher or lower two to four years out: 'I'm gonna err on the side of saying it's probably about the same', while 'the amount of power that is being consumed by the thermal management system may be less', letting operators redirect power to computing.

AI wafer intensity (CEO Christophe Fouquet), using NVIDIA as the example: today's NVIDIA system (transcribed as 'black wall system') needs 'about 2.5 wafers to create the product', while the 2027 NVIDIA product (transcribed as 'revenue product') will need 10 wafers, so 'NVIDIA will need 4x more wafer than today', driving capacity extensions. For the most advanced AI products the transistor requirement has grown '16x every 2 years' vs Moore's-law 2x; when scaling cannot fit enough transistors, 'the only option will be to make more wafers'. Advanced logic and advanced memory are to grow 'more than 20% year-on-year for the foreseeable future' vs the historical 'about 6%, 7% year-on-year', and rising EUV layer counts at key customers raise litho intensity.
about 2.5 wafers today to 10 wafers in 2027 (4x more wafer); advanced logic and memory more than 20% year-on-year

EUV roadmap: revenue was recognized on the first 5200B, the High-NA high-volume manufacturing tool, which was shipped, installed and accepted by a customer (unnamed) looking at putting it into high-volume manufacturing for its leading nodes. High-NA customers are still qualifying the tools with good results; 2026 is a year to prepare for insertion, with the first products manufactured using High NA in 2027, '28, and High NA enabling the shift to more advanced technology around '28-'29 for DRAM and logic. The vast share of 2026 EUV growth will be Low NA going into high-volume manufacturing. The number of EUV layers is increasing at key customers, raising litho intensity. R&D: the lion's share goes to EUV across 3 work streams (High NA, Low NA and the 'high productivity platform'); the high productivity platform is an EUV platform for early next decade that can take Low NA optics (more than 400 wafer per hour), High NA optics and potentially Hyper NA optics, letting ASML decide later when to introduce Hyper NA.
first 5200B revenue recognized; first High NA products 2027, '28; high productivity platform more than 400 wafer per hour early next decade

CALL - THE AI INTERCONNECT CONTENT THESIS ENTERING 2026: the CEO stressed breadth 'up and down the stack of AI' - 'the big web scale folks', 'the cloud, the Neo cloud', equipment manufacturers, and 'companies who are designing the chips and the architecture around those chips'. Customers' 'investment plans are all going up', and 'upgrades of the technology embedded in those data centers' require 'a higher technology, more complex, higher content degree of interconnect.' Amphenol participates in 'bringing the power in, power to the racks', in 'the data communication within racks, within adjacent racks', and now, with CommScope, in 'the broader fiber optic opportunity' - 'getting a signal from a GPU to a GPU or from a central office home somewhere'. Asked about an eventual move to 800-volt data-center power (the analyst's framing), the CEO answered: 'what we care about, Joe, is that there's more of everything... they go to different voltages. They go to different speeds... The ultimate what comes out of that is more complexity', adding that with CommScope Amphenol is 'even stronger than we were before' to help customers with these trade-offs.

Scale-up optics timing (CEO, answering a CPO/scale-up question): 'we do not have a significant revenue amount for scale-up included in this most recent SpringBoard upgrade', so it would be on top. Photons use 'greater than three times lower power' than electrons even over very short links, and the advantage 'can be 20 times or more' at longer reach or higher bit rate. There is a broad effort to bring optics into scale-up, closer to the GPUs and switch ASICs; he believes those links going to photons, with Corning's innovations playing a significant role, is inevitable. On timing, some scenarios fall between now and 2028 and others start 'primarily starting immediately in 2028 and beyond', so the plan treats timing conservatively.
no significant scale-up revenue in the upgraded plan; photons greater than three times lower power, 20 times or more at longer reach/higher bit rate; timing between now and 2028 or 2028 and beyond
